facts: Abalone are sea snails that cling to rocks, and wild stocks are protected in many places.
The inside of the shell is iridescent mother-of-pearl, prized for jewellery and inlay.
In East Asian cooking, abalone is often braised slowly for a long time to soften its firm flesh.
abalone.visual: one whole raw abalone in its shell, rough brown outer shell with a shiny rainbow interior, lying on its side
abalone.what: A large sea snail with a shiny shell and firm meat.

facts: Absinthe was first made in Switzerland in the late 1700s, and became popular in France.
It was banned in France and many other countries in the early 20th century.
It is traditionally diluted with iced water, which turns it cloudy in a process called louching.
absinthe.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale green liquid
absinthe.what: A strong spirit flavoured with aniseed and wormwood.

facts: Aburaage is made by deep-frying thin slices of tofu until they puff and turn golden.
It is a traditional Japanese ingredient, used to wrap inari sushi and in miso soup.
The name combines the Japanese words for oil and fried food.
aburaage.visual: a whole thin golden-brown fried tofu pouch, slightly puffed, lying flat
aburaage.what: Thin fried tofu pouches, often simmered in sweet soy.

facts: It crystallises more slowly than most honeys, so it stays runny for longer.
It is especially popular in Central Europe, where black locust trees grow widely.
acacia-honey.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with pale golden honey that is clear and runny
acacia-honey.what: A pale, mild honey that stays liquid for a long time.

facts: Acerola is native to tropical America, from Central America through to northern South America.
Acerola is widely grown in Brazil, where it is often pressed into juice.
Despite its name, acerola is not closely related to cherries, which belong to a different plant family.
acerola.visual: a small heap of bright red acerola fruits, round and glossy, lying loosely together
acerola.what: A tart red tropical fruit, also called Barbados cherry.

facts: The word achiote comes from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, and names annatto seeds.
The paste is a classic of Yucatán cooking in south-east Mexico, often used to season pork.
Annatto gives the paste its characteristic deep orange-red colour.
achiote-paste.visual: a plain glass jar without a label holding a dense, brick-red paste
achiote-paste.what: A brick-red seasoning paste of annatto, citrus and spices.

facts: Acini di pepe means peppercorn seeds in Italian, a name that describes the pasta's shape.
Pastina is the Italian term for tiny pasta shapes, and acini di pepe is one of the best known.
Small pasta shapes like this are traditionally added to broths and soups in Italian cooking.
acini-di-pepe.visual: a small loose heap of tiny, round, pale cream pasta beads, seen from above
acini-di-pepe.what: Tiny round pasta, like peppercorns, for soup and salad.

facts: Ackee and saltfish is widely regarded as Jamaica's national dish.
Ackee is native to West Africa and grows widely in Jamaica.
Only fully ripe fruit is eaten, because unripe fruit and seeds are poisonous.
ackee.visual: a ripe ackee fruit split open to show three glossy black seeds in pale yellow flesh, lying on its side
ackee.what: A Jamaican fruit with soft yellow flesh, eaten cooked.

facts: Squashes were domesticated in the Americas thousands of years ago, and acorn squash is one of them.
Its name comes from its shape, which resembles an acorn.
It is often halved, seeded and roasted until its flesh turns soft and nutty.
acorn-squash.visual: one whole acorn squash, dark green ridged skin with a patch of orange on one side
acorn-squash.what: A small ridged winter squash with sweet orange flesh.

facts: Adobo comes from the Spanish verb adobar, meaning to marinate or season.
Chipotle chillies are smoked, dried jalapeños, which give the sauce its smoky flavour.
Filipino adobo is a different dish, a meat braised in vinegar and soy sauce.
adobo-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, dark red adobo sauce, glossy
adobo-sauce.what: A smoky, tangy chilli sauce from Mexican cooking.

facts: Adobo is a Spanish word for a marinade or seasoning, and the name refers to marinating meat.
Latin American versions often include garlic, oregano, black pepper and cumin.
Adobo blends vary widely from country to country, and they are used on meat, fish and vegetables.
adobo-seasoning.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of reddish-brown ground spice blend, fine and powdery
adobo-seasoning.what: A garlicky spice blend used across Latin America.

facts: Advieh is the Persian word for spice or seasoning, and the term covers many different blends.
Persian cooks use advieh to flavour rice dishes, stews and sweets.
advieh.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, dusty pinkish-brown spice blend with visible dried petal pieces
advieh.what: A fragrant Persian spice blend with rose and cardamom.

facts: Advocaat is a Dutch liqueur, traditionally made with eggs, sugar and brandy.
It is commonly used in baking and desserts, where its custard-like flavour adds richness.
advocaat.visual: a clear drinking glass of thick, pale yellow advocaat
advocaat.what: A thick, creamy yellow liqueur made from eggs and brandy.

facts: Red bean rice, called sekihan, is served at celebrations in Japan.
Adzuki beans have been grown in East Asia for many centuries.
adzuki-beans.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dry, glossy, dark red adzuki beans, small and oval
adzuki-beans.what: Small, dark red beans with a sweet, nutty flavour.

facts: Agar is extracted from red seaweeds and has long been used in Japanese and Asian desserts.
Unlike gelatine, it is made from seaweed, so it suits vegetarian cooking.
Once set, agar keeps its firmness at warmer temperatures than gelatine does.
agar-agar.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, pale off-white agar powder
agar-agar.what: A seaweed-based setting powder that makes firm jellies.

facts: Agave syrup is produced from the sap of agave plants, mainly in Mexico.
Agave is a spiky succulent that grows in dry, sunny regions.
The name agave comes from a Greek word meaning noble or admirable.
agave-syrup.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of runny golden-amber syrup
agave-syrup.what: A mild, runny sweetener made from the agave plant.

facts: Traditional balsamic vinegar is made in and around Modena and Reggio Emilia in northern Italy.
It is made from cooked grape must, which is then aged in a series of barrels of different woods.
Over time the vinegar becomes thicker and more concentrated as water evaporates through the barrels.
aged-balsamic-vinegar.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of very dark, syrupy aged vinegar, with a small cork
aged-balsamic-vinegar.what: A dark, syrupy vinegar aged for years in wooden barrels.

facts: Gouda is named after the town of Gouda in the Netherlands, where the cheese has long been sold.
The small crunchy crystals in aged Gouda are mostly amino acids, which form as the cheese matures.
aged-gouda.visual: a block of aged gouda cheese with one wedge cut away, pale golden paste showing small crystals
aged-gouda.what: A hard Dutch cheese, aged until it tastes rich and nutty.

facts: Pepper sauces made with vinegar are a long-standing part of Caribbean and Southern US cooking.
Chilli peppers originated in the Americas and were carried to Asia and Africa by European traders.
Vinegar is used to preserve the sauce and to give it its sharp tang.
aged-pepper-sauce.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with deep red sauce
aged-pepper-sauce.what: A tangy red pepper sauce, aged in vinegar for depth.

facts: Agedashi tofu is dusted in starch before frying, which gives the cubes a thin crisp coat.
Dashi is a basic Japanese stock, often made from kelp and dried bonito flakes.
agedashi-tofu.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of golden-brown fried tofu cubes in a clear pale broth
agedashi-tofu.what: Soft tofu cubes lightly fried and served in a dashi broth.

facts: Agen prunes are named after Agen, a town in south-western France in the Lot-et-Garonne department.
Prunes wrapped in bacon and grilled make a savoury British snack often called devils on horseback.
agen-prune.visual: a small heap of soft, dark brown dried prunes, glossy and wrinkled
agen-prune.what: A soft, dark dried plum from south-western France.

facts: Agnolotti come from Piedmont in north-west Italy, where they have long been made.
Traditional fillings include roast meats, sometimes mixed with greens.
They are simmered in salted water and often served with melted butter or sage.
agnolotti.visual: a small heap of uncooked pale yellow pasta parcels, each one pinched shut
agnolotti.what: Small pinched pasta parcels, often filled with roast meat.

facts: Agretti, also called monk's beard, is a salt-tolerant plant that grows around the Mediterranean.
It has long been eaten in Italy, where it is often blanched briefly and served as a side dish.
Its needle-like leaves grow in tufts, which gives the plant its spiky appearance.
agretti.visual: a loose bunch of fresh bright green agretti, thin spiky leaves on pale stems, lying on a plain background
agretti.what: A spiky Italian green often served blanched with lemon.

facts: Aioli comes from the Provençal words for garlic and oil.
Traditional aioli was pounded by hand in a mortar with garlic and oil.
Modern versions often add egg yolk to help the oil emulsify.
aioli-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, pale yellow aioli
aioli-sauce.what: A thick, garlicky sauce made from olive oil and garlic.

facts: Aji amarillo is a key chilli in Peruvian cooking, used in sauces, stews and marinades.
Its name means yellow chilli, from amarillo, the Spanish word for yellow.
The pepper is often sold as a paste, and dried peppers keep well for use through the year.
aji-amarillo.visual: a few whole bright orange-yellow chilli peppers, slender and tapering, with short green stalks, lying on the background
aji-amarillo.what: A Peruvian yellow chilli with a fruity, warm flavour.

facts: Aji amarillo means yellow chilli in Spanish, and it is a staple of Peruvian cooking.
The chilli has been grown in Peru for centuries and is central to its cooking.
The paste is made by blending the chillies, giving a fruity, tangy flavour.
aji-amarillo-paste.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with bright orange-yellow chilli paste
aji-amarillo-paste.what: A bright yellow chilli paste with a fruity, medium heat.

facts: Ajvar is especially associated with Serbia and North Macedonia, where it is a staple condiment.
Peppers and aubergines are traditionally roasted over fire, peeled, then cooked slowly down.
ajvar.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, glossy red-orange relish, smooth and spreadable
ajvar.what: A smoky, sweet relish of roasted red peppers and aubergine.

facts: Ajwain is the seed of a plant in the parsley family, grown in India and parts of the Middle East.
The seeds smell of thyme because they contain thymol, although the plant is not related to thyme.
Ajwain is often added to breads, pastries and fried snacks, where its sharp flavour stands out.
ajwain.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with tiny greyish-brown ajwain seeds, oval and ridged
ajwain.what: Small seeds, sharp and thyme-like, used in Indian snacks.

facts: Akkawi takes its name from the coastal city of Akka, also known as Acre.
It is a white brined cheese, traditionally made from cow's or goat's milk.
It is often used in kunafa, a sweet pastry from the Levant.
akkawi.visual: one block of pale white brined cheese with a single slice cut away, lying directly on the background
akkawi.what: A mild, salty white cheese from the Middle East.

facts: Alaska pollock is a cold-water fish found across the North Pacific and the Bering Sea.
Its mild, white flesh makes it a common choice for fish fingers and fish cakes.
Pollock is also a major source of surimi, the processed fish paste used in imitation crab.
alaska-pollock.visual: one raw white fish fillet lying flat on the background, pale greyish-white flesh with a fine flaky texture
alaska-pollock.what: A mild white fish with delicate, flaky fillets.

facts: Albacore is the species used for white tuna, and it is sold canned in many countries.
Albacore is a fast-swimming ocean fish that travels across warm and temperate seas.
albacore-tuna.visual: a single raw albacore tuna loin with pale pink flesh, lying directly on a plain background
albacore-tuna.what: A pale-fleshed tuna with a mild taste, often sold canned.

facts: Its flakes are often described as fruity and raisin-like, with a slightly oily texture.
Similar pepper flakes are also made in Turkey, and both are used to season meats, salads and dips.
aleppo-pepper.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl holding a small heap of coarse, dark red pepper flakes
aleppo-pepper.what: Fruity, mildly hot dried chilli flakes from Syria.

facts: Alexanders is a wild plant of coastal Europe that was once grown as a vegetable in medieval gardens.
The young stems can be eaten raw or cooked, in the same way as celery.
alexanders.visual: a small bunch of pale green hollow stems, with glossy leaves at the top
alexanders.what: A wild coastal plant with celery-flavoured stems.

facts: Alfalfa is a flowering plant in the pea family, long grown as fodder for livestock.
Sprouts are grown by soaking seeds in water and rinsing them over several days.
The name alfalfa is generally traced to Arabic, meaning something like 'best fodder'.
alfalfa-sprouts.visual: a small loose heap of fresh alfalfa sprouts, thin pale white stems with tiny green leaves, lying on a plain background
alfalfa-sprouts.what: Fine, mild, crunchy sprouts grown from alfalfa seeds.

facts: Fettuccine Alfredo is the classic dish made with this sauce, served in many Italian-American restaurants.
Jarred versions are often thickened with starch, while home cooks may make it from scratch with butter, cream and cheese.
Parmesan gives the sauce its characteristic nutty, salty flavour.
alfredo-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, thick, pale ivory sauce, glossy
alfredo-sauce.what: A rich, creamy sauce of butter, cream and cheese.

facts: Puff pastry rises because steam from the water in butter pushes the thin dough layers apart as it bakes.
In France it is called pate feuilletee, roughly meaning layered dough.
It is used for pies, sausage rolls and vol-au-vents.
all-butter-puff-pastry.visual: a neatly rolled-out sheet of pale golden puff pastry, its thin layered edge visible, lying flat
all-butter-puff-pastry.what: Light, flaky pastry built from thin layers of butter.

facts: Almond paste was a staple of medieval European cooking, used in sweets and sauces.
Unlike peanut butter, almond butter is made from tree nuts rather than legumes.
almond-butter.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth pale golden-brown almond butter
almond-butter.what: A smooth spread made by grinding almonds into a paste.

facts: Almond extract is made by steeping almonds, or their oil, in alcohol to capture their flavour.
Its strong marzipan-like taste comes mainly from a compound called benzaldehyde.
It is a standard flavouring in cakes, biscuits and cherry bakes across Britain and Europe.
almond-extract.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden liquid, cap on
almond-extract.what: A concentrated flavouring made from almonds for baking.

facts: Almond milk is made by soaking and grinding almonds in water, then straining out the solids.
Almonds are native to the Middle East and Central Asia and were grown there in ancient times.
Almond-based milks have a long history in Spanish and Middle Eastern cooking.
almond-milk.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale creamy almond milk
almond-milk.what: A thin, nutty milk made from ground almonds and water.

facts: Almond oil is pressed from sweet almonds and has a gentle, nutty taste.
almond-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden almond oil
almond-oil.what: A mild, sweet oil pressed from almonds for cooking.

facts: Almond paste is a mix of ground almonds and sugar, used to fill pastries and cakes.
Marzipan is a close relative, finer and smoother, and often moulded into shapes.
almond-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale beige almond paste, dense and smooth, with a slightly crumbly surface
almond-paste.what: A sweet, coarse paste of ground almonds and sugar.

facts: Almonds have been cultivated in the Middle East for thousands of years.
Ground almonds are a key ingredient in marzipan and frangipane pastry.
almonds.visual: a small heap of whole raw almonds, pale brown oval nuts with smooth skins, loose on the background
almonds.what: A sweet, crunchy nut used whole, sliced or ground.

facts: Alphabet pasta is made in small letter shapes that children often enjoy in soup.
Pastina is the general name for small pasta shapes that are used in broths.
alphabet-pasta.visual: a small heap of dry uncooked alphabet pasta, tiny letter shapes in pale yellow
alphabet-pasta.what: Tiny pasta cut into letter shapes, often served in soup.

facts: Alphonso mangoes are grown mainly in Maharashtra, especially around the Ratnagiri region.
Alphonso is a grafted variety, so new trees are propagated by grafting rather than from seed.
The season for Alphonso is short, usually from late spring to early summer.
alphonso-mango.visual: a whole ripe Alphonso mango, golden-orange skin with a faint blush, on a plain background
alphonso-mango.what: A famous Indian mango, prized for its sweet, buttery flesh.

facts: Amaranth was an important food crop in the Americas, especially among the Aztecs, long before European contact.
The plant belongs to the same family as spinach and beetroot, and its leaves can be eaten as greens.
When cooked, the seeds swell into a thick, porridge-like texture that sets quickly as it cools.
amaranth.visual: a small heap of tiny pale beige amaranth seeds, loose, lying on a plain background
amaranth.what: Tiny seeds from a leafy plant, cooked like a porridge.

facts: Amaranth is a genus of plants, with many species native to the Americas, and its leaves have been eaten there for centuries.
In Caribbean cooking the leaves are used in soups and stews, including the dish callaloo.
Amaranth seeds are also eaten, and the plant has long been grown as a grain-like crop.
amaranth-leaves.visual: a bunch of fresh amaranth leaves, soft oval green leaves on pale pink-tinged stems, lying flat on the background
amaranth-leaves.what: Soft, mild leafy greens eaten widely across the tropics.

facts: Amarena is a sour cherry variety grown in northern Italy, especially in the Emilia-Romagna region.
The cherries are preserved in a thick sugar syrup, which gives them their dark colour and sweet-sour taste.
They are often spooned over ice cream, and their syrup is used in cocktails and desserts.
amarena-cherry.visual: a plain glass jar without a label holding dark red, glossy cherries in deep red syrup
amarena-cherry.what: A dark, sour Italian cherry preserved in sweet syrup.

facts: Amaretti take their name from amaro, the Italian word for bitter.
The town of Saronno, in Lombardy, is closely associated with amaretti.
amaretti-biscuits.visual: a small heap of round, pale golden Italian biscuits with cracked tops
amaretti-biscuits.what: Crisp, pale Italian biscuits made with ground almonds.

facts: Amaretto takes its name from the Italian word amaro, meaning bitter.
Many versions are flavoured with apricot kernels, which give a bitter almond taste.
amaretto.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of golden-amber liquid, cap on
amaretto.what: A sweet Italian liqueur with a flavour of almonds.

facts: Amazake is a traditional Japanese drink made from cooked rice and koji, a mould used in fermentation.
Traditional amazake contains very little alcohol and is often served warm in Japan.
The name is often read as sweet sake, which reflects its taste and its rice base.
amazake.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, creamy off-white liquid, smooth and slightly glossy
amazake.what: A sweet, thick Japanese drink made from fermented rice.

facts: Amberjacks are fast, powerful fish of the jack family, found in warm and temperate seas around the world.
Amberjack are caught on lines and nets, and some are also raised on fish farms.
amberjack.visual: a fillet of amberjack, pale pink flesh with silvery skin along one edge, lying flat
amberjack.what: A firm, mild-tasting sea fish that is good raw or grilled.

facts: Amchur is made by drying slices of unripe green mango in the sun and grinding them into powder.
It is widely used in Indian cooking, especially in chaat, pakoras and dal, to add sourness.
amchur.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, pale yellow-brown powder
amchur.what: Tangy powder made from dried unripe green mangoes.

facts: The slices are made from processed cheese, which blends cheese with emulsifying salts.
Processed cheese is especially popular in the United States, where it tops many burgers.
american-cheese-slices.visual: a neat stack of pale orange-yellow square cheese slices, lying flat on a plain background
american-cheese-slices.what: Soft, processed cheese slices that melt easily.

facts: Amontillado is a style of sherry from Jerez in southern Spain, first aged under flor, then oxidised.
Sherry is a fortified wine, with added grape spirit that raises its strength.
Amontillado is often served as an aperitif or with light snacks.
amontillado-sherry.visual: a clear drinking glass of amber-brown sherry, bright and clear
amontillado-sherry.what: An amber sherry with a nutty, toasty flavour.

facts: Anago is a saltwater conger eel, distinct from the freshwater unagi.
In Japan it is usually simmered in a sweet soy sauce before it is served on sushi.
Its flesh is delicate, so it is often cooked gently rather than fried hard.
anago.visual: one whole sea eel, slender grey-brown body, smooth skin, lying in a gentle curve
anago.what: A soft, mild sea eel prized in Japanese sushi.

facts: Its name comes from Anaheim in California, where it became a major commercial crop.
It is commonly roasted, which loosens the skin, and is used in Mexican and Southwestern cooking.
anaheim-chilli.visual: one whole long green chilli pepper, glossy and slightly curved, lying on its side
anaheim-chilli.what: A mild, long green chilli for roasting.

facts: Anardana is made by drying the seeds of sour pomegranates, often in the sun.
Its name combines the Persian word for pomegranate with the Persian word for seed.
It is widely used in North Indian cooking, especially in chutneys, and the seeds are often ground into a powder.
anardana.visual: a small heap of dried pinkish-brown pomegranate seeds, wrinkled and loose, on a plain background
anardana.what: Dried pomegranate seeds with a sour, tangy flavour.

facts: Ancho is the dried form of the poblano, a mild green chilli long associated with Puebla in Mexico.
Ancho chillies are a key ingredient in mole sauces, where they add depth and sweetness.
Its name comes from the Spanish word for wide, referring to the broad shape of the pod.
ancho-chilli.visual: a small heap of whole dried ancho chillies with wrinkled dark red-brown skins
ancho-chilli.what: Dried poblano pepper with a mild, sweet, raisin-like taste.

facts: Anchovies are small oily fish, traditionally salted or packed in oil around the Mediterranean.
Anchovy is used to flavour Worcestershire sauce and many Caesar dressings.
anchovy-essence.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of thin amber-brown anchovy essence
anchovy-essence.what: A thin, salty liquid extracted from anchovies.

facts: Anchovies are small oily fish, and they are preserved by salting or curing.
Anchovies are a traditional ingredient in Worcestershire sauce and in Caesar dressing.
Anchovies melt into sauces, adding savoury depth to many Italian dishes.
anchovy-fillets-in-oil.visual: a plain glass jar without a label holding several dark anchovy fillets in pale oil
anchovy-fillets-in-oil.what: Salty fish fillets preserved in oil, very savoury.

facts: Salted and preserved fish, including anchovies, has been made around the Mediterranean since ancient Roman times.
The paste is made by grinding salted anchovies, often with oil or vinegar, into a smooth spread.
Anchovies are a traditional ingredient in Worcestershire sauce, which adds a salty depth.
anchovy-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth dark pinkish-brown anchovy paste
anchovy-paste.what: A salty, savoury paste made from salted anchovies.

facts: It is a common ingredient in gumbo and jambalaya.
Andouille is closely associated with Louisiana's Cajun cooking, where it is used in everyday dishes.
andouille-sausage.visual: a whole smoked andouille sausage link, dark reddish-brown casing, lying in a gentle curve
andouille-sausage.what: A coarse, smoked pork sausage seasoned for Cajun dishes.

facts: Andouillette is strongly associated with the city of Troyes in north-eastern France.
It is traditionally grilled and often served with mustard.
andouillette.visual: a single andouillette sausage link, pale greyish-pink casing, lying in a gentle curve
andouillette.what: A pungent French sausage made from tripe and chitterlings.

facts: Anelletti means little rings in Italian, a name that describes the shape of the pasta.
A timballo is a pasta dish baked in a drum-shaped crust, popular in southern Italy.
Like other short pastas, anelletti is often used in soups and in simple baked dishes with tomato.
anelletti.visual: a small heap of dried anelletti pasta, tiny pale rings with a smooth surface, on a plain background
anelletti.what: Small Sicilian ring pasta, often used in a baked timballo.

facts: Anelli means little rings in Italian, from the word anello for ring.
Pasta of this kind is traditionally made from durum wheat semolina and water.
anelli.visual: a small heap of tiny dried pasta rings, pale yellow
anelli.what: Tiny ring-shaped pasta, often used in soups.

facts: Angel hair is called capelli d'angelo in Italian, meaning angel's hair, for its very fine strands.
It is one of the thinnest pastas, so it suits light sauces better than heavy ones.
Its other name, capellini, means little hairs in Italian.
angel-hair-pasta.visual: a loose twisted heap of uncooked, very thin pale pasta strands, lying on a plain background
angel-hair-pasta.what: Very fine Italian pasta strands that cook in minutes.

facts: Angelica is a tall plant in the carrot family, and its stems are candied for cake decoration.
The root has a musky flavour and is used to flavour some liqueurs and gins.
angelica.visual: a bunch of fresh angelica, pale green ribbed stems and leaves tied together
angelica.what: A tall herb whose candied stems add green sweetness.

facts: Aniseed comes from the anise plant, which is native to the eastern Mediterranean and the Middle East.
It is the main flavour in drinks such as ouzo, pastis and sambuca.
Aniseed is also used in some German breads and Italian biscuits.
aniseed.visual: a small heap of pale brown aniseed seeds, oval and slightly ridged
aniseed.what: Small sweet seeds with a liquorice flavour for baking.

facts: Aniseed flavour comes from anethole, a compound also found in star anise and fennel.
Anise-flavoured spirits such as pastis and ouzo are popular around the Mediterranean.
In France and Greece these drinks are often diluted with water, which turns them cloudy.
aniseed-liqueur.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle holding a pale, clear liquid
aniseed-liqueur.what: A sweet spirit flavoured with aniseed, like liquorice.

facts: Ankimo is a Japanese dish, traditionally made by steaming monkfish liver.
It is often served in thin slices with ponzu sauce and grated daikon radish.
Its rich texture leads cooks to call it the foie gras of the sea.
ankimo.visual: a whole, firm, pale beige liver lobe, smooth and slightly glossy
ankimo.what: Monkfish liver, steamed to a rich, silky texture.

facts: Annatto comes from the achiote tree, which is native to tropical regions of the Americas.
It is used to colour some English cheeses, such as Red Leicester.
Its red pigment was traditionally used to dye fabric and to paint the body.
annatto-seeds.visual: a small heap of brick-red annatto seeds, glossy and slightly angular
annatto-seeds.what: Small brick-red seeds used to colour food warm orange.

facts: Anthotyro is traditionally made from whey left over after other cheeses have been made.
Many Greek whey cheeses are made by heating the whey until its proteins set into soft curds.
anthotyro.visual: a soft, crumbly block of pale white cheese with one wedge cut away, lying on a plain background
anthotyro.what: A soft, crumbly Greek whey cheese, lightly salty.

facts: Salad potatoes are waxy, with less starch, so they hold their shape after boiling.
Potatoes belong to the nightshade family and grow from tubers that form underground on the plant's stems.
In Peru, hundreds of potato varieties are still grown in the Andes.
anya-potato.visual: a whole raw potato, long and slender with thin, pale skin
anya-potato.what: A slender, waxy potato with a nutty flavour for salads.

facts: Appam is traditionally associated with Kerala, in southern India.
The batter is fermented, then swirled in a small pan so the edges crisp and lace.
It is often served with coconut milk stew or a spiced meat curry.
appam.visual: one thin lacy appam, crisp edges and a soft pale centre, on a plain white plate
appam.what: A lacy-edged South Indian pancake made from fermented rice.

facts: Appenzeller is made in the Appenzell region of north-eastern Switzerland.
The cheese is washed in a herbal brine during ageing, which gives it a distinctive rind.
Appenzeller is one of the traditional Swiss cheeses that has been made for centuries.
appenzeller.visual: a block of firm pale cream cheese with one thick wedge cut away, a thin greenish-brown rind
appenzeller.what: A firm Swiss cheese with a spicy, herby, fruity aroma.

facts: Chutney comes from the Hindi word chatni, meaning a relish or sauce.
Chutneys were brought back to Britain from India during the colonial period.
Sultanas are seedless dried white grapes, a common ingredient in British baking.
apple-and-sultana-chutney.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, glossy brown chutney, smooth on top
apple-and-sultana-chutney.what: A sweet, spiced relish of apples and dried fruit.

facts: Crumble is a British dessert, with a topping of flour and butter baked over fruit until golden.
The topping is made by rubbing cold butter into flour until it forms a loose, crumbly mix.
Apple is the classic filling, but rhubarb, plums and berries are also common.
apple-crumble-topping.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of loose pale golden crumble mix, buttery and crumbly
apple-crumble-topping.what: A buttery, crumbly mix that bakes over fruit.

facts: Apple cucumbers are named for their round shape, which resembles a small apple.
They are an heirloom variety, grown in many home gardens.
Their thin skin means they are often eaten raw in salads without peeling.
apple-cucumber.visual: a whole small round apple cucumber, pale yellow-green with smooth skin
apple-cucumber.what: A small, round, pale cucumber with a mild flavour.

facts: Apple jelly is made by straining cooked apples, so the result is clear rather than cloudy.
Apples contain pectin, a natural setting agent that helps jellies firm up.
apple-jelly.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with clear pale golden apple jelly, glossy and set
apple-jelly.what: Clear, pale fruit jelly made from apples, mild and sweet.

facts: Apples were first grown in Central Asia, in the mountains of what is now Kazakhstan.
Cider, the fermented version, is often made from the same pressed juice.
apple-juice.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden apple juice
apple-juice.what: Juice pressed from apples, sweet and clear or cloudy.

facts: It is used in fruit salads, cold drinks and sauces, adding a gentle mint flavour.
It spreads readily in gardens, so it is often grown in pots to keep it in check.
apple-mint.visual: a small bunch of bright green, soft, downy apple mint leaves on their stems
apple-mint.what: A fruity, soft-leaved mint with a hint of apple.

facts: Apple pie spice usually combines cinnamon with nutmeg, allspice and sometimes cloves.
Spiced apple dishes have a long history in European baking, from medieval pies to modern crumbles.
apple-pie-spice.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine reddish-brown ground spice mix, level on top
apple-pie-spice.what: A warm spice blend, mostly cinnamon, for apple desserts.

facts: Apple sauce has long been served as an accompaniment to roast pork in English cooking.
Apples have been stewed into sauces in Europe for centuries, often with a little sugar and spice.
Its tartness balances the richness of fatty meats such as pork and goose.
apple-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with smooth, pale golden apple sauce
apple-sauce.what: Tart stewed apple, traditionally served with roast pork.

facts: Smoked cheese is made by exposing cheese to smoke from burning wood.
Applewood smoking uses wood from apple trees, which gives a mild, fruity smoke.
Cheddar is a firm cheese named after the village of Cheddar in Somerset.
applewood.visual: a block of golden, smoked cheddar-style cheese with one wedge cut away, lying directly on the background
applewood.what: A firm, cheddar-style cheese with a smoky flavour.

facts: The fruit reached the Mediterranean along trade routes such as the Silk Road.
Turkey is a major producer, and dried apricots are a staple in Middle Eastern cooking.
apricot.visual: one whole ripe apricot, golden-orange skin with a soft rosy blush, lying on its side
apricot.what: A soft, sweet-tart stone fruit, good roasted or in jam.

facts: Apricot glaze is usually made by heating apricot jam with a little water and straining it smooth.
Its French name, nappage, comes from the verb napper, meaning to coat a dish with a sauce.
Brushing a warm glaze over fruit tarts gives a shine and helps keep the fruit from drying out.
apricot-glaze.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, filled with clear, amber, glossy apricot glaze
apricot-glaze.what: A smooth, glossy amber coating made from apricot jam.

facts: Apricots are close relatives of the plum and the peach.
apricot-jam.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with glossy orange-gold apricot jam
apricot-jam.what: Sweet, tart fruit preserve made from apricots and sugar.

facts: The name aquavit comes from the Latin aqua vitae, meaning water of life.
It is typically flavoured with caraway, and sometimes with dill, fennel or other herbs.
Aquavit is often served chilled alongside cured fish in Scandinavia.
aquavit.visual: a clear drinking glass of colourless spirit, filled to just below the rim, on a plain background
aquavit.what: A clear Scandinavian spirit flavoured with caraway seed.

facts: Arame is a brown seaweed from Japan, traditionally sold dried and soaked before cooking.
It is often simmered with soy sauce, mirin and vegetables as a classic Japanese side dish.
Dried arame swells considerably when soaked, so a small amount goes a long way.
arame.visual: a small heap of dried black seaweed shreds, fine dark strands curling slightly
arame.what: Fine, dark strands of mild, sweet seaweed, sold dried.

facts: Arbequina is a small olive variety, grown mainly in Catalonia in north-east Spain.
Its name is linked to the town of Arbeca in the Lleida area of Catalonia.
arbequina-olive-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with pale golden-green olive oil
arbequina-olive-oil.what: A mild, fruity Catalan olive oil with a hint of almond.

facts: The name arbol is the Spanish word for tree.
They are long, thin and bright red, and are most often sold dried.
arbol-chilli.visual: a small loose heap of dried arbol chillies, slender deep red pods with their stems attached
arbol-chilli.what: A slender, very hot dried red chilli from Mexico.

facts: Arborio rice is named after the town of Arborio in Piedmont, northern Italy.
Risotto is made by slowly adding hot stock to the rice and stirring until the grains release their starch.
Arborio is one of several Italian short-grain rice varieties, alongside Carnaroli and Vialone Nano.
arborio-rice.visual: a small heap of short, plump white arborio rice grains, loose and dry
arborio-rice.what: Plump Italian rice that turns creamy as it is stirred.

facts: Arbroath smokies take their name from the Scottish fishing town of Arbroath on the east coast.
They are traditionally smoked over wood fires, which cooks the fish as well as flavouring it.
They are usually eaten warm, often with butter.
arbroath-smokie.visual: a pair of small smoked haddock, golden-brown skin, lying side by side
arbroath-smokie.what: Hot-smoked haddock from Scotland, sold in pairs.

facts: Arctic char live in cold northern lakes and coastal waters across the Arctic and sub-Arctic.
It belongs to the Salmonidae family, the same family as salmon and trout.
Arctic char is farmed in Iceland and Scandinavia as well as caught in the wild.
arctic-char.visual: a single raw skin-on fillet of pinkish-orange arctic char, silver skin visible, lying flat on the background
arctic-char.what: A cold-water fish related to salmon and trout.

facts: Argan trees grow mainly in south-west Morocco, where they are an important local crop.
The oil is traditionally made by pressing roasted kernels, often by women's cooperatives.
Its nutty flavour is used in amlou, a Moroccan paste of almonds, honey and argan oil.
argan-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of golden argan oil
argan-oil.what: A nutty Moroccan oil pressed from argan tree kernels.

facts: Armagnac is produced in Gascony in south-west France, from wine distilled and aged in oak casks.
Armagnac is traditionally aged in oak barrels, which give it colour and a rich, woody flavour.
Prunes soaked in Armagnac are a traditional French dessert from the region.
armagnac.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with amber-coloured brandy
armagnac.what: A rustic French brandy from the Gascony region.

facts: Aromatic bitters are made by steeping herbs, spices and other botanicals in alcohol.
Bitters are used in small dashes because they are very concentrated in flavour.
Bitters are an essential ingredient in many classic cocktails, such as the Old Fashioned.
aromatic-bitters.visual: a plain unlabelled dark glass bottle with a dropper top, small and tapered, containing deep amber liquid
aromatic-bitters.what: A concentrated spiced liquid for drinks and baking.

facts: Aronia berries are native to eastern North America, and the plant is also grown in parts of Europe and Russia.
The berries are very astringent when raw, so they are usually cooked and sweetened into jams, juices and syrups.
The common name chokeberry refers to the dry, astringent feel of the fruit in the mouth.
aronia-berry.visual: a small heap of glossy, dark purple-black berries, each berry round and smooth
aronia-berry.what: A small, dark, tart berry, often made into jam.

facts: Arrabbiata means angry in Italian, a name for the sauce's fiery chilli heat.
The sauce comes from Rome and is traditionally made with garlic, chilli and tomatoes.
It is traditionally served with penne, a short tube-shaped pasta.
arrabbiata-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, deep red sauce, flecked throughout by small red chilli pieces
arrabbiata-sauce.what: A hot, tomato-based pasta sauce flavoured with chilli.

facts: The starch is extracted from the rhizomes, the thick underground stems of the plant.
Arrowroot sauces stay clear and glossy, unlike those thickened with flour.
The plant is native to tropical America and is now grown in many tropical countries.
arrowroot.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with fine white arrowroot powder
arrowroot.what: A fine white starch from tropical roots, used to thicken.

facts: Indigenous peoples of the Americas cultivated arrowroot for food long before European contact.
The starch is extracted from the root and used as a thickener, especially for sauces and puddings.
Arrowroot is grown in warm regions across the Caribbean, South America and parts of Asia.
arrowroot-tuber.visual: a whole knobbly brown arrowroot tuber with fibrous skin and small root tips, lying on its side
arrowroot-tuber.what: A mild, starchy tropical root eaten boiled like potato.

facts: Its strong sulphurous smell mellows when fried in oil, giving a savoury onion-like flavour.
It is widely used in Indian cooking, especially in dals and vegetable dishes.
asafoetida.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl holding a little fine, pale yellowish-brown powder
asafoetida.what: A pungent resin, used in tiny pinches in Indian cooking.

facts: Asiago takes its name from the Asiago plateau in the Veneto region of northern Italy.
Fresh asiago is milky and mild, while aged versions become firm and sharp.
Its name is protected under European rules, so only cheese made in the area can carry it.
asiago.visual: one wedge of asiago cheese, pale straw-coloured paste with small holes, lying flat
asiago.what: A firm Italian cheese, mild when young, sharp when aged.

facts: Asian pears are native to East Asia and have been grown in China and Japan for centuries.
Their texture is crisp and watery, closer to an apple than to a soft European pear.
Nashi is the Japanese word for pear, and it is another common name for this fruit.
asian-pear.visual: a whole round Asian pear, pale golden-green skin with small brown speckles, lying on its side
asian-pear.what: A round, crisp pear with juicy, mildly sweet white flesh.

facts: Asparagus is the young shoot of a perennial plant, cut from the soil before it unfolds into ferny growth.
White asparagus is the same plant, grown under soil or mounded earth so it never turns green.
Asparagus has been eaten since ancient times and was prized by the Romans.
asparagus.visual: a bunch of fresh green asparagus spears, stem ends cut straight, tight tips
asparagus.what: Tender green spears of a plant from the lily family.

facts: Atlantic cod has been a staple food in Northern Europe and North America for centuries.
Dried and salted cod, known as bacalao in Spain and Portugal, is a long-standing tradition.
Fish and chips made with cod became a popular British dish in Victorian Britain.
atlantic-cod-loin.visual: a thick raw cod loin fillet, firm pale white flesh with a neat cut edge, lying flat
atlantic-cod-loin.what: A thick, mild white fish cut from the back of a cod.

facts: Atlantic salmon hatch in rivers, migrate to the sea to feed, then return to their home rivers to spawn.
Salmon has been a staple of northern European and North American cooking for centuries.
atlantic-salmon-fillet.visual: a single raw Atlantic salmon fillet, pink flesh with pale fat lines, skin on, lying flat
atlantic-salmon-fillet.what: A rich, pink fish fillet, cut from Atlantic salmon.

facts: Aubergine is native to South Asia and was grown there for a very long time before spreading west.
In the UK it is called aubergine, while in the United States it is called eggplant, after white varieties.
It is widely used in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern and Asian cooking, such as in moussaka and baba ganoush.
aubergine.visual: a whole glossy dark purple aubergine with a green cap, lying on its side
aubergine.what: A glossy purple fruit with spongy flesh that softens.

facts: Aubergine pickle is a popular condiment across India and Pakistan, served with flatbreads.
Pickles in South Asia are often preserved in oil, salt and spices, which helps them keep.
aubergine-pickle.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with chunks of dark aubergine in a spiced, glossy pickle
aubergine-pickle.what: Chunks of aubergine pickled with chilli and spices.

facts: Avocados are native to Mexico and Central America, where people have eaten them for thousands of years.
The name avocado comes from the Nahuatl word ahuacatl, the language of the Aztecs in central Mexico.
Avocados ripen after picking, so they are often bought firm and left to soften at home.
avocado.visual: a whole ripe avocado with dark green bumpy skin, lying on its side
avocado.what: A pear-shaped fruit with soft, buttery flesh.

facts: It is pressed from the fleshy part of the avocado fruit rather than the stone.
Avocados are native to Mexico and Central America, where people have grown them for thousands of years.
avocado-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with pale green oil
avocado-oil.what: A mild, pale green oil pressed from avocado flesh.

facts: Ayran is a traditional drink in Turkey and neighbouring regions, made by whisking yoghurt with water and salt.
In Iran, the similar drink doogh is often flavoured with mint.
ayran.visual: a tall clear drinking glass of pale frothy white ayran with a thin layer of foam on top
ayran.what: A cold, lightly salted drink made from yoghurt and water.

facts: Baba ganoush is a dip from the Levant, made from charred aubergine.
Its smoky flavour comes from charring the aubergine skin over a flame.
It is eaten across the Middle East and is often served with flatbread.
baba-ganoush.visual: a smooth, smoky, pale greyish-brown aubergine dip filling a small plain white ceramic bowl
baba-ganoush.what: A smoky dip made from roasted aubergine.

facts: Artichokes are the flower buds of a thistle plant, grown mainly in the Mediterranean region.
In Italy and Spain, young artichokes are often fried whole, with the leaves and heart eaten.
Artichokes belong to the daisy family, Asteraceae, which also includes sunflowers and lettuces.
baby-artichoke.visual: one whole small raw baby artichoke, tightly closed green leaves tinged purple, stem trimmed
baby-artichoke.what: A small, tender artichoke, often eaten whole when young.

facts: Aubergines originated in India and Southeast Asia, where they have been grown for a very long time.
The name aubergine comes from French, while many other countries use the word eggplant.
Baby aubergines are picked young, and tend to have softer flesh and fewer seeds.
baby-aubergine.visual: one whole baby aubergine, small and glossy, deep purple skin with a green cap
baby-aubergine.what: A tiny, tender aubergine, sold whole and good for curries.

facts: Baby back ribs are cut from the upper part of the pig's rib cage, next to the loin.
The 'baby' in the name refers to the smaller size of these ribs, not to young animals.
Ribs are slow-cooked or barbecued, and the dish is closely linked to American barbecue traditions.
baby-back-ribs.visual: a whole rack of raw pork ribs, pale pink meat over curved bones, lying flat
baby-back-ribs.what: Small, tender pork ribs cut from near the spine.

facts: Baby bananas, also called finger bananas, are a small variety with a sweeter, creamy flesh.
Banana plants grow from a large underground stem, and the fruit forms in hanging clusters.
In many tropical countries, small bananas are fried or eaten as a snack.
baby-banana.visual: one whole small yellow banana, slim and short, lightly speckled skin, lying on its side
baby-banana.what: A small, sweet banana, often eaten whole or fried.

facts: Button mushrooms are the young form of the cultivated white mushroom, Agaricus bisporus.
Cultivated mushrooms are grown on compost rather than in soil.
As they mature, button mushrooms open up and become cremini, then portobello.
baby-button-mushroom.visual: a small heap of tiny, smooth, pale cream-coloured button mushrooms with closed caps
baby-button-mushroom.what: Tiny, tender mushrooms with closed caps, used whole.

facts: Baby carrots are either small varieties grown for the purpose, or larger carrots cut and trimmed to size.
Carrots were first grown in Central Asia, and early roots were purple or yellow rather than orange.
Baby carrots are usually steamed, roasted or boiled whole, and they cook quickly.
baby-carrot.visual: a small heap of slim, bright orange baby carrots, each about the length of a finger
baby-carrot.what: Small, sweet, tender carrots, sold ready to cook whole.

facts: The leek is the national emblem of Wales, and it has been eaten there for centuries.
Baby leeks are picked young, before the stems thicken, so they cook in minutes.
They can be braised, grilled or roasted whole, and they are common in French cooking.
baby-leek.visual: a small bunch of baby leeks with slim white stems and pale green tops, roots trimmed short
baby-leek.what: A young leek, slim and tender, eaten whole.

facts: Octopus is eaten in many coastal cuisines, including Greece, Spain and Japan.
Octopuses have blue blood, carried by copper-based proteins.
Small octopus cooks quickly, while larger ones need long, slow cooking to become tender.
baby-octopus.visual: a small raw baby octopus, pale pinkish-grey body and curled tentacles, lying flat on the background
baby-octopus.what: A small octopus with tender flesh, often grilled whole.

facts: Pak choi, also called bok choy, is a Chinese brassica with a mild flavour.
Its name is often given as white vegetable in Cantonese.
Baby pak choi is often steamed whole or stir-fried, and its stalks take longer to cook than its leaves.
baby-pak-choi.visual: a whole baby pak choi with pale green leaves and white stalks
baby-pak-choi.what: Small, tender Chinese cabbage with crisp, mild leaves.

facts: Potatoes were first domesticated in the Andes of South America, where many varieties still grow.
Baby potatoes are harvested early, before the plant fully matures, which keeps their skins thin.
Potatoes reached Europe from the Americas and later became a staple crop in many countries.
baby-potato.visual: a small heap of tiny, smooth-skinned baby potatoes, some with a little soil still clinging
baby-potato.what: Small, young potatoes with thin skins, good for roasting.

facts: Spinach is thought to have originated in Persia, and it reached Europe through the Arab world.
Baby spinach is simply spinach harvested young, before the leaves grow large and tough.
baby-spinach.visual: a small loose heap of baby spinach leaves, bright green, smooth and crisp
baby-spinach.what: Young, tender spinach leaves with a mild, fresh taste.

facts: Baby squid are simply young squid, and they are caught in many coastal waters.
In Mediterranean cooking they are often dusted in flour and fried until golden.
Squid are cephalopods, and they are closely related to octopus and cuttlefish.
baby-squid.visual: a small heap of tiny raw baby squid, pale translucent bodies with short tentacles
baby-squid.what: Tiny squid, quick to cook on a grill or in a pan.

facts: Baby sweetcorn is harvested young, before the kernels develop, which is why the whole cob is edible.
Baby corn is widely used in Thai and Chinese stir-fries and soups.
Maize, the parent crop, was domesticated in Mexico thousands of years ago.
baby-sweetcorn.visual: a small loose heap of slender pale yellow baby corn cobs
baby-sweetcorn.what: Tiny immature corn cobs, eaten whole in stir-fries.

facts: Turnips are a root vegetable that have been cultivated in Europe and Asia for thousands of years.
The leaves, known as turnip greens, are eaten as a leafy vegetable in many countries.
baby-turnip.visual: a small bunch of baby turnips with pale purple-tipped roots and green leafy tops still attached
baby-turnip.what: Young turnips picked small, before the roots turn woody.

facts: Back bacon is cut from the loin, the lean muscle along the back, rather than from the fattier belly.
A rasher is a thin slice of bacon, and the word is common in British English.
back-bacon.visual: three thin raw back bacon rashers, pink lean meat with a white ribbon of fat along one edge, lying flat
back-bacon.what: Lean, meaty rashers from the loin, with a ribbon of fat.

facts: Bacon is cured pork, usually from the belly or back, smoked or unsmoked.
Crumbled bacon is often scattered over salads, potatoes and soups.
Salt curing is one of the oldest ways of preserving pork.
bacon-bits.visual: a small heap of crisp cooked bacon bits, golden-brown and irregular in shape
bacon-bits.what: Crisp, crumbled bacon pieces, ready to scatter over dishes.

facts: Cooks have long saved bacon fat to use for frying eggs and vegetables.
In the American South, bacon grease is a traditional cooking fat, especially for cornbread.
Rendering means melting the fat slowly and then straining out the solid pieces.
bacon-fat.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with pale amber solid bacon fat, smooth and opaque
bacon-fat.what: The smoky, savoury fat rendered from frying bacon.

facts: A bacon joint is a larger cut of cured pork than the thin rashers sold for frying.
In Britain, bacon joints are traditionally boiled and served with parsley sauce.
Curing with salt has been used to preserve pork for centuries in many countries.
bacon-joint.visual: one whole uncooked bacon joint, pink cured pork with a thin layer of fat on top, lying on its side
bacon-joint.what: A cured pork joint that is boiled or roasted, then sliced.

facts: Lardons are small strips or cubes of cured pork fat or bacon, used in French cooking.
The name comes from the French word lard, meaning pork fat.
bacon-lardons.visual: a small heap of raw bacon lardons, small cubes of pink meat with white fat
bacon-lardons.what: Small cubes of cured pork, often cut from the belly.

facts: Bagels were brought to North America by Eastern European Jewish immigrants and grew popular in New York.
The name is thought to come from the Yiddish word beygl, meaning ring.
bagel.visual: a whole plain bagel with a glossy golden-brown crust and a round central hole, lying on its side
bagel.what: A dense, chewy ring of boiled and baked bread.

facts: Bagoong is a fermented seafood paste from the Philippines, made by salting shrimp or small fish.
Salted fish pastes like this are part of many Southeast Asian kitchens, from the Philippines to Thailand.
bagoong.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pinkish-grey shrimp paste, smooth and moist
bagoong.what: Salty Filipino paste of fermented shrimp or fish.

facts: Baharat is the Arabic word for spices, and blends vary from household to household across the region.
Typical blends include black pepper, cumin, coriander, cinnamon and cloves.
Baharat is used to season meat, rice and stews across the Gulf and Levant.
baharat.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine reddish-brown ground spice powder
baharat.what: A warm, aromatic Middle Eastern blend of ground spices.

facts: Its name means white liquor, a reference to its clear colour.
Baijiu is traditionally distilled from sorghum, wheat or other grains, fermented with a starter called qu.
It is often served in small glasses at celebrations and banquets across China.
baijiu.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with clear, colourless liquid, standing alone on a plain background
baijiu.what: A strong, clear Chinese spirit made from grain.

facts: Haricot beans are dried white beans, native to the Americas, and are used widely across Europe.
Baked beans are traditionally made by simmering the beans slowly with sugar, tomato and seasonings.
baked-beans.visual: a small plain white bowl of cooked haricot beans in a smooth orange-red tomato sauce
baked-beans.what: Haricot beans cooked in a sweet tomato sauce.

facts: Baked beans in tomato sauce are a British breakfast and snack staple, often eaten on toast.
The beans are usually haricot beans, small dried white beans.
baked-beans-with-sausages.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of baked beans in orange tomato sauce, small pork sausages half-sunk among the beans
baked-beans-with-sausages.what: Beans in tomato sauce, served with small pork sausages.

facts: The jacket potato is a British favourite, usually baked in the oven until the skin is crisp.
Potatoes were brought to Europe from the Americas in the sixteenth century.
baked-potato-jacket.visual: a baked jacket potato with a crisp golden-brown skin, served whole on a plain white plate
baked-potato-jacket.what: A ready-baked potato, crisp-skinned and soft inside.

facts: Baker's ammonia, also called ammonium bicarbonate, releases gases when heated, which lifts thin bakes.
It was a traditional raising agent in German and Scandinavian biscuits.
It works best in thin bakes, since the gases escape easily and leave a crisp, open texture.
baker-s-ammonia.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine white powder, loose and dry
baker-s-ammonia.what: A raising agent for very crisp biscuits and crackers.

facts: Bakewell tart is named after the Derbyshire market town of Bakewell in England.
It has a shortcrust pastry base, a layer of jam and a sponge made with ground almonds.
Bakewell pudding, from the same town, is a related dish with a different filling.
bakewell-tart.visual: a golden slice of almond tart showing pale sponge on a pastry base, on a plain white plate
bakewell-tart.what: A jam and almond pastry tart from Derbyshire, England.

facts: Baking powder combines an acid and an alkali, which release gas when they are mixed with liquid.
Double-acting baking powder releases gas twice, once when mixed and again when heated in the oven.
Chemists began developing commercial baking powders in the nineteenth century to make home baking easier.
baking-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine white baking powder, levelled smooth across the top
baking-powder.what: A raising agent that makes cakes and scones rise.

facts: Traditional balsamic vinegar comes from Modena and Reggio Emilia in northern Italy, made from cooked grape must.
A glaze is made by simmering balsamic vinegar until it thickens and turns syrupy.
It is often drizzled over salads, strawberries and grilled dishes.
balsamic-glaze.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, dark brown, glossy balsamic glaze
balsamic-glaze.what: Thick, sweet syrup made by reducing balsamic vinegar.

facts: Traditional balsamic vinegar comes from the Modena and Reggio Emilia areas of northern Italy.
A vinaigrette is a simple mix of oil and vinegar that separates, so it must be shaken or whisked before use.
balsamic-vinaigrette.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with thin glossy dark brown dressing
balsamic-vinaigrette.what: A dark, sweet dressing made from balsamic vinegar and oil.

facts: Traditional balsamic vinegar is aged for many years in a series of wooden barrels.
Traditional balsamic comes from Modena and Reggio Emilia in northern Italy and has a protected name.
Many everyday bottles are made by blending wine vinegar with cooked grape must.
balsamic-vinegar.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of dark, glossy balsamic vinegar, closed by a stopper
balsamic-vinegar.what: A dark, sweet-sour vinegar made from grape must in Italy.

facts: The balti style is named after the deep, wok-like pan it is traditionally cooked in.
Balti dishes became popular in Britain in the 1970s, especially in Birmingham restaurants.
Balti dishes are cooked quickly over high heat, which gives them a glossy, fast-cooked style.
balti-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, deep orange-red paste with a smooth surface
balti-paste.what: A thick, garlicky tomato paste for stir-fried curries.

facts: Bamboo salt is traditionally made in Korea by roasting sea salt in bamboo tubes sealed with clay.
Cooks use it as a finishing salt or stir it into soups and sauces.
bamboo-salt.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of coarse, grey-tinged bamboo salt crystals
bamboo-salt.what: Sea salt roasted in bamboo tubes, with a mellow flavour.

facts: Bamboo shoots are the young growth of bamboo, which is a giant grass, and they emerge from the ground as the plant grows.
Bamboo shoots are eaten across China, Japan and South-East Asia, where they feature in soups, stir-fries and curries.
Fresh shoots contain a bitter compound, so they are usually boiled before eating.
bamboo-shoots.visual: a whole young bamboo shoot, pale cream and conical, with brown papery leaf sheaths
bamboo-shoots.what: Young, tender bamboo shoots with a crisp, mild bite.

facts: Bananas are thought to have originated in Southeast Asia, where wild relatives still grow.
The banana plant is technically a giant herb, not a tree, because its trunk is made of leaf stalks.
banana.visual: one whole ripe yellow banana with a few brown speckles on its skin, lying on its side
banana.what: A long, sweet fruit with yellow skin and creamy flesh.

facts: Peeling away the tough outer bracts reveals pale, tender petals beneath.
The blossom hangs at the end of the flower stalk, below the developing fruit.
Banana blossoms are used in salads and curries across South and Southeast Asia.
banana-blossom.visual: a single whole banana blossom, a large deep purple-red teardrop-shaped bud with overlapping petals
banana-blossom.what: The purple flower of a banana plant, eaten as a vegetable.

facts: Custard is a sweet sauce usually made from milk, sugar and egg yolks, thickened by gentle heat.
Custard powder was invented in England in the 1830s, giving a quick way to make custard.
banana-custard.visual: a small plain white bowl of smooth, pale yellow custard, soft and glossy on top
banana-custard.what: A smooth, sweet custard made with sliced ripe bananas.

facts: Artificial banana flavour is often made from isoamyl acetate, a compound that smells of bananas.
Many banana flavourings are made without any real banana in them.
banana-flavouring.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with pale yellow banana flavouring
banana-flavouring.what: Sweet banana essence used to flavour cakes and milkshakes.

facts: Banana ketchup is said to have started in the Philippines when tomatoes were scarce.
banana-ketchup.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, bright red ketchup
banana-ketchup.what: A sweet, bright red condiment made from bananas.

facts: Banana leaves are used across South-East Asia, Latin America and Africa to wrap food before cooking.
Warming the leaves over a flame makes them softer and easier to fold.
Indonesian pepes and Filipino suman are both wrapped in banana leaves before cooking.
banana-leaf.visual: one whole large glossy green banana leaf, flat and unfolded, with fine parallel veins visible
banana-leaf.what: A large, glossy leaf used to wrap and steam food.

facts: Banana peppers are a mild type of chilli pepper, grown for pickling and eating fresh.
Their name refers to their shape and colour, which resemble a banana.
They are often sold pickled in jars, especially in North America.
banana-pepper.visual: one whole raw banana pepper, long curved shape, pale yellow waxy skin, lying on its side on a plain background
banana-pepper.what: A long, mild yellow pepper with a gentle tang.

facts: Banana shallots are a long, elongated variety of shallot, valued for their mild flavour.
Their name is thought to come from Ascalon, an ancient city in the Levant.
banana-shallot.visual: one whole banana shallot with long, pale copper skin, lying on the background
banana-shallot.what: A long, mild shallot shaped like a small banana.

facts: Banon is a goat's cheese made in Provence, in the south of France.
The cheese is traditionally wrapped in chestnut leaves and tied with raffia.
banon.visual: a single whole round cheese wrapped in dark green chestnut leaves tied with raffia, lying on the plain background
banon.what: A small goat's cheese wrapped in chestnut leaves.

facts: Steamed buns, called bao or baozi, are a popular snack across China.
Steaming gives them their soft, pillowy texture rather than baking.
Taiwanese gua bao are folded around braised pork and crushed peanuts.
bao-bun.visual: a single soft, pillowy white steamed bun, folded in half, on a plain white plate
bao-bun.what: A soft, fluffy steamed bun, often folded around a filling.

facts: Magret is a thick duck breast fillet, often cooked with the skin scored and crisped.
The meat is darker and richer than chicken and is often served pink.
barbary-duck.visual: one whole raw Barbary duck, dark red-brown skin on the breast, lying on its breast on the background
barbary-duck.what: A large, lean duck with a meaty breast and dark flesh.

facts: Dry rubs of this kind are rubbed onto meat before it is smoked or grilled.
Paprika, which gives many rubs their colour, is made from ground dried red peppers.
American barbecue styles, from Texas to the Carolinas, each have their own rub recipes.
barbecue-rub.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, reddish-brown barbecue spice rub
barbecue-rub.what: A sweet, smoky mix of spices, sugar and paprika.

facts: Barbecue sauce varies widely, from thin vinegar sauces in North Carolina to thick tomato versions.
Kansas City-style sauces are typically thick and sweet, with a tomato base.
Barbecue refers to slow-cooking meat over low heat, often with smoke.
barbecue-sauce.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with thick dark reddish-brown sauce
barbecue-sauce.what: A smoky, sweet, tangy tomato sauce for ribs and burgers.

facts: Dates are the fruit of the date palm, which has long been grown across the Middle East.
Fresh barhi dates are eaten crisp, and they soften to a toffee-like texture as they ripen.
barhi-date.visual: a small heap of plump golden-yellow barhi dates, smooth-skinned
barhi-date.what: A round, golden date eaten fresh while still firm.

facts: It is a traditional ingredient in bagel boiling water and in some brown breads.
Malt has long been used in brewing, where sprouted grain supplies the sugars for fermentation.
barley-malt-syrup.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, holding thick dark brown barley malt syrup
barley-malt-syrup.what: A thick, dark, earthy syrup made from sprouted barley.

facts: Miso is a Japanese seasoning made by fermenting soybeans with salt and koji, a mould.
Miso styles differ by the grain used for the koji, such as rice, barley or soybeans.
Miso has been made in Japan for many centuries.
barley-miso.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, dark golden-brown paste, thick and glossy
barley-miso.what: A rustic Japanese paste of fermented barley and soybeans.

facts: Barley sugar is a hard boiled sweet made by heating sugar until it sets into a glassy mass.
The name comes from an old recipe that boiled barley in water and then mixed in sugar.
Traditional twisted sticks are made by pulling and twisting the warm, soft sugar mass by hand.
barley-sugar.visual: a small heap of amber barley sugar twists, glossy and translucent, on a plain background
barley-sugar.what: An amber, old-fashioned boiled sweet, mild and smooth.

facts: Barm cakes are known as stotties in parts of the North East, especially on Tyneside.
The name barm comes from the Old English word for yeast froth, which is used to raise the dough.
Barm cakes are often split and filled with cooked meats, cheese or salad for lunch.
barm-cake.visual: one whole soft, pale floury bread roll, round and slightly flattened, dusted with flour
barm-cake.what: A soft, floury bread roll from northern England.

facts: Brie-style cheeses take their name from the Brie region of France, east of Paris.
Soft cheeses like this are ripened with a white mould on the outside, which gives a bloomy rind.
Suffolk is a county in East Anglia, in the east of England.
baron-bigod.visual: a round of pale, soft cheese with a white bloomy rind, one wedge cut away to show a creamy interior
baron-bigod.what: A rich, soft, farmhouse brie-style cheese from Suffolk.

facts: Barracudas are fast, slender fish found in tropical and subtropical seas around the world.
Barracuda is eaten in many tropical countries, where it is often grilled whole.
barracuda.visual: one whole raw barracuda, long silver body with dark markings, lying on its side
barracuda.what: A long, toothy predatory fish with firm, mild white flesh.

facts: Barramundi is a native of the Indo-Pacific, found in coastal waters and rivers.
Its name comes from an Aboriginal Australian language.
Many fish farms raise barramundi, and it is often pan-fried or steamed.
barramundi.visual: a whole raw barramundi, silver-grey skin with a bluish back, lying on its side
barramundi.what: A mild, buttery white fish from the Indo-Pacific.

facts: Basil oil is made by blending fresh basil leaves into a neutral oil, then straining the mixture.
In Italy, basil is famously paired with tomato and mozzarella in the Caprese salad.
basil-oil.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with bright green basil oil
basil-oil.what: Bright green oil infused with basil, for drizzling on food.

facts: In India and South-East Asia, the seeds are soaked and added to drinks and desserts.
Dried seeds keep for a long time, and they swell when soaked in water.
basil-seeds.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with tiny dark basil seeds
basil-seeds.what: Tiny black seeds that swell into jelly in cold drinks.

facts: The name basmati comes from a Hindi word associated with fragrance.
It is grown mainly in the Indian subcontinent, especially in the Punjab region.
Basmati grains lengthen noticeably when cooked, which is part of its appeal.
basmati-rice.visual: a small heap of raw basmati rice, long slender white grains piled loosely
basmati-rice.what: Long, fragrant rice grown in the Himalayan foothills.

facts: It sits between a baguette and a round boule in shape, and is common in French bakeries.
Bakers shape the dough by hand and score the top before baking to guide its rise.
batard.visual: one whole batard loaf, short and fat with a golden crust and a score line across the top, lying on its side
batard.what: A short, fat French loaf with a tender, open crumb.

facts: Bavarian sweet mustard is traditionally served alongside weisswurst, a Munich veal sausage.
It is sweetened with sugar, which gives it a mild flavour compared with hot mustards.
Munich is the main city associated with this style, in the Bavarian region of southern Germany.
bavarian-sweet-mustard.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, golden-brown sweet mustard
bavarian-sweet-mustard.what: A sweet, mild Bavarian mustard, often eaten with sausages.

facts: Bavette is a cut from the bottom sirloin, close to the flank.
In France it is often served with shallots, as in the classic bavette a l'echalote.
bavette.visual: one raw bavette steak, long and flat, with a coarse grain and a thin band of fat along one edge
bavette.what: A lean, flat steak with an open grain and bold flavour.

facts: Bay boletes grow in woodland, often near pine trees, mainly in Europe.
Like other boletes, it has spongy pores under the cap in place of gills.
Its firm flesh holds its shape well when sliced and fried.
bay-bolete.visual: a whole fresh bay bolete mushroom, glossy brown cap and pale stem, lying on a plain background
bay-bolete.what: A wild mushroom with a firm, glossy brown cap.

facts: Bayonne ham takes its name from the French town of Bayonne in the Basque Country.
The ham is salted and then air-dried over many months, a method long used in the region.
bayonne-ham.visual: a neatly cut slice of air-dried ham, deep rose-red meat with a thin rim of white fat, lying flat on the background
bayonne-ham.what: A French air-dried ham with a gently salty, sweet flavour.

facts: It is an emulsion of egg yolks and melted butter, flavoured with reduced vinegar and shallots.
It is traditionally served with grilled steak and chips, and is a classic of French restaurant cooking.
bearnaise-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, pale golden sauce speckled with green tarragon
bearnaise-sauce.what: A rich, buttery sauce flavoured with tarragon and vinegar.

facts: Eggs are used to bind mixtures such as burgers and fishcakes, because they set when heated.
Beaten egg is brushed on pastry before baking to give it a golden, glossy finish.
beaten-egg.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, pale yellow beaten egg, lightly frothy at the surface
beaten-egg.what: Whole eggs whisked smooth, used to bind, glaze and enrich.

facts: Beaufort is made in the Savoie region of the French Alps from cow's milk.
beaufort.visual: a wheel of pale golden cheese, one wedge cut away to show a smooth pale interior
beaufort.what: A firm Alpine cheese with a sweet, fruity flavour.

facts: Bechamel is one of the five mother sauces of classical French cooking, from which many other sauces are made.
Bechamel is the base of dishes such as lasagne, macaroni cheese and moussaka.
bechamel-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, ivory-coloured bechamel, thick and glossy
bechamel-sauce.what: A smooth white sauce made from milk, butter and flour.

facts: Savoury crisps flavoured with onion are a long-standing British snack, sold in many variants.
Thin fried potato crisps are associated with the United States, and flavoured versions are now sold worldwide.
The name crisps is British, while in America the same snack is usually called chips.
beef-and-onion-crisps.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with thin, golden, flavoured potato crisps
beef-and-onion-crisps.what: Thin, savoury potato crisps flavoured with beef and onion.

facts: Mince is meat that has been passed through a grinder to make small, loose pieces.
Mixing beef and pork is a long-standing practice in meatballs, meatloaf and sausage.
In Italy, a mix of beef and pork is often used for polpette, or meatballs.
beef-and-pork-mince.visual: a small heap of raw minced beef and pork, pink and marbled with a fine, loose texture
beef-and-pork-mince.what: Minced beef and pork blended together for juicy meatballs.

facts: Bone broth is made by simmering bones and connective tissue in water for many hours.
Beef stock forms the base of many soups, stews and sauces in classic French cooking.
Stocks and broths have been central to European and Asian kitchens for centuries.
beef-bone-broth.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with clear golden-brown beef broth
beef-bone-broth.what: A rich, savoury liquid made from long-simmered beef bones.

facts: Brisket is cut from the lower chest of the cow, a muscle that does a lot of work.
Texas-style barbecue and Jewish-style salt beef are both traditionally made from brisket.
The meat needs long, slow cooking to break down its connective tissue and become tender.
beef-brisket.visual: one whole raw beef brisket, a large flat cut with a thick fat layer on top, lying flat on the background
beef-brisket.what: A tough chest cut that turns tender with slow cooking.

facts: The name burger is linked to Hamburg, the German city associated with minced beef steaks.
A patty is shaped by hand or in a press, then grilled, griddled or fried.
beef-burger-patty.visual: a single raw beef burger patty, round and even, pale pink with flecks of white fat, lying flat
beef-burger-patty.what: Minced beef pressed into a round, ready for the grill.

facts: Fillet is a very tender cut, because the muscle does little work during the animal's life.
Thinly sliced raw beef appears in several cuisines around the world.
beef-carpaccio-fillet.visual: a neat fan of paper-thin raw beef fillet slices, deep red with a fine edge of white fat, lying flat on the plain background
beef-carpaccio-fillet.what: Raw beef fillet, sliced very thinly and served cold.

facts: Beef cheek is the muscle that works the jaw, so it is firm and needs slow cooking.
Cheeks are braised in wine or stock so the connective tissue softens.
Ox cheek is a traditional cut in Spanish cooking, where it is often braised in red wine.
beef-cheek.visual: one whole raw beef cheek, deep red meat with thin streaks of white fat, lying on its side
beef-cheek.what: A dense, lean cut that becomes silky when slow-braised.

facts: In British butchery, clod is cut from the shoulder, where muscles work hard and need slow cooking.
Slow braising breaks down the connective tissue in this type of cut, leaving the meat soft and easy to shred.
beef-clod.visual: one whole raw beef clod, a dense dark red cut of meat with a thin layer of fat, on a plain background
beef-clod.what: A tough shoulder cut that turns tender with slow cooking.

facts: Dripping is the fat that melts off meat during roasting and sets as it cools.
British cooks have long saved beef dripping to fry food and roast potatoes.
beef-dripping.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of set, creamy-white beef dripping, smooth surface
beef-dripping.what: Rendered beef fat for crisp roast potatoes.

facts: Beef extract was developed in the nineteenth century as a way to preserve meat flavour.
It is used to add deep savoury flavour to stews, gravies and soups.
beef-extract.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label holding thick, glossy, dark brown beef extract paste
beef-extract.what: A thick, dark paste made by reducing beef stock.

facts: Fillet is cut from the psoas muscle, which does little work, so the meat is very tender.
Beef fillet is called tenderloin in the United States and filet mignon when cut into steaks.
beef-fillet.visual: a whole raw beef fillet, deep red meat, thin layer of fat, lying on a plain background
beef-fillet.what: The most tender cut of beef, from along the loin.

facts: The fillet is a long, tender muscle that runs along the underside of the beef loin.
Beef stroganoff, a dish linked to Russia, is traditionally made with thin strips of beef.
beef-fillet-tail.visual: a raw tapered piece of beef fillet, deep red with fine marbling, lying flat
beef-fillet-tail.what: The tender tapered end of the beef fillet, lean and mild.

facts: Instant noodles were first developed in Japan in 1958 by Momofuku Ando.
Cup and pot versions add hot water and wait a few minutes for the noodles to soften.
beef-flavour-noodle-pot.visual: a small heap of dry, curly instant noodles, pale yellow and crinkled
beef-flavour-noodle-pot.what: Instant noodles in a pot, flavoured with beef seasoning.

facts: Gravy is traditionally made from the juices left in the roasting tin, thickened with flour.
A roast dinner in Britain is often served with gravy, roast potatoes and vegetables.
Stock or stock cubes are often used to give gravy more depth of flavour.
beef-gravy.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, glossy, deep brown gravy, its surface lightly shining
beef-gravy.what: A rich brown sauce made from meat juices and stock.

facts: Gravy powders became popular in the twentieth century as a quick way to flavour sauces.
Powdered gravy is usually made from dried stock, starch and seasoning, mixed with hot water.
beef-gravy-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, dark brown beef gravy powder
beef-gravy-powder.what: Instant powder that makes a quick beef gravy.

facts: The English word jerky comes from the Spanish word charqui, itself from Quechua, for dried meat.
Drying and salting meat was an early way of preserving it before refrigeration.
Jerky keeps well without refrigeration, which made it a popular travel food.
beef-jerky.visual: a few dark brown strips of dried beef, glossy and slightly curled, on a plain white plate
beef-jerky.what: Chewy strips of dried, salted and spiced beef.

facts: Meatballs appear in many cuisines, from Swedish köttbullar to Italian polpette.
Spaghetti and meatballs is an Italian-American dish developed in the United States.
beef-meatballs.visual: a small heap of round, browned beef meatballs on a plain white plate
beef-meatballs.what: Small rounds of minced beef, shaped by hand and cooked.

facts: Minced beef is made by passing cuts of beef through a grinder, often with some fat for flavour.
