coconut-oil.what: A white fat from coconut flesh that is solid when cool.

facts: Coconut vinegar is made by fermenting the sap tapped from coconut palm flower buds.
It is widely used in Southeast Asia, especially the Philippines, in dips and marinades.
coconut-vinegar.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle, half full of cloudy pale golden liquid
coconut-vinegar.what: A mild, cloudy vinegar made from fermented coconut sap.

facts: Coconut water is the clear liquid found inside a young green coconut.
People in tropical countries have drunk it for centuries as a simple, refreshing drink.
Coconut milk is made by grating the white flesh of mature coconuts and pressing it with water.
coconut-water.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale, slightly cloudy coconut water, filled to the top
coconut-water.what: A clear, faintly sweet liquid found inside young coconuts.

facts: It is made by culturing coconut milk with bacteria, much as dairy yoghurt is made.
coconut-yoghurt.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, creamy white yoghurt
coconut-yoghurt.what: A creamy, lightly tropical yoghurt made from coconut milk.

facts: Cocoyam is a common name for the Colocasia and Xanthosoma plants, grown for their starchy corms.
In West Africa the corms are often boiled and pounded into a smooth dough.
The leaves of some cocoyam plants are also cooked as a green vegetable in parts of Africa and the Caribbean.
cocoyam.visual: a whole raw cocoyam corm, brown hairy rough skin, round and knobbly, lying on the background
cocoyam.what: A starchy corm from tropical regions, boiled or pounded.

facts: Cod is a white fish that lives in cold northern seas, including the North Atlantic.
Salted and dried cod has long been a way to keep fish for many months.
Cod cheeks are usually fried or roasted, and they are prized for their firm, tender texture.
cod-cheeks.visual: a small heap of raw white cod cheeks, pale and glossy, each a small rounded piece of fish
cod-cheeks.what: Small, tender cuts from a cod's head, sweet and rich.

facts: Cod was a major food fish in Europe and North America for centuries.
Salted and dried cod, known as bacalao, has long been traded around the world.
Fish and chips is a popular British dish, often made with cod or haddock.
cod-fillet.visual: one raw cod fillet, thick and pale white with a slightly flaky surface, lying flat
cod-fillet.what: A thick, mild white fish that flakes into large pieces.

facts: Cod liver is traditionally tinned in Norway and sold as a delicacy.
The liver is soft and fatty, which gives it a rich, creamy texture.
Cod livers were valued in northern fishing communities for centuries.
cod-liver.visual: a whole raw cod liver, smooth and pale pinkish-cream, lying flat
cod-liver.what: Smooth, rich fish liver, often tinned or served on toast.

facts: Cod is a white fish from cold northern seas, and it was a staple of British fish and chip shops.
Cod was salted and dried for centuries to preserve it, and salt cod remains important in Portuguese cooking.
A cod loin is the thick central part of the fillet, which holds together well when roasted or pan-seared.
cod-loin.visual: one raw centre-cut cod loin, thick, moist and pale white, lying flat
cod-loin.what: A thick, meaty centre cut from a cod fish.

facts: Cod roe is sold fresh, or salted and smoked, which helps it keep for longer.
In Greece, a paste called taramasalata is traditionally made from salted fish roe.
In Japan, salted cod roe, known as tarako, is a popular food eaten with rice.
cod-roe.visual: a raw cod roe sac, smooth pale pink membrane, lying in a gentle curve on a plain background
cod-roe.what: A soft, pale sac of fish eggs from a cod.

facts: Roasting turns green beans brown by caramelising their sugars and developing their aroma.
Coffee plants are widely thought to have originated in the highlands of Ethiopia.
coffee-beans.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dark brown roasted coffee beans with a glossy sheen
coffee-beans.what: Dark roasted seeds of the coffee plant, ground for brewing.

facts: Coffee liqueurs are made by steeping coffee in a spirit, then sweetening the result with sugar.
Cream liqueurs combine a spirit with dairy cream, which gives them a thick, smooth texture.
The Irish-style cream liqueur was developed in Ireland and is now copied around the world.
coffee-cream-liqueur.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle, half full of creamy dark brown liqueur
coffee-cream-liqueur.what: A sweet, creamy liqueur flavoured with coffee.

facts: Coffee grows as a shrub or small tree in tropical highlands, and its beans are roasted.
Coffee extract is used to flavour cakes, buttercream and tiramisu.
coffee-extract.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of dark brown, thick coffee extract
coffee-extract.what: A dark, sweet concentrate made from brewed coffee.

facts: Coffee liqueurs are sweetened spirits made by steeping or blending coffee with alcohol.
Mexico is well known for coffee liqueur, and the style is now made in many countries.
It is a common ingredient in tiramisu, white Russians and espresso martinis.
coffee-liqueur.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with glossy dark brown coffee liqueur
coffee-liqueur.what: A sweet spirit flavoured with coffee for desserts.

facts: Cognac is made from white wine grapes that are distilled and then aged in oak casks.
It is named after the town of Cognac in western France, in the Charente region.
The name is legally protected, so only brandy made in the region may be called Cognac.
cognac.visual: a clear drinking glass of amber grape brandy
cognac.what: A premium brandy from the Cognac region of France.

facts: Coho salmon are native to the North Pacific, where they are also called silver salmon.
Coho salmon spawn in rivers and streams, returning from the sea to the fresh water where they hatched.
coho-salmon.visual: a fillet of raw coho salmon with pale pink-orange flesh and silver skin, lying on the background
coho-salmon.what: A mild wild Pacific salmon with a delicate texture.

facts: Cokelek is made by heating buttermilk or whey so that soft curds form.
It is a common part of Turkish breakfast tables, usually eaten fresh.
cokelek.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of loose, crumbly white curd, with a soft moist texture
cokelek.what: A crumbly, tangy Turkish curd made from buttermilk.

facts: The name cola comes from the kola nut of West Africa, which was an early flavouring in the drink.
Cola drinks were developed in the United States in the late nineteenth century.
Cola is often used in cooking to glaze ham and in cakes, where its sugar caramelises.
cola.visual: a clear drinking glass of dark brown fizzy cola, bubbles rising through it
cola.what: A sweet, fizzy, dark soft drink flavoured with spices.

facts: Colatura di alici comes from Cetara, a fishing village on the Amalfi Coast of Italy.
It is made by layering salted anchovies and collecting the liquid that drains from them.
Cooks often drizzle it over pasta or vegetables as a seasoning.
colatura-di-alici.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with clear, amber-gold liquid
colatura-di-alici.what: A golden, salty essence drained from salted anchovies.

facts: It is a close relative of cheddar, but softer and more moist.
colby.visual: a block of orange-yellow Colby cheese with one wedge cut away, lying on the background
colby.what: A mild, soft American cheese, similar to cheddar.

facts: Cold brew is made by steeping coffee grounds in cold water for many hours rather than brewing with heat.
Cold brew tends to taste smoother and less bitter than coffee brewed with hot water.
cold-brew-coffee.visual: a clear drinking glass of dark, smooth cold brew coffee, no ice
cold-brew-coffee.what: Coffee steeped in cold water for many hours, then strained.

facts: Rapeseed belongs to the mustard family and is widely grown across Britain and Europe.
Cold pressing extracts oil using mechanical pressure rather than heat or chemical solvents.
Canola is the name used in North America for low-erucic-acid rapeseed varieties.
cold-pressed-rapeseed-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with clear golden cold-pressed oil
cold-pressed-rapeseed-oil.what: A golden, nutty oil pressed from rapeseed, for dressings.

facts: Coley is a member of the cod family, Gadidae, and lives in the North Atlantic.
Coley is also called saithe, and its flesh turns from greyish to white when cooked.
coley-fillet.visual: one raw coley fillet, greyish flesh with the skin on, lying flat directly on the background
coley-fillet.what: A white fish from the cod family, cheaper than cod.

facts: Collards are a non-heading cabbage relative that has been eaten since ancient times.
In the American South they are often braised slowly, traditionally with smoked pork.
collard-greens.visual: a bunch of dark green collard greens, thick pale stems and ruffled glossy leaves
collard-greens.what: Sturdy dark leafy greens from the cabbage family.

facts: Indian indentured workers brought curry traditions to the Caribbean in the nineteenth century.
It typically includes coriander, mustard seed, turmeric and cumin, and suits goat, chicken and fish.
colombo-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine yellow-brown curry powder, gently mounded
colombo-powder.what: A mild, golden spice blend from the Caribbean.

facts: Its French name, Doyenne du Comice, roughly means the leader of the agricultural show.
Comice pears are often served with blue cheese, a pairing that is popular in Britain and France.
Pears ripen best after picking, which is why they are often sold firm for ripening at home.
comice-pear.visual: a single whole ripe pear with green-yellow skin and a soft red blush, its stalk attached
comice-pear.what: A round, juicy pear with buttery flesh and honey notes.

facts: Comté is made in the Jura mountains of eastern France, from raw cows' milk.
It is a protected designation cheese, with rules on where and how it can be made.
Wheels are aged for several months in cellars, which develops its nutty, caramel flavour.
comte.visual: a block of pale golden hard cheese with one wedge cut away, showing the paste, a thin rind on the outside
comte.what: A firm, nutty French cheese from the Jura mountains.

facts: Conch is a large sea snail whose meat is eaten across the Caribbean and Florida.
Its firm meat is often pounded before cooking to make it tender.
Conch fritters and conch chowder are popular in the Bahamas.
conch.visual: a few thin pale cream slices of raw conch meat lying flat, firm and glossy
conch.what: A large sea snail with firm, sweet white meat.

facts: The name conchiglie is Italian for shells, which is what the pasta resembles.
Their hollow cups trap sauce and small pieces of filling.
conchiglie.visual: a small heap of dry uncooked conchiglie pasta shells, ridged and pale cream coloured, loose on the surface
conchiglie.what: Small hollow pasta shaped like seashells.

facts: Conchiglioni is the augmentative of conchiglie, the Italian word for shells.
Shell-shaped pasta is a classic Italian family of shapes, and the largest are often stuffed with cheese or meat.
Cooks often bake stuffed shells in tomato sauce, topped with melted cheese.
conchiglioni.visual: a small heap of uncooked large pasta shells, pale cream and ridged, scattered loosely
conchiglioni.what: Very large pasta shells, suited to stuffing and baking.

facts: The Concord grape was bred in Concord, Massachusetts, in the 1840s.
Concord grapes are a traditional variety in the eastern United States and are grown widely there.
concord-grapes.visual: a small bunch of dark purple Concord grapes, their skins lightly dusted by a pale bloom
concord-grapes.what: Dark purple American grapes with a strong, foxy flavour.

facts: Pears are members of the rose family, the same family as apples and plums.
Pear trees have been cultivated for thousands of years, with fruit eaten fresh or dried.
concorde-pear.visual: a whole ripe slender pear, long tapering shape, green-yellow skin with brown speckles
concorde-pear.what: A slender, sweet pear with a hint of vanilla flavour.

facts: Condensed milk was patented in the United States in 1856.
Condensed milk is made by heating milk with sugar until much of the water has evaporated.
In Britain, sweetened condensed milk is the basis of many fudge and caramel recipes.
condensed-milk.visual: a small plain glass jar of thick, pale cream condensed milk, smooth and glossy, without a label
condensed-milk.what: Sweetened milk, thickened into a rich, sticky syrup.

facts: The Conference variety was bred in Britain and is widely grown there.
Pears ripen after picking, so they are often chosen firm and left to soften at home.
Pears are good poached in wine or spiced syrup, as the flesh holds its shape.
conference-pear.visual: a whole green-skinned pear with a long, narrow neck and small brown speckles
conference-pear.what: A long, juicy pear with a green, slightly brown skin.

facts: Conger eels live in the Atlantic and Mediterranean, often hiding in rocky holes on the seabed.
The name comes from the Latin 'conger', the word used for this sea eel.
Its firm, meaty flesh holds together well in slow-cooked dishes such as stews and soups.
conger-eel.visual: a whole raw conger eel with dark grey skin and a pale belly, lying in a loose curve
conger-eel.what: A large sea eel with firm flesh, good in hearty stews.

facts: Beetroot is a cultivated form of the wild sea beet, grown for its swollen root.
Beetroot gives its deep colour to borscht, the traditional Eastern European soup.
Sugar beet, a close relative, is grown mainly as a source of sugar.
cooked-beetroot.visual: a whole cooked beetroot, deep magenta and smooth, with the skin peeled away and glossy flesh visible
cooked-beetroot.what: Beets, already cooked and peeled, ready for salads.

facts: Ham is pork from the hind leg, often brined or salted, then cooked until tender.
Salting pork to preserve it has been practised for centuries, long before refrigeration was common.
cooked-ham.visual: a neat fan of thin, pale pink slices of cooked ham, lying flat
cooked-ham.what: Pork leg, salted in brine and cooked, sold sliced.

facts: Lobsters are large marine crustaceans with a long tail and two big claws.
The meat is found in the tail, the claws and the knuckles of the animal.
A lobster roll, a classic New England dish, is made with picked lobster meat in a split bun.
cooked-lobster-meat.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of picked cooked lobster meat in pale pinkish-white chunks
cooked-lobster-meat.what: Ready-picked meat from a cooked lobster, sweet and firm.

facts: Prawns are small shellfish found in seas and rivers around the world.
In Britain, prawns are a traditional filling for sandwiches and the classic prawn cocktail.
cooked-prawns.visual: a small heap of cooked prawns, curled pink shells on, lying loosely on the background
cooked-prawns.what: A small pink shellfish, already cooked and ready to eat.

facts: Cooking chocolate is designed to melt smoothly into cakes, sauces and icings.
Chocolate was made into a drink in Mesoamerica long before it became a solid bar.
cooking-chocolate.visual: one whole unwrapped dark chocolate bar, plain and glossy
cooking-chocolate.what: A plain bar of chocolate sold for baking and melting.

facts: Chorizo is a pork sausage flavoured with smoked paprika, widely eaten across Spain and Portugal.
Cooking chorizo is softer than dried chorizo, so it is often fried or simmered.
cooking-chorizo.visual: a whole raw chorizo sausage link, deep red colour and coarse texture visible, lying in a gentle curve
cooking-chorizo.what: A spiced pork sausage that releases red oil when cooked.

facts: Vegetable oils are pressed or extracted from seeds such as sunflower, rapeseed and soya.
Rapeseed plants are grown widely in Britain, and their seeds yield a pale, mild cooking oil.
Neutral oils have little flavour of their own, so they let the taste of the food come through.
cooking-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden oil with a plain metal cap
cooking-oil.what: A neutral oil used for frying, roasting and greasing.

facts: Cooking sprays use a propellant to push a fine, even mist of oil out of the container.
cooking-spray.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden cooking oil, simply capped
cooking-spray.what: A fine oil mist for lightly greasing non-stick pans.

facts: Cooking wine is a lower-priced wine intended for sauces and braises rather than drinking at the table.
Some cooking wines have salt added, so they should be used with care when seasoning a dish.
Wine has been used in cooking for centuries, adding acidity and depth to stews and sauces.
cooking-wine.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden-brown liquid, plain cap
cooking-wine.what: A cheap wine sold for use in cooking, not for drinking.

facts: Coppa is an Italian meat made from the neck or shoulder of the pig, salted and air-dried.
Its other name, capocollo, comes from Italian words meaning head and neck.
coppa.visual: one thin slice of coppa lying flat, rose-red pork with creamy white fat marbled through it
coppa.what: Air-dried pork neck, salted and spiced, sliced thin to eat.

facts: Coriander is also called cilantro in North America, and its leaves are the basis of this chutney.
coriander-chutney.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with smooth, bright green coriander chutney
coriander-chutney.what: A fresh, zesty green sauce made from coriander leaves.

facts: Coriander is the leaf and seed of the same plant, and its roots are used widely in Thai cooking.
Thai cooks pound coriander root with garlic and pepper to make curry ppastes.
coriander-root.visual: a small cluster of whole coriander roots, pale cream and brown, with thin hairy rootlets, lying loosely together
coriander-root.what: A knobbly, fragrant root from the coriander plant.

facts: Coriander seeds are the dried fruit of the coriander plant, whose fresh leaves are called cilantro in America.
They are a common spice in Indian curries and are also used in pickling and in some baking.
The plant has been grown for thousands of years around the Mediterranean and across Asia.
coriander-seeds.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dried coriander seeds, pale brown, round and ridged
coriander-seeds.what: Dried seeds from the coriander plant, nutty and citrusy.

facts: Corn-fed chickens are raised on a diet based on maize, which gives their skin a golden colour.
In France, the Bresse chicken is a famous example of a bird raised on corn and milk.
The yellow colour of the skin comes from plant pigments the bird absorbs from its feed.
corn-fed-chicken.visual: a whole raw corn-fed chicken, plump and trussed, its golden-yellow skin smooth and unbroken
corn-fed-chicken.what: A plump bird whose diet of maize gives it golden skin.

facts: In Britain it is known as cornflour, and in the United States the same starch is called cornstarch.
It is used to thicken custards, sauces and gravies, and to make light crisp coatings.
corn-flour.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine white corn flour, level and smooth
corn-flour.what: A fine white maize starch used for thickening sauces.

facts: Corn oil is made mainly from the germ, the small embryo part of the corn kernel.
It has a high smoke point, which makes it suitable for deep-frying.
Corn was first domesticated in Mexico from a wild grass called teosinte.
corn-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of golden corn oil
corn-oil.what: A neutral golden oil, good for frying and baking.

facts: Corn relish is a preserve of sweetcorn kernels cooked with vinegar, sugar and spices.
corn-relish.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, filled with chunky yellow and red relish
corn-relish.what: A chunky, sweet-sour relish of sweetcorn and peppers.

facts: Salsa means sauce in Spanish, and the word covers a huge range of fresh and cooked sauces.
Corn salsa is a popular side dish in Mexican and Tex-Mex cooking.
Sweetcorn is charred in a hot pan or over a flame to add a smoky flavour.
corn-salsa.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of chunky yellow sweetcorn kernels with flecks of green and red
corn-salsa.what: A chunky, tangy salsa of sweetcorn and fresh herbs.

facts: It was used in American recipes, such as pecan pie, for its smooth texture.
Corn syrup stops sugar from crystallising, which keeps candies and icings smooth.
corn-syrup.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of thick, clear golden syrup
corn-syrup.what: A thick, sweet syrup made from processed corn starch.

facts: Corn tortillas have been made in Mexico and Central America for a very long time.
The dough, called masa, is made from maize soaked in lime, then ground and pressed.
Corn tortillas have a stronger, earthier flavour than wheat flour tortillas.
corn-tortilla.visual: a small heap of round, pale golden corn tortillas, thin and flat, lying loose
corn-tortilla.what: A thin, soft flatbread of corn dough, used for tacos.

facts: It is often served with chilli, beans or barbecue in the United States.
Recipes vary, with some made sweet with sugar and others savoury with no sweetness.
cornbread.visual: a square of golden cornbread with a crumbly texture, one piece cut and lying flat on a plain background
cornbread.what: A golden, crumbly bread made with cornmeal.

facts: Cornflakes were first made in the United States as a breakfast cereal.
They are made by cooking maize, flaking it, and toasting the flakes until crisp.
Cornflakes are often served with milk, sugar or fruit, and are eaten in many countries.
cornflakes.visual: a small plain white bowl of golden, crisp cornflakes
cornflakes.what: Crisp toasted maize flakes, often eaten with milk.

facts: Cornflowers grow wild in cereal fields across Europe, and they were once a common sight among crops.
The petals are edible and have been used to colour drinks and decorate cakes.
cornflower-petals.visual: a small heap of loose, vivid blue cornflower petals, slightly crumpled
cornflower-petals.what: Blue petals from a meadow flower, used mostly for colour.

facts: Cornichons are small, young gherkins, picked and pickled before they grow large.
They are a classic accompaniment to pâté, charcuterie and cold meats in France.
They are traditionally pickled in vinegar, sometimes with tarragon added.
cornichons.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label holding tiny bright green gherkins in clear pickling liquid
cornichons.what: Tiny, crunchy French gherkins, pickled sour in vinegar.

facts: Brie-style cheeses ripen from the outside inwards as a white bloomy mould grows over the surface.
Brie takes its name from the Brie region of France, where soft cheese has been made for centuries.
cornish-brie.visual: a round of soft white-rinded cheese, one wedge cut away to show the pale creamy interior
cornish-brie.what: A soft, mild British cheese with a white bloomy rind.

facts: Pasties were traditionally a portable lunch for Cornish tin and copper miners.
The Cornish pasty has protected designation status in the EU, so only pasties made in Cornwall can use the name.
Traditional fillings are beef, potato, swede and onion, seasoned with salt and pepper.
cornish-pasty.visual: a whole baked Cornish pasty on a small plain white plate, golden crimped edge
cornish-pasty.what: A crimped pastry case filled with beef, potato and swede.

facts: Cornish Yarg is a fairly modern cheese, first made in Cornwall in the late twentieth century.
Its name is Gray spelled backwards, a nod to the family who created it.
cornish-yarg.visual: a whole round cheese wrapped in dried green nettle leaves, pale rind showing at one edge
cornish-yarg.what: A Cornish cheese wrapped in nettle leaves.

facts: Croakers are named for the drumming sounds some species make with their swim bladders.
Corvina is popular across Latin America, where it is often marinated in lime juice to make ceviche.
Its white flesh is firm and mild, so it holds its shape well when cooked or marinated.
corvina.visual: one whole raw corvina fish with silvery grey skin, lying flat on its side
corvina.what: A mild, firm-fleshed sea fish from the croaker family.

facts: In North America the same lettuce is usually called romaine.
Cos has long, upright leaves with a firm rib that holds its shape in salads.
cos-lettuce.visual: one whole upright cos lettuce, long crisp leaves in pale green with a pale yellow-green heart
cos-lettuce.what: A tall, crisp lettuce with sweet, sturdy leaves.

facts: Côte de boeuf is French for beef rib, and the cut is sold thick enough to share.
The bone is left in while the steak cooks, then the meat is carved off it.
The cut comes from the rib section of the cow, close to the ribeye.
cote-de-boeuf.visual: one thick raw bone-in beef rib steak, deep red meat, marbled, a curved rib bone at one edge, lying flat
cote-de-boeuf.what: A thick bone-in beef rib steak, sold to share.

facts: Cotija is named after the town of Cotija in Michoacán, Mexico, where it has long been made.
It is made from cow's milk, salted and aged, which dries it and makes it crumble.
Cotija is often compared to feta, though it is drier and more crumbly.
cotija.visual: a crumbly white block of cheese, one wedge cut away to show a fine, dry texture
cotija.what: A salty, crumbly Mexican cheese, often grated over dishes.

facts: Double Gloucester is a firm English cheese made in Gloucestershire for centuries.
The Cotswolds are a range of limestone hills in southern England.
Traditionally made from cow's milk, it has a close, firm texture when matured.
cotswold.visual: a wedge of pale golden cheese, speckled with green flecks
cotswold.what: A Double Gloucester cheese flecked with chives and onion.

facts: Cottage cheese was traditionally made at home from soured skimmed milk.
Curd size varies, from small and fine to large and chunky.
cottage-cheese.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of soft, lumpy white cottage cheese curds
cottage-cheese.what: Soft, fresh white curds made from skimmed or whole milk.

facts: Its name is said to come from its shape, which resembles a cottage with a small round roof on top.
Bakers shape the dough as a large base with a smaller round top, pressed together with a finger through the centre.
It is a traditional English bread that was once common in bakeries across the country.
cottage-loaf.visual: a whole cottage loaf with two stacked round tiers and a golden floury crust, on a plain background
cottage-loaf.what: A traditional English loaf with two stacked round tiers.

facts: Coulommiers takes its name from the town of Coulommiers, east of Paris.
It is made from cow's milk and ripened with a white mould, as brie is.
It is typically eaten at room temperature, when its interior has turned soft and creamy.
coulommiers.visual: a whole small round soft cheese with a pale white bloomy rind, on a plain background
coulommiers.what: A small, soft cheese with a white rind, like a mild brie.

facts: Courgettes are young marrows, picked before the fruit grows large.
In Britain the vegetable is called a courgette, while Americans call it zucchini, from the Italian word for small squash.
courgette.visual: one whole glossy dark green courgette lying on its side, pale stalk end visible
courgette.what: A slim, quick-cooking summer squash with glossy skin.

facts: Courgette flowers are eaten in Italian cooking, often stuffed with cheese and fried.
The flowers are fragile and wilt quickly, so they are best used the same day.
courgette-flowers.visual: a small bunch of bright yellow courgette flowers with open, trumpet-shaped petals
courgette-flowers.what: Bright yellow edible blossoms from the courgette plant.

facts: Couscous is made from semolina wheat rolled into tiny granules, a staple of North African cooking.
Traditionally it was hand-rolled and steamed above a pot of stew.
Couscous is widely eaten across Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia.
couscous.visual: a small heap of pale golden couscous grains, tiny round granules, loose and dry
couscous.what: Tiny steamed semolina grains that fluff up in minutes.

facts: Couverture is chocolate with a higher share of cocoa butter than ordinary chocolate, which helps it set glossy.
Chocolatiers temper couverture by heating and cooling it carefully, so it sets with a snap and shine.
Couverture is a French word meaning covering, because it was used to coat sweets and pastries.
couverture-chocolate.visual: a whole block of dark couverture chocolate with a glossy surface and a neatly broken corner
couverture-chocolate.what: Chocolate with extra cocoa butter for a glossy, fluid melt.

facts: Cowpeas were first domesticated in Africa and are now grown across the tropics and subtropics.
Black-eyed peas, a type of cowpea, are traditionally eaten on New Year's Day in the Southern United States.
Cowpeas belong to the legume family, which also includes beans, lentils and peas.
cowpeas.visual: a small heap of dried cowpeas, pale cream seeds with a dark eye mark, loose on the background
cowpeas.what: A small, hardy bean with a creamy skin and earthy taste.

facts: Cox's Orange Pippin is an English apple variety that was raised in Buckinghamshire.
Its flavour is aromatic and sweet-sharp, and its skin blushes red over yellow-orange.
It is valued mainly for eating fresh, though it can also be used in cooking.
cox-s-orange-pippin.visual: a whole red and gold apple with a green stalk, lying on its side
cox-s-orange-pippin.what: A crisp English dessert apple, sweet and sharp.

facts: Crab apples are the small-fruited wild relatives of the cultivated apple.
Their sharp flavour makes them ideal for making jelly and chutney.
Crab apples have grown wild across Europe, Asia and North America for thousands of years.
crab-apple.visual: a small heap of tiny round crab apples, red and yellow-green, some with short stalks still attached
crab-apple.what: A small, sour wild apple, often turned into jelly.

facts: Crab apples are small, sour apples that grow on wild trees across Europe and North America.
Crab apple jelly is made by boiling the fruit and straining the juice through muslin.
Crab apples contain a lot of natural pectin, which helps the jelly set.
crab-apple-jelly.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with clear rosy pink jelly
crab-apple-jelly.what: A clear, rosy jelly made from small, tart wild apples.

facts: Crab claws are the large pincers of crabs, and their meat is firm and sweet.
Crabs use their claws to catch food and to defend themselves, so the claws are strong and heavily shelled.
crab-claws.visual: a small heap of cooked crab claws, red-orange shells cracked open to show pale meat
crab-claws.what: Cooked, cracked claws from a crab, eaten with the fingers.

facts: Surimi is a paste of white fish that is washed, pounded and shaped, and it was developed in Japan.
Crab sticks are made from surimi, flavoured and coloured to resemble the flesh of crab legs.
Surimi has been made in Japan for centuries, and the paste is used in dishes such as kamaboko.
crab-sticks.visual: a small heap of crab sticks, white with bright orange-red bands, lying loose and slightly curved
crab-sticks.what: Pressed fish paste, shaped and coloured to look like crab.

facts: Cracked wheat is made by breaking whole wheat kernels into coarse pieces rather than grinding them fine.
It is a staple across the Middle East and North Africa, where it appears in pilafs, salads and porridges.
Cracked wheat cooks more quickly than whole grains because its pieces have a large surface area.
cracked-wheat.visual: a small heap of coarse pale golden cracked wheat grains piled loosely
cracked-wheat.what: Coarse wheat pieces, cracked rather than finely ground.

facts: Cranberries grow on low trailing vines in bogs, and are often harvested by flooding the fields.
Cranberry sauce is traditionally served with roast turkey, especially at Thanksgiving in the United States.
cranberry.visual: a small heap of fresh, glossy, bright red cranberries on a plain surface
cranberry.what: Strong, leafy tops of celery, good in soups and salads.

facts: Sourdough is leavened by a culture of wild yeasts and bacteria, rather than by commercial yeast alone.
Cranberries are native to North America, and they were eaten there long before European settlers arrived.
Walnuts have been grown for thousands of years and were valued across the ancient Mediterranean.
cranberry-and-walnut-sourdough.visual: one whole round sourdough loaf with a dusted floury crust and a scored top, on a plain background
cranberry-and-walnut-sourdough.what: Tangy sourdough studded with tart cranberries and walnuts.

facts: Cranberries are native to North America, where they have long been gathered in the wild.
At harvest, many growers flood the beds so the berries float to the surface.
Cranberries are very tart, so juice is usually sweetened for drinking.
cranberry-juice.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with bright red cranberry juice
cranberry-juice.what: A tart red juice pressed from cranberries.

facts: Cranberries are native to North America, and the sauce is a traditional dish for Thanksgiving in the United States.
Cranberries grow in bogs and are often harvested by flooding the fields.
cranberry-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of glossy, deep red cranberry sauce with a smooth surface
cranberry-sauce.what: A tart, sweet red sauce made from cranberries.

facts: Wensleydale is a cheese traditionally made in the Yorkshire Dales in northern England.
Cranberries grow on low trailing vines in bogs, mainly in North America.
cranberry-wensleydale.visual: a block of pale ivory cheese flecked with bright red cranberries, one wedge cut away
cranberry-wensleydale.what: A crumbly, creamy English cheese studded with cranberries.

facts: Crayfish live in freshwater rivers, streams and lakes across many parts of the world.
In Scandinavia they are often boiled whole with salt and dill during summer parties.
crayfish.visual: a whole raw crayfish, dark reddish-brown shell, claws folded close, lying on its side
crayfish.what: Small freshwater shellfish, similar to a tiny lobster.

facts: Cream cheese was first made commercially in the United States in the nineteenth century.
It is a key ingredient in cheesecake, bagel spreads and many frostings.
cream-cheese.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, pale cream cheese
cream-cheese.what: A soft, mild, unripened cheese, smooth and slightly tangy.

facts: Red velvet cake is traditionally paired with it, and its tang balances the sweet crumb.
Cream cheese is a soft, fresh cheese, which is why frostings made with it need careful chilling.
cream-cheese-frosting.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, pale cream frosting with a soft peak
cream-cheese-frosting.what: A smooth, tangy icing made from cream cheese and butter.

facts: Cream cheese developed in the United States in the late 1800s.
It is spread on bagels and also used in cheesecake, dips and frosting.
cream-cheese-spread.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, pale cream cheese spread with a lightly textured top
cream-cheese-spread.what: A soft, smooth cheese spread for bagels and sandwiches.

facts: Cream crackers are a British style of cracker, often served with cheese and chutney.
They are made from wheat flour and fat, and baked until dry and crisp.
cream-cracker.visual: a neat stack of plain, pale golden square crackers on a small plain white plate
cream-cracker.what: A plain, crisp, savoury cracker, good with cheese.

facts: This style of cream liqueur was developed in Ireland in the 1970s.
It is usually made with Irish whiskey, cream, sugar and flavourings such as cocoa or vanilla.
It is often poured over ice, stirred into coffee or used to flavour desserts and cakes.
cream-liqueur.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with thick creamy beige liquid
cream-liqueur.what: A sweet, creamy drink made from whiskey and cream.

facts: Cream of tartar is a by-product of winemaking, forming as crystals inside wine barrels.
Chemically it is potassium bitartrate, a salt of the acid naturally found in grapes.
Mixed with bicarbonate of soda, it makes baking powder, which helps cakes rise.
cream-of-tartar.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with fine white cream of tartar powder
cream-of-tartar.what: A tangy white powder that stiffens whisked egg whites.

facts: Cream sherry is a sweetened version of oloroso, a sherry from the Jerez region of southern Spain.
Sherry takes its English name from Jerez, the town in Andalusia where it is made.
Cream sherry is a popular ingredient in British trifle and Christmas cake.
cream-sherry.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of deep amber cream sherry
cream-sherry.what: A sweet, rich fortified wine, often used in trifle.

facts: Cream soda is a sweet, carbonated drink that is sold widely in North America.
Its flavour usually comes from vanilla, and it is often pale golden or clear.
It is often used as a mixer, or in ice cream floats.
cream-soda.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale golden cream soda, bubbles rising
cream-soda.what: A sweet, fizzy soft drink flavoured with vanilla.

facts: Creamed horseradish is a traditional partner for roast beef in Britain.
Grating the root breaks its cells, releasing the compounds that give horseradish its sharp heat.
creamed-horseradish.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale, creamy horseradish sauce with fine flecks of grated root
creamed-horseradish.what: Grated horseradish root blended into a creamy sauce.

facts: Crème de cassis is made by steeping blackcurrants in spirit and sweetening the result.
The French region of Burgundy, around Dijon, is known for blackcurrant liqueur.
Kir, a cocktail of white wine and cassis, is a classic French aperitif.
creme-de-cassis.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with deep red-purple liquid
creme-de-cassis.what: A dark, sweet blackcurrant liqueur used in kir.

facts: Crème de menthe is a French liqueur, and its name means cream of mint.
It is a classic ingredient in cocktails such as the Grasshopper.
It is often used in chocolate desserts, where its mint flavour pairs well with dark chocolate.
creme-de-menthe.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with bright emerald-green liqueur
creme-de-menthe.what: A sweet green mint liqueur, often used in desserts.

facts: Creme fraiche is a cultured cream, thickened and soured by bacteria, and widely used in French cooking.
Its high fat content helps it resist curdling when heated in sauces.
creme-fraiche.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, smooth, off-white creme fraiche with a softly rippled surface
creme-fraiche.what: Thick, lightly soured French cream that resists curdling.

facts: Crème pâtissière is a French pastry cream made from milk, sugar, egg yolks and flour.
Its name is French for pastry cream, and it is thickened on the stove before cooling.
It is often flavoured with vanilla and sets thicker as it chills.
creme-patissiere.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, smooth pale yellow pastry cream
creme-patissiere.what: A thick, eggy custard used to fill tarts and eclairs.

facts: Creole cooking developed in New Orleans, blending French, Spanish and African influences.
Creole seasoning often includes paprika, garlic, onion and oregano.
creole-seasoning.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine reddish-brown seasoning powder, speckled with herbs
creole-seasoning.what: A blend of herbs and spices used in New Orleans cooking.

facts: Crêpes are associated with Brittany in north-western France, where thin pancakes have long been made.
The French word crêpe comes from the Latin crispa, meaning curled or crisped.
Crêpe Suzette is a French dessert of crêpes in an orange butter sauce, often flamed at the table.
crepe.visual: one thin golden crepe folded into a quarter, on a small plain white plate
crepe.what: A thin French pancake, folded or rolled around fillings.

facts: The ridges come from a wavy blade that cuts the potato into a zigzag shape.
In Britain, chips are what Americans call French fries.
crinkle-cut-chips.visual: a small heap of raw crinkle-cut chips, pale yellow ridged potato sticks lying loosely together
crinkle-cut-chips.what: Ridged frozen potato chips, ready for the oven or fryer.

facts: The Swedish word knäckebröd means crack bread, referring to the snap it makes when broken.
Crispbread keeps for a long time because it is dried, which made it practical for storage.
crispbread.visual: one round crispbread, pale golden rye cracker with a light pattern of holes, lying flat
crispbread.what: A thin, dry, crisp cracker, traditionally made from rye.

facts: Peking duck is roasted until the skin is crisp, then served in thin pancakes with hoisin sauce.
Cantonese cooks roast ducks with aromatic spices and display them hanging in shop windows.
crispy-aromatic-duck.visual: a small plain white plate of shredded crispy roast duck, dark golden and glossy
crispy-aromatic-duck.what: Roast duck, shredded and crisped, often eaten in pancakes.

facts: Wings contain more skin and bone than breast meat, so they are often cooked at high heat to crisp the skin.
Baking wings with a little salt and oil helps the skin turn crisp and golden.
crispy-chicken-wings.visual: a few golden crispy baked chicken wing pieces, served plainly on a small plain white plate
crispy-chicken-wings.what: Seasoned wings, oven-baked until the skin is crisp.

facts: Fried onion is a common topping for salads, curries and casseroles.
In South Asian cooking, crisp fried onions are known as birista.
Onions have been eaten for thousands of years, and were grown in ancient Egypt.
crispy-fried-onions.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of golden crispy fried onion pieces
crispy-fried-onions.what: Thin onion slices fried until golden and crisp.

facts: Seaweed has been eaten in Japan, Korea and China for centuries, often as thin dried sheets.
Nori, a red seaweed used to wrap sushi, is a common base for crisp snacks.
Seaweed snacks are usually cut into thin sheets, seasoned and dried until crisp.
crispy-seaweed-crisps.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with thin, crisp dark green seaweed crisps
crispy-seaweed-crisps.what: Light, salty crisps made from thin sheets of seaweed.

facts: Crocodile meat is eaten in parts of Australia, Southeast Asia and Africa.
Crocodiles are farmed in several countries for their skins and meat.
crocodile-tail.visual: a single raw boneless cut of pale white crocodile tail meat with a firm texture, lying on the plain background
crocodile-tail.what: Mild, firm white meat from a large reptile.

facts: Croissant is French for crescent, which is the shape of the pastry.
Croissants are made by folding cold butter into dough many times to create layers.
croissant.visual: a single whole golden-brown croissant, crescent-shaped, with visible flaky layers, lying on its side
croissant.what: A buttery, flaky crescent of laminated yeasted dough.

facts: Crottin is an AOC cheese made from goat's milk in the Sancerre area of the Loire.
Its name, crottin, is an old French word for a small pile of animal droppings.
crottin-de-chavignol.visual: one small round goat's cheese, pale wrinkled white rind, sitting on its base
crottin-de-chavignol.what: A small goat's cheese from the Loire valley, France.

facts: The word crouton comes from the French croûte, meaning a crust.
Croutons are a traditional way to use up stale bread by toasting or frying it.
They are often added to soups and Caesar salads.
croutons.visual: a small heap of golden, crisp bread croutons, cubed and toasted
croutons.what: Small cubes of toasted bread, crisp and golden.

facts: Crowdie is a traditional Scottish cheese made from skimmed milk curds.
Cream crowdie is a richer version, made by mixing cream into the soft curd.
Crowdie is a fresh cheese, eaten soon after it is made rather than aged.
crowdie.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale, crumbly white cheese, moist and irregular in texture
crowdie.what: A fresh, tangy Scottish cheese with a crumbly texture.

facts: Winter squashes have a hard skin that lets them be stored for months after harvest.
Its dense flesh holds its shape when roasted and works well in soups and purées.
crown-prince-squash.visual: one whole blue-grey squash with a knobbly skin, lying on its side on a plain background
crown-prince-squash.what: A blue-grey winter squash with dense, sweet orange flesh.

facts: Crumpets are cooked on one side only, which creates their characteristic holes.
Crumpet batter is traditionally made from flour, water, milk and yeast.
Crumpets are a popular teatime food in Britain, toasted and served with butter.
crumpet.visual: one toasted crumpet on a plain white plate, golden top with a pocked, open-holed surface
crumpet.what: A small, spongy, pocked round for soaking up butter.

facts: Crumpets are a close relative, made from a yeasted batter, which is what gives them their holes.
Pikelets are a common treat in Australia and New Zealand, often spread with butter and jam.
Scotch pancakes, also called drop scones, are a close cousin of the pikelet.
crumpet-style-pikelets.visual: a neat stack of three round pikelets on a plain white plate, small bubbles visible on the golden top surface
crumpet-style-pikelets.what: Small thin griddle cakes, often toasted and buttered.

facts: Peanuts are native to South America and are botanically legumes, not true nuts.
Crunchy varieties are made by leaving pieces of roasted nut in the paste.
crunchy-peanut-butter.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, pale brown peanut butter with visible chopped nut pieces
crunchy-peanut-butter.what: A spread of ground peanuts with bits of roasted nut.

facts: Eton mess, a British dessert, combines broken meringue with whipped cream and fresh fruit.
Crushed meringue is sometimes used as a crunchy topping for ice cream and fruit.
crushed-meringue.visual: a small heap of crisp, broken white meringue pieces, pale and airy
crushed-meringue.what: Crunchy broken shards of baked egg white and sugar.

facts: Ginger is the rhizome of a tropical plant that originated in Asia.
Preserving ginger in sugar was a traditional way to keep it for long periods.
It is popular in Christmas baking, such as ginger cake and biscuits.
crystallised-ginger.visual: a small heap of sugar-coated ginger pieces, pale golden with a glittering sugar crust
crystallised-ginger.what: Chewy ginger pieces simmered in sugar until candied.

facts: Cubanelle peppers are common in Cuban and Italian-American cooking.
They have thin walls, so they soften quickly when fried.
They have little or no heat, unlike many chilli peppers.
cubanelle-pepper.visual: a whole long, thin, yellow-green pepper, its skin slightly wrinkled
cubanelle-pepper.what: A long, thin, mild pepper that is good for frying.

facts: Cube sugar is made by moistening granulated sugar, pressing it into moulds and drying it.
Sugar cubes are often served with tea and coffee, especially in Britain and Europe.
cube-sugar.visual: a small heap of white sugar cubes, sharp-edged and evenly sized on a plain background
cube-sugar.what: Compressed white cubes of sugar, for tea and coffee.

facts: Cubeb is the dried unripe fruit of a climbing plant native to Indonesia.
It was traded along Asian and Middle Eastern routes and used in medieval European cooking.
cubeb-pepper.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dried, wrinkled, dark grey-brown berries, each with a short stalk
cubeb-pepper.what: A dried, peppery berry with a woody, allspice-like taste.

facts: Cucamelons come from Mexico and Central America, where they are known as sandiitas or mouse melons.
Cucamelons belong to the gourd family, the same family as cucumbers and melons, and are often pickled.
cucamelon.visual: a small heap of tiny green cucamelons, each about the size of a grape, with glossy striped skin
cucamelon.what: A tiny cucumber-like fruit with a sharp, lemony taste.

facts: Cucumbers belong to the gourd family and are thought to have originated in South Asia.
They have been cultivated for thousands of years, and were grown in ancient Egypt.
Most cucumbers are eaten raw in salads, but they are also pickled and used in soups.
cucumber.visual: a whole fresh green cucumber, long and smooth-skinned, lying on the background
cucumber.what: A cool, crisp, watery fruit that is eaten as a vegetable.

facts: Kimchi is a Korean family of salted, seasoned vegetables that are fermented.
Oi-kimchi, made from cucumbers, is a summer dish in Korea.
Traditionally, kimchi was stored in earthenware jars so it could ferment slowly.
cucumber-kimchi.visual: a small plain white bowl of cucumber chunks coated in red chilli seasoning
cucumber-kimchi.what: Crisp, quick-fermented Korean cucumbers with chilli.

facts: Culantro is native to tropical America and is widely used in Caribbean and Latin American cooking.
Its flavour resembles coriander but is more intense.
In Vietnam it is called ngò gai and is used in soups and salads.
culantro.visual: a small bunch of culantro, long narrow spiky-edged green leaves on thin pale stems
culantro.what: A strong, spiky-leaved herb, also called sawtooth coriander.

facts: Culatello comes from the Parma area of northern Italy and is made from the rear leg of the pig.
It is traditionally wrapped in pig's bladder and aged in damp cellars in the Po valley.
It is usually eaten thinly sliced, as an antipasto, and is valued for its soft texture.
culatello.visual: one whole round culatello, a pale pink cured pork ham with a thin dark rind, uncut
culatello.what: A soft, aged ham made from the heart of a pig's leg.

facts: Cultured butter is made by adding live cultures to cream before churning, which gives it a tang.
Butter has been churned from cream for thousands of years in many parts of the world.
Making butter from soured cream was a traditional method in parts of Northern Europe.
cultured-butter.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale yellow butter, smooth and soft-looking
cultured-butter.what: Tangy butter made from soured cream, pale and creamy.

facts: It is a traditional British cold sauce, often served with cured ham and pork.
It is usually made from port, redcurrant jelly, orange zest and juice, and sometimes mustard.
Redcurrant jelly gives the sauce its tart, sweet flavour and its deep red colour.
cumberland-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with glossy, deep ruby-red sauce, smooth and set
cumberland-sauce.what: A fruity sauce of port, orange and redcurrant for ham.

facts: Cumberland sausage comes from Cumbria in north-west England and is traditionally made from coarsely minced pork.
Its generous seasoning of black pepper gives it a warm, peppery flavour typical of the region.
cumberland-sausage.visual: one coiled raw Cumberland sausage, a long pale pink pork coil lying flat on the background
cumberland-sausage.what: A peppery pork sausage sold in a tight, long coil.

facts: Cumin comes from a small plant in the parsley family, and it is grown in many hot, dry regions.
Cumin seeds are often toasted in a dry pan or fried in oil to bring out their aroma.
Cumin is a key spice in Indian, Mexican and Middle Eastern cooking.
cumin-seeds.visual: a small heap of slender, ridged, greenish-brown cumin seeds
cumin-seeds.what: Small, ridged seeds with a warm, earthy flavour.

facts: Salt has been used to preserve meat for thousands of years, long before refrigeration.
The pink colour is added so the salt is not mistaken for ordinary table salt.
curing-salt.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with pink crystalline salt
curing-salt.what: Pink salt with nitrite, used for charcuterie and bacon.

facts: Frisée is widely used in French bistro salads such as salade lyonnaise, often with bacon lardons.
It grows best in cool weather, and is often blanched by covering the plant to make the inner leaves paler.
curly-endive.visual: a whole head of curly endive, frilly pale green outer leaves with a paler centre
curly-endive.what: A frilly, bitter salad leaf with pale, crisp hearts.

facts: Kale was a common food in Europe long before potatoes arrived there.
Crisp kale chips are made by baking the leaves at a low heat until they are brittle.
curly-kale.visual: a bunch of curly kale with dark green ruffled leaves and thin pale stems
curly-kale.what: A frilly, hardy green leaf from the cabbage family.

facts: Parsley is a plant native to the Mediterranean region, grown there for centuries.
Parsley butter and stuffings are classic British uses for the herb.
curly-parsley.visual: a small bunch of bright green curly parsley sprigs, fresh and frilly, lying flat on the background
curly-parsley.what: A frilly green herb with a fresh, mild flavour.

facts: Dried currants are made from a small seedless grape variety, not from the red or black currant berry.
The name currant comes from Corinth, the Greek region linked to the grapes they were originally dried from.
They are a traditional ingredient in British Eccles cakes and Christmas pudding.
currant.visual: a small heap of dark dried currants on a plain background
currant.what: A small, tart dried grape, often used in baking.

facts: Curry flavours reached Britain through trade and British rule in India.
Each cook's blend of curry powder is different, so the flavour varies from one dish to another.
curried-egg.visual: two halves of a boiled egg coated in pale yellow curry sauce, in a small plain white bowl
curried-egg.what: A boiled egg in a mild curry mayonnaise.

facts: Mango is a tropical stone fruit, closely related to the cashew and the pistachio.
Mango is native to South Asia and has been cultivated there for a very long time.
Chutneys and fruit-based sauces are traditional alongside curries in South Asian meals.
curried-mango-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth golden-orange sauce, glossy and thick
curried-mango-sauce.what: A mild, fruity dip made from mango and curry spices.

facts: Instant noodles were first developed in Japan in the mid twentieth century.
curry-flavour-instant-noodles.visual: a small plain white bowl of cooked curry-flavoured instant noodles, glossy and golden
curry-flavour-instant-noodles.what: Quick noodles with a spiced, curry-flavoured seasoning.

facts: Curry leaves come from a tree native to India and Sri Lanka.
Cooks in southern India often fry curry leaves in hot oil at the start of a dish.
The leaves are not the same as curry powder, which is a blend of spices.
curry-leaf-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dark green paste, thick and slightly glossy
curry-leaf-paste.what: A thick green paste of curry leaves and spices.

facts: Curry leaves come from the curry tree, Murraya koenigii, which is native to India and Sri Lanka.
They are a key flavour in South Indian cooking, often fried in oil at the start of a dish.
curry-leaves.visual: a small bunch of bright green curry leaves on thin stalks, glossy oval leaflets
curry-leaves.what: Fragrant leaves that sizzle in hot oil for tempering.

facts: The word curry is thought to come from the Tamil word kari, meaning sauce or relish.
Curry powder is widely used in British cooking, from chicken curries to coronation chicken.
curry-powder.visual: A small plain white ceramic bowl of fine golden-brown curry powder, smooth and evenly mixed.
curry-powder.what: A mild, all-purpose spice blend of turmeric and cumin.

facts: Curry sauce became popular in Britain through Indian restaurants and takeaways in the twentieth century.
It is based on Indian spice cooking, adapted over time to suit British tastes.
In British takeaways, curry sauce is often poured over chips or rice.
curry-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, mild golden-orange curry sauce, thick and glossy
curry-sauce.what: A mild, smooth gravy of spices, onion and tomato.

facts: Curtido is a cabbage slaw from El Salvador, traditionally served with pupusas, thick stuffed corn tortillas.
The cabbage is salted and then pickled in vinegar for a short time, often with onion and oregano.
Lightly fermented cabbage is a shared tradition, and kimchi from Korea is perhaps the best-known example.
curtido.visual: a small plain white bowl of finely shredded pale green cabbage slaw, loosely packed
curtido.what: A tangy Salvadoran slaw of lightly fermented cabbage.

facts: Custard is made by gently heating milk or cream with egg yolks, which thickens it.
Custard powder, a cornflour-based mix, is a quicker alternative to making it from eggs.
It is traditionally served warm over sponge puddings, crumbles and other British desserts.
custard.visual: a small plain white bowl of smooth pale yellow custard, glossy and thick
custard.what: A thick, sweet sauce of milk, sugar and egg yolk.

facts: Cherimoya, one member of the group, comes from the high valleys of the Andes.
The soft flesh is eaten with a spoon, while the skin and large black seeds are discarded.
custard-apple.visual: a whole custard apple with knobbly green segmented skin, lying on its side
custard-apple.what: A knobbly tropical fruit with creamy white flesh.

facts: Custard creams are British biscuits, made of two thin biscuits joined by a sweet vanilla filling.
custard-creams.visual: a small stack of round pale biscuits on a plain white plate, smooth and cream-coloured
custard-creams.what: Round biscuits with a soft vanilla cream filling.

facts: Custard powder was developed in England in the 19th century as a quick way to make custard.
It is mainly cornflour and flavouring, mixed with milk and heated until it thickens.
custard-powder.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled to the top with fine pale yellow powder, lid removed
custard-powder.what: Yellow vanilla-flavour powder for making custard.

facts: Cuttlefish ink is used in Mediterranean cooking, notably in risotto and pasta, to colour them black.
Cuttlefish is popular in Mediterranean and East Asian cooking, grilled, stewed or fried.
cuttlefish.visual: one whole raw cuttlefish, pale mottled skin, flat fins along its soft body
cuttlefish.what: A sea creature related to squid, with firm, sweet flesh.

facts: Black flake salt is used as a finishing salt, sprinkled over food just before serving.
Food-grade charcoal is sometimes added to foods simply to colour them black.
cyprus-black-flake-salt.visual: a small heap of dark grey-black pyramid-shaped salt flakes, glossy and loose
cyprus-black-flake-salt.what: Dark pyramid-shaped salt flakes, coloured with charcoal.

facts: The dab is a common flatfish found around the coasts of northern Europe.
It is often sold whole and is cooked on the bone.
dab.visual: one whole raw dab, flat body with brownish skin and pale underside, lying flat on a plain background
dab.what: A small, flat sea fish, a relative of the plaice.

facts: Daikon is a large white radish from East Asia, eaten raw, pickled or cooked.
Its name comes from Japanese words meaning big root.
Daikon is used in Japanese pickles such as takuan and in many soups and stews.
daikon.visual: one whole large white daikon radish, long, tapering and smooth-skinned, lying on its side
daikon.what: A large, mild white radish, pickled or simmered.

facts: Damsons are a type of plum, and the fruit is especially popular in Britain for jam and gin.
Damsons are cooked down with sugar to make jams, fruit cheeses and sauces.
damson.visual: a small heap of whole damsons, oval dark purple-blue fruit with a dusty bloom
damson.what: A small, tart, dark purple plum grown in Britain and Europe.

facts: Damsons are small, oval plums with a sharp flavour and a dark blue-purple skin.
Damson trees have long grown in Britain, and the fruit was often turned into jam, jelly or a thick preserve.
damson-jam.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with dark purplish-red damson jam
damson-jam.what: Dark, tart jam made from small, sharp damson plums.

facts: The name refers to the carrying poles that street vendors used to sell the noodles.
The dish comes from Sichuan province in south-west China.
The sauce is typically made with sesame paste, chilli oil and Sichuan peppercorns.
dan-dan-noodles.visual: a small plain white bowl of thin yellow noodles coated in a glossy red chilli sauce
dan-dan-noodles.what: Thin wheat noodles in a spicy, nutty chilli sauce.

facts: It has been sold in Britain for well over a century, and is still widely found in shops.
Its name comes from its two main flavourings, burdock root and the dandelion plant.
Burdock is a plant whose root is eaten in Japan as gobo.
dandelion-and-burdock.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale amber, slightly cloudy, fizzy drink with a few bubbles at the surface
dandelion-and-burdock.what: An old British fizzy drink flavoured with roots and herbs.

facts: The name comes from the French dent de lion, meaning lion's tooth, after the shape of the leaves.
Young leaves are eaten raw in salads, while older leaves are often wilted in a hot pan.
dandelion-leaves.visual: a small bunch of fresh dandelion leaves, deeply toothed bright green leaves on pale stems
dandelion-leaves.what: Bitter, jagged green leaves of the common dandelion plant.

facts: Dangmyeon is a Korean noodle and the key ingredient in japchae, a stir-fried noodle dish.
They turn clear when cooked and absorb sauce well, so they suit stir-fries and soups.
dangmyeon.visual: a small loose heap of dried, translucent grey-white glass noodles
dangmyeon.what: Springy, translucent noodles made from sweet potato starch.

facts: Its blue veins come from Penicillium mould, which grows through the cheese during ripening.
danish-blue.visual: a wedge of crumbly white cheese with blue-green veins, the cut face showing, lying directly on the background
danish-blue.what: A sharp, salty blue cheese from Denmark that crumbles well.

facts: Danish pastry is said to have been introduced to Denmark by Viennese bakers in the nineteenth century.
In Denmark the pastry is called wienerbrød, meaning Viennese bread.
Its layers come from folding cold butter into dough many times, a method known as laminating.
danish-pastry.visual: a single golden pastry swirl with flaky layers and a glossy finish, on a plain white plate
danish-pastry.what: A sweet, buttery pastry, often with jam or custard.

facts: Rugbrød is a dense rye bread from Denmark, often made with sourdough.
Danish open sandwiches, called smørrebrød, are traditionally built on slices of rye bread.
Rye bread is dense because rye flour does not rise as strongly as wheat flour.
danish-rye-bread.visual: one thick slice of dark, dense rye bread lying flat, seeds visible across the crust
danish-rye-bread.what: A dark, dense, seeded loaf used for open sandwiches.

facts: Dark chocolate is made from roasted, ground cacao beans mixed with sugar, and sometimes cocoa butter.
Cacao trees come from the Americas, where the beans were used long before chocolate reached Europe.
dark-chocolate.visual: a snapped piece of dark chocolate with a glossy surface and a clean broken edge
dark-chocolate.what: Bittersweet chocolate with a high share of cocoa solids.

facts: Cocoa beans grow in pods on the cacao tree, which is native to the tropical Americas.
Dark chocolate is made from cocoa mass with sugar and often cocoa butter, and has a bitter-sweet taste.
Chocolate chips are shaped to hold their form when baked, so they stay as distinct pieces in cookies.
dark-chocolate-chips.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of small, glossy dark chocolate chips
dark-chocolate-chips.what: Small, glossy drops of dark cocoa chocolate for baking.

facts: Dark liquid seasoning is typically made from soy or vegetable protein.
Savoury liquid seasonings like this are widely used across the Caribbean, West Africa and Asia.
dark-liquid-seasoning.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of dark brown liquid, cap on
dark-liquid-seasoning.what: A dark, salty sauce for adding savoury depth to dishes.

facts: Its moist texture comes from the syrup that clings to its crystals.
Muscovado is traditionally produced in sugar-growing regions such as Mauritius, Barbados and the Philippines.
dark-muscovado-sugar.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dark brown, moist, slightly clumped muscovado sugar
dark-muscovado-sugar.what: A rich, moist brown sugar with a deep treacle flavour.

facts: Rum is distilled from sugar cane products such as molasses or fresh cane juice.
Dark rum is aged, often in oak barrels, which gives it colour and a deeper flavour.
The Caribbean, particularly Jamaica and Barbados, has a long tradition of rum production.
dark-rum.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with deep amber-brown rum
dark-rum.what: A molasses-based spirit, richer and darker than white rum.

facts: Dark soft brown sugar keeps some molasses in the crystals, which gives it its moisture and flavour.
Brown sugars are traditionally used in gingerbread and sticky toffee puddings.
dark-soft-brown-sugar.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of damp, dark brown soft sugar, lightly heaped
dark-soft-brown-sugar.what: Moist brown sugar with a deep molasses flavour.

facts: Dark soy sauce is made from soybeans and wheat that have been fermented for several months.
It was developed in China, where it is used to darken and glaze braised meat.
Its colour comes from longer fermentation and, in some brands, added caramel.
dark-soy-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, dark brown soy sauce with a glossy surface
dark-soy-sauce.what: A thick, dark soy sauce used to colour braises.

facts: Dashi is a basic Japanese stock, traditionally made by steeping dried bonito flakes and kelp in water.
Dashi powder is a concentrated, dried version of the stock, sold so it dissolves quickly in hot water.
The word dashi simply means stock or broth in Japanese, and the stock is the base of many dishes.
dashi-powder.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, filled with pale brown fine granules
dashi-powder.what: Instant granules that make a quick Japanese stock.

facts: Its main flavour comes from kombu, a dried kelp, and katsuobushi, dried smoked bonito.
Kombu is steeped in water and katsuobushi is added off the heat, so the broth stays clear.
dashi-stock.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale golden clear dashi stock
dashi-stock.what: A light broth of kelp and dried bonito flakes.

facts: Date sugar is made by drying dates and grinding them into a granular powder.
Unlike white sugar, date sugar keeps the flavour of the whole fruit.
date-sugar.visual: A small plain white ceramic bowl of coarse, dark brown date sugar with small flecks of dried fruit.
date-sugar.what: Ground dried dates, coarse, fruity and slow to dissolve.

facts: Date syrup has been made in the Middle East for centuries, by boiling down ripe dates.
Silan is the Hebrew name for date syrup, and it is widely used in Israeli cooking.
date-syrup.visual: a plain glass bottle without a label, filled with dark amber syrup
date-syrup.what: A thick, dark syrup made from pressed, boiled dates.

facts: Date vinegar is made by fermenting ripe dates, a fruit long grown across the Middle East.
Date palms have been cultivated in the Middle East for thousands of years.
date-vinegar.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of dark amber vinegar, with a plain cork stopper
date-vinegar.what: A mellow vinegar made from fermented dates.

facts: Datterino is Italian for little date, a name that refers to the tomato's elongated shape.
Small tomatoes like these are often roasted or eaten raw in salads.
datterini-tomato.visual: a small bunch of bright red, elongated tomatoes still attached to a short green stem
datterini-tomato.what: A small, elongated tomato with a very sweet flavour.

facts: Decaffeination removes most of the caffeine from green coffee beans before they are roasted.
Common methods include water processing, solvent methods and carbon dioxide.
Coffee is thought to have originated in Ethiopia before it spread to Arabia and then Europe.
decaf-coffee.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with dark, freshly brewed coffee
decaf-coffee.what: Coffee with its caffeine removed, for a mellow flavour.

facts: Frozen pizzas were developed so that the dish could be stored and cooked at home.
Deep pan bases are baked in a tin, which gives a softer, thicker crust than a thin base.
deep-pan-frozen-pizza.visual: a whole round thick-crust pizza with a soft golden edge and an even reddish topping, served on a plain white plate
deep-pan-frozen-pizza.what: A thick, bready frozen pizza with a soft crust.

facts: Deep pan pizza uses a thick dough pressed into a deep tin, which gives a soft interior.
Pizza as a dish is closely associated with Naples, where topped flatbreads have long been baked.
The dough is usually left to rise before it is pressed into the tin.
deep-pan-pizza-base.visual: one thick round of raw, pale pizza dough, soft and slightly risen at the edge, lying flat
deep-pan-pizza-base.what: A thick, doughy pizza base with a crisp golden bottom.

facts: Deglet Noor is often translated from Arabic as 'date of light'.
The variety is grown mainly in Algeria, Tunisia and California, and is prized for its firm flesh.
Dates have been cultivated in the Middle East and North Africa for thousands of years.
deglet-noor-date.visual: one whole date with a glossy amber-brown skin, lying on its side
deglet-noor-date.what: A firm, drier variety of date with a mild, honeyed taste.

facts: Delicata is also called the sweet potato squash because of its sweet, creamy flesh.
Its skin is thin enough to eat once cooked, so the squash does not need peeling.
Delicata is a type of winter squash, harvested in autumn and stored for use through winter.
delicata-squash.visual: one whole delicata squash, a small oblong shape with cream-coloured skin and green stripes, on a plain background
delicata-squash.what: A small striped winter squash with thin, edible skin.

facts: It is partly refined, so it keeps some molasses, which gives its golden colour.
British bakers often sprinkle demerara on crumbles and use it in flapjacks.
demerara-sugar.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with large golden-brown sugar crystals
demerara-sugar.what: Golden, coarse sugar crystals with a light toffee flavour.

facts: A baguette is a long, thin French loaf, and its name is French for a stick or wand.
Its crisp crust and light, airy crumb make it a classic base for filled sandwiches in France.
demi-baguette.visual: one whole short golden-brown baguette loaf, crisp crust with a few diagonal slashes, lying directly on the background
demi-baguette.what: A short, crisp French-style loaf, sized for one sandwich.

facts: Demi-glace is one of the classical French sauces, traditionally made by combining brown stock with espagnole.
The name demi-glace is French for half glaze, and the sauce is used to finish meat dishes.
demi-glace.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of glossy, dark brown demi-glace, thick and shiny
demi-glace.what: A glossy, rich brown sauce of reduced meat stock.

facts: Desiccated coconut is made by drying and finely shredding the white flesh of mature coconuts.
It is widely used in British cakes and biscuits, and in curries across South Asia.
The coconut palm is grown across tropical coastal regions, and its fruit is dried commercially for export.
desiccated-coconut.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with fine, pale white dried coconut shreds
desiccated-coconut.what: Finely shredded dried coconut flesh, sweet and crumbly.

facts: Desiree is a Dutch potato variety, bred in the Netherlands in the twentieth century.
It has a red skin and pale yellow flesh, and is grown in Britain and across Europe.
Cooks use it for mash, roast potatoes and chips.
desiree-potato.visual: one whole raw potato, smooth pinkish-red skin, oval and firm, lying on its side
desiree-potato.what: A red-skinned potato that is good for mashing or roasting.

facts: Devilled refers to a dish seasoned with hot spices, such as mustard and cayenne pepper.
Halved eggs are filled by mashing the cooked yolks with mayonnaise or mustard, then piping them back in.
devilled-egg.visual: two halved boiled eggs, cut side up, each filled with a piped pale yellow yolk filling, on a small plain white plate
devilled-egg.what: Boiled egg halves with a creamy, spiced yolk filling.

facts: Dhansak is a dish of the Parsi community of western India, shaped by Persian cooking traditions.
Traditionally the sauce is made from dal, a cooked lentil dish, and is served with rice.
Its sweet and sour balance often comes from jaggery and tamarind.
dhansak-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, dark orange-brown sauce with a smooth texture
dhansak-sauce.what: A sweet and sour spiced lentil sauce from Parsi cooking.

facts: Stewing beef is usually cut from tougher muscles, which become tender with long, slow cooking.
Beef stews appear in many cuisines, including French boeuf bourguignon, braised in red wine.
Cattle were domesticated in the Near East thousands of years ago.
diced-beef.visual: a small heap of raw, deep red beef cubes, a little white fat showing at the edges
diced-beef.what: Cubes of beef from the shoulder or shin, for stews.

facts: Lamb has been eaten across the Middle East and Mediterranean for thousands of years.
Tagine is named after the clay pot it is cooked in, and is a slow-cooked stew popular in Morocco.
diced-lamb.visual: a small heap of raw diced lamb, bright red cubes with creamy white fat edges
diced-lamb.what: Small cubes of lamb, good for kebabs, stews and curries.

facts: Shoulder is a well-worked muscle with fat running through it, so it suits slow cooking.
Pork has been eaten across Europe and Asia for thousands of years.
diced-pork.visual: a small heap of raw diced pork, pink cubes with some pale fat visible, lying loosely together
diced-pork.what: Cubes of pork shoulder, for stews, curries and kebabs.

facts: They are made with wholemeal flour and are a staple of British tea time.
digestive-biscuits.visual: a small loose heap of round, pale golden digestive biscuits, speckled, lying on the background
digestive-biscuits.what: Crumbly wheaty biscuits, often used as cheesecake bases.

facts: Dijon mustard takes its name from the city of Dijon in Burgundy, eastern France.
It is a staple of French vinaigrettes and mustard sauces.
dijon-mustard.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label holding smooth, pale brown mustard paste
dijon-mustard.what: A smooth, sharp mustard from the French city of Dijon.

facts: Dill seeds and fronds flavour the brine, and garlic is often added for extra bite.
dill-pickles.visual: three whole green pickled cucumbers with bumpy skin and a slight sheen, lying on the background
dill-pickles.what: Cucumbers pickled in brine with dill and garlic.

facts: Dill is an herb of the carrot family, related to parsley, fennel and caraway.
Dill seeds are added to brines for pickled cucumbers and other vegetables.
Scandinavian breads, including rye loaves, often include dill seed for flavour.
dill-seeds.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale brown, oval, ridged seeds
dill-seeds.what: Small, pungent seeds of the dill plant, used for pickling.

facts: It ripens in late summer, earlier than most apples.
Apples belong to the rose family, and the cultivated apple is thought to come from Central Asia.
Early apple varieties are picked before the main autumn harvest begins.
discovery-apple.visual: a whole red-flushed apple with pale yellow-green patches and its stalk still attached, on a plain background
discovery-apple.what: A red apple, sweet and fresh, with a hint of strawberry.

facts: Distilled white vinegar is made from grain alcohol that is fermented into acetic acid and then distilled clear.
Vinegar has been used to preserve food since ancient times, and remains central to pickling.
The word vinegar comes from the French vin aigre, meaning sour wine.
distilled-white-vinegar.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with pale, clear liquid
distilled-white-vinegar.what: A clear, sharp vinegar made from distilled grain alcohol.

facts: Ditalini means little thimbles in Italian, a name that refers to its tiny tube shape.
It is traditionally added to minestrone and to pasta e fagioli, a bean and pasta soup.
Like most dried Italian pasta, ditalini is made from durum wheat semolina.
ditalini.visual: a small heap of dried ditalini pasta, short pale tubes with open ends, on a plain background
ditalini.what: Very small short tube pasta, used in soups and bakes.

facts: Diver scallops are gathered by hand by divers rather than dredged from the seabed.
Scallops are eaten in many cuisines, from Japan to the Mediterranean.
diver-scallops.visual: one whole raw scallop in its ridged fan-shaped shell, the plump cream-white meat visible
diver-scallops.what: A large sea scallop, picked by divers for its sweet meat.

facts: Doenjang is made by fermenting dried soybean blocks, then ageing them in brine.
It has been a staple of Korean cooking for many centuries.
It is often stirred into soups and stews, such as doenjang-jjigae.
doenjang.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dark brown thick soybean paste with a smooth surface
doenjang.what: A thick, salty Korean paste made from fermented soybeans.

facts: Dopiaza is often said to mean two onions, from Persian words for two and onion.
In many recipes the onions are added in two stages, so that some are browned and some stay soft.
The dish is widely served in Indian restaurants in Britain and across the Indian subcontinent.
dopiaza-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, reddish-brown onion curry sauce, smooth and glossy
dopiaza-sauce.what: An onion-based medium curry sauce from Indian kitchens.

facts: Dorset Blue Vinney is a traditional West Country cheese from Dorset, England.
The name is thought to come from an old English word for mould, which fits its blue veining.
It was traditionally made from skimmed milk, which was left over once the cream had been taken off.
dorset-blue-vinney.visual: a block of pale white cheese with blue-green veining, one wedge cut and set beside it on a plain background
dorset-blue-vinney.what: A hard, crumbly English blue cheese from skimmed milk.

facts: Dosas originated in South India and are made from a batter of fermented rice and lentils.
The batter ferments overnight, which gives dosas their slightly sour taste and light texture.
Dosas are often served with sambar, a spiced lentil stew, and coconut chutney.
dosa.visual: a thin golden dosa folded in half, lying flat on a plain white plate
dosa.what: A thin, crisp South Indian pancake of fermented batter.

facts: Doubanjiang comes from Pixian county in Sichuan province in south-west China.
It is a key seasoning in dishes such as mapo tofu.
The paste is made by fermenting broad beans with chilli and salt.
doubanjiang.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of deep red, glossy bean paste
doubanjiang.what: A hot, salty paste of fermented broad beans and chilli.

facts: Tomato paste is made by cooking tomatoes down until most of their water has evaporated.
Concentrated tomato purées are made by evaporating more water, so a small amount gives strong flavour.
double-concentrate-tomato-puree.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, deep red tomato paste with a glossy surface
double-concentrate-tomato-puree.what: A very thick tomato paste, sold in tubes for small amounts.

facts: In Britain, double cream is thicker than single cream and is used for whipping or pouring.
Cream rises to the top of unhomogenised milk and can be skimmed or separated off.
Double cream is used for whipping, for trifles and for thickening sauces.
