double-cream.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, pale ivory cream, with a soft ridge on its surface
double-cream.what: Rich, thick cream that whips well and holds its shape.

facts: Double Gloucester is a traditional cheese from Gloucestershire, England.
Traditionally it is made from cow's milk, and orange versions are coloured with annatto.
double-gloucester.visual: a block of firm golden Double Gloucester cheese with one wedge cut away, showing a smooth pale interior

duck-gizzards.visual: a small heap of raw duck gizzards, dark reddish-brown and firm, lying loose
duck-gizzards.what: A duck's muscular stomach, tender only after slow cooking.

facts: Duck confit is a French dish in which the leg is salted, then cooked slowly in its own fat.
Duck leg meat is dark and rich, and is well suited to slow cooking.
duck-leg.visual: a single raw duck leg, thigh and drumstick joined, pale pinkish skin, lying flat on the background
duck-leg.what: The thigh and drumstick of a duck, with rich, dark meat.

facts: Duck liver is a classic ingredient in French terrines and parfaits, prized for its smooth texture.
In French, the word foie means liver, as in foie gras, a dish made from the liver of a goose or duck.
Duck liver is sold fresh or frozen, and is often cooked gently to keep it soft.
duck-liver.visual: one small raw duck liver, smooth glossy dark reddish-brown lobe, lying flat
duck-liver.what: A rich, soft duck liver used for pâté and terrines.

facts: Spring rolls are eaten across China and Southeast Asia, with many regional variations.
Hoisin is a thick, sweet sauce from Cantonese cooking, often paired with roast duck.
duck-spring-rolls.visual: two golden crisp spring rolls, one cut in half to show the pale shredded filling, on a plain white plate
duck-spring-rolls.what: Crisp rolls filled with shredded duck and sweet hoisin.

facts: Roast duck is a classic Cantonese dish, and ducks have been raised in China for centuries.
Duck fat is widely used in French cooking, especially for roasting potatoes.
Duck wings are often braised or roasted in soy and sugar glazes, a style common in Chinese cooking.
duck-wings.visual: one raw duck wing with pale skin and small bones, lying directly on a plain background
duck-wings.what: Rich, fatty wings from a duck, good for roasting.

facts: Dukkah is a traditional Egyptian condiment, often eaten by dipping bread in olive oil first.
It is often made with hazelnuts, sesame, coriander and cumin.
Every cook's recipe varies, so dukkah can be mild or strongly spiced.
dukkah.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of coarse dukkah, a mix of pale seeds, crushed nuts and dark spices
dukkah.what: An Egyptian blend of toasted nuts, seeds and spices.

facts: Dulce de leche means sweet of milk in Spanish.
Argentina and Uruguay are known for dulce de leche, which is spread on pastries and cakes.
dulce-de-leche.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick golden caramel with a smooth glossy surface
dulce-de-leche.what: Thick golden caramel made from slowly cooked sweet milk.

facts: Dulse is a red seaweed that grows on rocky shores in the North Atlantic, including Ireland, Scotland and Canada.
Coastal communities in Ireland and Scotland have gathered dulse for centuries, eating it fresh or dried.
Dulse is often dried and sometimes fried or roasted, which gives it a smoky, bacon-like flavour.
dulse.visual: a small heap of dried red seaweed, dark purple-red fronds, crinkled and flat
dulse.what: A dark red seaweed, dried and often eaten as a snack.

facts: Dulse is a red seaweed that grows on rocks in cold northern Atlantic and Pacific coastal waters.
Dulse has long been gathered and dried for food on the coasts of Ireland and Scotland.
When fried, dulse becomes crisp and takes on a flavour often compared to bacon.
dulse-flakes.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dark reddish-brown dried seaweed flakes
dulse-flakes.what: Dried red seaweed flakes with a smoky, bacon-like taste.

facts: Dumpling wrappers are thin rounds of dough made from wheat flour, water and sometimes salt.
Chinese jiaozi and Japanese gyoza are two dishes that use these wrappers.
Wrappers are folded around fillings and then boiled, steamed or pan-fried.
dumpling-wrappers.visual: a neat stack of thin, pale, round dumpling wrappers, lightly dusted with flour
dumpling-wrappers.what: Thin, round sheets of dough for folding around fillings.

facts: Dungeness crabs are named after Dungeness, a town on the Olympic Peninsula in Washington state.
They are fished along the Pacific coast from Alaska down to California.
Crab is often steamed or boiled whole, then cracked open to reach the sweet meat.
dungeness-crab.visual: one whole raw Dungeness crab, greyish-brown shell with a purple tinge, legs folded neatly beneath its body
dungeness-crab.what: A sweet-fleshed crab from North America's Pacific coast.

facts: Dunlop takes its name from the village of Dunlop in Ayrshire, Scotland, where it has long been made.
It is a firm, pale cheese made from cow's milk, with a mild, sweet flavour.
dunlop.visual: a block of pale golden cheese, one thick wedge cut away and lying beside it
dunlop.what: A mild, creamy Scottish cheese, a little like cheddar.

facts: Durian is native to South-East Asia, and it is widely eaten in Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia.
Some public transport and hotels in the region ban durian because of its strong smell.
In parts of South-East Asia it is nicknamed the king of fruits.
durian.visual: one whole spiky green durian fruit, its husk sharply thorned, lying on its side
durian.what: Spiky fruit with custard-like flesh and a strong smell.

facts: Durum is a hard wheat that is widely grown around the Mediterranean and is ideal for pasta.
Semolina is the coarse middling left after milling durum wheat.
In Italy, semolina is the traditional flour for many types of dried pasta.
durum-wheat-semolina.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of coarse golden semolina, granular and slightly sandy
durum-wheat-semolina.what: Coarse golden flour milled from hard durum wheat.

facts: The alkali process was developed by Coenraad van Houten in the Netherlands in 1828.
It gives chocolate cakes and biscuits a darker colour and a smoother flavour.
dutch-process-cocoa.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, very dark brown cocoa powder
dutch-process-cocoa.what: Cocoa powder treated with alkali, for a darker flavour.

facts: Dwarf beans are a bush form of the common bean, growing low without needing supports.
Common beans originated in the Americas and reached Europe in the 16th century.
In France, slender green beans like these are called haricots verts, meaning green beans.
dwarf-beans.visual: a small heap of fresh green dwarf beans, slim pods with pointed tips, lying loose
dwarf-beans.what: Small, bushy green beans with tender pods.

facts: The bergamot flavour is added to black tea leaves, and the blend is a classic British drink.
Bergamot oil is pressed from the peel of the fruit, which is grown mainly in southern Italy.
earl-grey-tea.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dry, dark twisted black tea leaves, loose and uncut
earl-grey-tea.what: Black tea flavoured with bergamot, a Mediterranean citrus.

facts: Parboiling partly cooks the grains in their husks before milling, which helps them stay firm.
Parboiled rice is widely eaten in South Asia and parts of Africa.
Its grains stay separate after cooking, which suits salads and pilafs.
easy-cook-rice.visual: a small heap of raw, pale golden parboiled long-grain rice grains
easy-cook-rice.what: Parboiled long-grain rice that stays separate when cooked.

facts: Edam takes its name from the town of Edam in the Netherlands, north of Amsterdam.
Edam is traditionally coated in red wax, which protects the cheese during storage and transport.
Edam is made from partly skimmed cow's milk and is often sold young and mild.
edam.visual: a whole round cheese with a smooth, deep red wax coat, standing on its base
edam.what: A mild, slightly salty Dutch cheese in a red wax coat.

facts: Pansies, violets, nasturtiums and borage are among the flowers commonly eaten in Britain.
Rose petals are used in Middle Eastern sweets and drinks, such as rose syrup.
Flowers have been used in cooking for centuries in many cultures, including China.
edible-flowers.visual: a small heap of fresh edible flowers, including pansies and violets, in pink, yellow and purple
edible-flowers.what: Fresh blooms used to decorate cakes and salads.

facts: Sugar decorations have a long history in European confectionery, dating back to medieval feasts.
It sticks to wet surfaces such as icing, and is sometimes added to drinks for sparkle.
edible-glitter.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine gold and silver glitter flakes
edible-glitter.what: Sparkling, shiny decoration for cakes and drinks.

facts: Jellied eels were a traditional London street food, sold from stalls in the East End.
Eel has been eaten in Europe for centuries and is still smoked or grilled in many countries.
eel.visual: one whole raw eel, dark olive skin with a pale belly, lying in a gentle curve
eel.what: A long, rich, oily fish that is often smoked or stewed.

facts: Egg custard is made by gently cooking eggs and milk until they just set.
Custard desserts are common across Europe, from French crème caramel to British baked custard.
egg-custard.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl holding a wobbly, set pale yellow baked egg custard, its top golden
egg-custard.what: A baked pudding of eggs and milk, set to a soft wobble.

facts: Mayonnaise is an emulsion of oil, egg yolk and an acid such as vinegar or lemon juice.
Egg mayonnaise is a long-standing sandwich filling in Britain and many other countries.
egg-mayonnaise.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of chopped boiled egg in creamy pale mayonnaise
egg-mayonnaise.what: Chopped boiled egg stirred into mayonnaise for sandwiches.

facts: Egg noodles are made by mixing flour with beaten eggs, then kneading until smooth and elastic.
egg-noodle-dough.visual: a smooth, pale yellow ball of fresh egg noodle dough with a light dusting of flour
egg-noodle-dough.what: Flour and egg dough, rolled thin and cut into noodles.

egg-noodle-nests.visual: one dried pale golden egg noodle nest, a tightly coiled bundle of fine noodles
egg-noodle-nests.what: Dried egg noodles pressed into neat coiled portions.

facts: Egg noodles are made from wheat flour mixed with eggs, which gives them their yellow colour.
Egg noodles are common in Chinese and Central European cooking, often served in soups.
Dried egg noodles keep for a long time and cook quickly in boiling water.
egg-noodles.visual: a neatly coiled nest of dried golden egg noodles, fine yellow strands
egg-noodles.what: Long strands of pasta made with egg, golden and springy.

facts: Egg pasta is made with eggs mixed into the dough, giving it a yellow colour.
Nidi, the Italian word for nests, is the name used for these curled pasta shapes.
Long strands are wound into nests before they are dried.
egg-pasta-nests.visual: a small heap of dried yellow egg pasta nests, tightly curled ribbons, pale golden colour
egg-pasta-nests.what: Dried egg pasta curled into neat, round nests.

facts: Egg wash is a simple mixture of beaten egg, sometimes thinned with water or milk, brushed over pastry before baking.
As it bakes, the egg browns, which is why brushing before baking gives pastry a rich colour.
Egg wash is used across European baking, including in pies, sausage rolls and bread glazes.
egg-wash.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, glossy pale yellow beaten egg
egg-wash.what: Beaten egg, brushed onto pastry to give a golden shine.

facts: When whisked, egg white traps air and forms the foam used in meringues and souffles.
Pavlova, a meringue-based dessert, is named after the ballerina Anna Pavlova.
Egg white turns opaque and firm as it heats, which is why it helps set custards and bakes.
egg-white.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of clear, glossy raw egg white
egg-white.what: The clear, runny part of an egg that whisks into a foam.

facts: Egg white powder is made by drying liquid egg whites, and it can be mixed back with water.
Bakers use it for meringue and royal icing, where whipped egg white forms a stable foam.
Powdered egg whites keep for a long time in a cupboard, without needing refrigeration.
egg-white-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, pale cream egg white powder, dry and smooth
egg-white-powder.what: Dried egg white, ground to a fine powder that keeps well.

facts: Hollandaise and mayonnaise are both emulsions built on egg yolk.
Fresh pasta dough in Italy is often enriched with yolks, giving it a golden colour.
egg-yolk.visual: a single raw egg yolk, glossy and round, in a small plain white ceramic bowl
egg-yolk.what: The rich, golden centre of an egg, used to enrich dishes.

facts: Eggnog is thought to descend from posset, a medieval British drink of hot milk and ale or wine.
Eggnog became popular in the American colonies, where rum and whiskey were often added.
It is traditionally served at Christmas and winter celebrations in many countries.
eggnog.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with thick, pale yellow eggnog
eggnog.what: A creamy, festive drink of egg, milk and nutmeg.

facts: Russet describes an apple with a rough, brownish skin rather than a smooth, coloured one.
Egremont Russet is an English dessert apple, prized for its nutty flavour and dry flesh.
egremont-russet.visual: one whole Egremont Russet apple, rough golden-brown russeted skin, lying on its side on a plain background
egremont-russet.what: A nutty, russet-skinned English apple with dry flesh.

facts: Elbow macaroni is a short, curved pasta, named for its resemblance to the bend of an arm.
Macaroni cheese is a dish in Britain and America made by coating cooked pasta in a cheese sauce.
Pasta is made from durum wheat semolina mixed with water, shaped and dried.
elbow-macaroni.visual: a small heap of dry elbow macaroni, pale golden, curved tubes scattered loosely
elbow-macaroni.what: Short, curved pasta tubes, classic for macaroni cheese.

facts: Elder is a common shrub across Europe, western Asia and North Africa.
Raw elderberries are not eaten uncooked, so they are normally cooked into syrups, jams or jellies.
Elderflower cordial, made from the blossom, is a traditional British summer drink.
elderberry.visual: a small bunch of dark purple-black elderberries on their green stalks
elderberry.what: Small dark purple wild berries that grow on elder trees.

facts: Elder is a shrub or small tree, and its dark berries are cooked into jellies, syrups and wines.
Elderberry has long been used in British and European country cooking, including cordials and wines.
elderberry-jelly.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with glossy dark purple-red elderberry jelly
elderberry-jelly.what: A dark, glossy jelly made from elderberries and sugar.

facts: Elder is a shrub or small tree found across Britain and Europe, and it is common in hedgerows.
Elderflower cordial is traditionally made by steeping the blossoms in sugar and water with lemon.
Elderflower is also used to flavour gooseberry puddings, a traditional British pairing.
elderflower.visual: a small bunch of creamy-white elderflower heads, flat clusters of tiny blossoms on green stems
elderflower.what: Fragrant, creamy-white blossoms from the elder tree.

facts: Elderflower cordial is made by steeping elderflower blossoms in sugar syrup, often with lemon.
Elder is a common shrub across Europe, and its white flowers appear in early summer.
The shrub's berries are used for jams and wines, while the flowers are used for cordial.
elderflower-cordial.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden elderflower cordial
elderflower-cordial.what: A floral, sweet syrup made from elderflower blossom.

facts: Elderflowers come from the elder tree and are traditionally gathered in early summer in Britain.
Elderflower cordial, a non-alcoholic cousin of the liqueur, is a popular British summer drink.
Liqueurs like this are often made by steeping the flowers in a spirit and then adding sugar.
elderflower-liqueur.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with pale golden liquid
elderflower-liqueur.what: A sweet, floral liqueur made from elderflower blossom.

facts: Elder is a shrub or small tree, and its creamy flowers open in late spring and early summer.
The syrup is traditionally made by steeping the flower heads in sugar and water, sometimes with lemon.
Elderflower is often paired with gooseberries in puddings and drinks.
elderflower-syrup.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with pale golden syrup
elderflower-syrup.what: A sweet, floral syrup made from elder tree blossoms.

facts: Each bulb contains a few large cloves, which are milder than common garlic.
The cloves can be roasted whole and eaten like a vegetable.
elephant-garlic.visual: one whole large pale bulb, papery off-white skin with faint purple streaks, lying on its side
elephant-garlic.what: A giant, mild garlic-like bulb that is related to leeks.

facts: Eliche is Italian for propellers, which the twisted shape resembles.
Its ridges and twists help thick sauces cling to the pasta.
eliche.visual: a small heap of dried, pale golden propeller-shaped pasta spirals with ridged surfaces
eliche.what: A short, chunky spiral pasta that holds sauce well.

facts: Elm oyster mushrooms naturally grow on elm wood, and they are also cultivated for sale.
Oyster mushrooms are named for their fan-shaped caps, which resemble the shape of an oyster shell.
elm-oyster-mushroom.visual: a cluster of pale cream elm oyster mushrooms, fan-shaped caps joined at the base
elm-oyster-mushroom.what: A pale, firm mushroom with a crisp bite and mild flavour.

facts: Emmental takes its name from the Emme valley in the canton of Bern, Switzerland.
The holes form as gas bubbles develop during the slow ripening of the cheese.
It is a popular cheese for fondue and for melting in Swiss cooking.
emmental.visual: a block of pale yellow hard cheese, one wedge cut away to show large round holes
emmental.what: A pale Swiss cheese with big holes and a nutty taste.

facts: Emu is farmed commercially in Australia and sold as fillets, steaks and mince.
Emus are the second-tallest living birds, after the ostrich, and they cannot fly.
emu-fillet.visual: one raw emu fillet, deep dark red, smooth-surfaced, lying flat directly on a plain background
emu-fillet.what: Lean, tender red meat from a large flightless bird.

facts: Belgian endive is grown by forcing chicory roots in darkness, a method developed in Belgium.
Endive leaves are often served raw in salads, or braised with butter and lemon.
endive.visual: one whole pale yellow-white endive, tightly closed and elongated, lying on its side
endive.what: A pale, slightly bitter leaf vegetable grown in the dark.

facts: English breakfast tea is usually a blend of black teas from India, Sri Lanka and Africa.
Tea reached Britain in the 1600s and became an everyday drink in the 1700s.
Tea leaves are withered, rolled and oxidised to make black tea.
english-breakfast-tea.visual: a small plain white bowl of dark, twisted black loose tea leaves, dry and slightly glossy
english-breakfast-tea.what: A robust blend of black teas, strong enough for milk.

facts: English muffins are cooked on a griddle rather than baked, which gives them a flat shape.
They are traditionally split with a fork rather than cut, which leaves rough, pocketed edges.
In Britain, English muffins are often eaten toasted, with butter or jam.
english-muffin.visual: one whole round English muffin with a pale, slightly rough top, lying flat
english-muffin.what: A flat, round bread roll, usually split and toasted.

facts: English mustard is traditionally hot and is often served with roast beef.
It was long made in Norwich, a city in eastern England that became known for its mustard.
Mustard is made from the seeds of a plant in the cabbage family, ground and mixed with liquid.
english-mustard.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled to the top with bright yellow paste
english-mustard.what: A fiery yellow paste ground from mustard seed and flour.

facts: Enoki are grown in the dark on sawdust or grain, which gives them their pale colour and slender shape.
They are widely eaten in Japan, Korea and China, where they are used in soups and hotpots.
Enoki is the Japanese name, and the mushroom is also sold as the golden needle mushroom.
enoki-mushroom.visual: a small bunch of enoki mushrooms, long slender pale stems with tiny white caps
enoki-mushroom.what: Long, thin white mushrooms with tiny caps and crisp stems.

facts: Epazote is native to tropical America and has long been used in Mexican cooking.
It is traditionally simmered with black beans, adding a sharp, resinous flavour.
epazote.visual: a small bunch of fresh green epazote sprigs with narrow, serrated leaves
epazote.what: A strong-smelling Mexican herb used to season beans.

facts: Époisses is a French cheese from the village of Époisses in Burgundy.
It holds protected AOC status, so it must be made in a defined area under set rules.
Its strong aroma comes from bacteria that develop on the orange rind during ripening.
epoisses.visual: a round soft cheese with one wedge cut out, orange-washed rind and creamy yellow interior
epoisses.what: A pungent soft cheese from Burgundy, washed in brandy.

facts: Escarole is a kind of endive, closely related to chicory.
It is popular in Italian cooking, where it is often braised or added to soups.
Blanching the leaves by keeping them from light makes them paler and less bitter.
escarole.visual: a whole head of escarole, broad pale-green ruffled leaves, lying on its side
escarole.what: Broad, mildly bitter leaves, good in soups or braised.

facts: Escolar is a snake mackerel, a large fish found in warm seas around the world.
In many markets it is sold under the name white tuna, though it is not a tuna.
Its flesh is naturally oily, which gives it a soft, buttery texture when cooked.
escolar.visual: a skinless fillet of pale ivory fish, firm and glossy, lying flat
escolar.what: A rich, buttery white fish from warm deep ocean waters.

facts: Espagnole is one of the classic mother sauces in French cooking.
It is made from browned stock thickened with a roux and flavoured with tomatoes.
Its name refers to Spain, though the sauce is French in origin.
espagnole-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, glossy, dark brown sauce
espagnole-sauce.what: A rich, slow-cooked brown sauce, a classic mother sauce.

facts: The espresso method was developed in Italy, where it has been a café staple for over a century.
The word espresso means pressed out in Italian, referring to the brewing method.
Espresso is the base of drinks such as cappuccino and caffè latte.
espresso.visual: a small clear glass of dark espresso, topped with a thin golden crema
espresso.what: A small, very strong coffee brewed under pressure.

facts: Potatoes originated in the Andes of South America and were domesticated there thousands of years ago.
Yellow-fleshed potatoes are widely grown in Europe, and waxy varieties hold their shape when boiled.
Floury potatoes break down when cooked, which suits mash and roast potatoes.
estima-potato.visual: a small heap of smooth-skinned, oval, pale yellow potatoes
estima-potato.what: A yellow-skinned, creamy potato that suits most cooking.

facts: Korarima is grown in the highlands of southern Ethiopia, where it is widely used in local cooking.
It is used to flavour coffee and spiced stews, and it is sometimes called false cardamom.
ethiopian-korarima.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dried, dark brown korarima pods, ridged and slightly wrinkled
ethiopian-korarima.what: Smoky, camphor-edged Ethiopian pods, a cousin of cardamom.

facts: Unlike condensed milk, it has no added sugar.
Its long shelf life in cans made it useful before fridges were common.
evaporated-milk.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, pale creamy liquid
evaporated-milk.what: Milk thickened by heating to remove water, sold in cans.

facts: The bagel is a ring-shaped bread that is boiled and then baked, traditionally made in Jewish communities in Eastern Europe.
The everything bagel is commonly associated with New York bakeries, where it is topped with many seasonings.
Poppy and sesame seeds are the main toppings, and the dried onion and garlic add a savoury flavour.
everything-bagel.visual: one whole round golden-brown bagel, its top speckled with seeds, lying directly on the background
everything-bagel.what: A ring-shaped bread roll coated in seeds and spices.

facts: Everything bagel seasoning is mainly used as a topping for bagels in the United States.
Sesame seeds, one of its main ingredients, have been used in cooking for thousands of years.
everything-bagel-seasoning.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of mixed seeds and dried onion and garlic flakes
everything-bagel-seasoning.what: A mix of seeds, garlic, onion and salt for sprinkling.

facts: Tofu is made by curdling hot soya milk, then pressing the curds into blocks.
Extra-firm tofu is pressed more to remove water, giving a dense texture for frying and grilling.
Tofu has been eaten in China for many centuries and is now widely used across East Asia.
extra-firm-tofu.visual: a whole firm pale cream block of tofu, its surface lightly pressed, lying flat
extra-firm-tofu.what: A dense, pressed soy curd block that holds its shape.

facts: Extra mature cheddar is aged for a long time, which lets its flavour become intense and savoury.
Cheddar-style cheeses are made in many countries, and the name is often used for similar hard cheeses.
extra-mature-cheddar.visual: a block of extra mature cheddar cheese with one wedge cut away, pale golden crumbly interior and a flat cut face
extra-mature-cheddar.what: A crumbly, long-aged cheddar with a deep, savoury bite.

facts: Olive oil has been made around the Mediterranean for thousands of years.
Olive trees grow around the Mediterranean and can live for many centuries.
extra-virgin-olive-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with golden-green olive oil
extra-virgin-olive-oil.what: Fruity, peppery oil from the first pressing of olives.

facts: Faggots are a traditional British dish made from offal mixed with breadcrumbs and herbs.
Caul fat, a lacy membrane from the animal's abdomen, is used to wrap them.
faggots.visual: three round, dark-brown faggots, glossy and firm, served on a plain white plate
faggots.what: Savoury meatballs of minced offal, wrapped in caul fat.

facts: It is named for the circular rings it forms in grass, known as fairy rings.
It grows in pastures and lawns across Europe and North America.
The mushrooms dry naturally on the grass, and can be kept dried and rehydrated for cooking.
fairy-ring-champignon.visual: a small heap of tiny tan-coloured wild mushrooms with curled, dried-looking caps and pale gills
fairy-ring-champignon.what: A small wild mushroom that grows in grassy rings in fields.

facts: Fajitas grew out of Tex-Mex cooking in Texas, where grilled skirt steak was served in tortillas.
The name fajita comes from the Spanish word faja, meaning belt or strip.
Fajita seasonings typically combine chilli powder, cumin, garlic and paprika.
fajita-seasoning.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of reddish-brown ground spice blend, finely powdered
fajita-seasoning.what: A smoky, citrusy spice mix for Tex-Mex grilled meat.

facts: Traditional falafel is made from dried chickpeas or fava beans, rather than cooked ones.
Falafel is widely eaten across the Middle East and is often served in pitta bread.
falafel-mix.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale green-beige dried falafel mix, fine and crumbly
falafel-mix.what: A dry mix of chickpeas and herbs for frying into patties.

facts: Fallow deer have many coat colours, from pale to dark, and often have spots.
They were brought to Britain long ago and are now widespread in parks and woodland.
fallow-deer-haunch.visual: one raw fallow deer haunch, deep red meat with a thin layer of pale fat, lying on its side on a plain background
fallow-deer-haunch.what: A lean, mild venison from a medium-sized deer.

facts: Farfalle means butterflies in Italian, a name that comes from its shape.
It is thought to have been made in northern Italy, though its exact origin is uncertain.
The pinched middle is made by pinching a small rectangle of dough.
farfalle.visual: a small heap of dry farfalle pasta bows, pale yellow
farfalle.what: Bow-shaped pasta that holds creamy sauces well.

facts: Its mild flavour suits herbs, mustard and white wine.
Rabbit stew is a traditional dish in France, Italy and Spain.
farmed-rabbit.visual: a whole raw dressed rabbit, pale pink meat with a little white fat, lying on its side
farmed-rabbit.what: Mild, tender meat from domestic rabbits bred for eating.

facts: Bread made from wheat flour and water has been baked for thousands of years.
Crusty loaves are baked at high heat so the outside forms a firm, crisp crust.
Thick slices of crusty white bread are a classic base for British doorstop sandwiches.
farmhouse-loaf.visual: one whole crusty white loaf, floury golden-brown top, rustic oval shape, lying on its side
farmhouse-loaf.what: A large, crusty white loaf, ideal for thick sandwiches.

facts: Farro is the Italian name for ancient wheats such as emmer, which has been grown for thousands of years.
Emmer wheat was among the first cereals farmed in the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East.
Farro is popular in Tuscan cooking, often simmered in soups or served cold in salads.
farro.visual: a small heap of pale tan whole farro grains, oval and firm, on a plain background
farro.what: An ancient wheat grain with a firm, chewy bite.

facts: Fast-action yeast is a dried yeast that can be mixed straight into flour without first being dissolved.
Dried yeast was developed to be easier to store than fresh yeast, which spoils quickly.
It is widely sold in small sachets for home baking.
fast-action-dried-yeast.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale tan dried yeast granules
fast-action-dried-yeast.what: Granules that mix straight into flour for quick bread.

facts: Fat hen is a weed of the goosefoot family that grows on disturbed ground across much of the world.
It was an important food in prehistoric Europe, and its seeds have been found at ancient sites.
The name is thought to come from its past use as feed for fattening poultry.
fat-hen.visual: a loose bunch of soft grey-green fat hen leaves with a faint powdery sheen
fat-hen.what: A wild plant with soft leaves that cook like spinach.

facts: Fava beans are one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown around the Mediterranean and Near East for thousands of years.
In Egypt, fava beans are slow-cooked to make ful medames, a dish often eaten for breakfast.
Dried fava beans are soaked and peeled before they are cooked into purees and stews.
fava-beans.visual: a small heap of fresh shelled green fava beans, pale green and plump
fava-beans.what: A large green bean with a creamy, sweet taste.

facts: Feijoa is native to the highlands of South America, from Colombia down to Uruguay.
New Zealand is known for growing feijoas, and the fruit is very popular in home gardens there.
feijoa.visual: a whole oval green feijoa with smooth skin and a small dark tip at one end
feijoa.what: A green, perfumed fruit with gritty, sweet pulp inside.

facts: Felino salami takes its name from Felino, a town near Parma in northern Italy.
felino-salami.visual: one salami sausage lying on its side, one end cut to show deep red meat flecked with white fat
felino-salami.what: A fine-textured Italian sausage, dried and sliced thinly.

facts: Florence fennel is grown for its swollen leaf base, which is eaten as a vegetable.
The name fennel comes from the Latin feniculum, a diminutive of the word for hay.
Fennel seeds flavour Italian sausages and Indian cooking, and are often chewed after a meal.
fennel.visual: one whole fresh fennel bulb with feathery green fronds, pale white base and trimmed stalks
fennel.what: A crunchy bulb vegetable with a gentle aniseed flavour.

facts: Fennel is a Mediterranean plant, and its fronds, bulb and seeds are all eaten.
The aniseed flavour comes from anethole, a compound also found in star anise.
fennel-fronds.visual: a small bunch of fresh fennel fronds, fine feathery green stems and tufted tips, lying on a plain background
fennel-fronds.what: Feathery green tops of fennel with a soft aniseed taste.

facts: It has a sweet, honeyed flavour and is often sprinkled over roast pork or vegetables.
Wild fennel grows along coasts and roadsides in many parts of southern Europe.
fennel-pollen.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl holding fine golden-yellow pollen powder
fennel-pollen.what: Golden pollen from fennel flowers, used as a seasoning.

facts: Fennel seeds are the dried fruits of the fennel plant, a herb native to the Mediterranean.
In India they are known as saunf and are often chewed after meals.
They are a common flavouring in Italian sausages and in many breads.
fennel-seeds.visual: a small heap of pale green-brown fennel seeds, oval and ridged
fennel-seeds.what: Sweet, aniseed-flavoured seeds from the fennel plant.

facts: Fenugreek has been used in Indian, Middle Eastern and Mediterranean cooking for thousands of years.
Dried leaves, known as kasuri methi, are used in North Indian cooking.
fenugreek-seeds.visual: a small loose heap of small yellowish-brown fenugreek seeds, piled neatly
fenugreek-seeds.what: Small hard seeds with a bitter, maple-like flavour.

facts: Fermented bean curd is made by culturing tofu with moulds and salt, then ageing it.
It is widely used in Chinese cooking, often served as a small condiment with rice porridge.
fermented-bean-curd.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, holding small pale cubes of soft curd in a little liquid
fermented-bean-curd.what: Strong, salty cubes of soft tofu that has been fermented.

facts: Douchi are whole soybeans that have been fermented and salted, and they have been used in Chinese cooking for centuries.
Fermented black beans are a traditional seasoning in Cantonese cooking, often used with steamed fish.
The beans are fermented with moulds, and the process gives them a strong, salty and savoury character.
fermented-black-beans.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with dark, wrinkled fermented black soybeans
fermented-black-beans.what: Salty, pungent black soybeans preserved by fermentation.

facts: Garlic is native to central Asia, and has been used in cooking for thousands of years.
Fermentation turns sugars into acids, which gives the garlic a tangy, mellow flavour.
fermented-garlic.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with pale cream garlic cloves in cloudy brine
fermented-garlic.what: Garlic cloves slowly fermented in brine until mellow.

facts: Fermentation uses natural bacteria and yeasts to turn sugars into acids, which give a sharp taste.
Fermented chilli pastes are a long-standing part of Korean cooking, such as gochujang.
Hot sauces are often made from chillies that have been salted and left to ferment for weeks.
fermented-hot-sauce.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with bright red chilli sauce
fermented-hot-sauce.what: A tangy chilli sauce made by fermenting chilli mash.

facts: Sweet fermented rice is made from cooked glutinous rice, fermented with a starter of mould and yeast.
It is eaten on its own as a dessert in parts of China, or added to sweet soups.
fermented-rice.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of soft, pale rice grains in a little milky liquid
fermented-rice.what: Sweet, boozy fermented rice used in Chinese cooking.

facts: Tofu is inoculated with mould, then salted and left to ferment.
It is a long-established Chinese condiment, often eaten with rice porridge.
fermented-tofu.visual: a plain glass jar without a label holding soft, pale tofu cubes in brine
fermented-tofu.what: A pungent Chinese condiment made from soft tofu.

facts: Feta has protected designation of origin status in the EU, so only cheese made in Greece can be called feta.
Feta is traditionally made from sheep's milk, sometimes blended with goat's milk.
Feta is cut into blocks and kept in brine, which gives it its salty flavour and firm texture.
feta.visual: a block of white crumbly brined cheese, one side cut to show its crumbly texture
feta.what: A salty, crumbly white cheese from Greece, kept in brine.

facts: Fettuccine means little ribbons in Italian, from the word fettuccia.
Fettuccine Alfredo, a dish of butter and Parmesan, was created in Rome in the early twentieth century.
fettuccine.visual: a loosely coiled nest of dry, pale yellow fettuccine ribbons
fettuccine.what: Flat, ribbon-shaped pasta that holds rich, creamy sauces.

facts: Feuilletine is made from thin crepe-style pastry that is baked, broken and crumbled.
It is widely used in French pralines and chocolate confectionery for its crunch.
Its name comes from the French word feuillet, meaning a leaf or sheet of paper.
feuilletine.visual: a small heap of pale golden, crisp, paper-thin wafer flakes, loose, on a plain white background
feuilletine.what: Crisp golden flakes of crushed crepe, used in chocolates.

facts: Ficelle is French for string, a name that refers to the loaf's thin shape.
Its slender form gives a higher proportion of crust to crumb than a standard loaf.
ficelle.visual: a whole slender ficelle loaf, golden-brown with a crisp crust and a few slashes across the top
ficelle.what: A thin French stick of bread with a very crisp crust.

facts: Fiddleheads are the young, unopened fronds of certain ferns, picked while still tightly coiled.
Their name comes from the resemblance of the coil to the scroll of a violin.
They are usually boiled or steamed thoroughly before eating.
fiddlehead-ferns.visual: a small bunch of tightly coiled green fiddlehead fern fronds, stems trimmed
fiddlehead-ferns.what: Young coiled fern shoots, picked before they open.

facts: Figs are one of the oldest cultivated fruits, grown around the Mediterranean since ancient times.
Each fig is an inverted cluster of tiny flowers, which develop into the small seeds inside.
Figs are often roasted with goat's cheese, or wrapped in ham as a simple starter.
fig.visual: a whole ripe purple fig with a soft, slightly split skin
fig.what: A soft, sweet fruit with pink flesh and tiny seeds.

facts: Figs have been cultivated since ancient times, with some of the earliest evidence in the Middle East.
Fig jam is traditionally served with cheese, a pairing popular across Europe and the Mediterranean.
In many places figs are dried, and fig paste or jam is a traditional way to preserve the harvest.
fig-jam.visual: a plain glass jar without a label filled with dark purple fig jam, seeds visible on the glossy surface
fig-jam.what: A thick, seedy jam made from cooked figs and sugar.

facts: Fig leaves have a scent often compared to coconut, and cooks use them to flavour custards and creams.
Figs grow in the Mediterranean region and western Asia, where the trees have long been cultivated.
fig-leaf.visual: one whole fresh fig leaf, large and lobed, deep green with pale veins
fig-leaf.what: Large lobed leaf of the fig tree with a coconut-like scent.

facts: Fig paste is made by cooking dried figs down to a thick, sweet purée.
Figs have been dried and eaten across the Mediterranean since ancient times.
fig-rolls.visual: one soft golden biscuit cut across, showing a dark fig paste spiral inside
fig-rolls.what: A soft biscuit with a sweet fig paste rolled inside.

facts: Fillet steak comes from the tenderloin, a muscle that does little work in the animal.
Because it is very tender, fillet is usually cooked quickly over high heat.
fillet-steak.visual: one raw beef fillet steak, a neat cylinder of deep red meat, lying on its side
fillet-steak.what: A very tender, small cut of beef from the loin.

facts: Filo is a Greek word meaning leaf, and the dough is stretched extremely thin.
It is used across Greece, Turkey and the Middle East for pies such as spanakopita.
Layers are brushed with butter or oil between sheets so they bake crisp.
filo-pastry.visual: a loose, neatly folded stack of thin, pale golden filo sheets, slightly crinkled, lying flat
filo-pastry.what: Paper-thin sheets of dough used for baking crisp layers.

facts: Haricots verts is the French name for these beans, meaning green beans.
They are picked young, before the seeds inside the pods have fully developed.
Fine beans are a variety of French bean, often served blanched or steamed as a side dish.
fine-beans.visual: a small heap of slim, bright green fine beans, tips intact and ends trimmed
fine-beans.what: Very slim, tender green beans picked young.

facts: Breadcrumbs have long been used to coat food before frying, giving it a crisp golden crust.
Dried crumbs are made by drying stale bread and grinding it to a fine texture.
fine-breadcrumbs.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale golden fine dried breadcrumbs, loosely heaped
fine-breadcrumbs.what: Dry, fine crumbs of bread used to coat and crisp food.

facts: Maize was first domesticated in southern Mexico, and cornmeal is made by grinding its dried kernels.
Fine cornmeal gives a softer, more cake-like crumb than the coarser grinds used for polenta.
Cornbread is a classic of the southern United States, and is often made with cornmeal.
fine-cornmeal.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with fine, pale yellow cornmeal, smooth and level on top
fine-cornmeal.what: Finely ground dried maize, used for cakes and cornbread.

facts: Oats were a staple porridge grain in Scotland and northern England for many centuries.
Instant oats are cut finer and partly cooked before drying, so they soften in a short time.
Porridge is made by simmering oats in water or milk until the mixture thickens.
fine-instant-oatmeal.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, pale oat flakes, very finely cut and dry
fine-instant-oatmeal.what: Finely cut oats that turn creamy quickly with hot water.

facts: Fines herbes is a classic French blend, and its name simply means fine herbs.
fines-herbes.visual: a small heap of finely chopped fresh green herbs, fine mixed pieces of bright green leaf
fines-herbes.what: A French blend of finely chopped fresh green herbs.

facts: Finger limes grow wild in the rainforests of eastern Australia.
Their pulp forms small round vesicles that are often called citrus caviar.
Chefs now spoon the beads over oysters, fish and salads.
finger-lime.visual: a finger lime sliced in half lengthwise, showing clusters of pale green pearl-like beads inside
finger-lime.what: A slim Australian citrus with pearl-like, popping pulp.

facts: Fingerling potatoes are named for their long, slim shape, which resembles a finger.
Waxy potatoes hold their shape when boiled or roasted, unlike floury varieties.
Potatoes originated in the Andes of South America, where they were first cultivated.
fingerling-potato.visual: a small heap of raw fingerling potatoes, slender and knobbly, with thin golden skins
fingerling-potato.what: Small, slender potatoes with a firm, waxy flesh.

facts: Finocchiona comes from Tuscany, and its name comes from finocchio, the Italian word for fennel.
It is cured with whole seeds, which give it a sweet, aromatic flavour.
finocchiona.visual: one salami log with a round slice cut off, showing speckled pink meat and small dark seeds
finocchiona.what: A Tuscan salami flavoured with fennel seeds.

facts: Firefly squid are named for the light-producing spots on their bodies that glow blue.
They are caught in spring in Toyama Bay on Japan's Sea of Japan coast.
Firefly squid are often eaten raw or boiled, and are a local delicacy in the regions where they are caught.
firefly-squid.visual: a small heap of tiny raw squid, translucent pale bodies and small dark eyes, lying loosely
firefly-squid.what: A tiny glowing squid, eaten whole in Japan.

facts: Tofu is made by curdling hot soy milk and pressing the curds into blocks.
Firm tofu is pressed to squeeze out water, so it stays solid in stir-fries and on the grill.
Tofu has been a staple across East Asia for many centuries and is now eaten widely around the world.
firm-tofu.visual: one whole firm white block of tofu, pressed dry, with a smooth matte surface and straight edges
firm-tofu.what: Pressed soy curd that holds its shape when fried or baked.

facts: Fish balls are made from pounded fish paste, shaped into balls, then poached or fried.
They are a common topping for noodle soups in China, Hong Kong and Southeast Asia.
Their springy texture comes from working the fish paste until it becomes smooth and elastic.
fish-balls.visual: a small heap of pale, round, springy fish balls, lying loose on the background
fish-balls.what: Bouncy round balls of minced fish, popular in noodle soups.

facts: Fish stock is traditionally made from bones, heads and trimmings, simmered gently rather than boiled hard.
Fish frames, the skeletons left after filleting, are a common stock base in French cooking.
Fish stock forms the base of many classic dishes, including bouillabaisse from Marseille.
fish-bones.visual: a small heap of clean white fish bones and trimmings, pale and dry on a plain background
fish-bones.what: Bones and trimmings from white fish, simmered for stock.

facts: Fish heads are a traditional part of many cuisines, and the cheeks are prized for their soft flesh.
In parts of Asia and the Caribbean, fish heads are cooked in curries and stews.
Fish heads are often used to make stock, which adds body to the broth.
fish-head.visual: a whole raw fish head with silver-grey skin, lying flat on a plain background
fish-head.what: The head of a fish, valued for its rich cheek meat.

facts: Fish maw is traditionally made from the swim bladders of fish such as croaker or sturgeon.
It has been prized in Chinese cooking for centuries, especially in banquet soups.
Once soaked and cooked, it turns soft and silky and takes on the flavour of the broth.
fish-maw.visual: a small heap of pale ivory dried fish maw pieces, curled and irregular
fish-maw.what: The dried swim bladder of a fish, used to thicken soups.

facts: Fish paste is made by mashing cooked fish with butter, spices or other seasonings.
Fish paste spreads were a common sandwich filling in Britain.
Similar fish pastes, called surimi, form the base of many Japanese fish products.
fish-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth pale pink fish paste
fish-paste.what: A smooth, savoury spread made from blended fish.

facts: Fish pie is a traditional British dish, often topped with mashed potato.
Smoked haddock is a classic ingredient in British dishes such as kedgeree.
Mixed fish is usually baked in a sauce and finished under a potato topping.
fish-pie-mix.visual: a loose heap of raw, skinless fish chunks, some pink-orange and some pale white, cut into even pieces
fish-pie-mix.what: A ready-mixed blend of fish chunks for baking in a pie.

facts: Fish sauce has been made across Southeast Asia for centuries, from fish salted and left to ferment.
In Thailand it is called nam pla, and in Vietnam it is known as nước mắm.
It is a key seasoning in Thai and Vietnamese cooking, often mixed with lime and sugar.
fish-sauce.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of amber-brown liquid with a plain stopper
fish-sauce.what: A pungent, salty liquid made from fermented fish.

facts: Fish skin is fried until crisp in parts of Asia and Latin America and eaten as a snack.
In Japan, grilled salmon skin is a popular snack and a side dish served with rice.
fish-skin.visual: a small heap of golden, crisp fried fish skin pieces, curled and irregular, served on a small plain white plate
fish-skin.what: Crisp-fried fish skin, eaten as a crunchy snack.

facts: In French cooking a fish stock is called a fumet, and it is one of the classic base stocks.
It is simmered only briefly, because fish bones cook quickly and can turn bitter if overcooked.
Fish stock is the base for soups such as bouillabaisse, a fish stew from Marseille.
fish-stock.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale golden clear liquid
fish-stock.what: A light, clear broth made by simmering white fish bones.

facts: Dried stock cubes were developed in Europe to make broth quickly without long simmering.
Fish stock is made by simmering fish bones, trimmings and aromatic vegetables until the liquid is flavourful.
Fish stock is a common base for chowders and seafood soups, especially in coastal cooking.
fish-stock-cube.visual: a few pale cream-coloured stock cubes, pressed and crumbly, in a small plain white bowl
fish-stock-cube.what: A compressed block of dried fish stock for quick soup.

facts: Flageolets are a French variety of kidney bean, picked young while still pale green.
They are a classic partner for roast lamb in French cooking.
flageolet-beans.visual: a small heap of dried pale green flageolet beans, smooth and kidney-shaped
flageolet-beans.what: Small, pale green French beans with a delicate flavour.

facts: In Britain and Europe they are used to top cakes, pastries and biscuits.
They toast quickly, so they need watching closely in a dry pan or oven.
flaked-almonds.visual: a small heap of pale golden flaked almonds, thin and slightly curled
flaked-almonds.what: Thin slivers of almond, often toasted for crunch.

facts: Flaky salts form as pyramid-shaped crystals when seawater evaporates in shallow pans.
Salt has been produced from seawater by evaporation for thousands of years.
flaky-sea-salt.visual: a small heap of pale, pyramid-shaped sea salt flakes, glittering
flaky-sea-salt.what: Crisp salt flakes sprinkled over food just before serving.

facts: Flat iron steak is cut from the top blade of the shoulder, a muscle also known as the feather blade.
The name comes from its shape, which looks like an old-fashioned clothes iron.
It is best cooked quickly over high heat and sliced across the grain, as it can turn tough if overdone.
flat-iron-steak.visual: one raw flat iron steak, rectangular, deep red beef with a thin line of white fat, lying flat
flat-iron-steak.what: A tender, flavourful steak cut from beef shoulder.

facts: Flat-leaf parsley is also called Italian parsley, and is widely used across the Mediterranean.
Parsley is native to the Mediterranean region and has been cultivated there for centuries.
flat-leaf-parsley.visual: a small bunch of fresh flat-leaf parsley, dark green flat leaves on long stems
flat-leaf-parsley.what: A leafy herb with flat, toothed leaves and a clean taste.

facts: Flat mushrooms are the mature form of the cultivated white button mushroom, which is picked when its cap opens.
Mushrooms are fungi rather than plants, and they reproduce through spores found on the gills.
Cultivated mushrooms are grown on compost in darkened sheds, a method used in Britain for a long time.
flat-mushroom.visual: one whole large flat brown mushroom, broad cap open, gills dark underneath, lying on its side
flat-mushroom.what: A broad, open mushroom with a rich, savoury flavour.

facts: Flat peaches are grown in China and sold across Asia, and are now found in some Western shops too.
Peach trees originated in China, where they have been grown for thousands of years.
Peaches belong to the rose family, as do plums, cherries and apples.
flat-peach.visual: a whole flat peach with pale orange-blush skin, a squashed round shape and a dimple at the top, on a plain background
flat-peach.what: A squat, sweet peach with a scent of almonds.

facts: Rice noodles are a staple across South-East Asia, and many are made by steaming a thin sheet of rice batter.
In Cantonese cooking, flat rice noodles are called ho fun and are often stir-fried with beef.
Dried rice noodles are soaked in warm water rather than boiled for long, so they keep their shape.
flat-rice-noodles.visual: a small loose heap of dried flat rice noodles, pale off-white and slightly curled, lying on the background
flat-rice-noodles.what: Broad, flat rice noodles for pad thai and pho.

facts: Poha is a breakfast dish from India, made by softening and seasoning these flakes.
The rice is soaked, cooked, then pressed flat between rollers to make the flakes.
flattened-rice.visual: a small heap of thin, pale off-white flattened rice flakes, slightly irregular
flattened-rice.what: Rice pressed into thin flakes that soften in water.

facts: Couscous is a staple across North Africa, especially in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia.
Instant couscous is pre-steamed and dried, so it needs only hot water to soften.
flavoured-couscous-sachet.visual: a small heap of dry golden couscous grains with flecks of dried green herbs
flavoured-couscous-sachet.what: Quick-cook semolina grains seasoned with dried herbs.

facts: Flax has been cultivated for its fibre and seeds since ancient times.
Flaxseed oil is delicate and does not tolerate heat, so it is usually used cold.
flaxseed-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden oil
flaxseed-oil.what: A pale, delicate oil pressed from flax seeds.

facts: Fleur de sel is the delicate crust of salt that forms on the surface of evaporating seawater.
It is harvested by hand in Brittany and the Camargue, in France, where salt marshes have long been worked.
The name means 'flower of salt' in French, referring to its delicate surface crystals.
fleur-de-sel.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with pale, moist, greyish-white sea salt crystals
fleur-de-sel.what: Moist, delicate French sea salt, used to finish dishes.

facts: Flounder is a flatfish whose eyes move to one side of its head as it grows.
The name flounder is used for several flatfish species, including the European flounder.
Flounder are found in coastal waters around much of the world.
flounder.visual: one whole raw flounder, flat and oval, speckled brown on its upper side and white underneath, lying flat
flounder.what: A flat, mild white fish that lies on the seabed.

facts: Flour tortillas are associated with northern Mexico, where wheat was grown in drier regions.
Flour tortillas are made from wheat flour, fat and water, rolled thin and cooked on a hot griddle.
The word tortilla comes from Spanish, where it originally meant a small round cake.
flour-tortillas.visual: a stack of soft, pale, round flour tortillas on a plain white plate
flour-tortillas.what: Soft, thin wheat flatbreads, often folded around a filling.

facts: Baps are a regional bread roll found mainly in northern England and Scotland.
They are traditionally soft and floury, thanks to a dusting of flour on the top before baking.
A bap is often used for bacon rolls and sandwiches in the morning.
floury-bap.visual: one whole soft white bap roll, its top lightly floured
floury-bap.what: A soft white roll, dusted with flour on top.

facts: Flower sprouts are a hybrid of Brussels sprouts and kale, grown for clusters of small, leafy heads.
Their frilly leaves cook quickly and can be eaten whole in stir-fries or roasted.
They are sold in the UK and the US, where they are often roasted or stir-fried.
flower-sprouts.visual: a small bunch of flower sprouts, tight green rosettes with frilled leaves on thin stalks
flower-sprouts.what: A cross between sprouts and kale, sweet and nutty.

facts: The leaves are a main green in egusi soup, a rich dish of ground melon seeds.
In Igbo the vine is called ugu, and its leaves are a staple green in Nigerian cooking.
fluted-pumpkin-leaves.visual: a small bunch of fresh fluted pumpkin leaves, large dark green lobed leaves with thick veins
fluted-pumpkin-leaves.what: Dark green leaves of a West African climbing plant.

facts: Focaccia is a flat bread associated with Liguria in northwest Italy.
Its name is thought to come from the Latin word focus, meaning hearth.
focaccia.visual: one whole flat golden focaccia, dimpled, glossy and speckled across the top
focaccia.what: A flat, dimpled Italian bread, soft and golden.

facts: Foie gras is French for fat liver, made from the livers of ducks or geese.
France is closely associated with foie gras and is among its main producers.
Terrines and pâtés of foie gras are classic French preparations, often served with bread.
foie-gras.visual: one whole raw duck liver lobe, pale pinkish-beige, smooth and glossy, lying on the background
foie-gras.what: A rich, buttery liver from fattened duck or goose.

facts: Fondant is a sugar paste made from sugar and water, often with glucose added, kneaded until smooth.
In Britain it is often sold as ready-to-roll icing for covering celebration cakes.
The name fondant comes from the French verb fondre, meaning to melt.
fondant.visual: a block of smooth, soft white fondant with one neat slice cut from its edge, lying flat
fondant.what: Smooth sugar paste used to cover and decorate cakes.

facts: Icing sugar is granulated sugar ground to a fine powder, often mixed with a little cornflour to stop caking.
Fondant is a soft, pliable sugar paste used to cover cakes.
The name icing sugar reflects its use for making icings, glazes and frostings.
fondant-icing-sugar.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with fine white powdered sugar, soft and smooth
fondant-icing-sugar.what: Very fine icing sugar that gives glossy, smooth finishes.

facts: Fondue comes from the French word fondre, meaning to melt.
Classic Swiss fondue is made with cheeses such as Gruyère and Emmental, melted with white wine.
Fondue is a traditional communal dish in the Swiss Alps, eaten by dipping bread into the pot.
fondue-cheese.visual: a pale cream block of cheese with one wedge cut away, showing a smooth, slightly pale interior
fondue-cheese.what: A blend of nutty, mild cheeses for melting into fondue.

facts: Fontina is made in the Aosta Valley in the Italian Alps and has protected origin status.
It is the traditional cheese in fonduta, an Italian dish of melted cheese, butter and egg yolk.
fontina.visual: a block of pale ivory cheese with a thin brown rind and one wedge cut away to show a creamy interior
fontina.what: A nutty, rich Italian cheese that melts smoothly.

facts: Gel colourings are thicker than liquid ones, so they change the mixture less.
Only a small amount is needed, because the colour is very concentrated.
Food colouring has been used in baking and confectionery for a very long time.
food-colouring-gel.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with glossy deep red gel
food-colouring-gel.what: A strong paste used to colour icing and cake batter.

facts: Forced rhubarb is grown indoors in total darkness, which makes the stalks pale and more tender.
Forced rhubarb is famously grown in the Rhubarb Triangle of West Yorkshire.
Rhubarb is botanically a vegetable, but it is usually cooked with sugar and used in desserts.
forced-rhubarb.visual: a bunch of slender pale pink rhubarb stalks, with the leaves removed
forced-rhubarb.what: Pale pink, tender stalks of rhubarb, grown in the dark.

facts: The forerib is the top of the rib section, and it is the classic British roast beef joint.
In the United States the same cut is called a standing rib roast, because it is roasted on its bones.
The roast is traditionally served on Sundays in Britain, often with Yorkshire puddings.
forerib-of-beef.visual: a whole raw forerib of beef on the bone, a rectangular joint with a thick fat cap and deep red meat, lying on the background
forerib-of-beef.what: A large rib joint of beef, roasted on the bone.

facts: Fourme d'Ambert takes its name from the town of Ambert in the Auvergne region of central France.
The cheese is made from cow's milk and is aged in cool cellars, where blue moulds develop.
fourme-d-ambert.visual: a round wheel of pale cream cheese with blue-green veins, one wedge cut away to show the marbling inside
fourme-d-ambert.what: A mild, creamy blue cheese from central France.

facts: The frankfurter takes its name from Frankfurt, the German city where similar sausages were made.
Frankfurter sausages are made from pork, beef, or a mixture of both.
In the United States, frankfurters served in buns became a familiar street food and ballpark snack.
frankfurter.visual: one whole smooth pinkish-red frankfurter sausage, glossy skin, lying in a gentle curve
frankfurter.what: A smoked, pre-cooked sausage, usually eaten hot in a bun.

facts: Free-range chickens have access to outdoor space, under rules that vary between countries.
Domestic chickens descend from the red junglefowl of Southeast Asia.
free-range-chicken.visual: a whole raw chicken, plump with pale skin, lying breast side up on the background
free-range-chicken.what: A chicken raised with outdoor access, growing more slowly.

facts: Free-range hens are kept with access to outdoor space, as set out in farming rules.
Egg yolk colour varies largely depending on what the hen eats.
Hens were domesticated from wild jungle fowl in South-east Asia thousands of years ago.
free-range-egg.visual: a single whole raw brown egg with a slightly speckled, natural shell, lying on its side
free-range-egg.what: An egg laid by a hen that roams outdoors.

facts: Freekeh has been eaten in the Middle East for centuries, often in soups and pilafs.

freekeh.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with dull greenish-brown, cracked wheat grains
freekeh.what: Roasted young green wheat with a smoky, chewy bite.

facts: Freeze-drying removes water by freezing the food, then lowering the pressure so the ice turns straight to vapour.

freeze-dried-raspberries.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with bright pink-red freeze-dried raspberry pieces
freeze-dried-raspberries.what: Crisp, light raspberry pieces dried until they crunch.

facts: Freeze-drying removes water from frozen food, so the ice turns straight into vapour.
Freeze-dried strawberries can be ground to a powder and used to flavour icing.
Freeze-dried fruit keeps more of its shape and colour than fruit dried in a hot oven.
freeze-dried-strawberries.visual: a small heap of freeze-dried strawberry pieces, pink-red, light and crisp
freeze-dried-strawberries.what: Strawberries freeze-dried into light, crunchy pieces.

facts: Fregola is a traditional pasta from Sardinia, made by rolling moistened semolina into small pearls.

fregola.visual: a small heap of dry toasted fregola, tiny golden-brown round pasta pearls, on a plain white background
fregola.what: Toasted pasta pearls from Sardinia, with a nutty chew.

facts: The baguette is a long, thin loaf, and its French name means stick or wand.

french-baguette.what: A long, crisp-crusted French loaf with an airy inside.

french-breakfast-radish.visual: a small bunch of elongated red radishes with white tips, lying on a plain white background
french-breakfast-radish.what: A long, mild red radish with a white tip.

facts: Mustard helps the oil and vinegar stay combined, acting as an emulsifier.
In the United States, French dressing has long meant a sweet, orange-tinted bottled version.
french-dressing.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden, runny vinaigrette
french-dressing.what: Oil and vinegar dressing, sharpened with mustard.

facts: Marinated fresh anchovies, called boquerones in Spain, are soaked in vinegar and salt.
Fresh anchovies spoil quickly, so they are best eaten soon after they are caught.
fresh-anchovies.visual: a small heap of fresh whole anchovies, silvery blue-grey skin, glossy and firm
fresh-anchovies.what: Small silvery fish, eaten fresh, marinated or fried crisp.

facts: Basil comes from the mint family and is native to tropical regions of Asia and Africa.
Italian cooks pair it with tomatoes and mozzarella in the classic Caprese salad.
Its name comes from the Greek word basilikon, meaning royal.
fresh-basil.visual: a bunch of fresh basil, its bright green glossy leaves on fine stems
fresh-basil.what: A fragrant green herb with sweet, peppery leaves.

Fresh leaves are more floral than dried ones, and are often added whole to stocks and braises.
fresh-bay-leaf.visual: a small bunch of fresh glossy green bay leaves with their stems
fresh-bay-leaf.what: Glossy green leaves from the Mediterranean laurel tree.

facts: It is one of the traditional fines herbes of French cooking, alongside parsley, chives and tarragon.
Chervil loses its delicate flavour quickly when heated, so it is usually added at the end of cooking.
fresh-chervil.visual: a small bunch of fresh chervil, fine feathery bright green leaves on thin stems
fresh-chervil.what: A delicate, faintly aniseed herb with lacy green leaves.

facts: Chives grow wild across Europe, Asia and North America, and have been used in cooking for centuries.
Chive flowers are edible and share the stems' mild onion taste.
fresh-chives.visual: a small neat bunch of fresh chives, thin hollow green stems cut evenly, lying on a plain light background
fresh-chives.what: Thin green herb stems with a mild, oniony taste.

fresh-chorizo.visual: a small heap of raw, crumbly fresh chorizo, deep red with flecks of white fat, on a plain background
fresh-chorizo.what: Raw spiced pork, crumbled and fried for tacos and eggs.

Grated or shaved coconut is widely used in Indian, Thai and Caribbean cooking.
Coconut milk is made by soaking grated flesh in hot water and squeezing out the liquid.
fresh-coconut.visual: one whole fresh brown coconut with its fibrous husk, lying on its side
fresh-coconut.what: A large palm nut with white flesh and sweet, clear water.

Coriander is used across Mexican, Indian, Thai and Vietnamese cooking.
fresh-coriander.visual: a small bunch of fresh bright green coriander leaves and thin stalks, lying on the background
fresh-coriander.what: Bright green, citrusy leaves of the coriander plant.

Fresh dates are softer and juicier than the dried fruit most often sold in shops.
fresh-dates.visual: a small heap of plump fresh dates with smooth, shiny amber to reddish skins
fresh-dates.what: Soft, sweet fruit from a palm tree, eaten fresh or dried.

facts: Dill is a traditional herb in Scandinavian, Russian and Eastern European cooking.

fresh-dill.visual: a small bunch of fresh dill, feathery bright green fronds on thin pale stems
fresh-dill.what: Feathery green herb with a sweet, aniseed-like flavour.

fresh-egg-tagliatelle.what: Long flat ribbons of pasta made with fresh egg.

Dried fenugreek leaves, called kasuri methi, are an important flavour in north Indian and Pakistani cooking.
fresh-fenugreek-leaves.visual: a small bunch of fresh fenugreek leaves, small oval pale green leaves on thin stems
fresh-fenugreek-leaves.what: Bitter green leaves used in Indian curries and flatbreads.

The name garlic comes from Old English gar, meaning spear, and leac, meaning plant.
fresh-garlic.visual: one whole fresh garlic bulb with papery skin, lying on the background
fresh-garlic.what: A pungent bulb of cloves that turns mellow when roasted.

Ginger is thought to have originated in Asia and has long been used in Chinese and Indian cooking.
fresh-ginger.visual: a whole knobbly root of fresh ginger with thin pale tan skin, lying on its side
fresh-ginger.what: A knobbly, zingy root used in stir-fries and curries.

Fresh sheets are softer than dried ones and often need little or no pre-cooking.
fresh-lasagne-sheets.visual: a loose heap of flat fresh lasagne sheets, pale yellow with a slightly rough texture
fresh-lasagne-sheets.what: Thin, flat sheets of fresh egg pasta for layered bakes.

facts: Lovage is a perennial herb that has been grown in European gardens for centuries.

fresh-lovage.visual: a small bunch of fresh lovage, glossy dark green divided leaves on thin stems
fresh-lovage.what: Strong, celery-like herb leaves used sparingly in soups.

fresh-oregano.visual: a small bunch of fresh oregano sprigs with small oval green leaves on thin stems
fresh-oregano.what: A pungent Mediterranean herb for tomato sauces.

fresh-ravioli.visual: a few uncooked fresh ravioli squares, pale and crimped at the edges, arranged on a plain white plate
fresh-ravioli.what: Chilled pasta parcels filled with cheese, meat or veg.

fresh-rice-noodles.visual: a small heap of pale, wide rice noodle ribbons, soft and slightly glossy
fresh-rice-noodles.what: Soft, wide rice noodles sold fresh for stir-fries.

facts: Rosemary is native to the Mediterranean, where it grows wild on dry, sunny slopes.

fresh-rosemary.visual: a small bunch of fresh rosemary, narrow green needle-like leaves on woody stems
fresh-rosemary.what: A woody, piney herb with thin, needle-like leaves.

fresh-sage.what: Soft, grey-green herb with a musky, earthy flavour.

fresh-sardines.visual: a whole fresh sardine, silvery-blue with a glossy skin, lying on its side
fresh-sardines.what: Small oily fish, often grilled whole with the skin on.

fresh-savory.visual: a small bunch of fresh savory with thin green leaves on slender stems
fresh-savory.what: A peppery, thyme-like herb that goes well with beans.

Fresh pasta is usually eaten within a few days and cooks in only a couple of minutes.
fresh-spaghetti.visual: a loose nest of fresh spaghetti, pale yellow strands, glossy and soft, lying on a plain background
fresh-spaghetti.what: Long, soft pasta strands sold chilled rather than dried.

fresh-tarragon.visual: a bunch of fresh tarragon with narrow, bright green pointed leaves on thin stems
fresh-tarragon.what: A herb with narrow leaves and a sweet, aniseed taste.

fresh-thyme.visual: a small bunch of fresh thyme sprigs, tiny grey-green leaves on thin woody stems
fresh-thyme.what: A small, woody herb with tiny, fragrant leaves.

fresh-tortellini.visual: a small heap of fresh, pale yellow ring-shaped tortellini, plump and folded
fresh-tortellini.what: Small pasta rings filled with cheese or meat, sold chilled.

facts: Turmeric is native to South Asia and has been grown there for thousands of years.

fresh-turmeric.visual: a whole fresh turmeric root, knobbly tan skin, a few finger-like knobs, lying on its side
fresh-turmeric.what: An earthy, peppery orange root from the ginger family.

fresh-wasabi-root.visual: one whole fresh wasabi root, pale green knobbly rhizome, rough and irregular, lying on its side
fresh-wasabi-root.what: A knobbly root grated for a sharp, fast-fading heat.

fresh-white-breadcrumbs.what: Soft crumbs made from fresh white bread, not toasted.

fresh-yeast.visual: a whole soft block of pale beige fresh yeast, crumbly edges, lying on a plain background
fresh-yeast.what: A soft, crumbly block of live yeast used for bread.

fresno-chilli.what: A fruity red chilli with a medium heat and a blunt tip.

fried-egg.what: A hen's egg fried until the white is set.

facts: Shallots belong to the onion family, and they have been grown for thousands of years.

fried-shallots.what: Thinly sliced shallots, fried until golden and crisp.

facts: Fromage blanc is a fresh cheese made from cow's milk and is common across France.

fromage-blanc.what: A soft, fresh, spoonable cheese with a light, mild taste.

facts: Fromage frais is French for fresh cheese, and it is unripened.

fromage-frais.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, thick white fresh cheese
fromage-frais.what: A soft, mild, fresh cheese used in puddings and dips.

frosted-flakes.what: Crisp corn flakes coated in a sweet sugar glaze.

frozen-battered-fish-fillet.what: White fish coated in batter, frozen and ready to bake.

frozen-beef-burger-patties.what: Round minced beef patties, sold frozen ready for grilling.

facts: Blueberries are native to North America, where they have been gathered for centuries.

frozen-blueberries.what: Small, sweet-tart berries frozen soon after picking.

facts: Broccoli is a cultivated form of wild cabbage, bred for its flower buds.

frozen-broccoli.what: Tight green florets that are frozen soon after picking.

facts: Freezing cauliflower usually involves blanching it first, which stops enzymes that would spoil it.

frozen-cauliflower.visual: A loose heap of pale white frozen cauliflower florets with a light coating of frost.
frozen-cauliflower.what: Ready-cut florets of a cabbage-family vegetable, frozen.

frozen-cherries.what: Cherries picked ripe and frozen, pitted and ready to cook.

frozen-churros.visual: a few golden fried churros, ridged sticks lightly dusted with cinnamon sugar, on a plain white plate

frozen-dauphinoise.what: Potato slices baked in cream and garlic, sold frozen.

frozen-dim-sum.visual: a plain white plate of assorted steamed dumplings, pleated and pale, round and crescent shaped
frozen-dim-sum.what: Bite-sized steamed dumplings from Cantonese tea-houses.

facts: Suet dumplings are a traditional British addition to stews, made with beef suet and flour.

frozen-dumplings.visual: a small heap of pale, round frozen dumplings on a plain white plate
frozen-dumplings.what: Soft, doughy dumplings sold frozen, to simmer in stews.

facts: Falafel's origins are debated, with both Egypt and the Levant often named as its birthplace.

frozen-falafel.visual: a small heap of round, golden-brown falafel balls on a plain white plate
frozen-falafel.what: Spiced chickpea balls, made to bake or fry from frozen.

facts: Fish cakes are a long-standing British dish, often made from leftover fish and potato.

frozen-fish-cakes.what: Flaked fish and potato, shaped and coated in breadcrumbs.

frozen-fish-fingers.what: Breaded fish sticks, usually cod or pollock, sold frozen.

frozen-fish-pie-mix.what: A frozen pack of raw fish pieces for making fish pie.

facts: Green beans are the young, unripe pods of climbing or bush bean plants.

frozen-gyoza.what: Japanese pan-fried dumplings filled with pork and cabbage.

facts: Mango is native to South Asia and has been cultivated there for thousands of years.

frozen-mango-chunks.what: Ready-cut mango pieces, frozen for smoothies and sorbets.

facts: A classic margherita is topped with tomato, mozzarella and basil.

frozen-margherita-pizza.visual: one whole round baked margherita pizza, red tomato sauce and melted white cheese, golden crust, on a plain white plate
frozen-margherita-pizza.what: Tomato and mozzarella pizza, baked from frozen.

facts: Meatballs are usually made from minced meat mixed with breadcrumbs, egg and seasoning.

frozen-meatballs.what: Small seasoned meatballs, frozen ready to simmer in sauce.

facts: Frozen berries are picked and frozen soon after harvest, which keeps them usable year-round.

frozen-mixed-berries.what: A mix of berries, ready to simmer or blend.

frozen-mixed-vegetables.what: Peas, carrots and sweetcorn, frozen and ready to cook.

frozen-onion-rings.what: Breaded onion slices, sold frozen to fry or bake.

frozen-oven-chips.visual: a small heap of frozen oven chips, chunky pale-yellow potato pieces, lightly frosted
frozen-oven-chips.what: Pre-cut potato chips, frozen and ready to bake.

facts: Pakora are fritters of vegetables or paneer dipped in a spiced chickpea flour batter and deep-fried.
frozen-pakora.visual: a few golden-brown vegetable fritters, slightly frosted, on a plain white plate
frozen-pakora.what: Crisp spiced vegetable fritters from India, sold frozen.

frozen-pancakes.what: Ready-made thin pancakes, kept frozen until needed.

facts: Paratha comes from the Indian subcontinent and is cooked on a flat pan or griddle.

frozen-paratha.what: A flaky layered flatbread, cooked from frozen at home.

facts: Puff pastry is made by layering dough and butter, then folding and rolling it many times.

frozen-pastry-sheets.what: Ready-rolled pastry, frozen, to thaw and bake into pies.

facts: Freezing peas soon after picking keeps their sweetness, because their sugars turn to starch quickly.

frozen-peas.what: Small green peas, quickly frozen soon after picking.

facts: Pepperoni is a spicy cured sausage, usually made from pork and beef.

Giant couscous is a type of pasta made from semolina wheat, and it is larger than ordinary couscous.
Pearl couscous is another name for giant couscous, and it is known by several regional names.
giant-couscous.visual: a small heap of dry pale golden couscous pearls, each one round, smooth and uniform in size
giant-couscous.what: Large, toasted semolina pearls with a nutty flavour.

facts: As a puffball matures its interior turns yellowish and then powdery, releasing dark spores.
In Britain it is often cut into thick slices and fried in breadcrumbs.
giant-puffball.visual: one whole large round puffball mushroom, cream-white smooth skin, unbroken, sitting on the background
giant-puffball.what: A huge round wild mushroom, white inside when fresh.

facts: Yorkshire pudding is a batter of eggs, flour and milk, baked in hot fat until it rises.
Traditionally the batter was baked in the hot fat that dripped from roasting meat.
It is served in England as part of a Sunday roast, often with gravy.
giant-yorkshire-pudding.visual: One large golden, plate-sized Yorkshire pudding, puffed high with crisp edges, on a plain white plate.
giant-yorkshire-pudding.what: A large, crisp batter pudding from northern England.

facts: Giardiniera means gardener's style in Italian, a name for pickles made from garden vegetables.
In the United States, Chicago is known for serving giardiniera on beef sandwiches.
giardiniera.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, holding crisp mixed pickled vegetables in oil
giardiniera.what: Italian mixed vegetables pickled in vinegar or oil.

facts: Gigli means lilies in Italian, a name that refers to the flower-like shape of the pasta.
The ruffled edges catch sauce in their folds, so they suit creamy or chunky sauces.
gigli.visual: a small heap of dry gigli pasta, ruffled lily-shaped cones, pale cream colour, lying loose
gigli.what: Ruffled, lily-shaped Italian pasta for thick sauces.

facts: Gin's flavour comes mainly from juniper berries, with other botanicals such as coriander added.
Gin developed from genever, a juniper spirit first made in the Low Countries.
Gin is used in cocktails such as the gin and tonic, and in some recipes for cured salmon.
gin.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle, half full of clear liquid
gin.what: A clear spirit flavoured mainly with juniper berries.

facts: Ginger ale is a non-alcoholic fizzy drink, usually made with sugar, water and ginger flavouring.
Dry ginger ales are less sweet and are popular as a mixer in cocktails.
Ginger ale is also used in cooking, often in glazes and marinades for meat.
ginger-ale.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale golden ginger ale with bubbles rising through it
ginger-ale.what: A mildly spicy, fizzy soft drink flavoured with ginger.

facts: Ginger is a rhizome native to Southeast Asia, now grown across the tropics.
Ginger and garlic together form the base of many Indian, Pakistani and Bangladeshi curries.
Pastes like this are made ahead to save time when cooking curries and stir-fries.
ginger-and-garlic-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth pale beige paste
ginger-and-garlic-paste.what: A smooth, pungent paste of crushed ginger and garlic.

facts: Ginger beer has been made in Britain since the 18th century.
Traditional brewed ginger beer is fermented with a 'ginger bug' of wild yeast and bacteria.
It is a classic mixer in the Moscow Mule cocktail.
ginger-beer.visual: a clear drinking glass of golden, fizzing ginger beer with small bubbles rising
ginger-beer.what: A fizzy, spicy soft drink made from fresh ginger.

facts: Ginger biscuits, often called ginger nuts in Britain, are a tea-time favourite.
Ginger has been used in cooking in Asia for thousands of years.
Their crisp texture suits crushing into crumb bases for cheesecakes and tarts.
ginger-biscuits.visual: three round golden-brown ginger biscuits stacked neatly on a small plain white plate
