ginger-biscuits.what: Crisp, spiced biscuits, often made with ground ginger.

facts: Cordials were traditionally made by steeping fruit or herbs in sugar syrup to preserve their flavour.
Ginger is a root that has been used in cooking in Asia for thousands of years.
ginger-cordial.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden ginger syrup, with a cork
ginger-cordial.what: A sweet, spicy syrup made from ginger, diluted to drink.

facts: Marmalade is a preserve of citrus fruit cooked with sugar until it sets.
Stem ginger is root ginger preserved in sugar syrup, which makes it sweet and soft.
Marmalade is a popular breakfast spread in Britain, often eaten on toast.
ginger-marmalade.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, filled with amber marmalade and small pale pieces of ginger
ginger-marmalade.what: Orange marmalade studded with pieces of stem ginger.

facts: Ginger nuts are a hard, round British biscuit, popular for dunking in tea.
They are flavoured with ground ginger and often sweetened with golden syrup.
ginger-nuts.visual: a small heap of round golden-brown ginger biscuits, loosely piled on a plain white plate
ginger-nuts.what: A hard, spicy British biscuit made with ground ginger.

facts: Ginger is the underground stem, or rhizome, of a plant native to tropical Asia.
Ginger has been used in Chinese and Indian cooking for thousands of years.
Ginger puree is made by grinding peeled ginger root into a smooth paste.
ginger-puree.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth pale yellow ginger paste, slightly fibrous
ginger-puree.what: Crushed fresh ginger, sold as a smooth paste in a tube.

facts: Ginger syrup is made by simmering ginger root with sugar and water until thick.
Stem ginger is root ginger preserved in syrup, and is traditionally sold in jars in Britain.
ginger-syrup.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with thick, golden amber syrup
ginger-syrup.what: A spicy, sweet syrup made from stem ginger or fresh root.

facts: Gingerbread has been made in Europe since the medieval period, flavoured with imported spices.
Lebkuchen, a German festive gingerbread, is one of the best-known baked goods using this spice mix.
Cinnamon, ginger and clove reached Europe along historic trade routes from Asia.
gingerbread-spice.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with fine reddish-brown ground spice powder
gingerbread-spice.what: Cinnamon, ginger and clove, blended for festive baking.

facts: Ginkgo nuts are the seeds of female trees, and they are always cooked before eating.
In East Asia the nuts are added to congee and savoury egg custards such as chawanmushi.
ginkgo-nuts.visual: a small heap of smooth, oval, pale jade-green ginkgo nuts with their shells removed
ginkgo-nuts.what: Soft, jade-green seeds from the ginkgo tree, eaten in Asia.

facts: They grow in woodland soil, often in association with the roots of trees such as oak and pine.
Chanterelles are hard to cultivate, so most are gathered from the wild.
girolle.visual: a small heap of golden chanterelle mushrooms, funnel-shaped with wavy edges, lying loose on the background
girolle.what: A golden wild mushroom with a fruity, apricot-like smell.

facts: The name glacé means glazed in French, referring to the shiny sugar coating.
In Britain they are used to decorate Christmas cakes and fairy cakes.
glace-cherry.visual: a small heap of glossy bright red glacé cherries, some whole and some halved, on a plain background
glace-cherry.what: A cherry candied in sugar syrup, bright red and sweet.

facts: Glacé is French for iced or glazed, from the verb glacer, meaning to ice or freeze.
Glacé icing is poured or drizzled over buns and cakes while still runny, then sets to a shine.
Icing sugar is finely ground sugar mixed with a little starch to stop it clumping.
glace-icing.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, glossy white icing, thick enough to hold its shape
glace-icing.what: A simple glaze of icing sugar and water.

facts: Glass noodles are made from starch, often from mung beans, sweet potato or peas.
They are common in Chinese, Korean and Thai cooking, in soups and stir-fries.
In Korea, sweet potato glass noodles are a key part of the dish japchae.
glass-noodles.visual: a small loose heap of dried glass noodles, pale and translucent, in tangled strands
glass-noodles.what: Slippery starch noodles that turn clear when cooked.

facts: Globe artichoke is a cultivated form of the wild cardoon, a thistle.
Artichokes have been grown around the Mediterranean for centuries, especially in Italy and Spain.
globe-artichoke.visual: a whole raw green globe artichoke with tightly packed, pointed leaves and a short trimmed stalk
globe-artichoke.what: A thistle-like bud whose heart and leaf bases are eaten.

facts: Glucose syrup is made by breaking down starch, usually from corn or wheat, using acids or enzymes.
It is used in confectionery, ice cream and sorbets, where it helps control texture.
glucose-syrup.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with clear thick syrup
glucose-syrup.what: A clear, thick syrup that keeps sweets soft and smooth.

facts: Penne takes its name from the Italian word for quill, because its diagonal ends look like one.
Corn and rice flours are common in gluten-free pasta, as they can hold their shape when cooked.
Rice noodles have been eaten in China for many centuries, though they are quite different from penne.
gluten-free-penne.visual: a small heap of dry penne pasta, pale golden tubes with diagonal ends, lying loose
gluten-free-penne.what: Tube-shaped pasta made from corn and rice, without wheat.

facts: Spaghetti is a long, thin pasta associated with Italy, traditionally made from durum wheat.
Rice noodles have been made in East Asia for centuries, long before modern gluten-free pasta.
Gluten is a group of proteins found in wheat, barley and rye.
gluten-free-spaghetti.visual: a neat bundle of long dry pale cream spaghetti strands standing upright
gluten-free-spaghetti.what: Long pasta strands made from rice and corn, not wheat.

facts: Gluten is a group of proteins found in wheat, barley and rye that gives bread its elasticity.
Gluten-free breads often use a blend of rice, potato or tapioca flours to mimic wheat's texture.
gluten-free-white-bread.visual: a soft white sliced loaf with one slice pulled a little away from the rest, crumb showing
gluten-free-white-bread.what: Soft white sliced bread made without wheat gluten.

facts: Despite its name, glutinous rice contains no gluten; its stickiness comes from its starch.
Glutinous rice is eaten across Southeast Asia and Laos, often steamed in bamboo baskets.
Mango sticky rice is a Thai dessert of sweet glutinous rice, coconut milk and ripe mango.
glutinous-rice.visual: a small heap of raw, opaque white short-grain rice, pearly and round
glutinous-rice.what: A short-grain rice that turns very sticky when steamed.

facts: Despite its name, glutinous rice flour contains no gluten; the name refers to its stickiness.
It is made by grinding glutinous rice, a short-grain variety, into a fine powder.
It is used to make mochi in Japan and sweet tangyuan dumplings in China.
glutinous-rice-flour.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, bright white powder, soft and powdery
glutinous-rice-flour.what: A fine, starchy flour that makes chewy, sticky dough.

facts: Glycerine is a simple alcohol that is made from fats and oils, often as a by-product of soap making.
Glycerine helps icing and sugar-craft pieces stay soft, which is why bakers use it in fondant.
The name glycerine comes from the Greek word glykys, meaning sweet.
glycerine.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with clear, thick, syrupy liquid
glycerine.what: A thick, sweet, colourless liquid used to keep cakes moist.

facts: The name comes from Italian, where gnocchi means dumplings.
They are often rolled and ridged so the surface holds sauce.
gnocchi.visual: a small heap of uncooked potato gnocchi, pale cream dumplings with ridged surfaces
gnocchi.what: Small soft dumplings made from potato, flour and egg.

facts: Goat is eaten across Asia, Africa and the Caribbean, and is a staple in many curries.
goat-meat.visual: raw goat meat cut into cubes, dark red and fine-grained, lying directly on the background
goat-meat.what: Lean, gamey meat from young or adult goats.

facts: Cheddar is a cheese named after the village of Cheddar in Somerset, England.
Cheddar-style cheese is made by cheddaring, where curds are stacked and turned to drain the whey.
Goat's milk gives a whiter colour than cow's milk, so many goat's cheeses look pale.
goat-s-cheddar.visual: a block of firm pale cheese with one wedge cut away, showing a close texture
goat-s-cheddar.what: A hard goat's milk cheese, nutty and lightly tangy.

facts: Goat's cheese is often shaped into logs and rolled in herbs or ash for a distinctive look.
Goat's milk cheese is especially associated with France, where it is called chèvre.
Soft goat's cheese is usually eaten fresh, while harder goat's cheeses are aged for longer.
goat-s-cheese-log.visual: a whole log of soft white goat's cheese with a thin white rind, one end cut to show the creamy centre
goat-s-cheese-log.what: A soft, creamy log of goat's cheese, sliced onto toast.

facts: Goats were domesticated thousands of years ago and have long been kept for milk.
Goat's milk is used across many parts of the world, including the Mediterranean and South Asia.
Many soft cheeses, such as chèvre from France, are made from goat's milk.
goat-s-milk.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with creamy white goat's milk
goat-s-milk.what: Milk from goats, with a slightly tangy, sweet flavour.

facts: It is a key seasoning in kimchi and many other Korean dishes.
Its name combines gochu, the Korean word for chilli, with garu, meaning powder.
gochugaru.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with coarse, bright red chilli flakes
gochugaru.what: A coarse Korean chilli flake that is bright red and fruity.

facts: Gochugaru is the Korean red chilli powder used to make kimchi and gochujang.
It is made from dried red chillies that are ground into flakes or fine powder.
Coarse and fine versions exist; the fine kind blends smoothly into sauces.
gochugaru-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine bright red chilli powder
gochugaru-powder.what: A fine, mild-to-hot Korean red chilli powder.

facts: Gochujang is made from chilli powder, glutinous rice, fermented soybeans and salt.
It has been part of Korean cooking for centuries and is used in stews, marinades and sauces.
The name combines gochu, the Korean word for chilli pepper, with jang, a word for fermented paste.
gochujang.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, holding thick glossy red-brown paste
gochujang.what: A thick, sweet-hot red paste from Korean cooking.

facts: Goji berries grow on shrubs of the Lycium genus, which is native to parts of Asia.
The fruit has been used in Chinese cooking for centuries, often in soups, porridges and teas.
Goji is the Chinese name for the fruit, and wolfberry is the common English name for the same plant.
goji-berry.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with dried red goji berries, wrinkled and glossy
goji-berry.what: A small dried red berry with a tangy, chewy bite.

facts: Gold leaf has decorated food in several cultures, including Indian sweets such as mithai.
Gold is largely unreactive, which is why gold leaf is used as an edible decoration.
gold-leaf.visual: a single sheet of thin gold leaf, slightly crinkled, lying flat on the background
gold-leaf.what: Thin edible gold sheets for decorating desserts.

facts: Golden beetroot is a variety of the common beetroot, grown for its roots and leaves.
Beetroot has been cultivated in Europe and the Mediterranean for many centuries.
golden-beetroot.visual: a whole raw golden beetroot, smooth orange-gold skin, stem trimmed short
golden-beetroot.what: A mild, sweet beetroot with gold flesh that won't stain.

facts: Caster sugar is finer than granulated sugar, so it dissolves quickly in batters and creams.
Golden caster sugar is less refined than white sugar, so it keeps a trace of molasses flavour.
Sugar cane and sugar beet are the two main sources of the world's sugar.
golden-caster-sugar.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, pale golden sugar crystals, dry and free-flowing
golden-caster-sugar.what: Fine, pale golden sugar with a faint caramel taste.

facts: Golden Delicious was found as a chance seedling in West Virginia, in the United States.
It is one of the parents of many modern apple varieties, including Gala.
golden-delicious-apple.visual: one whole golden-yellow apple, smooth skin with a faint green tinge and a small stalk, lying on a plain background
golden-delicious-apple.what: A yellow-green apple with a soft, honeyed flavour.

facts: Golden kiwi is a cultivar of Actinidia chinensis, first bred in New Zealand.
Kiwifruit originated in China, where it was long known as the Chinese gooseberry.
golden-kiwi.visual: a whole golden kiwi fruit with smooth golden-brown skin and no fuzz
golden-kiwi.what: A smooth-skinned kiwi with sweet, golden flesh.

facts: Golden syrup is a by-product of refining cane sugar into a thick, amber liquid.
It is a traditional British ingredient in puddings, flapjacks and treacle tart.
golden-syrup.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, full of thick amber golden syrup
golden-syrup.what: A thick amber syrup, made from refined cane sugar.

facts: Golden Wonder is a traditional British maincrop potato, grown in the UK for many years.
Floury potatoes like this one break apart easily, which suits mashing and roasting.
Potatoes originated in the Andes of South America and were brought to Europe in the 16th century.
golden-wonder-potato.visual: a whole raw golden-brown potato with rough russet skin and a few small eyes, lying on its side
golden-wonder-potato.what: An old floury potato with russet skin and rich flavour.

facts: The name means sesame salt in Japanese, with goma meaning sesame and shio meaning salt.
It is sprinkled over rice, vegetables and salads, and is a common table seasoning in Japan.
gomashio.visual: a small heap of pale toasted seeds and coarse white crystals, loose and speckled
gomashio.what: A Japanese sprinkle of toasted sesame seeds and salt.

facts: Gomasio comes from Japan, where it has long been a table seasoning sprinkled over rice.
Traditional recipes grind the sesame and salt in a suribachi, a ridged Japanese mortar.
Sesame has been cultivated for thousands of years, and its seeds are pressed for oil.
gomasio.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of toasted sesame seeds and coarse salt crystals, evenly mixed
gomasio.what: Toasted sesame seeds ground with salt, sprinkled on food.

facts: Good King Henry is an old British pot herb, grown in cottage gardens for centuries.
Its young shoots can be cooked like asparagus, and its leaves like spinach.
good-king-henry.visual: a bunch of fresh, arrow-shaped dark green leaves with pale stems, lying loosely
good-king-henry.what: A leafy perennial green with a spinach-like flavour.

facts: Goose barnacles grow in clusters on rocks battered by Atlantic surf.
The name is linked to an old belief that the barnacles turned into barnacle geese.
In Spain and Portugal they are simmered briefly and eaten by pulling the meat from the stalk.
goose-barnacles.visual: a small heap of raw goose barnacles, each a leathery grey-brown stalk tipped with white and black plates
goose-barnacles.what: A stalked shellfish from Atlantic rocks, popular in Spain.

facts: Geese were domesticated for food thousands of years ago, and roast goose was once a common British festive dish.
Goose breast is dark, like duck, and is usually cooked slowly so the fat renders out and the skin crisps.
Goose fat was once prized in European kitchens for roasting potatoes and for frying.
goose-breast.visual: one whole raw goose breast fillet, dark red meat with a thin layer of pale skin, lying on its side
goose-breast.what: The rich, dark breast meat of a domestic goose.

facts: Goose eggs are much larger than hen's eggs, with a thicker shell and a rich yolk.
Goose eggs have been eaten in many countries since ancient times.
goose-egg.visual: one whole large pale cream goose egg with a smooth shell, lying on its side
goose-egg.what: A very large, rich egg laid by geese.

facts: Goose fat is prized in Europe for roasting potatoes.
In French cooking, goose fat is used in confit, a method of slow-cooking meat submerged in fat.
goose-fat.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of creamy, pale golden fat, set firm
goose-fat.what: Rich, golden fat rendered from a goose, used for cooking.

facts: A traditional Michaelmas dish in England, goose was often eaten in autumn.
In France, goose and duck legs are often cooked as confit, slowly cooked submerged in their own fat.
The leg has darker, richer meat than the breast, and its skin releases a lot of fat when roasted.
goose-leg.visual: a whole raw goose leg, pale skin, thigh and drumstick joined, lying on the background
goose-leg.what: A rich, fatty leg of goose, good for slow roasting.

facts: Gooseberries are native to Europe, northern Africa and western Asia.
Gooseberry fool is a traditional British dessert made from cooked fruit and cream.
Elderflower is often paired with gooseberries, as its floral taste balances their sharpness.
gooseberry.visual: a small heap of firm pale green gooseberries, round and slightly hairy, lying on a plain background
gooseberry.what: A sharp green berry, best cooked with sugar into desserts.

facts: Gooseberries are small, thin-skinned berries that are popular in Britain and northern Europe.
Gooseberry fool is a classic English pudding made by folding fruit pulp into cream.
Gooseberry sauce is a traditional English partner for mackerel.
gooseberry-jam.visual: a small plain glass jar of pale green gooseberry jam, thick and glossy, without a label
gooseberry-jam.what: A tangy jam made from green or red gooseberries.

facts: Gorgonzola is named after the town of Gorgonzola, near Milan in northern Italy.
It is a protected designation of origin, so only cheese made in designated areas of northern Italy can use the name.
The blue veins come from Penicillium moulds added during making, which are pierced so air reaches the cheese.
gorgonzola.visual: a wedge cut from a block of creamy pale ivory blue cheese with bluish-green veins running through it
gorgonzola.what: A creamy Italian blue cheese with a sharp, tangy flavour.

facts: Gorgonzola takes its name from the town of Gorgonzola, near Milan in northern Italy.
Piccante is the Italian word for sharp or spicy, and this version is aged longer than the milder dolce style.
The blue veins come from a mould added during making, which spreads through the paste as the cheese ages.
gorgonzola-piccante.visual: a single wedge of aged blue cheese, cut face showing creamy pale paste marbled with blue-green veins, rind edge visible
gorgonzola-piccante.what: A firm, aged Italian blue cheese with a sharp, bold tang.

facts: Gouda is named after the Dutch town of Gouda, where cheese was traded for centuries.
Gouda is made from cow's milk, and young cheese is soft and mild.
Mature Gouda develops a firmer texture and a deeper, caramel flavour as it ages.
gouda.visual: a block of pale yellow cheese, one wedge cut away, smooth rind edge visible
gouda.what: A mild, sweet Dutch cheese that melts well.

facts: Striped aubergines like this are associated with Sicily and southern Italy.
Aubergine is native to South Asia and was grown in the Mediterranean for many centuries.
Its flesh becomes soft and silky when cooked, which is why it suits roasting and braising.
graffiti-aubergine.visual: one whole raw aubergine, violet and white striped skin, oval shape, lying on its side
graffiti-aubergine.what: A small, striped aubergine with mild, delicate flesh.

facts: Grains of Paradise are the seeds of a plant in the ginger family, native to West Africa.
Medieval European traders sold them as a cheaper alternative to black pepper.
The spice was once known in Europe as Guinea pepper, reflecting its West African origin.
grains-of-paradise.visual: a small heap of glossy, reddish-brown seeds, loose on the surface
grains-of-paradise.what: Peppery West African seeds with a ginger and cardamom note.

facts: Grana Padano is made in the Po Valley in northern Italy.
It is a protected name, so only cheese made in designated areas of northern Italy can use it.
Its name refers to its grainy texture, which suits grating over pasta and risotto.
grana-padano.visual: a wedge of hard pale golden cheese with a thick natural rind, grainy and crumbly
grana-padano.what: A hard, milder cousin of parmesan, good for grating.

facts: This style of bread is made with malted wheat flakes, which give it a nutty flavour.
Malting means sprouting grain and then drying it, which gives the bread its sweet, toasty flavour.
Breads made from cracked and whole grains have been baked across Europe for centuries.
granary-bread.visual: one whole brown granary loaf with a speckled crust and visible grain flakes, on a plain background
granary-bread.what: A brown loaf with malted grain flakes and a chewy crumb.

facts: The variety began as a seedling grown by Maria Ann Smith in New South Wales, Australia.
Its name honours Maria Ann Smith, the orchardist known as Granny Smith.
Its firm flesh holds its shape when baked, so it is a classic choice for apple pies and tarts.
granny-smith-apple.visual: one whole bright green apple with a short brown stalk, smooth and shiny, lying on its side on a plain background
granny-smith-apple.what: A crisp, tart green apple from Australia.

facts: Early versions of granola appeared in the United States in the 1800s, made from baked grains.
The clusters form when oats are bound with sugar or honey and then baked until firm.
granola.visual: a small loose heap of golden baked oat clusters, glossy and crisp
granola.what: Baked oats, nuts and honey in crunchy clusters.

facts: Sugar is made from sugar cane or sugar beet, then refined into white crystals.
Granulated sugar is a standard sugar for everyday baking and tea.
The word sugar comes from the Sanskrit sharkara, meaning grit or gravel.
granulated-sugar.visual: a small heap of white granulated sugar crystals, loose and sparkling
granulated-sugar.what: Crystals of refined sugar used for baking and sweetening.

facts: Grape juice is made by crushing grapes and pressing out the liquid before it ferments.
Grapes were cultivated in the region between the Caucasus and the Middle East thousands of years ago.
grape-juice.visual: a clear drinking glass of deep purple grape juice, filled to near the top
grape-juice.what: Sweet juice pressed from grapes, for poaching and jelly.

facts: Grape molasses, called pekmez in Turkish, is made by slowly boiling down grape must.
It is traditional across Turkey, the Balkans and the eastern Mediterranean, often served with tahini or on bread.
Its thick texture and tang make it a sweetener for desserts and dips in the region.
grape-molasses.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, dark brown grape molasses, glossy
grape-molasses.what: Thick, dark syrup boiled from grapes, tangy and sweet.

facts: Grapefruit is believed to have arisen in the Caribbean, probably from a cross between pomelo and orange.
Grapefruit is often halved and grilled with a little sugar, or segmented for breakfast.
grapefruit.visual: a whole yellow grapefruit with a slightly textured skin, lying on its side
grapefruit.what: A large, tangy citrus fruit with a slightly bitter taste.

facts: Grapefruit is thought to be a natural cross between the pomelo and the sweet orange, first noted in Barbados.
Its name is said to come from the way the fruit grows in clusters, like grapes on a stem.
Curd is made by cooking citrus juice with eggs, sugar and butter until thick, the same method as lemon curd.
grapefruit-curd.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale pink-yellow grapefruit curd, thick and glossy
grapefruit-curd.what: A sharp, slightly bitter citrus curd, rich and smooth.

facts: Grapefruit is thought to have arisen in Barbados, probably as a cross between the pomelo and the sweet orange.
Grapefruit juice is a common breakfast drink in many countries.
grapefruit-juice.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with pale pink grapefruit juice
grapefruit-juice.what: A tangy, bitter-sweet juice pressed from grapefruit.

facts: Grapeseed oil is made from the seeds left over after grapes are crushed for wine.
Its mild taste and high smoke point make it popular for frying and for salad dressings.
Grapeseed oil is mainly used for cooking, though it is also found in some cosmetics.
grapeseed-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with pale golden oil, with a plain cap
grapeseed-oil.what: A light, neutral oil pressed from the seeds of grapes.

facts: Grappa is made from the pomace, the leftover skins, seeds and stalks left after winemaking.
It is traditionally sipped after a meal in Italy.
Grappa is usually clear, though some are aged in wooden barrels to take on colour.
grappa.visual: a clear drinking glass part-filled with a colourless spirit, plain background
grappa.what: An Italian brandy distilled from grape skins and pulp.

facts: Cheesemaking dates back thousands of years, in many regions of the world.
Pre-grated cheese often has a coating, such as potato starch, to keep strands from clumping.
grated-cheese.visual: a small heap of fine pale yellow shredded cheese strands, on a plain background
grated-cheese.what: Shredded melting cheese for pizzas and pasta bakes.

facts: Its name comes from grav, the Swedish word for grave, because salmon was once buried in the ground.
The dish is made mainly in Sweden and other parts of Scandinavia, and it is often served on rye bread.
Dill is the main herb used, and it gives the fish a fresh, grassy flavour.
gravadlax.visual: a few thin, translucent slices of orange-pink salmon laid flat on a plain background, edges slightly curled
gravadlax.what: Salmon salted and sweetened with dill, then sliced thin.

facts: Some versions also use goat's milk, and it is especially associated with Crete.
graviera.visual: a block of pale golden hard cheese, one thick slice cut away, a few small holes visible
graviera.what: A nutty Greek hard cheese made from sheep's milk.

facts: Gravy granules are a dry mix of starch, flavourings and salt that dissolves quickly in hot liquid.
Gravy is traditionally thickened with flour and the juices from roasted meat, which these granules replace.
Gravy is served across the UK with roast dinners, mashed potatoes and Yorkshire pudding.
gravy-granules.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine golden-brown granules, level and smooth
gravy-granules.what: A dried powder that thickens and flavours quick gravy.

facts: They are a type of common bean, Phaseolus vulgaris, grown widely in the United States.
Dried beans are usually soaked before cooking, and they keep their shape through long simmering.
great-northern-beans.visual: a small heap of dried white Great Northern beans, oval and smooth
great-northern-beans.what: Mild white beans that keep their shape in soups.

facts: Oregano belongs to the mint family, and its name comes from Greek words meaning mountain and joy.
It grows wild on dry, rocky hillsides across Greece and the wider Mediterranean.
greek-oregano.visual: a small loose bunch of fresh oregano sprigs, grey-green leaves and woody stems, lying on the background
greek-oregano.what: A wild, pungent herb with a resinous bite.

facts: Greek salad dressing is typically olive oil, lemon juice or vinegar, and dried oregano.
Oregano is native to the Mediterranean and is widely used in Greek cooking.
Olive oil is central to Greek cooking and is often poured over salads uncooked.
greek-salad-dressing.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with pale golden-green dressing and visible flecks of herb
greek-salad-dressing.what: A tangy dressing of olive oil, lemon and oregano.

facts: Greek yoghurt is strained to remove much of its whey, which makes it thicker than standard yoghurt.
Traditionally it was made from sheep's or goat's milk in Greece, though cow's milk is now more common.
greek-yoghurt.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, creamy white yoghurt with a smooth surface
greek-yoghurt.what: A thick, strained yoghurt with a rich, tangy taste.

facts: Green beans are the immature pods of the common bean, a plant first domesticated in the Americas.
They are picked young, before the seeds inside grow large, which is why they are eaten whole.
Runner beans are a different, larger species of pod, usually sliced before cooking.
green-beans.visual: a small bunch of fresh green beans, slender pods with stem ends trimmed
green-beans.what: Long, slender pods eaten whole, young and tender.

facts: Green cabbage is a staple in Eastern Europe, where it is used in soups, stuffed rolls and sauerkraut.
Sauerkraut is shredded cabbage fermented in salt, a method that keeps it for months.
green-cabbage.visual: one whole green cabbage, tight pale-green outer leaves, lying on its side
green-cabbage.what: A round, mild cabbage with tightly packed green leaves.

facts: Cardamom is native to the forests of southern India and Sri Lanka.
Green cardamom was traded along ancient spice routes and is used in coffee, tea and sweets.
green-cardamom-pods.visual: a small heap of pale green cardamom pods, papery and slightly rounded, lying loosely together
green-cardamom-pods.what: Aromatic seed pods with a floral, eucalyptus-like flavour.

facts: Chillies are native to the Americas and spread to Europe and Asia after European contact.
Green chillies are unripe; as they mature they often turn red, yellow or orange.
green-chilli.visual: a whole fresh green chilli with glossy smooth skin and a short stalk
green-chilli.what: A fresh, hot, grassy chilli, picked while still unripe.

facts: Figs are among the earliest cultivated fruits, grown in the Middle East for thousands of years.
In Mediterranean regions, fresh figs are often served with soft cheeses and cured ham.
The Latin name for fig, ficus, gave many European languages their word for the fruit.
green-fig.visual: a whole fresh green fig, pale yellow-green skin, slightly soft, with a short stem
green-fig.what: A pale-skinned fig, delicate and sweet when ripe.

facts: Green goddess dressing takes its name from a 1921 stage play, The Green Goddess.
The dressing is said to have been created at a San Francisco hotel, and is often served on salads.
green-goddess-dressing.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl holding a smooth pale green creamy dressing flecked with dark green herbs
green-goddess-dressing.what: A creamy green herb dressing, usually with anchovy.

facts: Grapes have been cultivated for thousands of years, in the Caucasus and the Near East.
Table grapes are eaten fresh and are also used in salads and served with cheese.
Many green grapes sold in shops are seedless varieties grown for eating fresh.
green-grapes.visual: a small bunch of pale green grapes on a stem, lying on a plain background
green-grapes.what: Crisp, sweet grapes with pale green skins.

facts: Its name comes from the Portuguese word jaca, which was itself borrowed from Malayalam.
Young jackfruit is used in savoury curries, while ripe fruit is eaten sweet.
green-jackfruit.visual: one whole unripe green jackfruit, large oval shape, knobbly spiny skin, lying on its side
green-jackfruit.what: An unripe tropical fruit that shreds like pulled meat.

facts: Lentils are among the oldest cultivated crops, grown in the Near East for thousands of years.
Puy lentils, grown in the Auvergne region of France, are a well-known green variety.
They are usually simmered gently until just tender, and they hold their shape well.
green-lentils.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dry, speckled green lentils, small and flat
green-lentils.what: Small, firm lentils that keep their shape when cooked.

facts: Green-lipped mussels are native to New Zealand and are farmed on ropes hanging in the sea.
Their shells have a distinct green rim, which gives them their name.
They are often steamed open and are sold fresh or frozen around the world.
green-lipped-mussels.visual: a small heap of raw green-lipped mussels in their shells, the pale green edges of the shells visible, lying on a plain background
green-lipped-mussels.what: A large New Zealand shellfish with a green-edged shell.

facts: Green mangoes are shredded into salads in Thailand, Vietnam and other South-East Asian cooking.
Their firm flesh holds its shape, so they are often pickled with salt, chilli or sugar.
green-mango.visual: one whole unripe green mango with smooth, firm pale-green skin and a slightly pointed end
green-mango.what: An unripe mango, firm, sour and crisp.

facts: Tapenade, a paste of black olives, capers and anchovies, comes from Provence in southern France.
Olives are soaked in brine or salt before eating, because raw olives are too bitter to enjoy.
green-olive-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, olive-green paste with a glossy surface
green-olive-paste.what: A smooth, bright green spread made from crushed olives.

facts: The olive tree has been cultivated around the Mediterranean for thousands of years.
Green olives are picked before they fully ripen, then cured, often in brine.
Spain is a major producer of table olives, including green varieties.
green-olives.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of brined green olives, bright green and glossy
green-olives.what: Unripe olives, picked green and cured in brine.

facts: Green papaya is the unripe fruit, eaten as a vegetable in many Southeast Asian dishes.
Som tam, the spicy green papaya salad of Thailand, is pounded together in a mortar.
Papaya is native to the tropical Americas and now grows across the world's warm regions.
green-papaya.visual: a whole unripe green papaya, firm pale-green skin and an oval shape, lying on its side
green-papaya.what: Unripe papaya, firm and pale green, shredded for salads.

facts: Peas have been grown as food since ancient times, in the Near East and beyond.
Dried split peas were a staple of medieval European diets, used in soups and pottages.
green-peas.visual: a small loose heap of fresh green peas, plump and bright green, smooth-skinned, on a plain background
green-peas.what: Small sweet seeds picked young from long green pods.

facts: Green peppers are unripe bell peppers, and they turn red, yellow or orange as they ripen.
Peppers are native to the Americas and were carried to Europe and Asia by traders.
The name bell pepper comes from the fruit's bell-like shape.
green-pepper.visual: a whole glossy green bell pepper with smooth skin and a small green stalk cap
green-pepper.what: An unripe bell pepper with a fresh, grassy bite.

facts: Green peppercorns are picked before they ripen, when they are still soft and green.
They come from the same vine as black and white pepper, Piper nigrum.
Green peppercorns are often used in creamy French pepper sauces.
green-peppercorns.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of soft green peppercorns, loosely piled
green-peppercorns.what: Unripe pepper berries with a mild, fresh flavour.

facts: Plantains are closely related to bananas but are starchier and usually cooked before eating.
In the Caribbean and Latin America, green plantain is often sliced, fried and flattened into tostones.
green-plantain.visual: a whole raw green plantain, firm green skin with dark streaks, slightly curved
green-plantain.what: An unripe, starchy fruit that is cooked before eating.

facts: Shiso is a member of the mint family, and it is widely grown across East Asia.
In Japan, the leaves are used as a garnish and wrapped around sashimi or tempura.
Green shiso is also called perilla, and its seeds and leaves are both used in cooking.
green-shiso.visual: a small bunch of bright green, jagged-edged shiso leaves on thin pale stems
green-shiso.what: A Japanese herb leaf with a mint-basil flavour.

facts: Sichuan pepper is not related to black pepper; it is the husk of a berry from the prickly ash tree.
It is a traditional part of Sichuan cooking in south-western China, often paired with chilli.
Green peppercorns are picked before they fully ripen, which gives a brighter, more lemony taste.
green-sichuan-peppercorns.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of small green peppercorns, loose, seen from above
green-sichuan-peppercorns.what: Small green berry husks with a citrusy, numbing bite.

facts: Split peas are dried peas that have been split along their natural seam, so no soaking is needed.
In Britain, slow-cooked green split peas traditionally make pease pudding and thick soup.
green-split-peas.visual: a small loose heap of dried pale green split peas, each a flat halved disc
green-split-peas.what: Dried green peas that cook down into a thick soup.

facts: Green tea leaves are dried or steamed soon after picking, which stops them oxidising.
Tea was first cultivated in China, and green tea is now grown across East Asia.
In Japan, matcha is a powdered form of green tea used in desserts and drinks.
green-tea.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, filled with dry loose green tea leaves
green-tea.what: A lightly processed tea with a fresh, grassy flavour.

facts: Green tomatoes are simply tomatoes picked before they have turned red.
Fried green tomatoes are a classic dish in the American South.
green-tomato.visual: one whole firm green tomato, pale green and unripe, lying on its side
green-tomato.what: An unripe, firm and tart tomato for chutney or frying.

facts: Greengages are plums, so they belong to the same family as cherries and apricots.
The name comes from Sir William Gage, who is said to have brought the plum to England.
Greengages are often used in tarts, jams and compotes, where their sweetness holds up well.
greengage.visual: one whole greengage plum, round and yellowish-green with a soft bloom
greengage.what: A small, round green plum with honey-sweet flesh.

facts: Greengages are a type of plum, named after Sir William Gage who brought them to England.
Greengages are a type of European plum, prized for their sweet, honeyed flesh.
They are grown across Europe and are often made into jam, compote or preserves.
greengage-jam.visual: a plain glass jar without a label filled with pale golden-green greengage jam, glossy surface
greengage-jam.what: A sweet, delicate jam made from small green plums.

facts: Greenland halibut lives in cold northern Atlantic and Arctic waters, often at considerable depth.
Despite its name it is a righteye flounder, not a true halibut.
Its firm, oily flesh suits smoking, and it is sold smoked in several northern countries.
greenland-halibut.visual: a raw fillet of Greenland halibut, pale pinkish-white flesh with a fine grain, lying flat
greenland-halibut.what: A deep-water flatfish with rich flesh, often smoked.

facts: Gremolata is the classic finishing mix served with osso buco, a dish from Milan.
The chopped herbs and zest are added at the end so their flavour stays fresh.
Lemon zest is the thin coloured peel of the fruit, grated or finely cut.
gremolata.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of finely chopped green herbs and bright yellow zest
gremolata.what: A bright garnish of lemon zest, parsley and garlic.

facts: Grenadine takes its name from the French word grenade, meaning pomegranate.
It is often used in cocktails such as the Tequila Sunrise.
Some commercial versions use flavourings and colouring instead of real pomegranate juice.
grenadine.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of bright red syrup
grenadine.what: A sweet, bright red syrup made from pomegranate juice.

facts: Duck breast is usually cooked skin-side down, so the fat slowly renders out and the skin crisps.
Peking duck is a famous Chinese dish of roasted duck served with thin pancakes.
gressingham-duck.visual: a whole raw duck with pale golden-cream skin, plump and neatly prepared, lying on its breast
gressingham-duck.what: A lean British duck with dark, richly flavoured meat.

facts: In the Mediterranean, the roe of grey mullet is salted and dried to make bottarga.
Mullet are known for leaping out of the water, a behaviour seen in many coastal areas.
grey-mullet.visual: a whole grey mullet, silver-grey back and pale belly, lying on its side with scales visible
grey-mullet.what: A mild, firm-fleshed fish with a silver-grey skin.

facts: Cheeses such as halloumi come from Cyprus and are traditionally made from sheep's and goat's milk.
Their firm texture lets them be grilled or fried without melting into a puddle.
The curd is traditionally heated in whey, which helps give the cheese its squeaky texture.
grilling-cheese.visual: a block of firm pale cheese with one thick slice cut away and lying beside it, on a plain background
grilling-cheese.what: A firm, squeaky cheese that holds its shape when grilled.

facts: Grissini come from the Piedmont region of north-west Italy, where they have been made for centuries.
They were traditionally baked as a thin, dry snack to be eaten with cured meats or cheese.
Their name is the plural of grissino, the Italian word for a breadstick.
grissini.visual: a small heap of thin, golden, crisp breadsticks lying loosely together
grissini.what: Thin, crisp Italian breadsticks, good with cured meats.

facts: Grits are a traditional maize dish of the Southern United States.
Hominy grits are made from maize soaked in an alkaline solution, a process called nixtamalisation.
In the Southern United States, grits are often served with butter, cheese or gravy.
grits.visual: a small heap of coarse yellow corn grits, loosely piled with a granular texture
grits.what: A coarse, porridge-like meal ground from dried maize.

facts: Ground almonds are made by grinding whole or blanched almonds into a fine meal.
Ground almonds are central to frangipane, a French almond cream used in tarts.
Almond meal has long been used in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern sweets, including marzipan.
ground-almonds.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, pale beige ground almonds
ground-almonds.what: Almonds ground to a fine meal for baking.

facts: Cardamom is the seed pods of plants in the ginger family.
The plant is native to the forests of southern India and Sri Lanka.
Cardamom is widely used in Indian cooking, Middle Eastern coffee and Scandinavian baking.
ground-cardamom.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale greenish-brown ground spice, fine and dusty
ground-cardamom.what: A sweet, perfumed spice powder ground from cardamom pods.

facts: Cassia comes from several Cinnamomum species, mainly grown in China, and is sold as a cheaper cinnamon.
Its bark is dried and rolled into quills, or ground, and has a stronger, coarser taste than true cinnamon.
Cassia has been traded across Asia and the Middle East for thousands of years.
ground-cassia.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of reddish-brown ground cassia powder
ground-cassia.what: Bold, strong-tasting powder ground from cassia tree bark.

facts: Cinnamon is the inner bark of trees in the genus Cinnamomum.
Ceylon cinnamon, from Sri Lanka, is milder than the cassia sold in many shops.
Cinnamon was traded across the Indian Ocean and the Middle East for centuries.
ground-cinnamon.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine reddish-brown ground cinnamon, a loose powder
ground-cinnamon.what: Warm, sweet spice made from ground dried cinnamon bark.

facts: Cloves are the dried flower buds of an evergreen tree native to the Maluku Islands in Indonesia.
Cloves were traded along old spice routes and were prized in Europe and China for centuries.
The name comes from the French clou, meaning nail, after the shape of the dried bud.
ground-cloves.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with fine dark reddish-brown ground clove powder
ground-cloves.what: Dried clove flower buds ground to a strong, warm powder.

facts: Coffee drinking spread from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula before reaching Europe.
Roasting turns the green beans brown and develops the aromatic flavours that make ground coffee distinctive.
ground-coffee.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, filled with dark brown ground coffee
ground-coffee.what: Roasted coffee beans ground into powder for brewing.

facts: Coriander seeds are the dried fruit of the coriander plant, whose leaves are called cilantro in North America.
Ground coriander is a common ingredient in curry blends across India, the Middle East and North Africa.
ground-coriander.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with fine, pale brownish-yellow ground coriander powder
ground-coriander.what: A mellow, citrusy spice made by grinding coriander seeds.

facts: Cumin is the seed of a small herb in the parsley family, native to the eastern Mediterranean.
Cumin is widely used in Indian, Mexican and North African cooking.
ground-cumin.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, pale brown ground cumin powder
ground-cumin.what: A warm, earthy spice ground from dried cumin seeds.

facts: Fennel is a Mediterranean plant whose seeds have been used as a spice for centuries.
Ground fennel is a common ingredient in Italian sausage seasoning.
Fennel seeds are the dried fruit of the plant, which is related to parsley.
ground-fennel.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine pale green-brown fennel powder
ground-fennel.what: A fine powder ground from dried fennel seeds.

facts: Fenugreek is a plant of the pea family, and its seeds are used as a spice.
Ground fenugreek is used in many Ethiopian spice blends, such as berbere.
Its Latin name, foenum graecum, means Greek hay.
ground-fenugreek.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine yellow-brown powder
ground-fenugreek.what: A bitter, maple-scented powder used in spice blends.

facts: Galangal is a relative of ginger and is native to Southeast Asia.
It is a key ingredient in Thai curry pastes, where the fresh root is usually used.
Ground galangal keeps on the shelf longer than the fresh root.
ground-galangal.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale golden-brown ground galangal powder
ground-galangal.what: Dried, peppery root powder from the galangal plant.

facts: Ginger is native to tropical Asia, and its rhizome has been used in cooking for thousands of years.
Ground ginger is made by drying the root and grinding it into a fine powder.
ground-ginger.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl holding a small heap of fine pale-brown ground ginger powder
ground-ginger.what: Dried, powdered ginger root with a warm, spicy flavour.

facts: Ground ginger is made by drying ginger root and grinding it into a fine powder.
It is a traditional ingredient in British gingerbread and parkin.
Ginger is thought to come from Southeast Asia and spread along ancient trade routes.
ground-ginger-spice.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine pale golden-brown ground ginger powder
ground-ginger-spice.what: A dry, peppery powder made from ground ginger root.

facts: Mace is the lacy outer covering of the nutmeg seed, dried before it is ground.
Mace has a warm, slightly citrus flavour that is milder than nutmeg.
It is used in British and Indian cooking, in cakes, sauces and sausages.
ground-mace.visual: a small heap of fine, orange-brown ground spice, loose and powdery
ground-mace.what: A warm, fine spice ground from the red coat around nutmeg.

facts: Nutmeg is the seed of the nutmeg tree, and mace is the lacy red covering around it.
Nutmeg was once highly valued in Europe and traded from islands in what is now Indonesia.
It is best grated fresh, as the flavour fades quickly once the spice has been ground.
ground-nutmeg.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, pale-brown ground nutmeg
ground-nutmeg.what: A warm, nutty spice from a tropical tree's seed.

facts: Turmeric is the rhizome of a plant related to ginger, grown in tropical South Asia.
The roots are boiled, dried and ground into the powder that gives curries their golden colour.
Turmeric has been used in South Asian cooking for centuries, both for flavour and colour.
ground-turmeric.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of bright golden-yellow turmeric powder
ground-turmeric.what: A bright yellow spice ground from dried turmeric root.

facts: It is milder than black pepper and is often used in pale sauces, where black specks would show.
White pepper is widely used in Chinese and French cooking, especially in pale sauces and soups.
ground-white-pepper.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl holding a fine, pale cream-coloured white pepper powder
ground-white-pepper.what: It is a pale, hot powder ground from peppercorns.

facts: Groundnut is another name for the peanut, which is a legume rather than a true nut.
Groundnut oil is widely used in West Africa, China and India for frying.
It has a high smoke point, so it suits deep-frying and stir-frying.
groundnut-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden oil
groundnut-oil.what: A light, high-heat oil pressed from peanuts.

facts: Groupers are large fish of the sea bass family, Serranidae, found in warm seas around the world.
In the Caribbean and the Gulf of Mexico, grouper is a popular fish for grilling, frying and stews.
grouper.visual: one whole raw grouper with speckled reddish-brown skin, lying on its side
grouper.what: A large, mild sea fish with firm, white, meaty flesh.

facts: Grouse shooting season on the British moors traditionally opens each August.
Grouse is traditionally roasted and served pink, a style popular in British game cookery.
grouse.visual: one whole raw plucked red grouse, plump and lying breast-down on a plain pale background
grouse.what: A small game bird from British moors, with rich dark meat.

facts: Gruyère takes its name from the Swiss village of Gruyères in the canton of Fribourg.
It is made from cow's milk and aged for several months, which gives it a firm, nutty texture.
It melts smoothly, which is why it is a classic cheese for fondue and French onion soup.
gruyere.visual: one wedge of pale yellow hard cheese, small holes visible, pale rind edge, lying flat on the background
gruyere.what: A nutty, savoury Swiss cheese for fondue.

facts: Guacamole comes from the Nahuatl word ahuacamolli, meaning avocado sauce.
Avocados are native to Mexico and Central America, where they have been eaten for thousands of years.
Traditionally guacamole is mashed by hand in a stone mortar called a molcajete.
guacamole.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of bright green, smooth mashed avocado dip with a few small pieces
guacamole.what: A dip of mashed avocado with lime and coriander.

facts: Guajillo is the dried form of the mirasol chilli, which is grown widely in Mexico.
It is often soaked, then blended into sauces, adobos and marinades.
Toasting the dried pods brings out a bright, berry-like flavour.
guajillo-chilli.visual: one whole dried chilli pod, smooth glossy deep red-brown skin, long and slender, lying on its side
guajillo-chilli.what: A dried, tangy Mexican chilli with a mild to medium heat.

facts: Guanciale comes from the cheek or jowl of the pig and is cured with salt, often with black pepper.
It is a key ingredient in Roman dishes such as carbonara and amatriciana.
Guanciale is left to dry for several weeks before it is ready to eat.
guanciale.visual: a thick cut piece of guanciale, pale pink meat with white fat running through it, lying flat
guanciale.what: Cured pork cheek, air-dried and used in Roman pasta.

facts: Guar is a legume plant grown widely in India, where its beans are eaten as a vegetable.
Guar gum, made from its seeds, is used as a thickener in many processed foods.
The plant suits hot, dry conditions, which is why it is grown across parts of India.
guar-beans.visual: a small heap of long, flat, bright green beans, loose on the surface
guar-beans.what: Flat, crisp green pods eaten across South Asia.

facts: Guava is native to tropical America, and it spread to Asia and Africa through trade.
In Mexico and India, guava is eaten raw, made into jam or juice, or cooked into sweet dishes.
Guava paste, known as goiabada in Brazil, is often served with cheese.
guava.visual: a whole yellow-green guava on a plain background, with one half cut to show pink flesh and small seeds
guava.what: A tropical fruit with a perfumed pink or white flesh.

facts: Guinea fowl were first domesticated in Africa, and were known to the ancient Greeks and Romans.
guinea-fowl.visual: one whole raw guinea fowl, pale plucked skin, plump breast, lying on its back
guinea-fowl.what: A small, lean bird with a mild, slightly gamey flavour.

facts: Guinea fowl were domesticated in Africa and reached Europe in ancient times.
Its meat is darker and firmer than chicken, with a richer flavour.
guinea-fowl-breast.visual: one raw guinea fowl breast, skin on, pale pink-purple meat, lying flat on the background
guinea-fowl-breast.what: Lean, firm meat from a small bird first farmed in Africa.

facts: Gurnard is a fish of the Triglidae family, and its name is thought to come from the grunting sound it makes.
Gurnard is a classic ingredient in bouillabaisse, the fish stew of Marseille in southern France.
Gurnard has firm white flesh that holds its shape well when poached or grilled.
gurnard.visual: a whole red-pink gurnard fish with spiky fins and a large bony head, lying on its side
gurnard.what: A firm, sweet-fleshed sea fish with a bony, spiky head.

facts: Gyoza are Japanese dumplings adapted from Chinese jiaozi, and are often dipped in soy and vinegar.
Gyoza dipping sauce is commonly a mix of soy sauce, rice vinegar and chilli oil.
The dip is served alongside the dumplings in Japanese restaurants and home kitchens.
gyoza-dipping-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of glossy dark brown dipping liquid
gyoza-dipping-sauce.what: A tangy soy and vinegar dip for dumplings.

facts: Gyoza originated in China and were adapted in Japan, where they are usually pan-fried.
A gyoza wrapper is folded into a half-moon and pleated along one edge before cooking.
The name gyoza is the Japanese reading of the Chinese word jiaozi, meaning dumpling.
gyoza-wrapper.visual: a neat small stack of round, thin, pale dumpling wrappers, lightly dusted with flour
gyoza-wrapper.what: A thin round dough wrapper for Japanese-style dumplings.

facts: The habanero chilli is thought to take its name from Havana, the capital of Cuba.
Habanero chillies are associated with the Yucatan peninsula of Mexico and the Caribbean.
Habanero sauces often combine the chillies with fruit such as mango or pineapple, and vinegar.
habanero-hot-sauce.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle, full of bright orange-red sauce
habanero-hot-sauce.what: A fiery, fruity sauce made from habanero chillies.

facts: The habanero chilli is native to the Yucatán peninsula in Mexico, where it has been grown for centuries.
Its fruity aroma suits tropical-style hot sauces, though its heat is stronger than a jalapeño's.
habanero-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine orange-red chilli powder
habanero-powder.what: A fine, fiery powder ground from dried habanero chillies.

facts: Haddock is a member of the cod family and is found mainly in the North Atlantic.
Smoked haddock is a classic British ingredient, including the Scottish Arbroath smokie.
Haddock is a traditional choice in British fish and chip shops.
haddock-fillet.visual: a raw skinless haddock fillet, firm flaky white flesh, lying flat
haddock-fillet.what: A mild, flaky white fish, often smoked or used in chowder.

facts: Haggis is traditionally cooked inside a sheep's stomach, though synthetic casings are now common.
It is Scotland's national dish and is often eaten on Burns Night in January.
It is traditionally served with mashed swede, called neeps, and mashed potatoes, called tatties.
haggis.visual: a portion of crumbly pale grey-brown haggis, served on a small plain white plate
haggis.what: A Scottish dish of spiced sheep offal and oats.

facts: Hairy bittercress is a common weed of gardens and cultivated ground across much of the world.
It belongs to the cabbage family, which includes watercress and mustard.
Its seedpods burst open suddenly when touched, scattering seeds widely, which is how it spreads.
hairy-bittercress.visual: a small bunch of hairy bittercress, bright green rosette leaves with tiny white flowers
hairy-bittercress.what: A small wild cress with peppery, slightly bitter leaves.

facts: Hake is a relative of cod, and it is widely eaten in Spain and Portugal.
In Spain hake is called merluza, and it features in many classic seafood dishes.
Hake has delicate flesh that flakes easily, so it is best cooked gently.
hake-fillet.visual: a single raw hake fillet with pearly white flesh and a flaky texture, lying flat
hake-fillet.what: A mild white fish with soft, delicate flakes.

facts: In the Basque Country, hake is often cooked in a sauce of garlic, parsley and stock called salsa verde.
Hake has soft, flaky flesh that breaks into large flakes when cooked.
hake-steak.visual: a raw hake steak, a thick cross-cut slice of pale white flesh with a central bone, lying flat on the background
hake-steak.what: A mild white fish related to cod, sold in steaks.

facts: Halibut is a large flatfish found in cold northern seas, including the North Atlantic and North Pacific.
Its name is traditionally said to come from holy flatfish, as it was eaten on holy days.
Its dense flesh holds its shape well when roasted or seared.
halibut-fillet.visual: one raw halibut fillet, firm pale white flesh with a faint grain, skin removed, lying flat
halibut-fillet.what: A firm, mild white fish that sears and roasts well.

facts: Halibut are large flatfish that live on the seabed in cold northern waters.
Young halibut swim upright, and their eyes gradually move to one side of the head as they grow.
The name is thought to come from words meaning holy flatfish, as the fish was often eaten on religious days.
halibut-steak.visual: one thick cross-cut halibut steak, firm white flesh around a central bone, pinkish-white edge
halibut-steak.what: A thick cross-cut slice of a large flatfish, good grilled.

facts: Halloumi comes from Cyprus, where it has been made for centuries.
Traditionally it is made from goat's or sheep's milk, sometimes mixed with cow's milk.
It has a high melting point, so it can be fried or grilled without melting.
halloumi.visual: a whole rectangular block of pale white halloumi cheese, with one thick slice cut away and lying beside it
halloumi.what: A firm Cypriot cheese that holds its shape when grilled.

facts: The name halva comes from an Arabic word meaning sweet.
Sesame is one of the oldest cultivated oilseed crops in the world.
halva.visual: a thick cut slab of pale tan sesame halva, crumbly and fibrous, with a clean cut face
halva.what: A crumbly sweet made from ground sesame seeds and sugar.

facts: A ham hock is the joint from the lower leg of a pig, usually salted or smoked before cooking.
Pea and ham soup is a traditional British dish, and a ham hock is often simmered to make its base.
Slow simmering draws flavour and gelatine from the bone and skin into the liquid.
ham-hock-stock.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with clear amber stock, its surface smooth and still
ham-hock-stock.what: A savoury liquid made by simmering a smoked ham hock.

facts: Ham is pork from the hind leg of the pig, cured or cooked and often served at celebrations.
Curing with salt was once a way to preserve meat, and many hams are still cured in this way.
ham-on-the-bone.visual: a whole cooked ham on the bone, glazed golden-brown, its fat cap lightly scored
ham-on-the-bone.what: A whole cooked ham, still on the bone, carved for feasts.

facts: Stock is a liquid made by simmering bones, meat or vegetables in water, and forms the base of many soups.
Curing pork with salt has preserved meat for centuries and gives ham its distinctive taste.
ham-stock.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of clear golden-brown stock
ham-stock.what: A salty, smoky broth made by simmering cured ham bones.

facts: Hard-boiled eggs are a key part of the Scotch egg, a British snack of sausage meat wrapped around an egg.
A firm yolk and white make a hard-boiled egg easy to slice, so it is common in salads and sandwiches.
hard-boiled-egg.visual: one whole peeled hard-boiled egg, smooth and white, lying on its side
hard-boiled-egg.what: An egg cooked in its shell until the yolk is firm.

facts: Goat's cheese has been made for thousands of years, and hard versions are aged for weeks or longer.
hard-goat-s-cheese.visual: a wedge of pale firm goat's cheese, cut flat to show a close white interior, lying on its side on a plain background
hard-goat-s-cheese.what: A firm, aged goat's cheese for grating or shaving.

facts: Hare is closely related to rabbit but larger, with darker, more strongly flavoured meat.
Jugged hare is a traditional dish in which the meat is slowly stewed in a sealed earthenware jug.
Hares have been hunted for food in Europe since prehistoric times.
hare.visual: one whole raw skinned hare, pale pinkish-red, lying on its side
hare.what: Dark, rich wild game meat from a relative of the rabbit.

facts: Hare is a wild game meat, and the saddle is the prized loin running along the back.
hare-saddle.visual: a raw hare saddle, a long dark red cut from the back, lying flat on the background
hare-saddle.what: The long, lean back cut of a wild hare.

facts: The name haricot is French and is applied to many small white bean varieties.
Haricot beans originated in the Americas and reached Europe after voyages of exploration.
Dried haricot beans are usually soaked overnight before they are simmered or baked.
haricot-beans.visual: a small heap of dried small white haricot beans, smooth and oval, loosely piled
haricot-beans.what: Small white beans used in cassoulet and baked beans.

facts: Harissa is most associated with Tunisia, where it is a staple of the local cuisine.
Traditional harissa is made by pounding dried chillies with garlic, caraway, coriander and olive oil.
The name is thought to come from an Arabic word meaning to pound or crush.
harissa.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, deep red chilli paste, glossy and smooth
harissa.what: A fiery North African paste of chilli, garlic and spices.

facts: Harissa is a chilli condiment widely used in Tunisia, Algeria and Morocco.
The name is often linked to an Arabic verb meaning to pound or crush.
The dried powder is stirred into soups, stews and couscous, or rubbed onto meat.
harissa-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with fine brick-red powder
harissa-powder.what: A fiery North African spice mix of chilli and caraway.

facts: Hash comes from the French word hacher, meaning to chop.
Hash browns are a traditional breakfast food in the United States and Canada.
They are made from grated potato, squeezed dry, then pan-fried.
hash-browns.visual: two golden fried hash brown patties, crisp and shredded in texture, on a plain white plate
hash-browns.what: Shredded potato patties, fried until crisp and golden.

facts: The Hass avocado grew from a seedling raised in California in the early twentieth century.
Avocados are native to Mexico and Central America, where they have been eaten for a very long time.
Its soft, buttery flesh makes it the usual base for guacamole.
hass-avocado.visual: one whole ripe fruit with dark purple-black bumpy skin, pear-shaped, lying on its side
hass-avocado.what: A creamy, pear-shaped fruit with dark, bumpy skin.

facts: Hatch chiles are named after the town of Hatch in southern New Mexico, where they are grown.
They are traditionally roasted over flame, which blisters the skin and brings out their sweetness.
hatch-chile.visual: one whole long green Hatch chile pepper, glossy skin, lying on its side on the background
hatch-chile.what: A green chile from New Mexico with a smoky, sweet flavour.

facts: Hatcho miso takes its name from the Hatcho district of Okazaki in Aichi Prefecture, Japan.
It is made from soybeans, salt and koji mould, then aged for a long time.
Like other miso, it is used in soups, glazes and marinades.
hatcho-miso.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dark reddish-brown miso paste, thick and glossy with a smooth surface
hatcho-miso.what: A dark, dense soybean paste that is intensely savoury.

facts: Havarti is named after the Danish farm where it was first made, according to tradition.
The cheese is made from cow's milk and is often eaten sliced in sandwiches or melted.
havarti.visual: a block of pale yellow havarti with one wedge cut away, showing small holes
havarti.what: A mild, buttery Danish cheese with a gentle tang.

facts: Black lava salt gets its colour from charcoal added during production.
Hawaiian sea salt is traditionally produced by evaporating sea water in shallow ponds.
Salt has been traded and used for seasoning for thousands of years.
hawaiian-black-lava-salt.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of coarse black salt crystals, dark grey-black and grainy
hawaiian-black-lava-salt.what: Coarse sea salt mixed with charcoal, for finishing dishes.

facts: Alaea salt gets its red colour from alaea, an iron-rich volcanic clay from Hawaii.
It is traditionally used to season kalua pig, pork cooked in an underground oven.
Hawaiians have harvested salt from sea water in shallow ponds for centuries.
hawaiian-red-alaea-salt.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of coarse, brick-red salt crystals
hawaiian-red-alaea-salt.what: A coarse red sea salt coloured by volcanic clay.

facts: Hawaij is a spice mix from Yemen, and the soup version is built around turmeric and black pepper.
A separate blend, flavoured with ginger, is used to season coffee.
Spice blends like this are part of everyday cooking across Yemen.
hawaij.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine yellow-brown ground spice
hawaij.what: A Yemeni blend of ground spices for soups and coffee.

facts: Hazelnuts are the fruit of the hazel tree, and Turkey is one of the largest producers.
Hazelnut spreads are made by grinding roasted nuts into a paste, sometimes with sugar and oil.
Hazelnuts have been gathered since prehistoric times and appear in archaeological sites across Europe.
hazelnut-butter.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with smooth, pale brown hazelnut butter
hazelnut-butter.what: A smooth spread made from ground, roasted hazelnuts.

facts: Hazelnuts grow on the hazel tree, which is native to Europe and western Asia.
Ground hazelnuts are used in many European cakes and biscuits.
Piedmont, in northern Italy, is famous for pairing hazelnuts with chocolate.
hazelnut-flour.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, pale tan hazelnut flour
hazelnut-flour.what: Finely ground hazelnuts, used in rich baking and cakes.

facts: Many hazelnut liqueurs are made by flavouring a neutral spirit with hazelnuts and sugar.
The Piedmont region of north-west Italy is famous for its hazelnuts and nut-based liqueurs.
Hazelnut liqueur is often poured over ice cream or stirred into coffee.
hazelnut-liqueur.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with pale amber hazelnut liqueur
hazelnut-liqueur.what: A sweet, nut-flavoured spirit used in desserts and coffee.

facts: Hazelnut milk is made by blending hazelnuts with water and then straining the liquid.
Hazelnuts come from the hazel tree, which grows widely across Europe and Asia.
It is often used as a dairy-free alternative in coffee and baking.
hazelnut-milk.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale creamy beige hazelnut milk
hazelnut-milk.what: A nutty, creamy drink made from ground hazelnuts and water.

facts: Hazelnut oil is made by pressing roasted or raw hazelnuts.
Turkey is one of the largest producers of hazelnuts in the world.
The oil is delicate and is best used in dressings rather than high-heat frying.
hazelnut-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of golden hazelnut oil
hazelnut-oil.what: A toasty nut oil pressed from hazelnuts, used in dressings.

facts: Hazelnuts grow on hazel shrubs and small trees, and each nut sits inside a leafy husk.
Gianduja, a mix of chocolate and ground hazelnut from Piedmont in Italy, is a classic use.
hazelnuts.visual: a small heap of whole shelled hazelnuts with smooth round brown skins lying loosely
hazelnuts.what: Round, sweet nuts with a toasty flavour, good for baking.

facts: Heather honey is made mainly in upland areas of Scotland, Scandinavia and northern Germany.
Heather honey is so thick that it is often pressed from the comb rather than spun out.
heather-honey.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, filled with dark amber honey that is thick and jelly-like
heather-honey.what: Dark, thick honey from wild heather moorland blossom.

facts: Heirloom tomatoes are older varieties, often grown from seed saved and passed down through families.
Heirloom tomatoes come in many colours, from yellow and orange to deep purple and striped.
heirloom-tomato.visual: one whole ripe heirloom tomato, misshapen and ribbed, with deep red and green-streaked skin
heirloom-tomato.what: A knobbly, multicoloured tomato, often sweet and juicy.

facts: Hemp has been grown for its seeds and fibre for thousands of years.
Hemp milk is made by blending hulled seeds with water, then straining the mixture.
It is popular as a dairy-free alternative in tea, coffee and porridge.
hemp-milk.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale, creamy beige hemp milk
hemp-milk.what: A pale, nutty milk made from crushed hemp seeds and water.

facts: Hemp is a plant grown for its fibre, seeds and oil, and it has been cultivated for thousands of years.
Hemp seeds are also sold hulled, for use in salads, porridge and baking.
hemp-seed-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale green oil
hemp-seed-oil.what: A grassy, nutty oil pressed from hemp seeds.

facts: Hemp has been cultivated for thousands of years, and its seeds have been eaten in Asia and Europe.
Hemp seeds are often sprinkled over salads, porridge and yoghurt.
hemp-seeds.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl holding a small heap of shelled hemp seeds, pale grey-beige and soft
hemp-seeds.what: Soft, nutty seeds from the hemp plant, sprinkled on salads.

facts: Chickens were domesticated in Asia thousands of years ago and are now kept worldwide.
An egg is a yolk surrounded by a clear white that sets when it is cooked.
hen-s-egg.visual: a single whole brown hen's egg with a smooth shell, lying on its side
hen-s-egg.what: A common egg from a hen, used boiled, fried or scrambled.

facts: Herbal liqueurs are traditionally made by steeping herbs and spices in a neutral spirit.
Recipes are closely guarded, and some have been made by monks since the 1700s.
herbal-liqueur.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle half-filled with pale yellow-green liquid
herbal-liqueur.what: A sweet, aromatic spirit flavoured with steeped herbs.

facts: The blend takes its name from Provence, the sunny region of south-east France.
Typical mixes include thyme, savory, rosemary and oregano, though recipes vary.
herbes-de-provence.visual: a small heap of dried mixed herbs, thin grey-green leaves and small twigs, loosely piled on a plain background
herbes-de-provence.what: A dried mix of classic French herbs for roasting.

facts: Carrots are thought to have been first domesticated in Central Asia, where early types were often purple or yellow.
Heritage varieties are older open-pollinated types, grown from seed saved and passed on rather than modern hybrids.
heritage-carrot.visual: a bunch of mixed heritage carrots in purple, yellow, orange and cream tones, green leafy tops still attached
heritage-carrot.what: Multicoloured carrots, often with a more varied flavour.

facts: For centuries it was salted, smoked or pickled so it would keep long after it was caught.
Pickled herring is a traditional dish across northern Europe, including Scandinavia and Germany.
herring.visual: one whole raw herring with silver skin, lying in a gentle curve
herring.what: A small oily sea fish, often salted, smoked or pickled.

facts: Herring roe is the egg mass of the herring, harvested when the fish are ready to spawn.
In Japan, herring roe is salted and seasoned as kazunoko, a traditional New Year food.
herring-roe.visual: a small heap of soft, pale orange herring roe, glossy grains clustered together
herring-roe.what: Tiny, delicate eggs from herring, often eaten on toast.

facts: Agua de jamaica is a Mexican drink brewed from dried hibiscus flowers and served cold.
In West Africa, the same plant is used in tart drinks such as bissap, popular in Senegal.
hibiscus-flowers.visual: a small heap of dried crimson hibiscus flowers, crinkled and dark ruby red
hibiscus-flowers.what: Tart crimson flowers that steep into a ruby-coloured drink.

facts: Hibiscus tea is made by steeping the dried calyces of the roselle plant.
Hibiscus tea is popular in West Africa, Mexico and the Caribbean, often served chilled.
In Mexico it is known as agua de jamaica.
hibiscus-tea.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with deep crimson liquid, plain and unadorned
hibiscus-tea.what: A tart red infusion made from dried hibiscus flowers.

facts: Hijiki is a seaweed from the coasts of Japan, Korea and China.
It is traditionally simmered with soy sauce and vegetables in Japanese home cooking.
It is sold dried, and it swells considerably when soaked in water before cooking.
hijiki.visual: a small heap of dried black hijiki seaweed strands, fine and wiry, loose on the background
hijiki.what: A dark, wiry seaweed, sold dried and soaked before use.

facts: Its pink colour comes from small traces of iron oxide within the salt.
It became popular in Western kitchens in recent decades as a finishing salt.
himalayan-pink-salt.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of coarse pale pink salt crystals
himalayan-pink-salt.what: A rosy rock salt, mined in Pakistan and mild in flavour.

facts: Pointed cabbages have been grown in parts of Europe for a long time, including the Netherlands and Germany.
Its leaves can be shredded raw for salads or charred in wedges.
hispi-cabbage.visual: one whole pointed hispi cabbage, pale green outer leaves and a tight conical head, lying on its side
hispi-cabbage.what: A small, tender, pointed cabbage that cooks quickly.

facts: The name hiyamugi means cold wheat, reflecting the way these noodles are served.
After boiling they are rinsed in cold water, which firms the noodles and stops the cooking.
In summer, cold noodles like these are commonly served with a dipping sauce.
hiyamugi.visual: a small heap of dry, pale cream wheat noodles, long straight strands, thin and even
hiyamugi.what: Thin Japanese wheat noodles, usually eaten cold.

facts: Hogget is sheep meat from animals older than lamb but younger than mutton, with a richer flavour than lamb.
hogget.visual: one raw hogget leg joint, deep pinkish-red meat with a cream-coloured fat cap
hogget.what: Meat from a sheep that is one to two years old.

facts: Hoisin is a Cantonese word meaning seafood, though the sauce contains no seafood.
It is traditionally served with Peking duck, where thin pancakes are spread with it.
Its recipes vary, but most include fermented soybeans, sugar, garlic and spices.
hoisin-sauce.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with thick, dark reddish-brown sauce
hoisin-sauce.what: A thick, sweet Chinese sauce made from fermented soybeans.

facts: Its leaves are traditionally used to wrap fish and tamales before steaming or grilling.
The flavour is often described as a mix of anise, sassafras and mint.
hoja-santa.visual: a single large fresh heart-shaped leaf with a velvety green surface and soft fuzzy underside, lying flat on the background
hoja-santa.what: Large heart-shaped Mexican leaf tasting of anise.

facts: Hojicha is made by roasting green tea leaves, which turns them reddish-brown.
Hojicha is a popular everyday tea in Japan, drunk hot or iced.
The roasting gives it a toasty, caramel-like flavour that is milder than most green teas.
hojicha.visual: A small plain white ceramic bowl of loose roasted tea leaves, reddish-brown and slightly twiggy.
hojicha.what: Japanese green tea leaves roasted until nutty and mellow.

facts: It is one of New Zealand's largest fisheries and is often sold as fillets.
Its flesh is mild and white, which makes it suited to crumbing and frying.
hoki.visual: one raw hoki fillet, pale pinkish-white flesh with a soft flaky texture, lying flat
hoki.what: A mild white fish from New Zealand, good for fish fingers.

facts: The dough is enriched with milk and often a cooked flour paste called tangzhong, which keeps the loaf soft.
Japanese milk bread is often baked in a tin, so it rises into a square, soft loaf.
In Japan the bread is widely known as shokupan, meaning eating bread.
hokkaido-milk-toast.visual: a pair of soft pale golden slices of milk bread fanned on a plain white plate
hokkaido-milk-toast.what: A soft, milky Japanese loaf with a fluffy, tender crumb.

facts: Hollandaise is one of the classic French mother sauces, traditionally finished with lemon juice or vinegar.
Eggs Benedict, a brunch dish of poached eggs and ham on muffins, is commonly served with hollandaise.
hollandaise.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, pale yellow hollandaise, glossy and thick
hollandaise.what: A rich, buttery sauce made from egg yolk and butter.

facts: Hollandaise is one of the five mother sauces of classic French cooking, the base for many other sauces.
It is the classic sauce for eggs Benedict, spooned over poached eggs on a toasted muffin.
It is made by whisking egg yolks with melted butter over gentle heat, and it can split if overheated.
hollandaise-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, pale yellow hollandaise, glossy and thick
hollandaise-sauce.what: A warm, rich sauce of egg yolks, lemon juice and butter.

facts: Holy basil is sacred in Hinduism, where it is called tulsi and often grown near homes.
It is a different plant from sweet basil, with a stronger, spicier taste.
In Thailand it is used in fiery stir-fries, often with chillies and garlic.
holy-basil.visual: a small bunch of fresh holy basil, purple-tinged stems and dark green, slightly hairy leaves
holy-basil.what: A fragrant herb with peppery, clove-like leaves.

facts: Nixtamalisation, the lime soaking process, comes from ancient Mesoamerica.
The process loosens the hulls and makes the maize easier to grind into masa.
Hominy is used in posole, a traditional Mexican stew.
hominy.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale cooked hominy kernels, plump and slightly translucent
hominy.what: Maize kernels soaked in lime until soft and chewy.

facts: Honey has been used as a sweetener since ancient times, long before cane sugar was common.
The colour and flavour of honey depend on the flowers the bees visited.
honey.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with clear golden honey
honey.what: A golden, sweet syrup made by bees from flower nectar.

facts: Mustard is made by grinding mustard seeds and mixing them with liquid such as vinegar or water.
Mustard seeds have been used as a seasoning for thousands of years.
honey-and-mustard-dressing.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth pale golden dressing, thick and glossy
honey-and-mustard-dressing.what: A sweet and sharp dressing of honey, mustard and vinegar.

facts: Barbecue sauces developed in many parts of the United States, each with its own style.
