The sugar in honey helps the sauce caramelise on meat as it cooks.
honey-bbq-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, glossy amber-brown barbecue sauce
honey-bbq-sauce.what: A sticky, sweet barbecue sauce flavoured with honey.

facts: Ready-to-eat breakfast cereals became popular in North America in the late nineteenth century.
Honey-coated cereals are typically made from puffed or flaked grains, coated in a sweet syrup.
Honey has been used as a sweetener since ancient times, long before refined sugar became common.
honey-coated-cereal.visual: golden, glossy cereal pieces in a small plain white bowl
honey-coated-cereal.what: Crisp, golden breakfast cereal in a sweet honey coating.

facts: Honey fungus grows in dense clusters on wood, both on living trees and on dead timber.
It takes its name from the honey-coloured caps that appear in autumn in many woodlands.
Cooks usually boil the mushrooms well before frying, as the raw fungus is not suitable to eat.
honey-fungus.visual: a cluster of honey-coloured wild mushrooms joined at the base, pale golden-brown caps with fine scales
honey-fungus.what: Clustered woodland mushrooms that need thorough cooking.

facts: Honey mustard combines mustard seed or powder with honey, often with vinegar or lemon.
It is commonly used as a glaze for ham, chicken and sausages, and as a dip.
Mustard comes from the seeds of mustard plants, which belong to the cabbage family.
honey-mustard.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth golden honey mustard, glossy
honey-mustard.what: A sweet, mellow sauce of mustard blended with honey.

facts: Ham is pork from the hind leg, traditionally cured by salting or smoking to preserve it.
Glazing ham and roasting it caramelises the outside, giving it a sweet, crisp crust.
honey-roast-ham.visual: a plain white plate holding overlapping thin slices of pink ham, with a golden-brown glazed edge
honey-roast-ham.what: Sliced pork ham, sweetened with a honey glaze.

facts: Peanuts are not nuts at all, but legumes that grow underground in pods.
Peanuts originated in South America and were later spread to Africa and Asia by Spanish and Portuguese traders.
Honey-roasting coats the nuts in a glaze of honey, often with sugar.
honey-roast-peanuts.visual: a small heap of glossy golden honey-roast peanuts, sticky and sugar-glazed
honey-roast-peanuts.what: Roasted peanuts coated in a sticky, sweet, honey glaze.

facts: Honeyberry grows wild in cold northern regions, including parts of Russia and Japan.
Honeyberry bushes flower early in the year and ripen early in summer.
honeyberry.visual: a small heap of elongated, dusky blue berries with a pale frosty bloom
honeyberry.what: A long, tart blue berry, related to honeysuckle.

facts: Honeycomb is the wax structure bees build to store honey and raise their young.
Beekeepers cut comb from the hive and sell it whole, or as a sweet to eat with bread.
honeycomb.visual: a single piece of golden honeycomb, its hexagonal wax cells filled with golden liquid, lying flat
honeycomb.what: Golden wax cells built by bees and filled with honey.

facts: The sweet is made by adding bicarbonate of soda to hot sugar syrup, which makes it foam.
Crushed honeycomb is a classic topping for ice cream in Britain.
honeycomb-pieces.visual: one rough-edged piece of golden honeycomb showing its open hexagonal wax cells
honeycomb-pieces.what: Crunchy, airy golden sweet with a bubbly texture.

facts: Tripe is the edible lining of a cow's stomach, eaten in many cuisines for centuries.
Honeycomb tripe comes from the second stomach, the reticulum, and has a net-like surface.
Italian trippa and Spanish callos are well-known tripe dishes simmered in tomato sauce.
honeycomb-tripe.visual: a piece of raw honeycomb tripe, pale cream-white with a neat grid of small pockets across its surface, lying flat on the plain background
honeycomb-tripe.what: A ridged, honeycomb-patterned lining from a cow's stomach.

facts: Honeydew is a type of muskmelon, and it is grown in many warm parts of the world.
Honeydew melons have a smooth, pale rind and ripen with a soft, sweet scent.
Spain is a major grower of honeydew melons, and they are often eaten with thin slices of cured ham.
honeydew-melon.visual: a cut wedge of honeydew melon showing pale green flesh and a thin pale rind, lying flat on the plain background
honeydew-melon.what: A pale green, sweet melon with a smooth rind.

facts: Hop plants are best known for their cones, which give beer its bitterness.
In parts of Italy, wild hop shoots are picked in spring and used in omelettes and risotto.
Hops grow from underground rhizomes that send up new stems each spring.
hop-shoots.visual: a small bunch of slender pale green hop shoots, stems trimmed, lying on the background
hop-shoots.what: Spring shoots of the hop plant, cooked like asparagus.

facts: Horchata has roots in Spain, where a tiger nut version called horchata de chufa is still popular.
In Mexico, rice horchata is a common sweet drink, often served chilled in hot weather.
horchata.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with a smooth, creamy, pale off-white drink
horchata.what: A sweet, milky drink flavoured with cinnamon and rice.

facts: Horned melon is native to Africa, and is also called kiwano.
It is now grown in New Zealand, Israel and parts of the United States.
The lime-green jelly inside has a tangy flavour often described as a mix of cucumber and banana.
horned-melon.visual: One whole spiky orange oval horned melon with bright yellow-orange spines, lying on its side.
horned-melon.what: A spiky orange fruit with lime-green jelly inside.

facts: Horse meat is eaten in parts of Europe, including France, Belgium and Italy.
In Japan, horse meat has long been eaten raw, and is sometimes called sakura, meaning cherry blossom.
horse-fillet.visual: a fillet of raw horse meat, deep red lean cut, smooth cylindrical shape, lying flat on the background
horse-fillet.what: Lean, sweet red meat cut from the loin of a horse.

facts: It is traditionally cooked into soups and stews, especially in South Indian home cooking.
Its beans are dark and firm and need long soaking before they are cooked.
horse-gram.visual: a small heap of dry, mottled brown horse gram seeds, loosely piled on a plain background
horse-gram.what: A small, earthy pulse popular in southern Indian cooking.

facts: Horse mackerel is the name used for several fish of the Trachurus genus, found in warm and temperate seas.
In Britain it is also known as scad.
In Japan it is called aji, and it has long been eaten there grilled or pickled.
horse-mackerel.visual: a whole raw horse mackerel, silver-blue back, lying on its side
horse-mackerel.what: A small, firm, oily fish, often grilled or pickled.

facts: Horse mushrooms grow in grassland, particularly in pastures and fields.
Horse mushrooms belong to the same genus as the common button mushroom, Agaricus.
horse-mushroom.visual: a whole raw horse mushroom with a broad, creamy white cap and a thick white stem, lying on its side
horse-mushroom.what: A large, meaty wild mushroom with a faint aniseed smell.

facts: Its sharp heat comes from compounds released when the root is cut or grated.
In Britain it is traditionally served as a sauce with roast beef.
horseradish-root.visual: one whole pale brown horseradish root, long and knobbly, with fine side rootlets, lying on its side
horseradish-root.what: A hot, sharp root that is grated to make a fiery sauce.

facts: Horseradish is a root from the mustard family, native to south-eastern Europe and western Asia.
Its sharp heat fades quickly once the root is grated, so the sauce is often made fresh.
horseradish-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of creamy pale horseradish sauce, smooth and thick
horseradish-sauce.what: A creamy, sharp sauce made from grated horseradish root.

facts: Chilli peppers come from the Americas and reached Asia and Europe in the 1500s.
Chilli powder is made by drying red chillies and grinding them, sometimes with other spices.
Hot chilli powder is a staple of Indian cooking, where it is used to season curries and pickles.
hot-chilli-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, bright red chilli powder, level on top
hot-chilli-powder.what: Ground dried red chillies, adding fiery heat to a dish.

facts: The cross on the bun is a Christian symbol, and the buns are traditionally eaten on Good Friday in Britain.
Spiced fruit buns like these have been sold in England for centuries, flavoured with dried fruit and mixed spice.
Many bakers now sell them year-round, though they are still most closely linked to the Easter season.
hot-cross-bun.visual: one whole hot cross bun, glossy golden-brown top with a pale icing cross, on a small plain white plate
hot-cross-bun.what: A sweet, spiced bun marked with a cross, eaten at Easter.

facts: The soft, split-top roll is designed to hold a sausage, and is widely used at fairs and barbecues.
Frankfurter rolls take their second name from the German city of Frankfurt, home of the frankfurter sausage.
hot-dog-roll.visual: one plain white split-top hot dog roll, soft and unfilled, lying on its side
hot-dog-roll.what: A soft, long bread roll made to hold a sausage.

facts: Hot fudge is a chocolate sauce often made with cream, butter and sugar.
It became a fixture of American ice cream parlours and sundaes in the early twentieth century.
The sauce thickens slightly when it meets cold ice cream, giving a firmer coating.
hot-fudge-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, glossy dark brown chocolate sauce
hot-fudge-sauce.what: A thick, glossy chocolate sauce poured hot over ice cream.

facts: Hot honey is often drizzled over pizza and fried chicken, especially in the United States.
Honey is made by bees from flower nectar, and it is naturally thick and sweet.
Chilli is steeped in the honey for some time, passing its heat and flavour into the sweetness.
hot-honey.visual: a plain clear glass jar without a label holding thick, glowing amber honey
hot-honey.what: Honey infused with chilli for a sweet and spicy kick.

facts: Vinegar helps preserve chillies, which is why many hot sauces are vinegar-based.
The word chilli comes from Nahuatl, an Indigenous language of central Mexico.
Hot sauces are popular across the Caribbean, the southern United States and many other regions.
hot-sauce.visual: a small plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with bright red chilli sauce
hot-sauce.what: A vinegary chilli sauce, used to add heat to food.

facts: Hot pimenton is made from hot chillies, while sweet versions are made from milder peppers.
Spanish cooks use it in chorizo, paella and grilled meats.
hot-smoked-paprika.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of deep red smoked paprika powder
hot-smoked-paprika.what: A deep red powder of smoked chillies with a spicy bite.

facts: Hot smoking cooks the fish with smoke at a warmer temperature than cold smoking.
Smoking fish has long been a way of preserving it in northern Europe.
Hot-smoked salmon is often flaked into salads, pasta and creamy dishes.
hot-smoked-salmon.visual: one thick fillet of hot-smoked salmon, orange-pink flesh, flaking apart, lying flat
hot-smoked-salmon.what: Salmon that is smoked until cooked and flaky.

facts: Huitlacoche is a fungus that grows on maize, swelling the kernels into dark grey masses.
Mexican cooks have eaten it for centuries, often in quesadillas, tacos and soups.
Its name comes from the Nahuatl language, and it is sometimes called the Mexican truffle.
huitlacoche.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dark grey swollen corn fungus, soft and velvety
huitlacoche.what: A dark corn fungus with an earthy, mushroomy taste.

facts: Humboldt squid live in the eastern Pacific Ocean, off the coasts of Mexico, Peru and Chile.
The squid is named after the Humboldt Current, which is named after the explorer Alexander von Humboldt.
humboldt-squid.visual: a whole raw Humboldt squid, reddish-purple skin, long body and tentacles, lying flat on the background
humboldt-squid.what: A large, muscular deep-sea squid with firm, thick flesh.

facts: The name comes from the Arabic word for chickpea, and the dip is found across the Levant.
Tahini, a paste of ground sesame seeds, gives hummus its nutty richness.
Hummus has become popular in Britain and beyond, often served with flatbread or crudites.
hummus.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth pale beige hummus with a shallow swirl on top
hummus.what: A smooth dip of chickpeas blended with sesame paste.

facts: In Britain, hundreds and thousands are a traditional decoration on fairy cakes.
The same sprinkles are known elsewhere as nonpareils.
hundreds-and-thousands.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of tiny multicoloured sugar balls, pink, yellow and blue
hundreds-and-thousands.what: Tiny coloured sugar balls used to decorate cakes.

facts: Peppers came to Hungary from the Americas, and paprika became central to Hungarian cooking.
Goulash, the stew at the heart of Hungarian cooking, is seasoned generously with paprika.
Hungarian paprika is graded by sweetness and heat, from mild and sweet to hot.
hungarian-paprika.visual: a plain glass jar without a label filled with bright red paprika powder
hungarian-paprika.what: A sweet, mild red powder ground from dried peppers.

facts: Hungarian wax peppers are popular in pickles, salads and as a mild stuffing pepper.
They are sold fresh as well as pickled, and their pale yellow colour sets them apart from green peppers.
hungarian-wax-pepper.visual: one whole glossy pale yellow tapered pepper, smooth waxy skin, lying on its side
hungarian-wax-pepper.what: A waxy yellow pepper with mild to medium heat.

facts: Hyssop is a member of the mint family and grows wild around the Mediterranean and in Central Asia.
It has long been grown in European gardens and is traditionally used to flavour some liqueurs.
hyssop.visual: a small bunch of narrow green hyssop leaves, with tiny blue-violet flowers on the stems
hyssop.what: A narrow-leaved, minty herb with a slightly bitter taste.

facts: Iberico pork comes from the Iberian pig, a breed raised mainly in Spain and Portugal.
Spanish cured hams from the same breed are among the best-known products of the Iberian pig.
iberico-pluma.visual: a single raw pork cut, thin rectangle of dark pink meat with creamy white fat marbling, lying directly on the background
iberico-pluma.what: A thin, fatty cut of pork from a black-hoofed pig.

facts: Iberico pigs are raised in Spain and Portugal, often on acorns in oak woodland.
Iberico ham is the best-known product of the breed, cured for long periods in Spain.
iberico-presa.visual: a raw pork steak with deep pink-red flesh and fine white fat marbling, lying flat
iberico-presa.what: A marbled cut of pork shoulder from the Iberian pig.

facts: Iberian pigs are raised in Spain and Portugal, and are often fed acorns in oak woodland.
iberico-secreto.visual: one raw, thick, dark-pink pork piece marbled with fine white fat, lying directly on the background
iberico-secreto.what: A marbled pork cut from the shoulder of the Iberian pig.

facts: Iced desserts made with snow, ice and fruit date back many centuries in Persia and China.
Modern ice cream became popular in the 19th century, when mechanical refrigeration improved.
Ice cream is churned while it freezes, which adds air and gives a smooth texture.
ice-cream.visual: a single round scoop of pale cream ice cream in a small plain white bowl
ice-cream.what: A frozen dessert made from cream, milk and sugar.

facts: Wafer cones are baked from a thin batter and shaped into cones while still warm.
Some cones are dipped in chocolate or coated in sugar for extra crunch and flavour.
ice-cream-cone.visual: one empty golden wafer cone, open end facing up, lying on a plain background
ice-cream-cone.what: A crisp wafer cone designed to hold scoops of ice cream.

facts: Wafer cones are made from a thin batter baked between heated plates until crisp.
ice-cream-cones.visual: a single crisp golden-brown wafer cone, pointed tip down, open rim up, shown on a plain background
ice-cream-cones.what: Crisp, hollow wafer cones that hold scoops of ice cream.

facts: Wafer cones are made by baking a thin batter between heated plates, then rolling it while still warm.
The word cornet comes from the French for a paper cone or horn-shaped container.
In Britain, a soft-serve cone topped with a chocolate flake is a popular seaside treat.
ice-cream-cornet.visual: one empty crisp golden wafer cornet, cone-shaped with a rolled ridged side, standing upright with its open end up
ice-cream-cornet.what: A crisp, rolled wafer cone that holds ice cream.

facts: Wafer biscuits have been baked in Europe for centuries, pressed between hot metal plates.
ice-cream-wafers.visual: a few thin round golden wafer biscuits arranged on a plain white plate
ice-cream-wafers.what: Thin, crisp wafer biscuits for sandwiching ice cream.

facts: Ice lollies are made by freezing liquid, such as fruit juice or flavoured water, in a mould with a stick.
In Britain, an ice lolly is the everyday word for what some people call an ice pop.
ice-lolly.visual: a single bright orange ice lolly on a short plain wooden stick, frosted surface
ice-lolly.what: A frozen treat of fruit juice or flavoured ice on a stick.

facts: The tiny bladders on its leaves look like ice crystals, which gives the plant its name.
Its leaves have been used as a salad green in parts of the Mediterranean.
The plant tolerates salty soil, which is why it grows near the coast.
ice-plant.visual: a small bunch of pale green succulent leaves covered in tiny glistening crystal-like bumps
ice-plant.what: A crunchy, salty succulent with leaves covered in bumps.

facts: Iceberg is a head lettuce with tightly folded leaves, and it is widely used in sandwiches and burgers.
The inner leaves stay pale because they grow tightly wrapped around one another in the head.
iceberg-lettuce.visual: one whole iceberg lettuce, a tight pale green head with crisp, pale-edged leaves, standing on its base
iceberg-lettuce.what: A pale, crisp, round lettuce with tightly packed leaves.

facts: Ichimi togarashi is a single-ingredient chilli powder, and 'ichimi' means 'one flavour'.
Togarashi is the Japanese word for chilli pepper, which Portuguese traders are thought to have introduced to Japan.
It is sprinkled over noodles, rice bowls and soups as a finishing spice.
ichimi-togarashi.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, bright red ground chilli powder
ichimi-togarashi.what: Ground Japanese chilli, sprinkled on noodles and soups.

facts: Icing sugar is ground very finely and usually mixed with a little cornflour to stop it clumping.
In Britain it is called icing sugar because it is used to make the smooth icing for cakes.
In North America it is more often called powdered sugar or confectioners' sugar.
icing-sugar.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with soft, fine white icing sugar
icing-sugar.what: Sugar ground to a fine powder for icing and dusting.

facts: Idiazabal is made in the Basque Country and Navarre from the raw milk of Latxa and Carranzana sheep.
idiazabal.visual: a block of firm pale golden cheese with one wedge cut away, its smoked brown rind visible on the outside, lying on a plain background
idiazabal.what: A firm, smoky sheep's cheese from the Basque Country.

facts: Pale ales were brewed in England and exported widely around the world.
Hops are the cone-shaped flowers of a climbing plant, and they give beer its bitterness and aroma.
The style is often linked to beer shipped from Britain to India in the colonial era, though the story is debated.
india-pale-ale.visual: a clear drinking glass of golden-amber beer with a small head of foam
india-pale-ale.what: A bitter, citrusy pale beer with a strong hop flavour.

facts: The leaf is called tej patta in Hindi and comes from a relative of the cinnamon tree.
It is not the same as the Mediterranean bay leaf, which comes from a different tree.
It is used across South Asia, especially in biryani, curries and rice dishes.
indian-bay-leaf.visual: a small heap of dried tej patta leaves, long and narrow, pale green-brown, with three visible veins
indian-bay-leaf.what: A fragrant, cinnamon-scented leaf used in rice and curry.

facts: Meat and potato pies are closely linked with northern England, where they are a familiar everyday food.
The filling of minced beef and potato is held in gravy and sealed inside a pastry case.
individual-meat-and-potato-pie.visual: a single golden pastry pie with a crimped edge, whole and uncut, on a plain white plate
individual-meat-and-potato-pie.what: A small pastry pie of minced beef and potato in gravy.

facts: Injera is traditionally made from teff, a tiny grain native to the Horn of Africa.
The batter is left to ferment for a day or more, which gives injera its tangy, sour taste.
In Ethiopian meals it serves as both plate and utensil, and diners tear pieces to scoop up stews.
injera.visual: one large round sheet of spongy grey-beige injera, bubbly surface full of small holes, lying flat
injera.what: A soft, spongy, sour flatbread from Ethiopia.

facts: Instant coffee is made by brewing coffee and then drying it into soluble granules or powder.
Instant coffee was developed in the early twentieth century as a quicker alternative to brewing.
Its roasted flavour pairs well with chocolate, so it is often added to cakes and desserts.
instant-coffee.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with dark brown instant coffee granules
instant-coffee.what: Dried coffee granules that dissolve quickly in hot water.

facts: Couscous is a staple of Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, traditionally steamed over a stew.
Instant couscous is steamed and dried before packing, so it only needs hot water.
instant-couscous.visual: a small heap of pale golden instant couscous, fine granules, lying on a plain background
instant-couscous.what: Pre-cooked granules of semolina that soften in hot water.

facts: Potatoes were first cultivated in the Andes of South America, thousands of years ago.
Dehydrated potato is made by cooking, drying and grinding potatoes into flakes or granules.
Mashed potato is a traditional British side dish, often served with sausages or gravy.
instant-mash.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale, dry potato flakes, thin and flat
instant-mash.what: Dried potato flakes that turn into mash with hot water.

facts: Miso is a fermented paste made from soybeans, often with rice or barley, used in Japanese cooking.
Miso soup is a traditional Japanese dish, often served alongside rice.
Instant versions dry miso and tofu so they rehydrate quickly in hot water.
instant-miso-soup-sachet.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dry, pale-brown miso granules, loose and powdery
instant-miso-soup-sachet.what: Dried miso and tofu pieces that dissolve in hot water.

facts: Instant noodles were first developed in Japan, and the idea has spread across Asia and beyond.
The noodles are steamed and then fried or air-dried, which lets them rehydrate quickly in hot water.
instant-noodle-pot.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of soft, cooked curly noodles in a pale savoury broth
instant-noodle-pot.what: Dried noodles and seasoning in a pot, ready with hot water.

facts: Instant noodles were invented in Japan in 1958 by Momofuku Ando.
They are made by steaming noodles and then drying or frying them.
instant-noodles.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of cooked yellow noodles, lightly coiled and glossy
instant-noodles.what: Dried noodles that cook in hot water in minutes.

facts: Maize, the grain behind cornmeal, was brought to Europe from the Americas.
Instant polenta is pre-cooked and dried, so it needs much less stirring than traditional coarse meal.
instant-polenta.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dry, pale yellow instant polenta, fine and granular
instant-polenta.what: Quick-cooking cornmeal, ready in a few minutes.

facts: Porridge is a traditional oat dish in Scotland and northern Europe, often cooked with water or milk.
Instant oats are pre-cooked and finely cut, so they absorb hot water quickly.
The word porridge is linked to pottage, a thick soup of grains or vegetables cooked in a pot.
instant-porridge-sachet.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine dry instant oat flakes, pale cream and loosely heaped
instant-porridge-sachet.what: Fine oats that cook into porridge with hot water.

facts: Instant puddings were developed in the twentieth century so that dessert could be made quickly.
The powder thickens when whisked into cold milk, then sets as it rests.
Custard powder, a close British relative, was made as an egg-free alternative for pouring custard.
instant-pudding-mix.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, pale cream-coloured powder, smooth and dry
instant-pudding-mix.what: A powdered mix that sets into a creamy dessert with milk.

facts: Instant noodles are dried so they can be stored for a long time and rehydrated with hot water.
In Vietnam they are used in pho, the noodle soup, and in many other noodle dishes.
instant-rice-noodles.visual: a small heap of thin, dried, pale rice noodles, straight and brittle
instant-rice-noodles.what: Thin, dried rice noodles that soften in boiling water.

facts: Udon is a thick Japanese wheat noodle made from flour, water and salt, kneaded into strands.
Instant udon is cooked and dried, so it only needs hot water or a short simmer to heat.
Udon is often served in a hot broth, sometimes with tempura or spring onions.
instant-udon.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with thick, cooked, pale udon noodles
instant-udon.what: Thick, pre-cooked Japanese noodles, quick to heat.

facts: Instant desserts are powders that thicken or set when whisked with cold milk, without any cooking.
instant-whip-dessert.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, pale cream dessert powder
instant-whip-dessert.what: Powder that whisks with milk into a light dessert.

facts: Invert sugar is made by breaking sucrose into glucose and fructose, usually with acid or an enzyme.
Confectioners use it because it stays smooth and resists turning grainy in fudge, fondant and sorbet.
The name comes from the way it inverts the direction of polarised light.
invert-sugar-syrup.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden syrup, thick and clear
invert-sugar-syrup.what: A smooth syrup of sugar split into two simpler sugars.

facts: The Irish name for whiskey, uisce beatha, means water of life.
Irish whiskey is spelled with an 'e', a difference from Scotch whisky.
irish-whiskey.visual: a clear drinking glass holding pale golden whiskey, no ice
irish-whiskey.what: A smooth whiskey from Ireland, often distilled three times.

facts: Isinglass is made from the dried swim bladders of fish, traditionally sturgeon.
For centuries it was used to clear beer and wine, and to set jellies.
isinglass.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, filled with pale translucent dried isinglass flakes
isinglass.what: A clear setting agent made from fish, for jellies.

facts: Cheddar is made by cheddaring, where curds are stacked and turned to drain whey.
Isle of Mull Cheddar is made on Mull, one of the Inner Hebrides off Scotland's west coast.
isle-of-mull-cheddar.visual: a block of pale golden cheddar cheese with one wedge cut away, crumbly edges and a smooth face
isle-of-mull-cheddar.what: Rich, tangy cheddar made on the Scottish island of Mull.

facts: The 00 grade describes how finely the flour is milled.
It is traditionally used for fresh egg pasta and for Neapolitan-style pizza dough.
Doppio zero is the Italian name for this flour, and means double zero.
italian-00-flour.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of very fine, bright white flour, soft and powdery
italian-00-flour.what: Very finely milled wheat flour for pasta and pizza.

facts: Its flavour comes from oil and vinegar seasoned with garlic, oregano and other dried herbs.
italian-dressing.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden oil-and-vinegar dressing
italian-dressing.what: A tangy oil and vinegar dressing with garlic and herbs.

facts: Salsa verde means green sauce in Italian, and versions are made across Italy.
italian-salsa-verde-mix.visual: a small heap of finely chopped fresh green herbs in bright green flecks on a plain background
italian-salsa-verde-mix.what: A chopped mix of green herbs for an Italian green sauce.

facts: Salsiccia is the Italian word for sausage, and many regional versions exist across Italy.
Fennel seeds are a traditional flavouring in many Italian pork sausages.
italian-sausage.visual: one whole raw Italian pork sausage link, pinkish-brown, lying in a gentle curve
italian-sausage.what: A fennel-scented pork sausage, often used in pasta sauces.

facts: Italian seasoning is a dried blend, usually of oregano, basil, rosemary, thyme and sometimes sage.
Oregano's name comes from Greek words meaning mountain and joy.
italian-seasoning.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dried green herb mix with small flakes and leaf pieces
italian-seasoning.what: A dried blend of herbs for pasta, pizza and tomato sauces.

facts: Ivy gourd is a climbing vine native to tropical Africa and Asia, grown for its small fruits.
In India it is known as tindora or kundru, and is commonly stir-fried or cooked in curries.
Cooks slice the gourds thinly or lengthwise, then fry them with spices or pickle them.
ivy-gourd.visual: a small heap of slim oval green ivy gourds with pale striped skin, lying loose
ivy-gourd.what: A small, crunchy green gourd eaten in South Asian cooking.

facts: Jabuticaba is native to Brazil, where it is a popular fruit.
The fruit grows directly from the trunk and branches of the tree, a habit called cauliflory.
Its thin skin and sweet, juicy flesh make it popular for jam and liqueur.
jabuticaba.visual: a small heap of round, glossy, dark purple-black berries lying loosely together
jabuticaba.what: Small, dark purple berries that grow on the trunk.

facts: Jackfruit grows on large trees in South and Southeast Asia, where it has long been eaten.
Young green jackfruit has a mild flavour and a texture close to shredded meat.
In parts of India and Sri Lanka the seeds are boiled or roasted.
jackfruit.visual: one whole green jackfruit with a knobbly, spiky skin, lying on its side
jackfruit.what: A giant tropical fruit, sweet when ripe, meaty when green.

facts: Jackfruit seeds are eaten boiled or roasted in parts of South and South-East Asia.
Each jackfruit holds many seeds, each one wrapped in a pod of sweet yellow flesh.
The English name jackfruit comes from the Portuguese word jaca, itself from a Malayalam word.
jackfruit-seeds.visual: a small heap of pale beige oval seeds, smooth-skinned and plump
jackfruit-seeds.what: Starchy seeds from a large tropical fruit, eaten cooked.

facts: The name refers to the Jaffa orange, which was once shipped from the port of Jaffa.
Jaffa Cakes were launched in Britain in 1927 by the biscuit maker McVitie's.
In 1991 a British court ruled that Jaffa Cakes are cakes, not biscuits, for tax purposes.
jaffa-cakes.visual: a single round sponge cake topped in orange jelly and dark chocolate, on a small plain white plate
jaffa-cakes.what: Sponge cakes topped with orange jelly and chocolate.

facts: Jaggery is made by boiling down sugarcane juice or palm sap until it thickens and sets.
It is a traditional sweetener across South Asia, and it is known as gur in Hindi.
jaggery.visual: a block of dark golden-brown jaggery, one corner broken away to show a grainy texture, lying on the background
jaggery.what: Unrefined sugar from palm or cane sap, sold in blocks.

facts: The jalapeno is named after Xalapa, the capital of Veracruz in Mexico.
Jalapenos ripen to red, and smoke-dried red jalapenos are sold as chipotles.
jalapeno.visual: a whole green jalapeno chilli with smooth, glossy skin and a short stem, lying flat
jalapeno.what: A medium-hot green chilli, popular in Mexican cooking.

facts: The jalapeno chilli is named after Xalapa, a town in Mexico.
Their heat varies, and removing the seeds and membrane reduces the spice.
jalapeno-poppers.visual: a few golden breaded jalapeno poppers, halved to show a pale creamy filling, served on a plain white plate
jalapeno-poppers.what: Green chillies stuffed with cheese, breaded and fried.

facts: Jalfrezi is a stir-fried curry style that became popular in British Indian restaurants.
Jalfrezi is usually made with peppers, onions and tomatoes, cooked fast over high heat.
Jars of ready-made paste are a shortcut for home cooks making jalfrezi.
jalfrezi-paste.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with thick red-orange paste
jalfrezi-paste.what: A hot paste of peppers and chilli for stir-fried curry.

facts: Jalfrezi is a stir-fried style of curry, cooked with peppers and onions and often served in British curry houses.
Green chillies are commonly used in jalfrezi, adding a sharp heat to the sauce.
Ready-made jalfrezi sauces are sold in jars and are often stirred into cooked meat or vegetables.
jalfrezi-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, glossy, deep orange-red sauce, full of small red and green flecks
jalfrezi-sauce.what: A hot curry sauce of peppers and onions.

facts: Jam roly-poly is a traditional British pudding made from suet pastry rolled around jam.
Suet, the hard fat from around beef or mutton kidney, has long been used in British pastry.
jam-roly-poly.visual: a slice of golden-brown jam roly-poly, rolled suet pastry showing a dark red spiral of fruit filling, on a plain white plate
jam-roly-poly.what: A rolled suet pastry pudding, spread with jam and steamed.

facts: The shortbread base is made from butter, sugar and flour, rubbed together and baked until crisp.
The jam centre is usually a fruit preserve such as raspberry or strawberry.
jam-sandwich-biscuits.visual: one round sandwich biscuit, pale golden shortbread edges, glossy red filling showing at the side, on a plain white plate
jam-sandwich-biscuits.what: Two shortbread biscuits sandwiched around a layer of jam.

facts: Jam tarts are a traditional British bake, made with shortcrust pastry and a fruit preserve.
Jam is made by cooking fruit with sugar until the mixture sets.
jam-tarts.visual: two small round jam tarts, golden shortcrust cases filled with glossy red jam, on a plain white plate
jam-tarts.what: Small shortcrust pastry cases with a spoonful of jam.

facts: Its character reflects the Indian indentured workers who arrived in Jamaica in the nineteenth century.
Allspice, native to the Caribbean, gives the blend its warm, clove-like flavour.
Goat curry is a popular Jamaican dish, often flavoured with this blend.
jamaican-curry-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of bright yellow-orange curry powder, fine and dry
jamaican-curry-powder.what: A warm, earthy spice blend used in Caribbean curries.

facts: Jamón ibérico comes from black Iberian pigs, which are raised mainly in western Spain and Portugal.
Many of these pigs roam oak woodland and feed on fallen acorns in the months before slaughter.
jamon-iberico.visual: a whole cured dark ham leg with a thin dark rind and marbled, creamy fat, lying flat
jamon-iberico.what: Cured ham from acorn-fed Iberian pigs, with nutty fat.

facts: The ham is salted and then left to air-dry for many months, often in cool mountain climates.
It is traditionally served thinly sliced on bread or as part of a tapas platter.
jamon-serrano.visual: a thin slice of dark pink cured ham with a rim of white fat, lying flat on a plain background
jamon-serrano.what: A dry-cured Spanish ham, thinly sliced for tapas.

facts: January King is a Savoy-type cabbage, a variety that is hardy enough to be harvested through the winter.
Cabbage has been grown in Europe for a very long time and is related to broccoli and kale.
january-king-cabbage.visual: a whole round January King cabbage, outer leaves tinged with purple and a pale green centre
january-king-cabbage.what: A hardy winter cabbage with purple-tinged leaves.

facts: Japanese aubergines are long and thin, with a skin that stays tender when cooked.
Nasu dengaku is a popular Japanese dish of aubergine grilled and glazed with sweet miso.
japanese-aubergine.visual: a whole slender purple Japanese aubergine with glossy dark skin, lying on its side
japanese-aubergine.what: A slim, sweet aubergine with thin skin and few seeds.

facts: It is made mainly with egg yolks, which gives it a richer texture than many Western mayonnaises.
Japanese mayonnaise was developed in the early twentieth century, when Western cooking was becoming popular in Japan.
It is often used on okonomiyaki, a savoury Japanese pancake.
japanese-mayonnaise.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale ivory mayonnaise with a soft, glossy surface
japanese-mayonnaise.what: A creamy, tangy mayonnaise from Japan, popular on salads.

facts: Shoyu is the Japanese word for soy sauce, and it has been made in Japan for many centuries.
Traditional Japanese soy is brewed from soybeans, wheat, salt and koji mould, over a long fermentation.
Soy sauce developed in East Asia over many centuries, and each country now has its own styles.
japanese-soy-sauce.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with dark amber soy sauce, standing upright
japanese-soy-sauce.what: A dark, balanced soy sauce for sushi and marinades.

facts: Satsumaimo is named after Satsuma Province in southern Japan, where it was widely grown.
Sweet potatoes reached Japan from China and became an important food crop, especially in lean years.
Yaki-imo, roasted sweet potato, is a traditional winter street food in Japan.
japanese-sweet-potato.visual: one whole raw Japanese sweet potato, red-purple skin, tapered oval shape, smooth and clean
japanese-sweet-potato.what: A red-skinned sweet potato with creamy, pale yellow flesh.

facts: Jarlsberg takes its name from the Jarlsberg estate in Norway.
Its large holes form as bacteria give off gas while the cheese matures.
jarlsberg.visual: a block of pale yellow cheese with large round holes, one wedge cut away
jarlsberg.what: A mild, sweet, nutty Norwegian cheese with large holes.

facts: Jasmine rice is grown mainly in Thailand, where it is named for its jasmine-like aroma.
The aroma comes from a natural compound found in the grain, and it is strongest in freshly harvested rice.
Jasmine rice is usually rinsed before cooking, which removes surface starch and loosens the texture.
jasmine-rice.visual: a small heap of long, slender, translucent white rice grains, uncooked
jasmine-rice.what: Fragrant long-grain rice that cooks soft and sticky.

facts: The practice of scenting tea with flowers has a long history in China, where jasmine is a favourite choice.
The name comes from jasmine, the fragrant plant whose blossoms are used in the scenting process.
jasmine-tea.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with dried green tea leaves and small pale jasmine flower buds
jasmine-tea.what: A floral green tea scented with jasmine blossoms.

facts: Jazz apples were bred in New Zealand from a cross of Royal Gala and Braeburn.
They are now grown in orchards in many countries around the world.
jazz-apple.visual: a whole red-and-yellow jazz apple, streaked red skin, glossy and firm
jazz-apple.what: A crisp, tangy-sweet apple that keeps its crunch in salads.

facts: Jellied eels were sold cheaply from street stalls in London's East End for generations.
The jelly sets as it cools because gelatine from the fish's skin and bones is released during cooking.
The dish is traditionally eaten cold, often with a splash of malt vinegar.
jellied-eels.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of cold jellied eel chunks set in pale grey-green jelly
jellied-eels.what: Chunks of eel set in cold savoury jelly, a London classic.

facts: Jelly babies are soft sweets made from gelatine, sugar and glucose syrup.
The sweets became popular in Britain in the twentieth century.
jelly-babies.visual: a small heap of soft, glossy jelly babies in red, green, yellow and orange
jelly-babies.what: Small, soft gummy sweets shaped like little people.

facts: Gelatine is made from collagen found in animal skin and bones.
Jelly was a popular party dessert in Britain in the Victorian era, often set in moulds.
Jelly sets as it cools because the gelatine forms a network that traps the liquid.
jelly-crystals.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dry, translucent jelly crystals
jelly-crystals.what: Powdered gelatine mix that sets into sweet, wobbly jelly.

facts: The word jelly comes from the Old French gelée, meaning something frozen or congealed.
jelly-cubes.visual: a small heap of firm, pale amber jelly cubes, slightly glossy
jelly-cubes.what: Concentrated jelly in cubes, dissolved in hot water.

facts: Edible jellyfish are eaten mainly in China, Japan and Korea, where they are salted and dried.
Before eating, dried jellyfish is soaked in water to remove salt and soften the texture.
Jellyfish have been part of East Asian cooking for centuries, and dried jellyfish is traded internationally.
jellyfish.visual: a small heap of thin, pale, translucent cured jellyfish strips, slightly curled
jellyfish.what: A translucent sea creature eaten crunchy after curing.

facts: Jerk seasoning originated in Jamaica, where it is traditionally used to season meat cooked slowly over wood.
Allspice, called pimento in Jamaica, is the main spice in jerk and gives it a warm, clove-like flavour.
jerk-marinade.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick dark reddish-brown paste with green flecks
jerk-marinade.what: A fiery Jamaican paste of allspice, chilli and herbs.

facts: Jerk seasoning comes from Jamaica, where it is traditionally rubbed onto pork and chicken.
Allspice, known in Jamaica as pimento, is the signature spice in jerk.
Jerk cooking is often linked to the Maroon communities of Jamaica's hills.
jerk-sauce.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of dark reddish-brown jerk sauce, half full, on a plain background
jerk-sauce.what: A spicy Jamaican sauce for marinating and grilling meat.

facts: Jerk cooking is traditionally linked to the Maroon communities of Jamaica.
Traditional jerk is cooked over pimento wood, which adds a smoky, aromatic flavour.
jerk-seasoning.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of coarse, dark brown spice paste with a rough texture
jerk-seasoning.what: A spicy Jamaican blend of allspice, thyme and chilli.

facts: Jersey cows are a small breed from the Channel Island of Jersey.
Jersey milk is rich in butterfat, which gives it a golden colour.
jersey-milk.visual: a clear drinking glass of golden milk, its thick cream line rising to the top
jersey-milk.what: Rich, golden milk from Jersey cows, with a thick cream top.

facts: Jersey Royals are grown on the island of Jersey in the Channel Islands.
They have a protected designation of origin, so only potatoes grown on Jersey can carry the name.
Farmers traditionally fertilised the fields with seaweed, a practice known locally as vraic.
jersey-royal-potato.visual: a small heap of small, oval new potatoes with thin, pale skins
jersey-royal-potato.what: A small early potato with a thin skin and nutty taste.

facts: Jerusalem artichoke is a sunflower species, native to eastern North America.
Its name is often linked to girasole, the Italian word for sunflower.
Europeans began growing it in the 1600s after it was brought back from North America.
jerusalem-artichoke.visual: one whole raw knobbly tuber, pale beige skin with irregular bumps and small knots, lying on its side
jerusalem-artichoke.what: A knobbly, nutty-tasting tuber, a sunflower relative.

facts: It is traditionally eaten at breakfast, often wrapped in warm flatbread.
jibneh-arabieh.visual: a block of soft white cheese with one wedge cut away, pale and moist, lying directly on a plain background
jibneh-arabieh.what: A soft, mild white cheese from the Gulf region.

facts: Jicama is a root vegetable native to Mexico and Central America, where it has long been eaten raw.
Its crisp, sweet white flesh is often sliced into sticks and sprinkled with lime and chilli powder.
Its name comes from the Nahuatl word xicamatl.
jicama.visual: one whole jicama root, round and bulbous, thin pale brown skin, a few fine root hairs, lying on its side
jicama.what: A crisp, juicy root, refreshing raw with lime and chilli.

facts: Soba is a Japanese noodle, and the word soba simply means buckwheat.
In Japan, soba is often served cold with a dipping sauce.
jiu-soba.visual: a small heap of dried thin brown buckwheat soba noodles, straight strands loosely tangled
jiu-soba.what: Thin Japanese noodles made mostly from buckwheat flour.

facts: The name is often linked to the French jaune dorée, meaning golden yellow, a nod to its colouring.
It lives in the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean, usually near the seabed in deeper water.
Fishermen across Europe have long valued its firm, delicate fillets, which hold their shape in the pan.
john-dory.visual: one whole raw fish with a tall, flattened oval body, golden-olive skin and a dark round spot on each side, lying on the background
john-dory.what: A deep-bodied sea fish with a fine, sweet white flesh.

facts: The jostaberry was developed in Germany by crossing gooseberry with blackcurrant.
The berries have a tart flavour and are often used in jams, crumbles and pies.
jostaberry.visual: a small bunch of glossy, dark purplish-black berries on a short stalk
jostaberry.what: A tart berry, a cross of gooseberry and blackcurrant.

facts: Jujube trees are native to China and other parts of Asia, and have been cultivated there for thousands of years.
Dried jujubes are added to teas and soups in Chinese cooking for a sweet, date-like flavour.
The fruit is sometimes called the Chinese date, though it is not related to the date palm.
jujube.visual: a small heap of glossy red-brown jujube fruits, oval with a wrinkled skin, some with short stems
jujube.what: A small oval fruit with crisp, sweet-tart flesh.

facts: Oat grains are steamed and then rolled flat to make flakes.
Oats are a traditional grain in Scotland, where porridge is a long-standing dish.
Flapjacks are a traditional British bake made with oats, butter and golden syrup.
jumbo-oats.visual: a small heap of large, flat rolled oat flakes, pale cream and dry
jumbo-oats.what: Thick, flat oat flakes that stay chewy when baked.

facts: Jungle curry, or gaeng pa, is a Thai curry traditionally made without coconut milk.
Thai curry pastes are traditionally pounded by hand in a mortar, though many cooks now use a blender.
Chillies first reached Asia from the Americas, and are now central to many Thai dishes.
jungle-curry-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with thick glossy red-brown paste
jungle-curry-paste.what: A fiery Thai paste of chilli and herbs for hot curries.

facts: Juniper is the defining flavouring of gin, and it is also used to season game and sauerkraut.
Juniper has long been used in northern European cooking, especially with game and pork.
juniper-berry.visual: a small heap of dark blue-black juniper berries with a pale dusty bloom, lying loose
juniper-berry.what: Small blue-black berries with a piney, peppery flavour.

facts: Jute mallow, known as molokhia in Egypt, is a leafy plant from the mallow family.
When cooked, its leaves have a naturally thickening quality, giving soups a silky texture.
Ewedu, a Nigerian name for the plant, is used in Yoruba cooking.
jute-mallow.visual: a loose bunch of bright green jute mallow leaves on their stems, fresh and glossy
jute-mallow.what: Silky green leaves used to make a classic Egyptian soup.

facts: Its skin is edible and softens when cooked, so it does not need peeling.
Kabocha is often used in tempura, where its dense flesh holds its shape when fried.
kabocha-squash.visual: a whole kabocha squash, dull dark green skin with pale speckles, squat and round
kabocha-squash.what: A dark green squash with sweet, fluffy, orange flesh.

facts: Kaffir lime is native to Southeast Asia, and its leaves are a key flavour in Thai cooking.
Cooks mostly use the zest and leaves, as the fruit's juice is small in quantity and sour.
kaffir-lime.visual: one whole knobbly kaffir lime, bumpy dark green skin, lying on its side
kaffir-lime.what: A knobbly citrus valued for its perfumed zest and leaves.

facts: Kala namak gets its pinkish-grey colour and sulphur smell from iron and sulphur compounds in the salt.
It is widely used in Indian chaat and in vegan dishes that imitate the taste of egg.
kala-namak.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dark pinkish-grey coarse salt crystals
kala-namak.what: A pungent Indian rock salt with a sulphurous, eggy smell.

facts: Kalamata olives take their name from the city of Kalamata in southern Greece.
They are usually cured in brine or vinegar, which softens their bitterness.
A Greek salad is one of their best-known uses, alongside feta cheese.
kalamata-olives.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of glossy dark purple olives
kalamata-olives.what: Large, purple Greek olives with a fruity, meaty flavour.

facts: It is a common topping for noodle dishes such as udon and ramen in Japan.
A pink-swirled version is traditionally served at New Year celebrations in Japan.
kamaboko.visual: one kamaboko fish cake log, white with a pink spiral pattern, one end cut to show the cross-section, lying on its side
kamaboko.what: A Japanese cake of steamed white fish paste, often sliced.

facts: Kamut is a trademarked name for khorasan wheat, an ancient grain related to durum wheat.
The name khorasan refers to an old region of Iran, Afghanistan and Central Asia.
Its large grains are often used in salads, soups and porridges.
kamut.visual: a small heap of large, plump, golden-brown kamut grains
kamut.what: Large, buttery ancient wheat grains with a chewy texture.

facts: Kangaroos are native to Australia, and their meat is sold there and exported abroad.
kangaroo-fillet.visual: a single raw kangaroo fillet, deep dark red meat, long and lean, lying flat
kangaroo-fillet.what: Lean, dark red meat cut from the back of a kangaroo.

facts: Kangaroo meat is sold in Australia and exported to other countries, including parts of Europe.
Because kangaroo is very lean, it is often cooked quickly or mixed with fat.
kangaroo-mince.visual: a small heap of raw, deep red minced meat with a fine, loose texture on a plain background
kangaroo-mince.what: Lean, dark red minced meat from the Australian kangaroo.

facts: It is made from stretched curd, a method also used for mozzarella and provolone.
kashkaval.visual: a block of pale yellow firm cheese with a smooth rind and one wedge cut away
kashkaval.what: A mild, pale Balkan cheese that melts well when fried.

facts: Kashmiri chillies come from the Kashmir region of northern India and are prized for their colour.
Chilli peppers reached India from the Americas, carried by Portuguese traders.
Kashmiri chilli powder gives dishes such as rogan josh their deep red colour.
kashmiri-chilli-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of vivid red chilli powder, fine and bright
kashmiri-chilli-powder.what: Mild, bright red chilli powder that gives colour, not heat.

facts: Kashmiri chillies take their name from the Kashmir region of northern India.
Cooks use them to colour curries a deep red while adding only mild heat.
The pods are dried, which wrinkles their skin and deepens the colour.
kashmiri-dried-chillies.visual: a small heap of dried, wrinkled, deep red whole chillies, their stalks still attached
kashmiri-dried-chillies.what: Dried red chillies prized for their colour more than heat.

facts: Like mozzarella, it is a stretched-curd cheese, with the curd kneaded in hot water.
It is often used for saganaki, a Greek dish of pan-fried cheese.
kasseri.visual: a pale ivory block of kasseri cheese with one thick wedge cut away, lying flat
kasseri.what: A mild Greek cheese with a buttery, slightly tangy taste.

facts: Fenugreek is grown widely across India and Pakistan, and its leaves are used fresh or dried.
Dried leaves are added near the end of cooking, so their aroma is released over a curry.
Fenugreek is a member of the pea family, and its seeds are also used as a spice.
kasuri-methi.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dried, crumbly grey-green fenugreek leaves, fine and papery
kasuri-methi.what: Dried fenugreek leaves with a sweet, celery-like aroma.

facts: Kataifi is made by pouring thin batter through a sieve onto a hot surface, forming fine threads.
It is used in Greek, Turkish and Middle Eastern desserts, often soaked in syrup.
kataifi-pastry.visual: a loose heap of fine pale kataifi pastry strands, thin golden threads tangled together
kataifi-pastry.what: Fine shredded pastry strands that bake up crisp and golden.

facts: Katsu curry is a Japanese dish of a breaded, fried cutlet served with curry sauce.
Japanese curry was influenced by British curry and became popular during the Meiji era.
The sauce is typically thick and sweet, often made with apple, honey and a roux.
katsu-curry-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, glossy golden-brown curry sauce
katsu-curry-sauce.what: A sweet, mild, golden sauce for Japanese-style curry.

facts: Kaya is a classic breakfast spread in Singapore and Malaysia, often spread on toast.
Pandan leaves are used across Southeast Asia for their grassy, sweet scent.
Kaya is made by slowly cooking coconut milk, eggs and sugar until thick.
kaya.visual: a plain glass jar without a label filled with a smooth, deep golden-brown coconut spread
kaya.what: A sweet coconut and egg spread, scented with pandan.

facts: The Indonesian word kecap is thought to be the source of the English word ketchup.
Kecap asin is made by fermenting soybeans, and it is a common seasoning across Indonesian cooking.
Asin means salty in Indonesian, which sets it apart from the sweet kecap manis.
kecap-asin.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle, three-quarters full of dark, glossy brown soy sauce
kecap-asin.what: A salty, dark Indonesian soy sauce, unsweetened.

facts: Naan is a leavened flatbread traditionally baked in a clay tandoor oven, across South Asia.
The word keema is generally traced to Persian, and it refers to minced meat cooked with spices.
Stuffed naans are a popular treat in Indian and Pakistani restaurants, especially in Britain.
keema-naan.visual: a whole round stuffed naan bread, golden and lightly charred on the surface, on a plain white plate
keema-naan.what: Naan bread filled with a spiced minced lamb mixture.

facts: In Greece it is often sliced and fried as saganaki, which crisps the outside.
Its firm, dry texture means it can be grated over pasta and other dishes.
kefalotyri.visual: a block of pale yellow hard cheese with one thick slice cut off and lying flat beside it
kefalotyri.what: A hard, salty Greek cheese, good for frying.

facts: Kefir is made by fermenting milk with kefir grains, which are cultures of bacteria and yeasts.
Kefir is traditionally associated with the Caucasus region, where it has been made for centuries.
kefir.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with a pale cream-white milky drink, a little foam at the top
kefir.what: A tangy, fizzy drink made from fermented milk.

facts: Its floury texture suits mash and chips, and it is a popular variety in Northern Ireland.
Its pink-tinted skin sets it apart from the plain brown-skinned potatoes common in shops.
It is a maincrop variety, harvested later in the season than early potatoes.
kerr-s-pink-potato.visual: a small heap of whole raw potatoes with pale rosy-pink skins and slightly rough, earthy surfaces
kerr-s-pink-potato.what: A floury, pink-skinned potato, superb for mash and chips.

facts: Kettle cooking fries thin potato slices in small batches in an open pan, giving an uneven, crunchy bite.
Crisps is the British term for thin fried potato snacks, which are called chips in the United States.
kettle-cooked-crisps.visual: a small heap of golden, irregular kettle-cooked potato crisps, rough-edged and uneven, lying loosely
kettle-cooked-crisps.what: Thick, crunchy potato crisps fried in small batches.

facts: Kewra water is made by distilling the flowers of the screwpine plant.
It flavours biryani and Indian sweets, and is especially popular in South Asia.
kewra-water.visual: a small plain unlabelled glass bottle of clear, pale liquid
kewra-water.what: A sweet, musky flavouring distilled from screwpine flowers.

facts: Key limes are smaller and rounder than common Persian limes and have a more intense aroma.
They are named after the Florida Keys, where they were once widely grown.
Key lime pie is a classic dessert made with lime juice, egg yolks and condensed milk.
key-lime.visual: one whole raw key lime, small and round, pale green-yellow skin
key-lime.what: A small, very fragrant lime with a sharp, sour flavour.

facts: Khubz is the Arabic word for bread, and it is eaten across the Arab world.
It is traditionally baked on a hot dome or in an oven, and it puffs up as it cooks.
Flatbreads like khubz are used to scoop up dips, stews and salads across the Middle East.
khubz.visual: one whole round flatbread, pale golden with a soft surface, on a plain white plate
khubz.what: A soft, round flatbread eaten across the Arab world.

facts: Kid is the name for a young goat, usually eaten before it is a year old.
kid-goat-leg.visual: one whole raw goat leg, pale pink meat and small shank bone, lying on a plain background
kid-goat-leg.what: A leg of young goat, mild and tender when slow-roasted.

facts: Kidney beans are a legume native to the Americas, first domesticated there long ago.
Red kidney beans are a common ingredient in chilli con carne.
Dried kidney beans must be boiled thoroughly before eating, and should never be eaten raw.
kidney-beans.visual: a small heap of dried dark red kidney beans, glossy and kidney-shaped, lying loosely
kidney-beans.what: Dark red, kidney-shaped beans, firm and good in stews.

facts: Kielbasa is the Polish word for sausage, and the name covers many styles.
Polish cooks often smoke kielbasa and simmer it in stews or serve it alongside sauerkraut.
kielbasa.visual: one whole smoked kielbasa sausage link, dark reddish-brown casing, gently curved, lying flat
kielbasa.what: A garlicky smoked Polish sausage, good in stews.

facts: It is made by salting vegetables and then mixing them with chilli, garlic and other seasonings.
Its sour flavour develops as lactic acid bacteria ferment the vegetables over days.
kimchi.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of red, chilli-coated kimchi, cabbage pieces glossy and packed
kimchi.what: Spicy Korean pickle, usually made with fermented cabbage.

facts: Kimchi is a traditional Korean dish of fermented vegetables, most often napa cabbage.
Gochugaru, the Korean chilli powder, is a key part of the paste, giving colour and mild heat.
Kimjang, the making of kimchi in large batches for winter, is a long-standing Korean tradition.
kimchi-paste.visual: a plain glass jar without a label filled with bright red kimchi paste, glossy and flecked with chilli
kimchi-paste.what: A red chilli seasoning used to make Korean kimchi.

facts: King crabs live in cold northern seas, including the North Pacific.
Their long legs are the part most often sold, and are usually steamed or boiled.
Crab legs are traditionally served with melted butter for dipping.
king-crab-legs.visual: a pair of long red-orange cooked king crab legs with spiny shells, lying side by side on the background
king-crab-legs.what: Large, sweet-tasting legs from a big deep-sea crab.

facts: King Edward is a long-established British potato variety, still widely grown in the UK.
It is a maincrop potato, which means it is harvested later in the season and stores well.
Its floury texture suits roast potatoes and fluffy mash, a staple of British Sunday dinners.
king-edward-potato.visual: one whole raw floury maincrop potato, oval, pale skin blushed pink, with a few small eyes
king-edward-potato.what: A floury potato that roasts crisp and mashes well.

facts: King oyster mushrooms are native to Europe and Asia and are now widely farmed, mainly in East Asia.
Its species name, eryngii, refers to sea holly plants, on whose roots it often grows in the wild.
Its thick stem can be sliced into rounds and seared, giving a texture similar to scallops.
king-oyster-mushroom.visual: a whole king oyster mushroom with a thick, pale cream stem and a small brown cap
king-oyster-mushroom.what: A thick-stemmed mushroom with a firm, meaty bite.

facts: King prawns are large penaeid prawns found in warm and tropical seas.
Many are farmed in Asia and Latin America.
The name king prawn is a trade term for several large species.
king-prawns.visual: one raw king prawn in its shell, curled body and long antennae, pale grey-pink with faint banding, on a plain background
king-prawns.what: A large sea prawn with plump, sweet meat.

facts: The king scallop is a large marine shellfish found around Europe, and its orange roe is also eaten.
Scallops swim by clapping their shells together, pushing water out to move away from predators.
king-scallops.visual: one raw king scallop, a plump round creamy-white muscle with a thin orange roe attached
king-scallops.what: A large, sweet sea scallop with a firm, pale flesh.

facts: Kingfish is a common name for several species of large ocean fish, not one single fish.
Yellowtail kingfish is found in warm waters around Australia and New Zealand.
kingfish.visual: a raw fish steak, its firm pale pink flesh and dark skin edge showing, lying flat on the background
kingfish.what: A firm, rich fish often cut into steaks for grilling.

facts: Kippers were a staple of the British breakfast table, especially in the Victorian and Edwardian eras.
Herring have long been a major catch in the North Sea fishing trade.
They are usually grilled, fried or poached before they are served.
kippers.visual: one kipper, a smoked herring split open and flattened, golden-brown skin, pale flesh
kippers.what: Smoked herring, split open and cured for breakfast.

facts: Traditional farmhouse Lancashire is crumbly and moist, unlike many hard cheeses.
Lancashire is a county in north-west England, and the cheese takes its name from it.
Lancashire cheese was traditionally made on farms, from milk from the farm's own herd.
kirkham-s-lancashire.visual: a block of pale crumbly cheese, one wedge cut away, lying flat
kirkham-s-lancashire.what: A crumbly, buttery cow's milk cheese from Lancashire.

facts: The name comes from the German word Kirsche, meaning cherry.
It is a classic flavouring in cheese fondue and in cakes such as Black Forest gateau.
kirsch.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of clear, colourless liquid
kirsch.what: A clear brandy distilled from cherries.

facts: Masala is a word for a mixture of spices, used across the Indian subcontinent.
Garam masala is a common blend in North Indian cooking, usually including cumin, coriander and cardamom.
kitchen-king-masala.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine reddish-brown masala powder
kitchen-king-masala.what: A warm, well-rounded blend of Indian spices for curries.

facts: Kiwi fruit originated in China, where it was known as the Chinese gooseberry.
Its tiny black seeds are edible and give a pleasing crunch.
kiwi-fruit.visual: a halved kiwi fruit showing bright green flesh and a ring of tiny black seeds, cut side up
kiwi-fruit.what: A tangy green fruit with tiny black seeds inside.

facts: Kiwiberries come from Actinidia arguta, a hardy vine native to East Asia.
Their skin is thin and smooth enough to eat, so they are usually eaten whole.
Kiwiberries are a close relative of the common kiwi, both members of the genus Actinidia.
kiwiberry.visual: a small heap of smooth, bright green grape-sized fruits, glossy and hairless
kiwiberry.what: A grape-sized kiwi relative with smooth, edible skin.

facts: In Poland, buttered noodles are often finished with poppy seeds, a sweet and nutty combination.
kluski.visual: a small heap of dried pale yellow egg noodles, short twisted strands in a loose pile
kluski.what: Tender Polish egg noodles with a soft, buttery texture.

facts: Knackwurst is a German sausage usually made from finely minced pork and beef, seasoned with garlic.
Its name comes from the cracking sound the casing makes when it is bitten or heated.
In Germany it is often served with sauerkraut and mustard.
knackwurst.visual: a whole raw knackwurst sausage link, pale pinkish-brown casing, smooth and plump, lying in a gentle curve
knackwurst.what: A plump, garlicky German sausage that snaps when cooked.

facts: Kohlrabi is a cultivated form of wild cabbage, grown for its swollen stem rather than its head.
Kohlrabi is popular in Germany, Austria and parts of India, where it is often cooked in curries.
kohlrabi.visual: a whole raw pale green kohlrabi bulb with small stalks attached, lying on its side
kohlrabi.what: A crisp, mild vegetable with a sweet, turnip-like taste.

facts: Koji is steamed rice or grain inoculated with the mould Aspergillus oryzae.
The mould is used across East Asia to make soy sauce, miso and sake.
Its enzymes break starches into sugars, which yeast can then turn into alcohol in sake.
koji.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of loose rice grains coated in a fine, powdery pale off-white mould
koji.what: Rice grains grown with a mould, used to make miso and sake.

facts: Its dark purple rind is dried in the sun and used to give curries a sour taste.
In Goa and Maharashtra it is used to sour fish curries and to make a cooling drink.
kokum.visual: a small heap of dried, dark purple-brown kokum rinds, leathery and flattened
kokum.what: A dried, sour fruit rind from western India.

facts: Kokuto is made by boiling down sugarcane juice and leaving the sugar unrefined.
It is especially associated with Okinawa, where sugarcane has long been grown.
kokuto.visual: a small heap of dark brown, slightly moist cane sugar granules, lying loose on a plain background
kokuto.what: Dark, moist Japanese cane sugar with a rich flavour.

facts: Kola nuts grow on evergreen trees of the genus Cola in the rainforests of West Africa.
Kola nuts are offered to guests in many West African communities as a sign of welcome.
The kola nut gave its name to cola drinks, which were first flavoured with its extract.
kola-nuts.visual: a small heap of irregular pinkish-red kola nuts, some split to show pale cream centres
kola-nuts.what: A bitter nut from West African trees, containing caffeine.

facts: Komatsuna is named after Komatsugawa, an area of Edo, which is now Tokyo.
It belongs to the brassica family, which also includes cabbage and mustard.
In Japan, komatsuna is often used in stir-fries and soups.
komatsuna.visual: a bunch of fresh komatsuna leaves, bright green with pale stems, loosely upright
komatsuna.what: A mild, tender Japanese leafy green, similar to spinach.

facts: Kombu is a kelp that grows in cold northern Pacific waters, notably around Hokkaido in Japan.
It is the basis of dashi, the stock used across Japanese cooking, often with dried bonito flakes.
Kombu has been dried and traded in East Asia for centuries, and is also used in Korean and Chinese cooking.
kombu.visual: a long dried strip of dark green-brown kombu seaweed, lying flat
kombu.what: Dried kelp seaweed, the savoury base of Japanese dashi.

facts: Dashi is the basic stock of Japanese cooking, used in soups, sauces and simmered dishes.
Kombu is a type of edible kelp that is dried before use and often soaked to make dashi.
Its savoury depth comes from natural compounds in the seaweed, not from meat or fish.
kombu-dashi.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with pale golden kombu stock
kombu-dashi.what: A light Japanese stock made by steeping dried kelp.

facts: Kombucha is made by fermenting sweetened tea with a living culture of bacteria and yeast.
Its origins are often traced to East Asia, though the exact history is uncertain.
kombucha.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale golden fizzy liquid, small bubbles rising through it
kombucha.what: A fizzy, sour drink made from fermented sweet tea.

facts: Kombucha is tea fermented with a symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast, sometimes called a SCOBY.
Kombucha is thought to have originated in East Asia, later spreading to Russia and Eastern Europe.
The culture consumes the tea's sugar during fermenting, leaving a sharp, acidic liquid behind.
kombucha-vinegar.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with pale golden, slightly cloudy vinegar
kombucha-vinegar.what: A sharp, tangy vinegar made from fermented sweet tea.

facts: Konjac is a plant grown in East and Southeast Asia for its large underground corm.
In Japan, konjac has long been made into firm, jelly-like blocks called konnyaku.
konjac.visual: a whole raw konjac corm, rounded and brown-grey, with a rough, mottled skin, lying on the background
konjac.what: A starchy corm whose flour makes springy noodles.

facts: Many Korean marinades use soy sauce, sesame, garlic and grated Asian pear.
Bulgogi roughly means fire meat in Korean.
korean-bbq-sauce.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with glossy dark brown sauce
korean-bbq-sauce.what: A sweet, savoury soy and sesame marinade for grilled beef.

facts: Chilli peppers reached Korea through trade from the Americas and became central to Korean cooking.
Long green chillies like these are often used whole in stews and soups.
Gochugaru, dried red chilli flakes, is a separate product used for kimchi and seasonings.
korean-green-chilli.visual: a whole fresh long green chilli pepper, slightly curved, glossy skin, stem still attached
korean-green-chilli.what: A long, crisp green chilli with moderate heat from Korea.

facts: Perilla is a member of the mint family, Lamiaceae.
In Korea the leaves are often wrapped around grilled meat, known as ssam.
In Japan the same plant is known as shiso and used in sushi and pickles.
korean-perilla.visual: a loose bunch of fresh, broad, serrated green perilla leaves with their stems together
korean-perilla.what: Broad green leaves with a nutty, slightly minty flavour.

facts: Korma is a mild dish associated with the Mughal cooking tradition of northern India.
Korma sauces are usually made with yoghurt or cream, ground nuts and gentle spices.
korma-curry-paste.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, filled with thick, smooth golden-brown curry paste
korma-curry-paste.what: A mild, creamy spice paste used to make korma sauce.

facts: The name korma is thought to come from a word meaning braising.
Korma is traditionally associated with Mughal cooking in northern India.
korma-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, pale cream-coloured korma sauce
korma-sauce.what: A mild, creamy sauce of almonds, coconut and spices.

facts: Koroneiki is a small olive variety grown mainly in Greece, especially in Crete and the Peloponnese.
Its name comes from the village of Koroni in the south-west of the Peloponnese.
Its small olives are rich in oil, which is why the variety is valued for pressing.
koroneiki-olive-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with golden-green olive oil
koroneiki-olive-oil.what: A small, intense Greek olive oil, peppery and herbal.

facts: Kosher salt gets its name from its use in koshering meat, a Jewish dietary process of salting.
Its large, flaky crystals are easy to pinch and spread evenly over food before cooking.
Because crystal sizes vary, the same measure of kosher salt can taste different in different brands.
kosher-salt.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with coarse white flaky salt crystals
kosher-salt.what: A coarse, flaky salt that is easy to pinch.

facts: Kumamoto oysters are named after Kumamoto Prefecture on the island of Kyushu in Japan.
They are farmed in coastal bays and are typically sold on the half shell.
kumamoto-oysters.visual: one whole raw oyster in its deep, rough grey shell, lying on its side
kumamoto-oysters.what: A small, creamy Japanese oyster with a mild, sweet taste.

facts: Kumquats are native to south-east China, where they have been cultivated for centuries.
The name comes from the Cantonese for 'golden orange'.
Their thin, sweet peel wraps a tart flesh, so the whole fruit is often eaten.
kumquat.visual: a small cluster of whole bright orange kumquats with glossy skins
kumquat.what: A tiny orange citrus fruit that is eaten peel and all.

facts: Kung pao dishes are popular in Sichuan-style cooking and in restaurants around the world.
It is a common stir-fry sauce in Chinese restaurants in Britain.
kung-pao-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of glossy reddish-brown sauce
kung-pao-sauce.what: A sweet, sour and spicy Chinese stir-fry sauce.

facts: Labneh is made by straining yoghurt until most of the whey has drained away.
It is often shaped into balls and kept in olive oil with herbs or spices.
labneh.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, smooth, creamy white labneh with a soft swirl on top
labneh.what: A thick, tangy strained yoghurt, often served as a dip.

facts: Lager ferments at cooler temperatures than ale, which gives it a crisp, clean taste.
Pilsner is a famous type of lager, first brewed in the Czech city of Pilsen in the 19th century.
lager.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale golden beer topped with a light foam head, plain background
lager.what: A crisp, pale beer brewed with bottom-fermenting yeast.

facts: Rice noodles are made from rice flour and water, then steamed or boiled.
Laksa has many regional styles, from curry laksa to Sarawak laksa.
laksa-noodles.visual: a small heap of thick, dried white rice noodles
laksa-noodles.what: Thick round rice noodles that hold their shape in soup.

facts: Laksa is a noodle soup with strong roots in Peranakan cooking in Malaysia and Singapore.
Pastes like this are usually pounded or blended from fresh aromatics before being fried.
Lemongrass is a tall grass native to tropical Asia, and its stalks are prized for their citrus scent.
laksa-paste.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with thick orange-red paste
laksa-paste.what: A spicy paste of lemongrass and chilli for noodle soup.

facts: Breast of lamb is often boned, rolled and stuffed before being slowly roasted.
It is an economical cut that becomes tender with long, slow cooking.
lamb-breast.visual: a whole raw breast of lamb, a rectangular slab of pale pink meat with a thick layer of fat
lamb-breast.what: A fatty cut from the lamb's belly, best slow-roasted.

facts: The chump lies at the back of the loin, next to the leg, and is cut into chops.
lamb-chump-chop.visual: one raw lamb chump chop, a thick rounded cut with a rim of creamy fat, lying flat
lamb-chump-chop.what: A thick, meaty chop cut from the rump end of a lamb.

facts: A cutlet is a small cut of meat, usually from the rib or loin, and the word comes from the French côtelette.
Lamb cutlets cook quickly, so they are often grilled, pan-fried or seared over high heat.
The rack is a row of rib bones, and cutting it between the bones gives individual cutlets.
lamb-cutlets.visual: two raw lamb cutlets, small pink chops with a thin rim of fat and a short exposed rib bone, lying side by side
lamb-cutlets.what: Small, tender lamb chops cut from the rack.

facts: Devilled kidneys, cooked with mustard and cayenne, are a traditional British dish.
Lamb's kidneys are smaller and milder than pig's or beef kidneys.
Kidneys are usually cooked quickly, because overcooking makes them tough.
lamb-kidneys.visual: two raw lamb kidneys, glossy reddish-brown, lying side by side
lamb-kidneys.what: Small organ meat from lamb with a mild, tender flavour.

facts: The word kofta comes from Persian, and the dish is made across the Middle East, South Asia and the Balkans.
The mince is pressed firmly around the skewer, so it holds its shape while grilling.
Lamb is a common choice for koftas, though beef and chicken versions are also made.
lamb-koftas.visual: two grilled lamb koftas, browned sausage-shaped mince on flat metal skewers, served on a plain white plate
lamb-koftas.what: Seasoned minced lamb, moulded onto skewers and grilled.

facts: Garlic and rosemary are classic partners, pushed into small cuts in the meat before roasting.
lamb-leg.visual: a whole raw leg of lamb, pale pink meat with a thin layer of white fat, the bone visible at one end
lamb-leg.what: A large roasting cut from the hind leg of a young sheep.

facts: A loin chop is the cut from the back of the lamb that looks like a miniature T-bone steak.
lamb-loin-chops.visual: a single raw lamb loin chop, small and lean, with a rim of white fat along one edge
lamb-loin-chops.what: Small, tender chops cut from the back of a young lamb.

facts: Lamb has been eaten across the Middle East and Central Asia for thousands of years.
Kofta is a spiced mince dish, shaped into balls or sausages, found from the Middle East to India.
Shepherd's pie, traditionally made with lamb, is an English dish topped with mashed potato.
lamb-mince.visual: a small heap of raw minced lamb, fine texture, pale red and flecked white
lamb-mince.what: Meat from a young sheep, minced finely for koftas and pies.

facts: Sheep were domesticated in the Near East many thousands of years ago, so lamb has long been eaten there.
Lamb is cooked in many cuisines, from Middle Eastern kebabs to British roasts.
lamb-neck-fillet.visual: one raw lamb neck fillet, long narrow boneless cut with deep red meat and a thin layer of white fat, lying flat
lamb-neck-fillet.what: A long, tender boneless cut from the lamb's neck.

facts: A noisette is named after the French word for hazelnut, from its small round shape.
Noisettes are usually cut from the loin, the tender muscle along the back.
lamb-noisettes.visual: three raw lamb noisettes, neat boneless rounds of pink-red meat, lying flat
lamb-noisettes.what: Small boneless rounds cut from the loin of a young sheep.

facts: Lamb ribs come from the breast, a fatty cut that suits long, low cooking.
lamb-ribs.visual: a rack of raw lamb ribs, meaty pink with a thick layer of white fat, lying flat
lamb-ribs.what: Fatty rib cuts from the breast, tender when slow-cooked.

facts: The rump is the cut from the top of the lamb's hind leg, near the loin.
lamb-rump.visual: one raw lamb rump, a boneless oval cut with a thin white fat cap and dark red meat
lamb-rump.what: A tender, lean cut from the leg, often roasted pink.

facts: Stuffed lamb's heart is a traditional British dish.
Offal, including heart, is eaten in many traditional cuisines around the world.
lamb-s-heart.visual: one whole raw lamb's heart, deep red, lying on its side on the background
lamb-s-heart.what: A dense, lean muscle from a young sheep, good for stuffing.

facts: Lamb's lettuce is also known as corn salad and mâche, the French name.
Despite its name, it belongs to the valerian family rather than the lettuce family.
lamb-s-lettuce.visual: a small bunch of tender dark green lamb's lettuce rosettes, the small rounded leaves still joined at the base, on the plain background
lamb-s-lettuce.what: A small, mild salad leaf with rounded green rosettes.

facts: Liver has been eaten as food for thousands of years in cultures around the world.
Lamb's liver is generally milder in flavour than beef liver.
lamb-s-liver.visual: a whole raw lamb's liver with a smooth reddish-brown surface, lying flat
lamb-s-liver.what: A soft, mild liver from a young sheep, usually fried.

facts: Lamb's tongue is usually simmered gently until tender, then peeled and sliced.
Tongue from cattle and sheep has been eaten in many European cuisines for centuries.
