lamb-s-tongue.visual: one whole raw lamb's tongue, pale pink, smooth and slightly curved, lying flat
lamb-s-tongue.what: The tongue of a young sheep, slow-cooked until tender.

facts: Lamb sausages appear in Middle Eastern, North African and Mediterranean cooking.
Harissa is a fiery chilli paste from Tunisia, flavoured with garlic, cumin and caraway.
Merguez is a spiced North African sausage, usually made from lamb or beef.
lamb-sausage.visual: a single raw lamb sausage link, pale pinkish-brown, lying in a gentle curve
lamb-sausage.what: A sausage of minced lamb, flavoured with mint or harissa.

facts: Shanks are the lower part of the leg, where the muscle works hard, so they need slow cooking.
The bone and connective tissue release flavour and body into the sauce as it cooks.
lamb-shank.visual: one raw lamb shank, a small lower leg cut with pale pink meat around a bare bone end
lamb-shank.what: A cut from the lower leg that turns tender when braised.

facts: Lamb shoulder contains connective tissue that softens into tender meat with slow, moist cooking.
lamb-shoulder.visual: one whole raw lamb shoulder joint, marbled pink meat, a thin layer of fat on top
lamb-shoulder.what: A fatty, flavourful cut from the front leg of lamb.

facts: Stock is made by simmering bones and aromatics for a long time to draw out flavour.
Scotch broth is a traditional Scottish soup of lamb, barley and vegetables.
lamb-stock.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of clear golden lamb stock
lamb-stock.what: A rich, savoury broth made by simmering lamb bones.

facts: Stock cubes were developed in the early twentieth century as a way to store concentrated flavour.
Cubes are dissolved in hot water to make a quick broth for soups, stews and sauces.
Concentrated stock cubes became popular in Britain as a convenient alternative to homemade broth.
lamb-stock-cube.visual: a pale brown compressed stock cube in a small plain white ceramic bowl
lamb-stock-cube.what: Dried lamb stock pressed into a cube for quick broth.

facts: Sweetbreads are glands from young animals, most often from lambs or calves.
They are blanched, pressed and then fried or braised in many European kitchens.
Sweetbreads are a traditional dish in French and British cooking, valued for their soft texture.
lamb-sweetbreads.visual: two pale pink raw lamb sweetbreads side by side, lobed texture visible
lamb-sweetbreads.what: Tender offal from young lamb, rich and creamy when cooked.

facts: Lambic is brewed mainly in the Senne valley around Brussels, where the cool air carries wild yeasts.
Its wild fermentation happens in open vessels exposed to the air, rather than with added cultured yeast.
Gueuze blends young and old lambics together, and kriek adds sour cherries to the beer.
lambic.visual: a clear drinking glass, half full of hazy golden beer under a thin white head of foam
lambic.what: A sour Belgian beer fermented by wild yeasts from the air.

facts: Lamian is a noodle from China, traditionally made from wheat flour and water.
The city of Lanzhou, in Gansu province, is known for a beef noodle soup made with these noodles.
lamian.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of long, pale, glossy wheat noodles, loosely coiled
lamian.what: Long, stretchy Chinese wheat noodles with a springy bite.

facts: Lampreys are jawless fish with a round sucker-like mouth lined with teeth.
Lamprey pie was a prized dish at medieval English tables.
In Bordeaux, lamprey is cooked in red wine in a classic dish called lamproie à la bordelaise.
lamprey.visual: one whole raw lamprey, long and eel-like, with olive-grey skin and a pale belly
lamprey.what: An eel-like jawless fish, once prized at medieval feasts.

facts: Lancashire cheese has been made in north-west England for centuries.
Historically it was made on farms, using milk from local herds.
lancashire.visual: a wedge of pale, crumbly cheese lying on its flat side, one cut face showing a clean edge
lancashire.what: A creamy, crumbly English cheese that melts beautifully.

facts: Land cress belongs to the cabbage family, Brassicaceae, along with mustard and rocket.
It grows in ordinary soil, unlike watercress, which grows in running water.
land-cress.visual: a small bunch of dark green land cress leaves on thin pale stalks, lying flat
land-cress.what: A peppery salad leaf related to watercress and mustard.

facts: Langoustines live on muddy seabeds in the North Atlantic and the Mediterranean.
The French name langoustine means little langouste, a spiny lobster.
Their meat is sweet and is often served grilled or in a rich bisque.
langoustine.visual: one whole raw langoustine, pale orange-pink shell, long claws, lying on its side
langoustine.what: A small, sweet-fleshed sea crustacean related to lobsters.

facts: It originated in Guizhou province in south-west China and is now sold widely.
It is often spooned over noodles, rice, dumplings and eggs.
lao-gan-ma.visual: a plain glass jar filled with dark red chilli oil and crisp brown fried flakes
lao-gan-ma.what: A crunchy chilli condiment of fried soybeans in oil.

facts: The name lap cheong means preserved sausage in Cantonese, and the sausages are air-dried.
They are made from minced pork and fat, seasoned with soy and sugar, then dried.
Lap cheong are a traditional part of Cantonese cooking, often sliced and steamed over rice.
lap-cheong.visual: a single whole dried pork sausage, reddish-brown and slightly wrinkled, lying in a gentle curve
lap-cheong.what: A sweet, dried Chinese pork sausage, often sliced thinly.

facts: Lapsang souchong comes from the Wuyi Mountains in Fujian province, southeast China.
Its smoky flavour comes from drying the leaves over fires of pinewood.
lapsang-souchong.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dark, wiry black tea leaves, smoky and dry
lapsang-souchong.what: A smoky black tea from China, dried over pine wood fires.

facts: Lard is rendered pork fat: the fat is melted down slowly and then strained.
For centuries, lard was a common cooking fat in kitchens across Europe and the Americas.
Its crystals give pastry a flaky texture, which is why it has long been used in pie crusts.
lard.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of soft, creamy white lard
lard.what: Soft white pork fat, used for flaky pastry and frying.

facts: Lardo is especially associated with the village of Colonnata in Tuscany, near the Carrara marble quarries.
Traditionally it was cured in marble basins with salt, garlic, rosemary and pepper.
Its name comes from the Latin lardum, meaning fat, which is also the root of the word lard.
lardo.visual: a thin slice of white cured pork back fat, translucent, with a faint pink edge, lying flat on the background
lardo.what: Cured pork back fat, sliced paper-thin for serving.

facts: Hens have been kept for their eggs for thousands of years.
Eggs bind, set and add lift to cakes, custards and sauces.
large-egg.visual: a single whole raw large brown hen's egg, lying on a plain pale background
large-egg.what: A larger hen's egg, the usual size called for in baking.

facts: Lasagne is made in many regions of Italy, each with different fillings and sauces.
Many modern recipes use no-boil sheets, which need no pre-cooking.
lasagne-sheets.visual: a neat pile of flat, dried pale yellow lasagne sheets, edges straight
lasagne-sheets.what: Flat, wide pasta sheets for layered baked dishes.

facts: Lassi is made by blending yoghurt with water and either salt, sugar or fruit.
lassi.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale creamy yoghurt drink, slightly frothy at the top
lassi.what: A chilled, creamy yoghurt drink from India and Pakistan.

facts: Lavash is traditionally baked against the inside walls of a clay oven, which makes it thin and quick to cook.
The bread is popular across Armenia, Iran, Georgia and the wider region, and is often used to wrap fillings.
Because it is thin and pliable, it can be rolled around grilled meats, herbs and salad.
lavash.visual: one large thin sheet of pale flatbread, lying flat and unfolded, with soft golden spots on its surface
lavash.what: A thin, soft Armenian flatbread that rolls easily.

facts: Lavender is native to the Mediterranean region and parts of Africa and Asia.
Its flavour is strong, so cooks use it sparingly in sweet and savoury dishes.
lavender-buds.visual: a small heap of dried lavender buds, grey-purple and fine-textured
lavender-buds.what: Dried, fragrant flower buds from the lavender plant.

facts: Lavender is native to the Mediterranean region and is now grown widely across Europe.
Its flavour is soft and floral, and it is often used in tea and desserts.
Honey is made when bees collect nectar and store it in the honeycomb.
lavender-honey.visual: a plain clear glass jar of pale golden honey, thick and slow-flowing
lavender-honey.what: Pale, floral honey made from bees feeding on lavender.

facts: Lavender grows around the Mediterranean, and its flowers have long been used to flavour food in southern Europe.
Lavender sugar is made by storing dried buds with sugar, so the scent passes into the crystals.
The name lavender is thought to come from the Latin lavare, meaning to wash.
lavender-sugar.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine white sugar with a few dried purple lavender buds scattered through it
lavender-sugar.what: Sugar scented with dried lavender buds, for baking.

facts: Laverbread is made from laver, a red seaweed simmered for hours until it becomes a soft purée.
In Wales it is often fried in bacon fat and served as part of a traditional breakfast.
Laver has been gathered along the Welsh coast for centuries, especially near Swansea.
laverbread.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, dark green seaweed purée, soft and glossy
laverbread.what: A dark green Welsh purée made from cooked seaweed.

facts: Gelatine is made by cooking animal collagen from skin and bones, usually from pigs or cattle.
Gelatine sets as it cools and melts again when warmed, which is why it is used in mousses and jellies.
Leaf gelatine is soaked in cold water to soften before it is melted into a warm liquid.
leaf-gelatine.visual: a small neat heap of thin, pale, translucent gelatine sheets lying flat
leaf-gelatine.what: Thin, clear sheets that set liquids into a firm jelly.

facts: Leaf lard comes from the fat that surrounds a pig's kidneys and has a very neutral flavour.
Lard has been used in cooking across Europe and the Americas for centuries.
leaf-lard.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth pale white lard, creamy and firm
leaf-lard.what: Mild, pure pork fat prized for flaky pastry.

facts: Minced beef is made by passing meat through a grinder, which breaks it into small pieces.
The word mince comes from the Old French mincier, meaning to cut into small pieces.
lean-beef-mince.visual: a small heap of raw minced beef with a fine, even texture and deep red colour
lean-beef-mince.what: Minced meat trimmed of most fat, good for quick sauces.

facts: Lebanese cucumbers are a short, slim variety that is popular across the Middle East.
They are usually eaten unpeeled, as their skin is thin and tender.
They are a traditional part of salads such as fattoush and Lebanese chopped salad.
lebanese-cucumber.visual: a whole slender dark green cucumber with a smooth, thin skin
lebanese-cucumber.what: A small, thin-skinned cucumber, crisp and very mild.

facts: Lebanese flatbread is baked on a very hot surface, so it puffs up as it cooks.
Similar thin breads are eaten across the Levant and the wider Middle East.
It is often torn up and used to scoop dips such as hummus.
lebanese-flatbread.visual: a plain white plate holding two soft round Lebanese flatbreads, lightly puffed and golden
lebanese-flatbread.what: A thin, soft round flatbread used for wraps and mezze.

facts: Seven spice is a blend used in Lebanese cooking, especially for kibbeh, a dish of minced meat and bulgur.
Despite its name, the blend does not always contain exactly seven spices, and recipes vary.
lebanese-seven-spice.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with fine reddish-brown ground spice blend
lebanese-seven-spice.what: A warm, ground spice blend for rice, meat and stews.

facts: Lecithin is found naturally in egg yolk and soya beans.
Its name comes from the Greek word for egg yolk, lekithos.
lecithin.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, full of pale tan lecithin granules
lecithin.what: A natural fatty substance that helps oil and water mix.

facts: Leeks are grown by earthing up the soil around their stems, which keeps them pale and tender.
Leeks are a national emblem of Wales, where they are traditionally worn on St David's Day.
leek.visual: a whole fresh leek with long dark green leaves and a pale white base, a little earth on the root
leek.what: A mild onion relative with layered, sweet white stems.

facts: Cheeses with holes, like Emmental, form when gas released by bacteria is trapped during ripening.
The Netherlands has a long dairy tradition, and cheese is one of its best-known exports.
leerdammer.visual: a block of pale yellow semi-hard cheese with round holes, one slice cut off and laid flat
leerdammer.what: A mild, nutty, semi-hard Dutch cheese with holes.

facts: Lemons are thought to have come from Asia and spread to the Mediterranean over many centuries.
Lemon trees are evergreen and grow fruit throughout much of the year in warm climates.
Lemon zest is the thin yellow outer peel, and it holds most of the fruit's fragrant oils.
lemon.visual: a whole ripe yellow lemon with a bumpy, glossy skin, lying on its side
lemon.what: A sour yellow citrus fruit, used for juice and zest.

facts: Lemon balm belongs to the mint family and grows across Europe and western Asia.
Its lemon scent fades when the leaves are dried.
lemon-balm.visual: a small bunch of bright green lemon balm leaves on a short stem, plain background
lemon-balm.what: A soft, lemon-scented herb from the mint family.

facts: Barley water has long been a British summer drink, served cold at picnics and parties.
It is made by simmering pearl barley in water, then straining and adding lemon and sugar.
lemon-barley-water.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with pale, cloudy yellow liquid
lemon-barley-water.what: A sweet, sharp drink made from barley, lemon and sugar.

facts: The herb is best added near the end of cooking, so its fresh flavour is kept.
lemon-basil.visual: a small bunch of fresh lemon basil, bright green leaves on slender pale green stems
lemon-basil.what: A basil with a strong lemon scent and fresh flavour.

facts: Lemon curd is a thick spread cooked slowly on the stove, set by egg yolks rather than gelatine.
It is traditionally spread on bread or toast, and used as a filling for tarts and sponge cakes.
In older British recipes it is sometimes called lemon cheese, though it contains no cheese.
lemon-curd.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, glossy pale-yellow lemon curd with a smooth, slightly peaked surface
lemon-curd.what: A smooth, tangy spread of lemon, eggs, sugar and butter.

facts: Boiled sweets are made by heating sugar and water to a very high temperature, then cooling and shaping them.
Lemon drops are sometimes dusted in sugar to stop them sticking together.
lemon-drops.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with pale yellow, glossy, sugar-coated lemon boiled sweets
lemon-drops.what: Tart lemon boiled sweets, often coated in sugar.

facts: Lemon extract is typically made by soaking lemon peel in alcohol to draw out its flavour.
Lemons are thought to have come from Asia and reached Europe through the Middle East.
Because it is so concentrated, a few drops of lemon extract go a long way in a recipe.
lemon-extract.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle holding pale yellow lemon extract liquid
lemon-extract.what: Concentrated lemon flavouring for icing and sponge cakes.

facts: Lemon glaze is made by mixing icing sugar with lemon juice until it is thin enough to pour.
Lemon drizzle cake is a classic British bake that is finished with a sharp lemon glaze.
lemon-glaze.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale yellow lemon glaze
lemon-glaze.what: A sharp, sugary icing that is drizzled over cakes.

facts: Olive oil is pressed from the fruit of the olive tree, a crop grown around the Mediterranean for thousands of years.
Infused oils are made by steeping flavouring ingredients such as citrus peel in oil over time.
The Mediterranean region is famous for lemons, which flavour fish, salads and sauces in many dishes.
lemon-infused-olive-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with pale yellow-gold olive oil
lemon-infused-olive-oil.what: Olive oil flavoured with lemon, good over fish or salad.

facts: Lemons are believed to have originated in Asia before spreading through trade.
Lemon juice is the sharp base of lemon curd and of the classic lemon meringue pie.
It is used across Greek, Italian and Middle Eastern cooking to brighten dishes.
lemon-juice.visual: a clear drinking glass half full of pale yellow lemon juice, slightly cloudy
lemon-juice.what: Sharp, fresh juice squeezed from ripe lemons.

facts: Marmalade takes its name from the Portuguese word marmelo, meaning quince, from which early versions were made.
Traditional British marmalade is usually made from Seville oranges, which are very bitter and set well.
Lemon marmalade is made by simmering sliced lemon peel, juice and sugar until the mixture sets.
lemon-marmalade.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, holding thick golden marmalade full of fine, translucent strands of lemon peel
lemon-marmalade.what: A tangy preserve of lemons, sugar and shredded peel.

facts: Lemon myrtle is a native Australian tree from the subtropical rainforests of the east coast.
Its leaves contain a strong citrus oil, which gives the herb its lemony scent.
lemon-myrtle.visual: a small bunch of fresh narrow pale-green lemon myrtle leaves with stems attached
lemon-myrtle.what: A leafy Australian herb with a bright lemon-lime flavour.

facts: Because it is so concentrated, only a few drops are needed in baking and sweets.
Citrus peel oils have long been used in cooking and perfumery.
lemon-oil.visual: a small plain unlabelled glass bottle of pale yellow oil, with a plain stopper
lemon-oil.what: An intensely zesty oil for sweets and baking.

facts: Lemon pepper is an American seasoning, popular for rubbing onto chicken and fish.
Black pepper has been traded across Asia and Europe for thousands of years.
Its name simply describes the mix: lemon peel for citrus and black pepper for heat.
lemon-pepper.visual: a small heap of coarsely cracked black pepper flecked with pale yellow dried zest
lemon-pepper.what: Cracked black pepper blended with dried lemon peel.

facts: Sea salt is made by evaporating seawater, leaving salt crystals behind.
Lemon zest is the thin coloured outer skin of the fruit.
lemon-salt.visual: a small heap of coarse pale salt flecked with yellow lemon zest
lemon-salt.what: Sea salt mixed with dried lemon zest for seasoning.

facts: Despite its name, the lemon sole is a flatfish and not a true sole.
It lives on sandy and muddy seabeds around the coasts of northern Europe.
Its delicate flesh suits quick cooking, such as pan-frying or grilling.
lemon-sole.visual: one whole raw lemon sole, flat oval body, pale yellowish-brown skin, lying flat
lemon-sole.what: A delicate white flatfish, often sold whole for frying.

facts: Its scent comes from natural oils held in the small leaves, which release when crushed or heated.
Thyme is native to the Mediterranean and has been used in cooking for thousands of years.
lemon-thyme.visual: a small bunch of fresh lemon thyme sprigs with tiny green leaves, lying on a plain background
lemon-thyme.what: A thyme variety with a fresh citrus scent and mild flavour.

facts: Lemon verbena is native to South America, and it is grown in Europe and elsewhere for its scented leaves.
The leaves are used to flavour teas, syrups and custards, and they are often infused in hot liquid.
Lemon verbena is a shrub and is not related to the common lemon tree, but its leaves are intensely lemony.
lemon-verbena.visual: a small loose bunch of long, pointed, pale green lemon verbena leaves on their woody stems
lemon-verbena.what: A herb with strongly lemon-scented leaves for infusing.

facts: Vinaigrette is a dressing of oil and an acid, traditionally vinegar.
Vinaigrettes are shaken or whisked so the oil and acid briefly combine.
lemon-vinaigrette.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale yellow dressing, standing upright
lemon-vinaigrette.what: A zesty dressing of lemon juice and oil.

facts: Street sellers in 17th-century Paris were known for selling lemonade.
In Britain, lemonade often means a fizzy, clear soft drink rather than a freshly squeezed one.
lemonade.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with pale yellow, cloudy lemonade
lemonade.what: A sweet, sharp drink of lemon juice, sugar and water.

facts: Lemongrass is a tall tropical grass native to South and Southeast Asia.
Its stalks are bruised or finely sliced before use to release the aroma.
It is widely used in Thai and Vietnamese cooking, in soups, curries and marinades.
lemongrass.visual: a bunch of fresh lemongrass stalks, pale at the base and green at the tips, with long thin leaves
lemongrass.what: A citrus-scented grass with tough, pale stalks.

facts: Lemongrass is a tall grass native to tropical Asia, grown for its fragrant stalks.
It is a staple of Thai and Vietnamese cooking, used in soups, curries and marinades.
lemongrass-paste.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with pale green lemongrass paste
lemongrass-paste.what: A smooth, citrusy paste made from ground lemongrass stalks.

facts: Lentils have been cultivated in the Near East for thousands of years.
Lentils are a staple in Indian, Middle Eastern and Mediterranean cooking.
lentil-pasta.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dried lentil pasta twists, golden-brown and matt
lentil-pasta.what: Pasta made from lentil flour, with an earthy flavour.

facts: Lentils are sprouted by soaking the seeds in water until small shoots appear, usually within a few days.
Lentils have been eaten in the Middle East and South Asia for thousands of years.
Lentil sprouts are often added to salads and sandwiches for their crunch.
lentil-sprouts.visual: a small heap of fresh, pale lentil sprouts, with thin white stems and small pale leaves
lentil-sprouts.what: Tender, nutty sprouts grown from lentil seeds.

facts: Fresh rhizomes are firm and are often sliced and pounded into spice pastes for curries.
Lesser galangal is grown in tropical gardens, and the underground stem is harvested rather than a true root.
lesser-galangal.visual: a small bunch of slender yellowish rhizomes with ringed, knobbly skin lying on a plain background
lesser-galangal.what: A slim, knobbly root with a sharp, camphor-like bite.

facts: Leyden cheese takes its name from the city of Leiden in the Netherlands.
Caraway and cumin are traditional flavourings in Dutch and German cheeses.
Its seeds are mixed into the curd before the cheese is pressed and aged.
leyden.visual: a rectangular block of pale yellow cheese with one wedge cut away, dark cumin seeds dotted through the cut face
leyden.what: A Dutch cheese flavoured with cumin and caraway seeds.

facts: Mayonnaise is an emulsion, with oil whisked into egg yolk until the two stay blended.
Its origin is disputed, with several accounts of where it was first made.
light-mayonnaise.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale creamy-white mayonnaise, smooth and glossy
light-mayonnaise.what: A pale, creamy sauce of egg yolk, oil and vinegar.

facts: Muscovado is an unrefined sugar made by boiling down cane juice without fully removing its molasses.
Its name is thought to come from the Portuguese 'mascavado', meaning unrefined.
It is produced in places including Mauritius and the Philippines.
light-muscovado-sugar.visual: a small heap of soft, pale brown muscovado sugar, clumpy and slightly damp-looking
light-muscovado-sugar.what: A soft, moist brown sugar with a mellow caramel flavour.

facts: Light olive oil is refined, which removes much of the stronger flavour and colour.
Refined olive oil has a higher smoke point than extra virgin oil, making it suited to frying.
Olive oil has been pressed from olives around the Mediterranean for thousands of years.
light-olive-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden olive oil, closed by a stopper
light-olive-oil.what: A mild, pale olive oil that is good for frying.

facts: Brown sugar keeps some molasses on the sugar crystals, which gives it its colour and moisture.
Sugar cane and sugar beet are the two main sources of sugar worldwide.
light-soft-brown-sugar.visual: a small heap of moist, pale golden-brown sugar crystals
light-soft-brown-sugar.what: Moist, fine sugar with a gentle caramel flavour.

facts: Soy sauce is made from fermented soybeans and roasted wheat.
Light soy is thinner and paler than dark soy and is used mainly for flavour, not colour.
Soy sauce was developed in China and spread across East Asia over many centuries.
light-soy-sauce.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of thin, pale brown liquid
light-soy-sauce.what: A thin, salty soy sauce for seasoning and dipping.

facts: Treacle is a thick, sweet syrup left over from refining sugar.
Light treacle is milder and paler than black treacle, which is more bitter.
Treacle is a traditional ingredient in British puddings such as treacle sponge.
light-treacle.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with thick golden treacle
light-treacle.what: Mild golden treacle, sweeter and lighter than black.

facts: Limes are thought to come from South-east Asia and spread through trade across the tropics.
Lime juice is widely used in cooking across Mexico, South-east Asia and many other regions.
lime.visual: a single whole fresh green lime with smooth glossy skin, slightly speckled
lime.what: A small green citrus fruit with sharp, aromatic juice.

facts: Cordial is a concentrated fruit syrup, usually diluted with water or soda before drinking.
It is usually made from lime juice concentrate, sugar and water, sometimes with added lime oil.
lime-cordial.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale green lime cordial
lime-cordial.what: A sharp, sweet concentrated lime syrup for mixing drinks.

facts: Lemon curd is the classic version, and lime curd is made the same way.
It is cooked gently in a bowl over simmering water until thick.
Lime curd is used as a filling for tarts and cakes, or spread on toast.
lime-curd.visual: a small plain glass bowl of pale green lime curd, smooth and glossy
lime-curd.what: A tangy spread made from lime juice, eggs and sugar.

facts: In the past, British sailors were given lime juice on long voyages at sea.
Lime juice is a key flavour in Thai and Vietnamese cooking.
Lime juice is used in many Latin American dishes, including ceviche.
lime-juice.visual: a clear drinking glass half filled with pale green lime juice
lime-juice.what: Sharp juice from green limes, used in drinks and cooking.

facts: Marmalade takes its name from marmelo, the Portuguese word for quince.
Lime marmalade follows the classic orange version but uses limes instead.
Marmalade is made by boiling citrus peel, juice and sugar until the mixture sets.
lime-marmalade.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with glossy pale green-gold lime marmalade, strips of peel visible
lime-marmalade.what: A tangy spread of lime fruit and peel set with sugar.

facts: Lime pickle is common across India and is often made with lime, salt, chilli and spices.
Many versions are left to mature for several weeks, so the lime rind softens and the flavour deepens.
It is served alongside rice, flatbreads and curries across South Asia.
lime-pickle.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with pale yellow-green pickled lime pieces in oil
lime-pickle.what: Salty, very hot pickle made from preserved limes.

facts: Limoncello is made by steeping lemon peel in alcohol, then adding sugar and water.
It comes from the Amalfi Coast and southern Italy, where lemons grow in abundance.
It is often served chilled after a meal, and it is also used in cakes and desserts.
limoncello.visual: a clear drinking glass holding bright yellow liqueur
limoncello.what: A sweet Italian liqueur made from lemon peel.

facts: Limpets are a type of sea snail, and they cling to rocks with a strong, muscular foot.
Limpets have been gathered from rocky coasts for food since prehistoric times, and their shells survive in old middens.
In parts of Britain they are traditionally cooked in their shells or simmered in stews.
limpets.visual: a small heap of raw limpets in their grey-brown conical shells, rough and ridged
limpets.what: A cone-shaped shellfish that clings to shore rocks.

facts: Lincolnshire sausages are traditionally seasoned with sage, which gives them a distinctive flavour.
They are often eaten fried or grilled, and sometimes served in a bread roll.
lincolnshire-sausage.visual: one whole raw Lincolnshire sausage link, coarse pinkish texture with flecks of green herbs, lying in a gentle curve
lincolnshire-sausage.what: A coarse, herby pork sausage from Lincolnshire, England.

facts: Ling is found in the cold North Atlantic, including the waters around Britain, Ireland and Norway.
Salted and dried ling has long been a staple in Scandinavia and the Faroe Islands.
ling-fillet.visual: one raw ling fillet with firm, pale white flesh, lying flat
ling-fillet.what: A firm, mild white fish related to cod.

facts: Lingcod is not a true cod; it belongs to a separate family of fish found along the Pacific coast of North America.
Lingcod is found from Alaska down to Baja California, along rocky coastal waters.
Its firm white flesh holds together well when baked, fried or grilled.
lingcod.visual: one whole raw lingcod, long mottled grey-green body with a large head, lying flat
lingcod.what: A large, firm-fleshed fish from the North Pacific coast.

facts: Lingonberries grow wild on low evergreen shrubs across the cold forests of Scandinavia.
Lingonberry jam is a classic accompaniment to Swedish meatballs.
lingonberry.visual: a small heap of fresh red lingonberries, tiny glossy round berries lying loosely together on a plain background
lingonberry.what: A tart red berry from Scandinavia, eaten with meatballs.

facts: Lingonberries grow wild across the forests of Scandinavia and northern Europe.
In Sweden, lingonberry jam is traditionally served with meatballs.
Lingonberries are naturally tart, so the jam is usually made with plenty of sugar.
lingonberry-jam.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with glossy deep red lingonberry jam
lingonberry-jam.what: A tart, red Nordic jam made from wild lingonberries.

facts: Linguine means little tongues in Italian, a name that reflects its shape.
Linguine is often served with clams, a classic pairing in Italian coastal cooking.
Dried pasta like linguine is made from durum wheat semolina and water.
linguine.visual: a small loose heap of dried linguine, flat pale ribbons of pasta
linguine.what: Flat, narrow ribbons of pasta that cling well to sauces.

facts: Linseed is the seed of the flax plant, which has been cultivated for thousands of years.
Linseed oil is pressed from the seeds and has long been used in paints and varnishes.
In British shops the seeds are often sold as linseed, while in North America they are called flaxseed.
linseed.visual: a small heap of golden linseeds, glossy and oval, loose on the background
linseed.what: Small, glossy seeds from the flax plant.

facts: Lion's mane is a tooth fungus that grows on hardwood trees such as oak and beech, not on the ground.
Its name comes from the long, dangling spines that resemble the mane of a lion.
In Japan it is known as yamabushitake and has long been used in Japanese and Chinese cooking.
lion-s-mane-mushroom.visual: a whole lion's mane mushroom, a shaggy white cluster of long dangling spines
lion-s-mane-mushroom.what: A shaggy white mushroom with a soft, shreddable texture.

facts: Liquid egg is pasteurised, a gentle heat treatment used to process eggs commercially.
Egg white whips into a foam because its proteins stretch and trap air bubbles.
Whisked egg whites are used in meringues, soufflés and light sponge cakes.
liquid-egg-white.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, clear, slightly cloudy liquid egg white
liquid-egg-white.what: Pasteurised egg white sold as a liquid, ready to whisk.

facts: Liquorice comes from the root of Glycyrrhiza glabra, a plant that grows in Asia and southern Europe.
Sweet liquorice flavoured with aniseed is especially popular in the Netherlands and Scandinavia.
Its name comes from the Greek word glykyrrhiza, meaning sweet root.
liquorice.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with glossy black liquorice sweets
liquorice.what: A dark, chewy sweet with an aniseed taste and bitter edge.

facts: Liquorice root has been used as a sweetener in Europe and Asia for thousands of years.
Its distinctive taste comes from a naturally sweet compound found in the root.
In Yorkshire, liquorice was long made into sweets such as Pontefract cakes.
liquorice-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, dark brown liquorice powder, level at the top
liquorice-powder.what: A fine, sweet-earthy powder made from liquorice root.

facts: Liquorice comes from the Glycyrrhiza plant, a legume native to parts of southern Europe and Asia.
Its sweetness comes from glycyrrhizin, a compound that tastes many times sweeter than sugar.
Pieces of the root are often steeped in hot water to make a sweet, mildly aniseed-flavoured drink.
liquorice-root.visual: one whole dried liquorice root, brown and wrinkled, lying on its side
liquorice-root.what: A sweet, woody root used to flavour teas and sweets.

facts: Little gem is a small type of cos lettuce, a group known for upright, long leaves.
Cos lettuce is often said to take its name from the Greek island of Kos.
little-gem-lettuce.visual: one whole small pale green lettuce head, compact and crisp, leaves packed in a tight rounded heart
little-gem-lettuce.what: A small, crisp lettuce with sweet, tender inner leaves.

facts: Livarot is a washed-rind cheese, meaning its rind is regularly brushed with brine during ripening.
Livarot is made in the Pays d'Auge area of Normandy, where it has been produced for centuries.
livarot.visual: a whole round soft cheese with a sticky orange-brown rind, wrapped in a band of reed-like sedge, lying on the background
livarot.what: A strong, soft cheese from Normandy, wrapped in reed bands.

facts: Liver sausage is a traditional German and Central European food, known there as leberwurst.
It is made by blending cooked pork liver with fat and spices, then packing it into casings.
liver-sausage.visual: one thick slice of smooth pinkish-brown liver sausage, cut edge showing, lying flat
liver-sausage.what: A smooth, spreadable sausage of pork liver and spices.

facts: Lo mein means tossed noodles in Cantonese, and the dish is served with a sauce rather than soup.
The noodles are boiled, then tossed in a sauce with vegetables or meat in a hot wok.
Egg noodles have been made in China for many centuries and are eaten across the country.
lo-mein-noodles.visual: a small loose heap of uncooked yellow egg noodles, lying on a plain background
lo-mein-noodles.what: Soft, chewy wheat-and-egg noodles for saucy stir-fries.

facts: Lobsters are marine crustaceans, related to crabs, shrimp and crayfish.
Lobster is traditionally steamed, grilled or poached, and it is often served with melted butter.
Live lobsters turn red when cooked, because the heat changes pigments in the shell.
lobster.visual: one whole raw lobster, dark blue-green shell, claws held in a relaxed curve, lying on a plain background
lobster.what: A large sea crustacean with sweet, firm meat.

facts: The tail holds much of a lobster's edible meat, which is why it is often sold separately.
Lobsters are crustaceans, related to crabs, shrimp and prawns.
Lobster tails are often split lengthways, then grilled or baked with butter.
lobster-tail.visual: one raw lobster tail in its shell, greyish-green, segments visible, lying on its side
lobster-tail.what: The sweet, firm meat from the tail of a lobster.

facts: The loganberry was bred in California in 1881 by James Harvey Logan.
It is a cross between a raspberry and a blackberry, so it tastes of both.
Loganberries are often cooked into jams, pies and syrups because they are quite tart.
loganberry.visual: a small heap of dark red loganberries, glossy and slightly elongated
loganberry.what: A tart berry bred from a raspberry and a blackberry.

facts: Lollo rosso is a loose-leaf lettuce with deep red frilled edges, widely grown across Europe.
Its ruffled leaves are popular in mixed salads, where they add colour as well as crunch.
lollo-rosso.visual: one whole head of lollo rosso lettuce, frilly leaves with red edges, standing upright on its base
lollo-rosso.what: A frilly red-tinged lettuce with a mild, sweet taste.

facts: Basmati and jasmine rice are both long-grain varieties with distinct aromas.
Rice is thought to have been first domesticated in China thousands of years ago.
long-grain-rice.visual: a small heap of raw long-grain white rice grains, slender and glossy
long-grain-rice.what: Slender grains that stay separate when cooked.

facts: Long pepper is the dried fruiting spike of a climbing plant from the same family as black pepper.
Romans used long pepper in their cooking before black pepper became common in Europe.
Its Sanskrit name is pippali, and it was traded widely across the Indian Ocean in earlier centuries.
long-pepper.visual: a small heap of slim dried long pepper catkins, dark brown and ridged, on a plain background
long-pepper.what: A slim dried catkin with a sweet, cinnamon-like heat.

facts: Longan is grown in southern China and across Southeast and South Asia.
Its Chinese name means 'dragon's eye', a reference to the dark seed seen through the flesh.
Dried longan is used in Chinese teas and sweet soups.
longan.visual: a small cluster of round, thin-skinned brown longan fruits still on their stalks
longan.what: A small sweet fruit with translucent white flesh.

facts: Similar sausages are found in Spain, Latin America and the Philippines.
In Spain, longaniza is commonly seasoned with garlic and paprika.
In the Philippines, longganisa varies by region, from sweet to garlicky.
longaniza.visual: one whole raw longaniza sausage, long and thin, rosy pork casing, in a gentle curve
longaniza.what: A long, thin pork sausage, spiced with garlic or aniseed.

facts: Loquats originated in southern China, where the tree has been grown for many centuries.
Loquats are now grown in Mediterranean countries such as Spain.
The fruit is often eaten fresh or poached, and it is sometimes made into jam.
loquat.visual: a small bunch of loquats on their stalks, pale orange oval fruit with a soft fuzzy skin
loquat.what: A small orange fruit with a sweet, apricot-like flavour.

facts: Lor is made by heating the whey left over from cheesemaking until it curdles.
It is often used in savoury pastries and is sold fresh in Turkey.
lor.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of soft white lor curd
lor.what: A soft, mild Turkish curd cheese made from whey.

facts: Lorne sausage is a Scottish speciality made from minced meat, rusk and spices, pressed into a block and sliced.
It is typically fried until crisp at the edges and eaten in a bread roll for breakfast.
lorne-sausage.visual: a single raw square slice of pale pinkish-brown sausage meat with an even flat surface
lorne-sausage.what: A thin, square, seasoned Scottish sausage slice.

facts: Lotus root is the rhizome of the sacred lotus, a water plant grown in ponds and paddies.
When sliced across, the root shows a pattern of holes that gives it a lace-like look.
In Japan the root is called renkon and is often simmered or pickled.
lotus-root.visual: a whole raw lotus root, pale beige and knobbed, lying on its side
lotus-root.what: The crunchy, underwater stem of the lotus plant, sliced.

facts: Lotus seeds come from the seed heads of the lotus, a water plant grown across Asia.
In Chinese cooking they are often used in sweet soups and desserts.
They have a mild, nutty flavour and a soft, starchy texture when cooked.
lotus-seeds.visual: a small heap of dried lotus seeds, pale ivory and oval with a slightly rough skin
lotus-seeds.what: Starchy, chewy seeds from the lotus plant.

facts: Lotus stems and roots are eaten in China, Japan and India, often sliced and stir-fried or simmered.
Lotus root has channels running through it, which show as round holes when it is sliced.
lotus-stem.visual: a slice of raw lotus stem, pale cream, lying flat and showing several round holes in the cut face
lotus-stem.what: A crisp, hollow lotus plant stem used in Asian cooking.

facts: Many Louisiana hot sauces are a tangy addition to Cajun and Creole cooking, used at the table and in the pot.
Hot sauce is found across the southern United States, and bottles often sit on the dinner table.
louisiana-style-hot-sauce.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of thin, bright orange-red hot sauce with a plain cap
louisiana-style-hot-sauce.what: A thin, tangy hot sauce made from chilli and vinegar.

facts: Lovage is a tall perennial herb long grown in gardens across Europe.
Its leaves and seeds carry a strong, celery-like flavour that suits soups and stews.
lovage-seed-salt.visual: a plain glass jar without a label of pale green-flecked salt, the lid off and set beside it
lovage-seed-salt.what: A savoury salt blended with lovage, a celery-flavoured herb.

facts: The word lox comes from the Yiddish laks, meaning salmon.
It is served thinly sliced, often on a bagel with cream cheese and onion.
lox.visual: thin, translucent slices of pinkish-orange salmon laid flat in an overlapping row
lox.what: Salmon preserved in brine, then sliced very thin.

facts: Young luffa is eaten as a vegetable, while mature fruits dry into the natural loofah sponge.
It is common in South and East Asian cooking, where it is added to curries and stir-fries.
luffa.visual: a whole young luffa gourd, long and slim, pale green with pronounced ridges running its length
luffa.what: A young, ridged gourd that turns silky when cooked.

facts: Lumache means snails in Italian, and the shape is named after the snail shell it resembles.
The ridged, curled shape traps sauce and suits chunky ragù or cheese-based sauces.
Like most dried pasta, lumache are made from durum wheat semolina and water.
lumache.visual: a small heap of uncooked dried lumache pasta, golden ridged shells, lying loose
lumache.what: Small snail-shaped pasta with ridges that hold sauce.

facts: Lumpfish are small, stocky fish found in cold northern seas around Iceland and Greenland.
The roe is often dyed black and sold as a cheaper alternative to caviar.
Its small grains are used as a garnish on blinis and cream cheese in Scandinavia.
lumpfish-roe.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of tiny glossy black fish eggs
lumpfish-roe.what: Small, salty black fish eggs that pop, from the lumpfish.

facts: Lupins are legumes related to peas and beans, and their seeds are very bitter when raw.
To make them edible, lupini beans are soaked and brined, which removes the bitterness.
They have been eaten around the Mediterranean since ancient times and are sold as a snack.
lupini-beans.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with pale yellow brined lupini beans, flat and round
lupini-beans.what: A brined, pale yellow bean eaten as a Mediterranean snack.

facts: Lutefisk is a traditional dish from Norway and Sweden, often eaten at Christmas and winter dinners.
The dried cod is soaked in water for a long time, then in lye, an alkali, before it is cooked.
The name is generally taken to mean lye-fish, referring to the lye used in its preparation.
lutefisk.visual: a single portion of soft, pale white lutefisk fish on a plain white plate
lutefisk.what: Dried cod soaked in lye, then rinsed to a soft texture.

facts: Lychee is native to southern China, where it has been cultivated for many centuries.
The fruit spoils quickly after picking, so it is often sold fresh in season or canned.
lychee.visual: a small bunch of fresh lychees on the stem, rough reddish-pink shells intact
lychee.what: A small red fruit with sweet, translucent white flesh.

facts: Maasdam was developed in the Netherlands in the Swiss style.
Like Emmental, it forms large holes as bacteria release gas during ripening.
maasdam.visual: a block of pale yellow cheese with one thick wedge cut away, showing large round holes
maasdam.what: A mild, nutty Dutch cheese with large holes.

facts: Macadamia nuts are native to the subtropical rainforests of eastern Australia.
The nut is named after John Macadam, a Scottish-born scientist who worked in Victoria, Australia.
Macadamia trees are widely grown in Hawaii and Australia for their nuts.
macadamia-nuts.visual: a small heap of shelled macadamia nuts, pale creamy-beige and round, lying loosely together
macadamia-nuts.what: Rich, buttery nuts with a very hard shell.

facts: The oil is pressed from the nut kernels and is valued for its high smoke point in cooking.
The nut is named after John Macadam, a Scottish-born Australian chemist.
macadamia-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden oil
macadamia-oil.what: A mild, buttery oil pressed from macadamia nuts.

facts: The name comes from the Italian word maccheroni, used for many short tube pastas.
Macaroni cheese, a British classic, bakes short curved pasta in a cheese sauce.
Southern Italy, especially Naples, has a long history of dried pasta production.
maccheroni.visual: a small heap of short, hollow, curved macaroni pasta tubes, uncooked and dry, lying on the background
maccheroni.what: Short, hollow pasta tubes, often curved, for baking.

facts: Mace is the aril, the lacy red covering, of the nutmeg seed, which is removed and dried.
Mace has a warm, delicate flavour and is used in baking, sauces, pickles and processed meats.
mace-blades.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dried mace blades, orange-red and lacy
mace-blades.what: Dried lacy covering of the nutmeg seed, used as a spice.

facts: Atlantic mackerel is a migratory fish found across the North Atlantic and along European coasts.
Mackerel has been eaten in Britain for centuries and is often served with gooseberry sauce.
Its oily flesh spoils quickly, so mackerel is usually cooked soon after it is caught or bought.
mackerel-fillet.visual: a fillet of raw mackerel with silver skin and dark blue-green markings across its back, lying flat
mackerel-fillet.what: A rich, oily sea fish with a strong, distinctive flavour.

facts: Madeira wine is made on the Portuguese island of Madeira, in the Atlantic Ocean.
Madeira cake is named after the wine, and the wine is also used in rich sauces and gravies.
madeira.visual: a clear drinking glass of deep amber, golden-brown fortified wine, filled to the top
madeira.what: A rich, amber fortified wine from the island of Madeira.

facts: Madeira cake is a traditional British sponge, a dense, plain cake made with butter, sugar, eggs and flour.
Lemon zest and citron peel are classic flavourings in traditional Madeira cake recipes.
madeira-cake.visual: a whole plain Madeira cake loaf with one thick slice cut away, pale golden crumb and a smooth domed top
madeira-cake.what: A plain, buttery sponge loaf with a light lemon flavour.

facts: Madras is a city in southern India, now known as Chennai, and gave its name to this curry style.
Madras-style curries became popular in British restaurants during the twentieth century.
The paste is usually built on chilli, tomato and spices such as cumin and coriander.
madras-curry-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, deep red-brown curry paste
madras-curry-paste.what: A hot, tomato-rich paste used in British curries.

facts: Madras is the former name of Chennai, a city on the south-east coast of India.
Madras-style dishes are hot curries that became popular in Britain as restaurant food.
Chilli, tomato and spices such as cumin and coriander are common in Madras-style sauces.
madras-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth deep red curry sauce
madras-sauce.what: A hot, tomato-based curry sauce for quick meals.

facts: It is an Italian pasta, traditionally made from durum wheat semolina and water.
Ruffled ribbon pastas suit rich meat and tomato sauces, which cling to their edges.
mafaldine.visual: A loose heap of dried, pale cream pasta ribbons, each with a ruffled edge.
mafaldine.what: Ribbon pasta with ruffled edges that catches sauce well.

facts: Mahi-mahi is found in warm, open waters of tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide.
It is also called dorado or dolphinfish, although it is not related to dolphins.
Its firm flesh suits grilling, and it is often served with fruit salsa.
mahi-mahi.visual: a whole raw mahi-mahi, bright blue-green and golden sides, and a deeply forked tail
mahi-mahi.what: A firm, mild white fish from warm tropical seas.

facts: It is a traditional flavouring in Middle Eastern and Levantine breads and pastries such as ma'amoul.
Its flavour is often described as a mix of bitter almond and cherry.
mahleb.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, pale beige ground mahleb powder
mahleb.what: Ground kernels from a wild cherry stone, used in breads.

facts: Mahón is a cheese from the Spanish island of Menorca, protected by a designation of origin.
mahon.visual: a block of firm pale yellow cheese with one wedge cut from it, lying flat on a plain background
mahon.what: A tangy Spanish cow's milk cheese from Menorca.

facts: Maitake is usually translated from Japanese as 'dancing mushroom'.
It grows in clusters at the base of trees, often oaks, in woodlands across Japan and North America.
In North America it is also called hen of the woods, a name for the same mushroom.
maitake-mushroom.visual: a cluster of raw maitake mushrooms with frilly grey-brown caps fanned out from one pale base
maitake-mushroom.what: Frilly, fan-shaped mushroom with a rich, earthy taste.

facts: The word makhani comes from makhan, the Hindi word for butter, which describes the sauce well.
The sauce is simmered with tomato, then enriched with butter and cream for a smooth, mild richness.
Cooks also use it for paneer and vegetable dishes, not only for chicken.
makhani-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, orange-red, glossy buttery sauce
makhani-sauce.what: A smooth tomato sauce made rich with butter and cream.

facts: Makrut lime is a citrus tree native to Southeast Asia, grown mainly for its leaves and rind.
Its leaves are used whole in Thai curries and soups and then removed before eating.
makrut-lime-leaves.visual: a small bunch of glossy dark-green double-lobed leaves, stems attached
makrut-lime-leaves.what: Aromatic leaves from a Southeast Asian citrus tree.

facts: Malabar spinach is not a true spinach; it comes from a climbing vine in the Basellaceae family.
It grows across tropical Asia and Africa, where its leaves are cooked in curries and stir-fries.
When cooked, the leaves release a natural gel, which is why they thicken soups and stews.
malabar-spinach.visual: a bunch of fleshy, glossy green Malabar spinach leaves with thick pale stems
malabar-spinach.what: Fleshy leaves from a climbing vine that thicken stews.

facts: Malanga is a corm, a swollen underground stem, grown in tropical America and the Caribbean.
Malanga is closely related to taro, and its flesh is pale with a fine, starchy texture.
malanga.visual: one whole brown malanga root, with rough, hairy-looking skin and an oval, knobbly shape
malanga.what: A starchy tropical root vegetable with a nutty flavour.

facts: Malbec originated in south-west France, where it was once a common grape in Bordeaux blends.
Argentina became closely associated with Malbec, and it is now the country's best-known red grape.
Malbec wine is often soft and fruity, with dark plum and blackberry notes.
malbec.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with deep ruby-red wine
malbec.what: A dark, plummy red wine grape, grown widely in Argentina.

facts: Salt has been made by evaporating seawater around the town of Maldon in Essex for a long time.
The flakes are pyramid-shaped, so they crunch easily and are usually sprinkled over food just before serving.
maldon-salt-flakes.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of delicate, pale, flaky white salt crystals
maldon-salt-flakes.what: Delicate, crunchy sea salt flakes made in Essex, England.

facts: The mallard is the wild ancestor of most domestic ducks and is found across the northern hemisphere.
mallard.visual: one whole raw wild duck, plump, with dark lean breast skin, lying on its side
mallard.what: A wild duck with dark, lean meat and a rich flavour.

facts: Malt loaf is a traditional British tea bread, sweetened and flavoured with malt extract.
Malted barley is also used in brewing beer and in malted milk drinks.
malt-extract.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, holding thick, dark brown syrup
malt-extract.what: A thick, dark, sticky syrup made from malted barley.

facts: Malt loaf is a traditional British teatime bread, often sliced and eaten with butter.
It is made with malt extract, which gives it a dark colour and a sticky, chewy texture.
malt-loaf.visual: a whole glossy dark brown malt loaf, one end cut to show a sticky, chewy crumb
malt-loaf.what: A sticky, chewy British loaf sweetened with malt extract.

facts: Malt vinegar is made by fermenting malted barley into ale, then turning the ale into vinegar.
It is a classic British condiment, traditionally splashed over fish and chips.
malt-vinegar.visual: A plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of amber-brown vinegar, the light glowing through it.
malt-vinegar.what: A brown, tangy vinegar made from malted barley.

facts: The name means badly cut in Italian, referring to its irregular shapes.
It is often served in soups and bean dishes, where its ragged edges catch the sauce.
Its shapes are cut by hand from rolled pasta sheets, which gives each piece a different shape.
maltagliati.visual: a small heap of rough, irregular triangular and diamond-shaped dried pasta pieces, lying on the background
maltagliati.what: Small, irregular pasta shapes, cut from pasta sheets.

facts: Malted milk powder is typically made from malted barley, wheat flour and milk, giving a toasted, sweet taste.
Malt is barley that has been allowed to sprout and then dried, which gives it a sweet flavour.
In Britain, biscuits are often dunked in tea, a habit enjoyed by many across the country.
malted-milk-biscuits.visual: a single round pale golden biscuit with a smooth, slightly domed top, lying directly on a plain background
malted-milk-biscuits.what: Mild, malty biscuits, often eaten with a cup of tea.

facts: Malted milk powder was first made in the United States in the late 19th century.
It is made from malted barley, wheat flour and dried milk, then sold as a powder.
It gives a toasty, sweet flavour to milkshakes and some baked goods.
malted-milk-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with pale golden malted milk powder
malted-milk-powder.what: A sweet powder of milk and malted barley for shakes.

facts: Manakish is a common breakfast food and snack across the Levant.
Common toppings include za'atar, cheese and minced meat.
manakish.visual: one round flatbread, golden and bubbled, topped with a green-brown herb paste, on a plain white plate
manakish.what: A Levantine flatbread often topped with za'atar and oil.

facts: Manchego takes its name from La Mancha, a region of central Spain.
It is made from the milk of Manchega sheep, a breed native to that region.
Manchego is traditionally eaten with membrillo, a thick quince paste.
manchego.visual: one wedge of pale ivory firm cheese with a darker zig-zag patterned rind and a smooth cut face
manchego.what: A firm, nutty cheese made from sheep's milk in Spain.

facts: Their loose skin makes them easy to peel, which is why they are popular as a snack.
Clementines and satsumas are both closely related to the mandarin.
mandarin.visual: one whole ripe mandarin, bright orange with a slightly loose, glossy peel
mandarin.what: A small, sweet citrus with loose skin that peels easily.

facts: Mangetout means eat all in French, because the whole pod is eaten.
Mangetout is grown in many parts of Asia and Europe and has been cultivated for centuries.
Snow peas are a key vegetable in Chinese stir-fries, where they are often added near the end of cooking.
mangetout.visual: a small heap of bright green flat mangetout pods, slightly curved, lying loose
mangetout.what: Flat, crisp green pea pods that are eaten whole.

facts: Mangoes are native to South Asia, where they have been cultivated for thousands of years.
Mango is the national fruit of India.
The fruit is used in chutneys, lassi, salsas and desserts across many cuisines.
mango.visual: a whole ripe mango, yellow-orange blushed with red, smooth skin, lying on its side
mango.what: A sweet, juicy tropical fruit with a large flat stone.

facts: The word chutney comes from the Hindi chatni, used for a range of spiced relishes.
mango-chutney.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick orange-brown chutney with a glossy, jammy texture
mango-chutney.what: A sweet, spiced relish made from mango, sugar and vinegar.

facts: Mango is the national fruit of India, the Philippines and Pakistan.
Mango pulp and juice are the base of the popular yoghurt drink mango lassi.
mango-juice.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with smooth, golden-orange mango juice
mango-juice.what: Sweet juice made from ripe tropical mangoes.

facts: Mango pickle is a South Asian preserve, made by salting and steeping raw mango in spices and oil.
Mustard oil is widely used in Bengali and North Indian cooking and gives pickles a pungent flavour.
Pickling raw mango is a long tradition in India, where the fruit is made into many regional varieties.
mango-pickle.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, full of golden-orange pieces of pickled mango in oil
mango-pickle.what: Sharp, spicy pickled mango preserved in mustard oil.

facts: Mango salsa is a classic partner for grilled fish and tacos, and it is especially popular in Mexico and the Caribbean.
Mangoes are native to South Asia and have been cultivated there for thousands of years.
mango-salsa.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of chunky orange mango salsa, dotted with tiny red pieces
mango-salsa.what: A chunky sauce of diced mango, onion, chilli and lime.

facts: Mangosteen is native to Southeast Asia, where it has been grown for centuries.
Its thick purple rind is inedible; the soft white segments inside are the edible part.
Mangosteens are traditionally eaten fresh, and the segments are often served as a dessert or in fruit salads.
mangosteen.visual: one whole round mangosteen, deep purple-brown skin, with a small green-tipped cap on top
mangosteen.what: A purple tropical fruit with sweet white segments inside.

facts: Manicotti means little sleeves in Italian, a name that refers to its tube shape.
Manicotti is traditionally from Italy, and in the United States it is often stuffed with ricotta.
The tubes are boiled until just soft, then filled and baked so they hold their shape.
manicotti.visual: a small heap of dried manicotti pasta tubes, ridged and pale cream, lying loose on the background
manicotti.what: Large tubes of pasta, stuffed and baked under a sauce.

facts: Manouri is traditionally made from the whey left after making feta or other cheeses in Greece.
It is traditionally made in Greece, especially in Thessaly and Macedonia.
manouri.visual: a soft white block of manouri cheese, one thick wedge cut away to show a creamy interior
manouri.what: A soft, creamy Greek cheese with a mild, milky taste.

facts: Mantis shrimp are not true shrimp; they belong to an order of crustaceans called stomatopods.
Some species have club-like or spear-like claws that they use to hunt prey.
In Japan, mantis shrimp, called shako, are often served sliced as sushi.
mantis-shrimp.visual: one whole raw mantis shrimp, pale orange-speckled shell, long segmented body, lying on its side
mantis-shrimp.what: A spiny sea creature with sweet meat, not a true shrimp.

facts: Mantou is a staple in northern China, where wheat foods are widely eaten.
The buns are made from a yeasted dough and steamed rather than baked, which keeps them soft.
They can be eaten plain or split and filled, and are often served with savoury dishes.
mantou.visual: a single plain white steamed bun with a smooth domed top, soft and matte, on a plain background
mantou.what: A soft, plain Chinese steamed bun with a mild taste.

facts: Manuka honey is made by bees that gather nectar from manuka, a shrub native to New Zealand and parts of Australia.
Manuka is a Māori name for the plant, and beekeepers have produced this honey in New Zealand for decades.
manuka-honey.visual: a plain glass jar without a label filled with dark amber honey
manuka-honey.what: A dark, strong-tasting honey from New Zealand.

facts: Manzanilla olives are grown mainly in Andalusia in southern Spain.
They are often stuffed with pimiento, a sweet red pepper.
They are usually cured in brine, which gives them a mild, salty flavour.
manzanilla-olives.visual: a small heap of shiny green Manzanilla olives, lying on the background
manzanilla-olives.what: Small green Spanish olives, cured in brine.

facts: Maple flavouring is a bottled essence used in baking and icings to give a maple taste.
Canada is the leading producer of maple syrup, and Quebec makes most of it.
maple-flavouring.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale amber liquid, cap closed
maple-flavouring.what: A concentrated, syrupy essence that tastes of maple.

facts: Maple sugar is made by boiling maple sap until nearly all the water has evaporated.
Maple sugaring was practised for centuries by Indigenous peoples of north-eastern North America.
maple-sugar.visual: a small heap of pale golden maple sugar crystals in a small plain white ceramic bowl
maple-sugar.what: A fine sugar made by boiling down maple tree sap.

facts: Maple syrup is made by boiling down the sap of sugar maple trees in late winter.
Quebec is famous for its maple syrup, and Canada is a leading producer.
Indigenous peoples of northeastern North America made maple syrup long before European settlers.
maple-syrup.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of amber maple syrup
maple-syrup.what: Sweet syrup boiled down from the sap of maple trees.

facts: Maras pepper comes from Kahramanmaraş, a city in southern Turkey, and takes its name from it.
The peppers are dried in the sun, then crushed into flakes that are rich and mildly hot.
Maras biber is used in Turkish dishes such as kebabs, stews and dips.
maras-pepper.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with coarse deep red pepper flakes
maras-pepper.what: Sun-dried Turkish chilli flakes, mild and slightly sweet.

facts: The name comes from maraschino, a liqueur distilled from marasca sour cherries.
Commercial cherries are usually bleached, dyed red and packed in sugar syrup.
They are a classic garnish for cocktails such as the Manhattan, and for ice-cream sundaes.
maraschino-cherry.visual: a single glossy, bright red maraschino cherry with a short green stem
maraschino-cherry.what: A bright red cherry preserved in sugar syrup.

facts: Maraschino is traditionally made in Zadar, a port city on the Croatian coast.
It is used in cocktails such as the Aviation and in some desserts.
maraschino-liqueur.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with a colourless liquid
maraschino-liqueur.what: A sweet, bittersweet liqueur made from cherries.

facts: Marcona is a traditional Spanish almond variety, grown mainly in eastern Spain.
They are often fried gently in olive oil, which gives them a soft, tender bite rather than a hard crunch.
Marcona almonds are commonly served as a snack with drinks in Spanish bars.
marcona-almonds.visual: a small loose heap of plump, pale golden almonds, seen from above
marcona-almonds.what: A round, plump Spanish almond with a rich, sweet bite.

facts: Margarine was developed in France in the nineteenth century as a cheaper alternative to butter.
Modern margarines are made by blending vegetable oils with water and emulsifiers to create a spreadable texture.
margarine.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale yellow soft margarine, smooth surface
margarine.what: A soft, butter-like spread made from vegetable oils.

facts: Pot marigold, also called calendula, is a flower that has long been used in European cooking.
marigold-petals.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of loose, dried orange marigold petals, bright and unarranged
marigold-petals.what: Golden flower petals used for colour in rice and soups.

facts: Marinara is a simple Italian sauce, usually made with tomatoes, garlic and herbs.
Traditional marinara contains no cheese or meat, and is often served with pasta.
Tomatoes reached Europe from the Americas, and became central to Italian cooking.
marinara-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, deep red sauce with a slightly chunky texture
marinara-sauce.what: A quick Italian sauce of tomato, garlic and herbs.

facts: Marionberry was developed at Oregon State University and named after Marion County in Oregon.
It is a cross of other blackberry varieties, bred for a rich flavour and firm berries.
marionberry.visual: a small heap of glossy dark purple-black berries, slightly oval and plump
marionberry.what: A dark, sweet blackberry-type fruit grown in Oregon.

facts: It is a widely grown British potato, popular for roast potatoes and chips.
Its floury, dry flesh breaks down easily, so it suits both roasting and mashing.
Potatoes originated in the Andes of South America before spreading to Europe.
maris-piper-potato.visual: one whole raw potato, oval with a thin tan skin and a few small eyes, lying on its side
maris-piper-potato.what: A floury British potato, good for roasting and mash.

facts: The flesh is dense and firm, which makes it suited to grilling and barbecuing.
Marlin is sometimes sold as a steak, cut across the body of the fish.
marlin-steak.visual: a raw marlin steak, thick firm dark-pink fish cut with a pale skin edge, lying on the background
marlin-steak.what: A thick, firm steak cut from a large ocean fish.

facts: The Marmande tomato is named after Marmande, a town in south-west France.
It is prized for its firm, meaty flesh.
Its ribbed shape makes it well suited to being stuffed and baked whole.
marmande-tomato.visual: a whole ripe Marmande tomato, deep red and deeply ribbed, lying on its side
marmande-tomato.what: A large, ribbed, juicy tomato good for stuffing.

facts: Maroilles takes its name from a town in the Nord department of northern France.
It has a washed rind, rubbed with brine during ripening, which gives it a strong smell.
maroilles.visual: one square block of soft pale cheese, orange-brown washed rind, one corner cut away, lying flat
maroilles.what: A strong, pungent cheese from northern France.

facts: Marrons glacés are a traditional French sweet, made over several days by soaking chestnuts in syrup.
The syrup is added in stages, so the sugar slowly replaces the water inside the chestnut.
They are often given as gifts around Christmas, especially in France.
marron-glace.visual: one whole glossy candied chestnut with a shiny sugar coat, pale amber-brown, lying on its side
marron-glace.what: A whole chestnut slowly candied in vanilla sugar syrup.

facts: A marrow is a large form of courgette, grown to a much bigger size than usual.
Marrows are a popular crop on British allotments and at village produce shows.
marrow.visual: one whole large cylindrical green-striped marrow with smooth glossy skin, lying on its side
marrow.what: A large, mild courgette-like squash, good for stuffing.

facts: Marrowfat is a type of pea grown for drying, rather than the fresh garden pea eaten in the pod.
Marrowfat peas are left to mature on the plant, so they are starchy and dry.
They are the basis of mushy peas, a traditional British dish often sold alongside fish and chips.
marrowfat-peas.visual: a small loose heap of dried pale green marrowfat peas, seen from above
marrowfat-peas.what: Large dried peas that soften into a thick, soft mash.

facts: Marsala takes its name from the port city of Marsala on the west coast of Sicily.
It is used in Italian cooking for dishes like veal escalope and in the dessert zabaglione.
marsala.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle, full of deep amber marsala wine
marsala.what: A fortified wine from Sicily, nutty and sweet.

facts: Marshmallow fluff was developed in the United States, where it became a popular sandwich spread.
Its base is egg whites whipped with sugar and corn syrup, giving a light, airy texture.
Cooks use it in fudge, frostings and fillings, and it is a classic ingredient in American sandwiches.
marshmallow-fluff.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with white, glossy whipped marshmallow spread, lid off
marshmallow-fluff.what: A sticky whipped spread for sandwiches and fudge.

facts: Marshmallows were once made from the root of the marsh mallow plant, a wetland herb.
Modern marshmallows are made with sugar, gelatine and whipped air rather than the plant.
marshmallows.visual: a small heap of plain white marshmallows, loosely piled
marshmallows.what: Soft, squidgy sugar puffs, often toasted over a fire.

facts: Marzipan is made by mixing ground almonds with sugar into a smooth, pliable paste.
It has been made in Europe for centuries and is often rolled over Christmas cakes.
In Germany and Italy, marzipan is moulded into small fruits and figures, a tradition still popular.
marzipan.visual: a small block of smooth, pale yellow marzipan, lying flat on the background
marzipan.what: A sweet paste of ground almonds and sugar for cakes.

facts: Masa harina is made by soaking dried maize in lime water, a process called nixtamalisation.
The process makes maize easier to grind and changes its flavour and how it binds.
Masa harina means dough flour in Spanish, and it is used to make dough for tortillas.
masa-harina.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, pale yellow flour with a soft, powdery texture
masa-harina.what: Maize flour treated with lime for tortillas and tamales.

facts: Masago is the roe of the capelin, a small smelt-like fish found in cold northern seas.
Many sushi bars use masago as a lower-cost alternative to tobiko, the flying fish roe.
The name masago is Japanese, and the roe is widely used in Japanese cooking.
masago.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of tiny, glossy, orange-yellow fish roe
masago.what: Small, crunchy fish roe used as a sushi topping.

facts: Mascarpone is traditionally made in northern Italy by curdling cream with an acid.
It is the cheese used in tiramisu, the layered dessert of coffee-soaked sponge biscuits.
mascarpone.visual: a soft white dollop of mascarpone heaped in a small plain white ceramic bowl
mascarpone.what: A thick, soft Italian cream cheese with a mild taste.

facts: Potatoes were first grown in the Andes of South America, thousands of years ago.
Mashed potato is traditionally made by boiling potatoes and mashing them with butter and milk.
Dried and instant potato products were developed in the twentieth century to save cooking time.
mashed-potato-pot.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, creamy mashed potato, a soft peak on top
mashed-potato-pot.what: Instant creamy mashed potato, sold ready to heat.

facts: Mashua is grown in the Andes of South America, where it has been cultivated for centuries.
It is one of several Andean tubers grown alongside potatoes and oca.
mashua.visual: a whole raw mashua tuber, waxy and pale yellow with curled, knobbly lobes, lying on its side
mashua.what: A knobbly Andean tuber with a peppery flavour.

facts: Masoor dal is a staple of South Asian cooking, especially in India, Pakistan and Bangladesh.
Because the lentils are split and husked, they cook far faster than whole lentils.
In India it is often cooked into a thick dal that is eaten with rice or flatbread.
masoor-dal.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dried split red lentils, pale orange-red and flat, loosely heaped
masoor-dal.what: Small split red lentils that melt into a golden purée.

facts: Massaman is a Thai curry that uses roasted spices and tamarind, which give it a rich, sweet-sour flavour.
Coconut milk and palm sugar are commonly added to massaman, making it richer and sweeter than many Thai curries.
massaman-curry-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, dark brick-red curry paste
massaman-curry-paste.what: A mild, warmly spiced Thai paste with peanuts and cardamom.

facts: Mastic is the resin of the mastic tree, which grows on the Greek island of Chios.
The resin is collected by cutting the bark, which releases droplets that harden.
It is traditionally chewed on its own and used to flavour Greek sweets and breads.
mastic.visual: a small heap of pale, translucent yellowish resin crystals, rounded like tears
mastic.what: Hard, pale resin with a piney, slightly cooling taste.

facts: Matcha comes from tea plants that are shaded before harvest, which deepens the leaves' green colour.
Matcha is whisked into hot water for drinking, and it is also used in Japanese sweets and baking.
matcha.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine bright green tea powder, smooth and even in colour
matcha.what: Finely ground green tea, used in drinks and baking.

facts: The fish are lightly salted and traditionally eaten without cooking in the Netherlands.
Hollandse Nieuwe, the first catch of the season, is a Dutch springtime tradition.
matjes-herring.visual: two pale herring fillets, silvery skin, lying side by side
matjes-herring.what: Young herring, lightly salted and mild, a Dutch favourite.

facts: Its Japanese name means pine mushroom, reflecting its link with pine forests.
It is highly prized in Japanese cooking, especially in autumn when it is in season.
Matsutake has not been cultivated easily, so most supply comes from wild forests.
matsutake.visual: a whole raw matsutake mushroom, tan cap closed over a thick white stem, lying on its side
matsutake.what: A prized wild mushroom with a spicy, resinous smell.

facts: Cheddar takes its name from the village of Cheddar in Somerset, south-west England.
Cheddar is made by a process called cheddaring, in which curds are cut, stacked and turned.
Mature cheddar is aged for many months, which develops sharper flavours and a crumbly texture.
mature-cheddar.visual: a block of mature cheddar cheese with one wedge cut off, pale golden crumbly interior showing, on a plain background
mature-cheddar.what: A firm, aged cheese with a sharp, tangy bite.

facts: Matzo is unleavened bread made without yeast, so the dough does not rise.
It is eaten during Passover, when Jewish tradition forbids leavened bread.
It is made from flour and water and baked quickly so that it does not ferment.
matzo.visual: a plain white plate holding a stack of thin, pale, square matzo crackers with small holes
matzo.what: Thin, crisp unleavened flatbread eaten at Passover.

facts: Matzo meal is made by grinding matzah, the unleavened flatbread eaten during Passover.
It is the traditional base for matzo balls, the dumplings served in chicken soup at Passover.
Because matzah contains no raising agent, matzo meal is used in place of flour in many Passover recipes.
matzo-meal.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with pale beige matzo meal, fine and crumb-like
matzo-meal.what: Ground matzah, used to bind dumplings and coat foods.

facts: Mayonnaise is thought to date from the eighteenth century, and its origins are still debated.
Its name is often linked to Mahón in Menorca, though historians disagree about that story.
Across Europe and beyond, it is spread on sandwiches and served with chips, and it forms the base of many dressings.
mayonnaise.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl holding smooth, pale yellow mayonnaise with a glossy surface
mayonnaise.what: A thick, creamy sauce of egg yolk whisked with oil.

meaux-mustard.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with coarse, pale brown grainy mustard
meaux-mustard.what: A coarse French mustard with a gentle, grainy heat.

facts: Dundee, in Scotland, is associated with a style of marmalade made from bitter Seville oranges.
The word marmalade is thought to come from the Portuguese word for quince, marmelo.
Seville oranges are often used for marmalade, as they are sour and contain plenty of pectin, which helps it set.
medium-cut-marmalade.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with amber marmalade flecked with fine strands of orange peel
medium-cut-marmalade.what: A bitter orange preserve, set and studded with peel.

facts: The name chow mein comes from Chinese words meaning 'fried noodles'.
Dried egg noodles are usually boiled or steamed before frying, so they stay springy.
medium-egg-noodles.visual: a loose nest of dried pale yellow egg noodles, curled ribbons lying in a heap
medium-egg-noodles.what: Springy wheat noodles made with egg, used in chow mein.

facts: Oatmeal has been eaten in Scotland for centuries and remains important to Scottish baking.
Oatcakes are thin, savoury biscuits made from oatmeal, water and fat, and are a traditional Scottish snack.
Haggis traditionally contains oatmeal, and the dish is strongly associated with Scotland and Burns Night.
medium-oatmeal.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with pale beige medium oatmeal, finely granular
medium-oatmeal.what: Oats ground to a medium grain, used in oatcakes and haggis.

facts: Dates have been cultivated in the Middle East for thousands of years, and were a staple food for many desert communities.
They are often stuffed with nuts or blended into sauces and desserts.
medjool-date.visual: one whole large date with wrinkled, glossy dark brown skin, lying on its side
medjool-date.what: A large, soft, sweet date with caramel flavour.

facts: Medlars are native to south-west Asia and were later grown across Europe for their fruit.
The fruit is hard and sour when picked, and it softens over time in a process called bletting.
Medlar jelly and medlar cheese, a thick fruit paste, are traditional ways to use the fruit.
medlar.visual: a whole round medlar fruit, russet-brown and firm, with a small open crown at the top
medlar.what: An old-fashioned autumn fruit, eaten only when very soft.

facts: Megrim is a flatfish related to turbot and brill, found in the Atlantic and North Sea.
Like other flatfish, megrim has both eyes on one side of its head as an adult.
megrim.visual: one whole raw flatfish, pale speckled brown skin, oval and flat, lying on its side
megrim.what: A lean flatfish with fine, delicate flesh, often grilled.

facts: Melba toast is made by slicing bread very thinly and baking it slowly until dry and crisp.
It is named after the Australian opera singer Nellie Melba.
melba-toast.visual: a few thin golden rectangles of toast fanned out on a plain white plate
melba-toast.what: Wafer-thin, crisp toast that is often served with pâté.

facts: Melon liqueur is a sweet spirit flavoured with melon and is often used in cocktails and sweet drinks.
Liqueurs like this are made by flavouring a neutral spirit and then sweetening it with sugar.
