The drink is named for the melon, a fruit grown in many warm parts of the world.
melon-liqueur.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with bright lime-green liquid
melon-liqueur.what: A sweet green spirit tasting of ripe honeydew melon.

facts: In West African cooking, ground melon seeds called egusi thicken soups and stews.
Roasted and salted watermelon seeds are a popular snack across China.
melon-seeds.visual: a small heap of flat, pale cream melon seeds lying loosely on a plain surface
melon-seeds.what: Flat, pale seeds from a melon, used whole or ground.

facts: Melton Mowbray pork pies take their name from the market town in Leicestershire, England.
The pastry is a hot-water crust, shaped by hand, and the filling is raw pork.
Pork pies are a common British picnic and pub food, and are often eaten cold.
melton-mowbray-pork-pie.visual: one whole golden-brown pork pie, tall bow-curved sides, raised hot-water pastry case
melton-mowbray-pork-pie.what: A hand-raised pork pie from Leicestershire, England.

facts: Mentsuyu is a Japanese dipping sauce made from soy sauce, mirin and dashi stock.
It is served chilled with cold soba or somen noodles, especially in summer.
mentsuyu.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of glossy, dark amber-brown liquid
mentsuyu.what: A soy and dashi dipping sauce for cold noodles.

facts: Merguez is popular across North Africa and in France, where it is often grilled.
Many recipes flavour it with harissa, paprika, cumin and coriander.
It is made with lamb or beef, and sometimes a mix of both.
merguez.visual: one whole raw merguez sausage link, deep red, slim and lying in a gentle curve
merguez.what: A spicy North African lamb sausage with cumin and chilli.

facts: Meringue is made by whisking egg whites with sugar until stiff, then baking slowly until dry.
It is a classic topping for lemon pies and is often served with cream and fruit.
Crushed meringue folded into cream and fruit makes Eton mess, a traditional English dessert.
meringue.visual: one whole crisp white baked meringue on a small plain white plate
meringue.what: Crisp, airy baked egg white and sugar, light and sweet.

facts: Meringue is made by whisking egg whites with sugar until stiff, then baking them slowly at low heat.
Nests are usually shaped by piping or spooning the mixture into rounds before it goes in the oven.
meringue-nests.visual: one whole white meringue nest, shallow bowl-shaped with a crisp, slightly craggy surface, standing upright on a plain white plate
meringue-nests.what: Crisp, baked egg-white shells, ready to fill with cream.

facts: Being dry, it keeps well on the shelf and does not need refrigeration.
It is commonly used to make royal icing for decorating biscuits and cakes.
meringue-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine pale cream powder
meringue-powder.what: A dried egg-white mix for stable icing and meringue.

facts: Merlot is a red grape variety grown in many wine regions around the world.
Merlot is a key grape in Bordeaux blends and is often the main grape in Pomerol.
Merlot is softer and less tannic than Cabernet Sauvignon, which is why it is often blended.
merlot.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with deep ruby-red merlot wine
merlot.what: A soft, plummy red wine made from the merlot grape.

facts: Mexican oregano is not botanically the same plant as the oregano used in Mediterranean cooking.
It is commonly added to chilli, bean dishes, pozole and salsas.
mexican-oregano.visual: a small loose heap of dried Mexican oregano leaves, dull green and crumbled
mexican-oregano.what: A citrusy, earthy dried herb suited to chilli and beans.

facts: The Meyer lemon is thought to be a cross between a lemon and a mandarin orange.
It was brought to the United States from China in the early twentieth century.
It is less sharp than a common lemon, so it is often used in desserts, curds and dressings.
meyer-lemon.visual: a whole Meyer lemon with smooth, deep yellow-orange skin, lying on its side
meyer-lemon.what: A sweet, round lemon with thin skin and a floral scent.

facts: Mezcal is made from many species of agave, and it is often produced in Oaxaca.
The agave hearts are traditionally roasted in earth pits, which gives mezcal its smoky character.
The name mezcal is generally traced to a Nahuatl word meaning oven-cooked agave.
mezcal.visual: a plain clear glass bottle without a label, filled with pale golden liquid
mezcal.what: A smoky Mexican spirit distilled from roasted agave.

facts: Mezze maniche means half sleeves in Italian, after the shape of the tube.
It is usually made from durum wheat semolina and dried.
Its wide, short shape holds chunky ragu and creamy sauces well.
mezze-maniche.visual: a small heap of dry, short, ridged pasta tubes, pale cream in colour, on a plain background
mezze-maniche.what: Short, wide pasta tubes that cling to chunky sauces.

facts: Mezzelune means half-moons in Italian, after the crescent shape of the pasta.
They are usually filled with cheese, spinach or meat, and cooked in boiling salted water.
mezzelune.visual: a few raw, fresh half-moon pasta parcels with crimped edges, pale yellow, lying on a plain white plate
mezzelune.what: A half-moon pasta stuffed with creamy filling, sold fresh.

facts: Microgreens became popular in restaurants in the late twentieth century as a decorative garnish.
They are grown in shallow trays and harvested once the first true leaves appear.
microgreens.visual: a small heap of tiny fresh green microgreen seedlings, fine stems and small round leaves
microgreens.what: Tiny vegetable or herb seedlings, picked when young.

facts: Basmati is often said to mean fragrant, and refers to long-grain rice grown in South Asia.
Basmati grains lengthen noticeably when cooked, which is part of what makes it distinctive.
microwave-basmati-rice-pouch.visual: a small plain white bowl of fluffy cooked long-grain basmati rice, grains separate and glossy
microwave-basmati-rice-pouch.what: Ready-cooked long-grain rice, heated in the microwave.

facts: Coconut rice is common across Southeast Asia, where rice is often cooked in coconut milk.
Coconut milk is made by grating the white flesh of a mature coconut and pressing it with water.
microwave-coconut-rice-pouch.visual: a small plain white bowl of cooked sweet coconut rice, creamy white grains, glossy and soft
microwave-coconut-rice-pouch.what: Sweet rice cooked in coconut milk, ready in minutes.

facts: Egg fried rice is a stir-fried dish of cooked rice mixed with beaten egg, popular in Chinese restaurants worldwide.
Fried rice is a common way to use leftover cooked rice, which dries slightly and fries more cleanly.
Microwave rice pouches are sealed packs of pre-cooked rice that are heated in their packaging.
microwave-egg-fried-rice-pouch.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with fluffy golden egg-fried rice, loose grains and small flecks of yellow egg visible
microwave-egg-fried-rice-pouch.what: Pre-cooked rice seasoned and mixed with scrambled egg.

facts: Noodles have been eaten in China for a very long time, with early examples found at ancient sites.
Fresh noodles are sold chilled and need only a brief reheat before eating.
microwave-noodles.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of cooked yellow noodles, curled and glossy, served plainly
microwave-noodles.what: Fresh noodles, pre-cooked and ready to warm in minutes.

facts: Pilau is a rice dish cooked with spices, found across South Asia, Iran and the Middle East.
The word pilau is linked to pilaf, a family of rice dishes that spread along trade routes.
Cumin and cardamom are among the spices often used to flavour pilau rice.
microwave-pilau-rice-pouch.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fluffy cooked pilau rice, pale golden, separate grains
microwave-pilau-rice-pouch.what: Spiced rice, sold ready-cooked in a sealed pouch.

facts: Popcorn has been eaten in the Americas for thousands of years.
Microwave popcorn was developed as a quick way to pop kernels at home.
microwave-popcorn-bag.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of freshly popped white popcorn, fluffy pieces piled loosely
microwave-popcorn-bag.what: Corn kernels sealed in a pouch to pop in a microwave.

facts: Quinoa is a seed from the Andes, grown in Bolivia and Peru for thousands of years.
Its seeds are naturally coated in a bitter layer called saponin, usually rinsed off before cooking.
microwave-quinoa-pouch.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of cooked quinoa, fluffy and separate seeds, light cream colour
microwave-quinoa-pouch.what: Cooked quinoa seeds, sold ready to heat in a pouch.

facts: Rice is grown in flooded fields called paddies, and most of the world's rice comes from Asia.
Rice has been cultivated in Asia for thousands of years and is now a staple food across much of the world.
microwave-rice-pouch.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fluffy, freshly cooked white rice
microwave-rice-pouch.what: Fully cooked rice sold in a sealed pouch, ready to heat.

facts: Middle bacon is cut from the pig's belly and back together, so it has fat and lean meat.
In Britain it is often grilled or fried, and it is common on a traditional full breakfast.
middle-bacon.visual: one long raw middle bacon rasher, pink lean meat with streaks of white fat, lying flat
middle-bacon.what: A British rasher with both streaky fat and lean back meat.

facts: Middle neck is a budget cut that becomes tender after slow cooking, as its connective tissue breaks down.
Lamb neck is used in Irish stews and Middle Eastern braises, cooked slowly with vegetables.
The bones add flavour to the cooking liquid in hotpots and tagines.
middle-neck-of-lamb.visual: one raw bone-in slice of lamb middle neck, pale pink meat, white fat and a round neck bone, lying flat
middle-neck-of-lamb.what: A bone-in neck cut, rich and good for slow cooking.

facts: Cheddar takes its name from the village of Cheddar in Somerset, in south-west England.
Cheddaring is the process of cutting, stacking and turning curds, which gives the cheese its texture.
Mild cheddar is aged for a shorter time than mature cheddar, so it has a softer flavour.
mild-cheddar.visual: a block of pale yellow cheddar cheese with one slice cut away, showing a smooth, creamy face
mild-cheddar.what: A gentle, creamy hard cheese that melts smoothly.

facts: Chilli sauces trace back to chilli peppers first domesticated in the Americas many centuries ago.
Vinegar helps preserve the sauce and gives it a sharp, tangy flavour.
Milder sauces use fewer chillies or sweeter peppers, so they add warmth without a strong burn.
mild-hot-sauce.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with bright red, smooth chilli sauce
mild-hot-sauce.what: A mild, vinegar-based chilli sauce with a gentle heat.

facts: Milk from cows has been used in cooking and drinking for thousands of years.
Milk is used in sauces, batters and porridge, and is the base for cheese, butter and yoghurt.
Fresh milk is kept cold because it spoils quickly at room temperature.
milk.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with fresh white milk
milk.what: A white liquid from cows, sold fresh and used in cooking.

facts: Shokupan means eating bread in Japanese, and the soft loaf became a staple of Japanese breakfasts.
Its tender crumb comes from a tangzhong, a flour and water paste cooked before mixing the dough.
Bakers shape the dough into a tall, square-sided loaf, so slices make wide, even pieces of toast.
milk-bread.visual: a whole soft white Japanese milk loaf with a golden top, lying on its side on a plain background
milk-bread.what: A soft, fluffy Japanese loaf enriched with milk.

facts: Milk chocolate was developed in Switzerland in the nineteenth century.
Chocolate is made by fermenting, drying and roasting cocoa beans, then grinding them.
milk-chocolate.visual: one unwrapped milk chocolate bar with two squares snapped off, lying flat, glossy brown
milk-chocolate.what: Sweet, creamy chocolate made with milk solids.

facts: Milk chocolate contains cocoa, sugar and milk solids, which give it a creamy texture.
The cacao tree grows in tropical regions close to the equator.
Chocolate was first prepared as a drink by peoples of Mesoamerica, long before it became a solid sweet.
milk-chocolate-buttons.visual: a small heap of glossy milk chocolate buttons in a small plain white bowl
milk-chocolate-buttons.what: Small, round discs of sweet, smooth milk chocolate.

facts: Milk chocolate is made from cocoa solids, sugar, milk solids and cocoa butter.
Chocolate chips are shaped to keep their form when baked, unlike block chocolate.
Chocolate chips became a staple of home baking in North America in the twentieth century.
milk-chocolate-chips.visual: a small heap of milk chocolate chips, glossy light brown drops, loosely piled on a plain white background
milk-chocolate-chips.what: Small drops of sweet milk chocolate for baking.

facts: In the Philippines the fish is called bangus and is a common everyday food.
Milkfish are farmed in ponds across South-East Asia and are sold fresh or salted.
Filipino cooks often marinate the fish in vinegar and garlic before frying it until crisp.
milkfish.visual: one whole raw milkfish with silvery scales and a forked tail, lying on its side
milkfish.what: A mild, silvery fish that is often marinated and fried.

facts: Millet has been cultivated in Africa and Asia for thousands of years.
Millet is a small-seeded grass, and the grains are the seeds of the plant.
It is a staple in parts of India and West Africa, where it is ground into flour.
millet.visual: a small heap of tiny, smooth, golden millet grains lying on the background
millet.what: Tiny round grains that cook into a light, fluffy base.

facts: Mimolette was developed in northern France as a French imitation of Dutch Edam.
Its orange colour comes from annatto, a natural colouring from the seeds of the achiote tree.
Aged for months, it becomes harder and nuttier, and its rind takes on a pitted texture.
mimolette.visual: a wedge cut from a round orange cheese, with a pitted pale brown rind and bright orange flesh
mimolette.what: A round, bright orange French cheese with a firm texture.

facts: Mincemeat once contained real meat, but modern British mince pies are filled with dried fruit, suet and spices.
Mince pies are traditionally eaten in Britain around Christmas time.
The name comes from mincemeat, a mixture of finely chopped fruit, spices and suet.
mince-pies.visual: a single round mince pie with a golden pastry lid and a star cut into the top, served on a plain white plate
mince-pies.what: Small, sweet pastry pies filled with spiced dried fruit.

facts: Mincemeat was once made with meat, and its name reflects that older tradition.
Mince pies filled with mincemeat are traditionally eaten in Britain at Christmas.
Traditional mincemeat is made in advance and left to mature so the flavours blend.
mincemeat.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of moist, dark brown mincemeat showing pieces of dried fruit
mincemeat.what: A sweet, spiced dried-fruit filling, often used in pies.

facts: Cucumbers have been cultivated for thousands of years and are eaten raw or pickled.
The name cucumber comes from the Latin word cucumis.
mini-cucumber.visual: one whole mini cucumber, bright green, slim and smooth-skinned, lying on its side
mini-cucumber.what: A small, sweet cucumber with thin skin and few seeds.

facts: Modern marshmallows are whipped mixtures of sugar, gelatine and air.
mini-marshmallows.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of white mini marshmallows, round and soft
mini-marshmallows.what: Tiny, soft, sugary sweets that puff up when heated.

facts: Pitta is a leavened flatbread eaten across the Eastern Mediterranean and the Middle East.
The pocket forms when the dough puffs sharply in a very hot oven, separating the layers.
mini-pitta.visual: a single small round pitta bread, lightly puffed, pale golden-brown, lying flat
mini-pitta.what: A small, soft flatbread with a hollow pocket for filling.

facts: Raised pork pies were traditionally made with a hot water crust pastry that holds its shape.
Melton Mowbray in Leicestershire is famous for its pork pies.
mini-pork-pie.visual: one small golden pork pie with a crimped pastry edge, served whole on a small plain white plate
mini-pork-pie.what: A small, savoury pastry case filled with seasoned pork.

facts: The name quiche is linked to the German word Kuchen, meaning cake.
Quiche Lorraine is the classic version, made with eggs, cream and bacon.
mini-quiches.visual: three small golden baked mini quiches arranged on a plain white plate
mini-quiches.what: Small savoury egg tarts, a bite-sized version of quiche.

facts: Scotch eggs are a British picnic and pub food, often eaten cold.
The origin of the name is uncertain, and the dish may not come from Scotland.
mini-scotch-egg.visual: a whole golden breaded mini scotch egg, crumb coating rough and crisp, lying on its side
mini-scotch-egg.what: A boiled egg wrapped in sausage meat, coated and fried.

facts: Sweet peppers are the same species as many chillies, but have been bred for a mild flavour.
Peppers originated in the Americas and spread across the world after European contact.
Their colour changes as they ripen, from green to yellow, orange or red.
mini-sweet-peppers.visual: a small heap of tiny glossy red and yellow sweet peppers, a few with their stalks
mini-sweet-peppers.what: Small, sweet peppers that are crisp enough to eat raw.

facts: Tortillas are flatbreads that have been a staple across Mexico and Central America for centuries.
Traditional corn tortillas are made from masa, a dough of ground maize treated with lime.
Flour tortillas became popular in northern Mexico and the American southwest.
mini-tortilla.visual: a neat stack of small, soft white flour tortillas on a plain white plate
mini-tortilla.what: Small, soft flatbreads for snacks and bite-sized tacos.

facts: Mint and chocolate is a popular flavour pairing in ice cream and sweets.
Mint ice cream is usually flavoured with mint leaves or mint extract.
mint-choc-chip-ice-cream.visual: a scoop of pale mint-green ice cream speckled throughout by dark chocolate flecks, in a small plain white ceramic bowl
mint-choc-chip-ice-cream.what: Cool mint ice cream with dark chocolate flecks.

facts: Peppermint is a natural hybrid of watermint and spearmint, and its oil flavours many sweets.
Dark chocolate is made from cocoa solids, cocoa butter and sugar, with little or no milk.
mint-chocolate.visual: a single dark chocolate square with a neat cut edge showing a pale green filling, lying directly on the background
mint-chocolate.what: Dark chocolate with a cool peppermint filling inside.

facts: Cooks make it by setting a mint-flavoured syrup with pectin, often with a splash of vinegar.
Mint jelly takes its flavour from mint, a herb in the Mentha genus.
Mint jelly is clear, because the leaves are strained out before it sets.
mint-jelly.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, holding clear bright green jelly
mint-jelly.what: A sweet, green, set jelly served with roast lamb.

facts: Mint sauce is traditionally made from chopped mint, vinegar and sugar, and served with roast lamb in Britain.
Mint has been grown and cooked with for centuries across Europe and the Middle East.
mint-sauce.visual: a small clear glass jar without a label, filled with bright green mint sauce and chopped mint flecks
mint-sauce.what: Chopped mint in sweetened vinegar, served with lamb.

facts: Mint has been grown and used around the Mediterranean and the Middle East for thousands of years.
mint-yoghurt.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, pale green yoghurt, flecked throughout by chopped mint
mint-yoghurt.what: Thick yoghurt with fresh mint stirred through it.

facts: The name refers to how quickly the thin cut cooks over high heat.
Because it is thin, it is best cooked quickly and not overcooked.
minute-steak.visual: one raw beef minute steak, thin and flattened to an even thickness, deep red with a little marbling, lying flat
minute-steak.what: A thin cut of beef, beaten flat so it cooks very quickly.

facts: Mirabelle plums are used to make a clear plum brandy called eau-de-vie.
The fruit is small and sweet and is often baked in tarts or preserved.
mirabelle-plum.visual: a few small round golden-yellow plums with a red blush, lying on the background
mirabelle-plum.what: A tiny golden plum with honeyed, sweet flesh.

facts: Hon-mirin is the traditional version, while cheaper mirin-style seasonings contain added sugar.
Mirin adds sweetness and gloss to teriyaki glazes and simmered dishes.
mirin.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden liquid
mirin.what: A sweet, low-alcohol rice wine used in Japanese cooking.

facts: Mirror glaze is a modern pâtisserie technique, widely seen on layered entremets cakes.
It is usually made by melting gelatine into sugar, glucose and cream or condensed milk.
It is poured over a frozen cake, which sets it into a smooth, shiny surface.
mirror-glaze.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of glossy pink liquid glaze
mirror-glaze.what: A glossy pourable coating that gives cakes a shine.

facts: Miso is a paste of fermented soybeans, usually mixed with salt and a grain such as rice or barley.
Miso has been a traditional seasoning in Japan for many centuries, used in soups and marinades.
Sesame adds a nutty flavour and is widely used alongside miso in Japanese cooking.
miso-dressing.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth pale golden-brown dressing, thick and glossy
miso-dressing.what: A savoury Japanese dressing based on soybean paste.

facts: Miso is a paste of fermented soybeans, often with rice or barley.
Miso has been made in Japan for centuries and is a staple in its cooking.
miso-gravy.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, glossy brown gravy
miso-gravy.what: A savoury gravy flavoured with miso, a Japanese soy paste.

facts: Miso is made by fermenting soybeans with salt and koji, a mould grown on rice or barley.
Miso has been made in Japan for centuries, and there are many styles, from pale and sweet to dark and rich.
Dashi is the basic stock of Japanese cooking, made from kombu seaweed and dried bonito flakes.
miso-soup-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, pale golden-brown miso paste
miso-soup-paste.what: A fermented soybean paste for quick Japanese soup.

facts: Mitmita is a spice blend from Ethiopia, used in dishes such as kitfo, a minced beef dish.
Mitmita is known for its fiery heat, which comes mainly from bird's eye chilli.
Cardamom and cloves give the blend a warm, aromatic note beneath its heat.
mitmita.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with a fine, bright red-orange spice powder, lightly textured and slightly flaky
mitmita.what: A fiery Ethiopian chilli and spice blend with cardamom.

facts: Jam is made by cooking fruit with sugar until it thickens, helped by pectin in the fruit.
Jam was traditionally a way to preserve summer fruit for the colder months.
Fruit jam is a classic filling for sandwiches, scones and Victoria sponge cakes in Britain.
mixed-fruit-jam.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with thick glossy deep red-purple fruit jam
mixed-fruit-jam.what: A thick, sweet spread of several fruits boiled with sugar.

facts: Drying herbs was a way to keep them through the winter before refrigeration was common.
mixed-herbs.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dried mixed herb flakes, green and brown
mixed-herbs.what: A dried blend of herbs for everyday cooking.

facts: Miso is a Japanese seasoning made from soybeans, salt and a grain such as rice or barley.
Awase miso is the name for a blend of different misos, usually red and white.
Red miso is generally aged for longer than white miso, giving it a deeper flavour.
mixed-miso.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, light brown miso paste, lightly textured on top
mixed-miso.what: A blend of red and white fermented soybean pastes.

facts: Cashews are the seeds of a fruit called the cashew apple, which grows on a tree native to Brazil.
Brazil nuts come from a tall rainforest tree in the Amazon and are often included in mixes.
Roasting nuts causes browning reactions that give them a toasty, deeper flavour.
mixed-nuts.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with salted roasted nuts in varied shapes and light browns
mixed-nuts.what: A salted, roasted blend of assorted nuts for snacking.

facts: Snack mixes of nuts and dried fruit are sold widely across Britain and Europe.
Raisins are dried grapes, and they have been made by sun-drying for thousands of years.
mixed-nuts-and-raisins.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with mixed shelled nuts and dark raisins
mixed-nuts-and-raisins.what: A snack mix of assorted nuts and dried raisins.

facts: Black and white peppercorns come from the same climbing plant, and the colour depends on how they are processed.
Pink peppercorns are the berries of a different plant, a tree related to the cashew.
Green peppercorns are unripe berries, often preserved in brine or dried.
mixed-peppercorns.visual: a small heap of mixed whole peppercorns in black, white, green and pink
mixed-peppercorns.what: A mix of black, white, green and pink peppercorns.

facts: Many recipes use mango, lime, chilli and mustard seeds.
In Hindi, pickles are called achar, and the word is used across much of South Asia.
mixed-pickle.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, full of chopped spiced pickled vegetables, glossy and golden
mixed-pickle.what: A hot, spiced pickle of mixed vegetables in oil.

facts: Mixed salad leaves combine several young leaves, such as lettuce, rocket and baby spinach.
Many salad leaves are picked young, when they are tender and milder in taste.
The term mesclun comes from a Provencal word meaning mixture, used for mixed young salad leaves.
mixed-salad-leaves.visual: a loose heap of mixed fresh salad leaves, red and green, crisp and tender
mixed-salad-leaves.what: A handy mix of tender, fresh leaves for quick salads.

facts: Mixed spice typically combines cinnamon, nutmeg, allspice, coriander and ginger.
It is used in hot cross buns, Christmas puddings and fruit cakes across Britain.
Recipes differ from one household to another, so each blend tastes slightly different.
mixed-spice.visual: a plain glass jar without a label holding a warm brown powdered spice blend
mixed-spice.what: A sweet British blend of warm spices for baking.

facts: Wild mushrooms are gathered from woodland and grassland, and their flavour varies with the season.
Many wild mushroom varieties are fragile and are best cooked soon after they are picked.
Chanterelles, morels and ceps are among the best-known wild mushrooms in European cooking.
mixed-wild-mushrooms.visual: a small heap of mixed wild mushrooms in brown, cream and golden tones, earthy and fresh, lying loosely together
mixed-wild-mushrooms.what: A seasonal mix of forest mushrooms, good for quick frying.

facts: Wild rice is not a true rice but the seed of an aquatic grass native to North America.
It has long been gathered from lakes and rivers in North America.
Wild rice has long, dark grains and a chewy texture when cooked.
mixed-wild-rice.visual: a small heap of mixed dark and pale rice grains, long and slender, lying loose
mixed-wild-rice.what: A blend of wild rice with white or brown rice for texture.

facts: Mizithra is made from whey, the liquid left after other cheeses have been made.
Fresh mizithra is soft and mild, while aged versions are firm, dry and sharp.
mizithra.visual: a block of pale, firm white cheese with one thick wedge cut away, lying flat
mizithra.what: A Greek whey cheese, soft when fresh and hard when dried.

facts: Mizuna is a Japanese mustard green, related to cabbage, broccoli and turnip.
Its leaves are often eaten raw in salads or stirred into soups at the last moment.
Its name is often translated as water greens, from the Japanese words for water and greens.
mizuna.visual: a small bunch of feathery mizuna leaves, deeply serrated pale green leaves on white stems
mizuna.what: A feathery Japanese salad leaf with a peppery bite.

facts: Mochi is made by pounding steamed glutinous rice until it forms a smooth, elastic dough.
Mochi is traditionally pounded at New Year in Japan and is used in many sweets and desserts.
mochi.visual: a soft white mochi rice cake, round and slightly glossy, on a plain white plate
mochi.what: A soft, chewy Japanese rice cake made from glutinous rice.

facts: Mojo picon is a Canarian sauce, traditionally served with papas arrugadas, or wrinkled potatoes.
It is traditionally pounded by hand with peppers, garlic, vinegar and oil.
The Canary Islands are a Spanish archipelago in the Atlantic, and their food mixes Spanish and African influences.
mojo-picon.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick orange-red sauce, smooth and glossy
mojo-picon.what: A smoky, spicy red sauce from the Canary Islands.

facts: Mojo is a family of sauces from the Canary Islands, which are part of Spain.
It is often served alongside grilled fish and the wrinkled potatoes called papas arrugadas.
mojo-verde.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl holding a vivid green, finely chopped sauce, flecked and smooth
mojo-verde.what: A tangy green herb sauce from the Canary Islands.

facts: Mole is a family of rich sauces from Mexico, and negro means black, after its very dark colour.
Mole negro is traditionally associated with Oaxaca, where cooks toast and grind dried chillies with spices.
mole-negro.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, very dark brown-black sauce, smooth and glossy
mole-negro.what: A dark, smoky Mexican sauce built on dried chillies.

facts: Mole comes from the Nahuatl word molli, meaning a sauce or mixture.
Mole poblano takes its name from Puebla, the city in central Mexico where it is traditionally made.
mole-poblano.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, glossy dark brown sauce
mole-poblano.what: A dark Mexican sauce of chillies, spices and chocolate.

facts: In Italy monkfish is known as coda di rospo, meaning toad's tail.
Its firm, white flesh holds together well in stews and when pan-fried.
monkfish-cheeks.visual: a small heap of pale pink-white monkfish cheeks, each a neat round piece, lying on the background
monkfish-cheeks.what: Small, firm, sweet pieces cut from the head of a monkfish.

facts: Monkfish, also called anglerfish, lies camouflaged on the seabed and lures prey close.
It is found in the north-eastern Atlantic, including the waters around Britain and Ireland.
monkfish-tail.visual: a whole raw monkfish tail, thick firm pinkish-white flesh, lying on its side
monkfish-tail.what: A firm, mild sea fish that holds its shape when cooked.

facts: Fresh Montasio is mild and milky, while aged versions become sharp and firm.
Frico is a crisp Friulian dish made by melting grated Montasio in a pan.
montasio.visual: a block of pale straw-coloured hard cheese with one wedge cut away, the cut face showing tiny holes
montasio.what: A hard, pale Italian cheese from the Friuli region.

facts: It is a semi-hard cheese that softens into a smooth melt, which is why it suits quesadillas and grilled cheese.
An aged version called dry Jack is firmer and is grated over pasta and salads.
monterey-jack.visual: a block of pale ivory cheese with one wedge cut out, lying on the background
monterey-jack.what: A mild, buttery American cheese that melts well.

facts: Typical blends include black pepper, coriander, garlic, dill and salt.
The mix is coarse, so the spices stay visible and form a crust when the steak is seared.
montreal-steak-seasoning.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with a coarse mix of dark pepper, herbs and crushed spices
montreal-steak-seasoning.what: A coarse, savoury spice blend for crusting grilled steak.

facts: Morbier comes from the Franche-Comté region in eastern France and is made from cow's milk.
morbier.visual: one cut wedge of pale ivory semi-soft cheese, with a thin dark line of ash running through its middle, lying flat
morbier.what: A soft, mild French cheese with a thin line of ash.

facts: Morcilla is made across Spain, and regional versions vary a great deal in flavour and spice.
Versions from Burgos and León are among the best known.
Blood sausages have been made in Europe for many centuries as a way to use the whole animal.
morcilla.visual: one whole dark morcilla sausage link, brown-black casing, lying in a gentle curve
morcilla.what: A Spanish blood sausage with rice and paprika.

facts: Morels are prized in French cooking, often cooked in butter or cream.
Dried morels keep for months and are soaked to soften them before use in soups and sauces.
morel.visual: a single whole fresh morel mushroom, honeycombed ochre cap on a pale hollow stem, lying on its side
morel.what: A honeycombed wild mushroom with a deep, earthy flavour.

facts: Morello cherries are too tart to eat fresh, so they are usually cooked with sugar.
Sour cherries like the morello are traditional in Black Forest gateau and kirsch desserts.
morello-cherry.visual: a small heap of dark red morello cherries with short stalks attached
morello-cherry.what: A tart, deep red cherry used for baking and preserves.

facts: Moreton Bay bugs are a type of slipper lobster, found in the warm coastal waters of Australia.
The name comes from Moreton Bay, an inlet off the coast of Queensland near Brisbane.
Most of the edible meat is in the tail, which is often grilled whole or split.
moreton-bay-bug.visual: one whole raw Moreton Bay bug, flat broad body, pale orange-brown shell, lying on its side
moreton-bay-bug.what: A flat Australian shellfish with sweet, rich tail meat.

facts: Moringa is a tree native to the Himalayan foothills and other parts of South Asia.
Its long, thin seed pods, known as drumsticks, are simmered in curries in southern India.
The leaves are cooked gently in dal or stir-fried, and the tree now grows across the tropics.
moringa-leaves.visual: a small bunch of fresh moringa leaves, tiny oval leaflets on pale green stems
moringa-leaves.what: Small green leaves of the drumstick tree, used in curries.

facts: Moroccan mint is a spearmint variety, prized for a gentler, sweeter taste than peppermint.
The leaves are usually steeped with sugar and green tea, then poured from a height to create a froth.
moroccan-mint.visual: a small bunch of fresh spearmint, bright green leaves on thin reddish stems
moroccan-mint.what: A sweet spearmint, used to flavour tea across Morocco.

facts: Mortadella is strongly associated with Bologna in northern Italy.
Pistachios are often added to mortadella, which gives it a speckled look.
mortadella.visual: a thick slice of pale pink mortadella with flecks of white fat through it, lying flat
mortadella.what: A smooth, pink Italian cold cut of finely ground pork.

facts: Moscato is made from Muscat grapes, a family of grapes cultivated for a very long time.
Moscato d'Asti comes from Piedmont in north-west Italy and is often gently sparkling.
The name Muscat is thought to come from musk, a nod to the scent of the grapes.
moscato.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale golden, lightly sparkling wine with small bubbles rising
moscato.what: A lightly fizzy, sweet white wine with grapey flavour.

facts: Moth beans are grown in dry regions of India and Pakistan, as they tolerate drought well.
Misal, a spicy dish from Maharashtra, is often made with sprouted moth beans.
Moth beans are known as matki in parts of western India.
moth-beans.visual: a small heap of dry, mottled brown moth beans on a plain white surface
moth-beans.what: A small, dry bean from India, popular in spicy misal.

facts: Traditional mozzarella is made from water buffalo milk in southern Italy, especially around Naples.
The cheese is made by stretching the curd in hot water, which gives it an elastic, springy texture.
Its name is thought to come from mozzare, the Italian for to cut, referring to how the curd is cut.
mozzarella.visual: one whole fresh mozzarella ball, smooth and glossy white, with a slightly moist surface
mozzarella.what: A soft, milky Italian cheese that stretches when melted.

facts: Fried mozzarella sticks became popular in American restaurants and are often served with a tomato dipping sauce.
The coating is usually dipped first in flour, then in beaten egg, then in breadcrumbs before frying.
Sticks are usually made from firmer, low-moisture mozzarella, which holds its shape in hot oil.
mozzarella-sticks.visual: a small plain white plate holding three golden breadcrumbed cheese sticks, one with a cut end showing melted cheese
mozzarella-sticks.what: Breadcrumbed cheese strips, fried until crisp and gooey.

facts: Mud crabs live in mud and mangrove areas along the Indo-Pacific coast.
They are sold live and are widely eaten across South-East Asia and Australia.
Chilli crab and black pepper crab are popular dishes made with mud crab in Singapore.
mud-crab.visual: a whole raw mud crab, shell brownish-green with thick claws, lying on its back
mud-crab.what: A large, meaty crab from tropical mangrove swamps.

facts: Muesli was developed in Switzerland as a raw oat dish by the doctor Maximilian Bircher-Benner.
Oats have long been eaten as porridge in Scotland and northern Britain.
The name muesli comes from Swiss German, meaning a little mash or purée.
muesli.visual: a small heap of loose muesli, pale oat flakes and speckled dried fruit pieces
muesli.what: A mix of raw oats, dried fruit and nuts, eaten with milk.

facts: In Japan the young leaves, called yomogi, are mixed into rice cakes.
Mugwort was used to flavour beer in Europe before hops became common.
mugwort.visual: a small bunch of fresh mugwort stems, with soft grey-green leaves whose undersides are silvery and downy
mugwort.what: A bitter, aromatic wild herb with grey-green leaves.

facts: Muhammara is traditionally associated with the city of Aleppo in Syria, where it is part of the mezze spread.
Walnuts give the dip its body, and pomegranate molasses is often added for a sweet-sour edge.
muhammara.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick deep red-brown dip, smooth glossy paste
muhammara.what: A rich, dark dip of roasted red peppers and walnuts.

facts: Mulato chillies are dried poblano peppers, left to ripen longer on the plant before drying.
They are a key ingredient in many mole sauces from Mexico.
Their flavour is often described as raisin-like, with hints of chocolate and liquorice.
mulato-chilli.visual: a small heap of dried mulato chillies, wrinkled dark brown skins, loose pods lying in a gentle pile
mulato-chilli.what: A dried, sweet, chocolatey Mexican chilli used in mole.

facts: Mulberry leaves feed silkworms, which is why the trees were widely planted for silk production.
The berries are very delicate and bruise easily, so they are usually eaten or cooked soon after picking.
mulberry.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of plump dark purple-red mulberries, slightly uneven in shape
mulberry.what: Soft, sweet berries from a tree that stain easily.

facts: Mulberry molasses is a traditional fruit syrup in Middle Eastern cooking, made by boiling down the juice.
The berries are cooked for a long time until the juice thickens into a dark, sticky syrup.
It is often drizzled over yoghurt, or used in sauces and to sweeten drinks.
mulberry-molasses.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with thick, dark purple-brown syrup
mulberry-molasses.what: A thick, dark, tangy syrup made from mulberries.

facts: Mulled wine, or glühwein in German, is traditionally served at Christmas markets.
Recipes vary, but cinnamon, cloves and orange peel are common in most versions.
Spiced warm wine has been drunk in Europe for many centuries.
mulled-wine.visual: a plain clear drinking glass filled with dark ruby-red mulled wine
mulled-wine.what: Red wine warmed with spices, citrus and sugar, served hot.

facts: Mulled wine is an old European drink, served hot and spiced with ingredients like these.
Cinnamon is the dried bark of a tree, rolled into sticks.
Cloves are the dried flower buds of a tropical evergreen tree.
mulling-spices.visual: a small heap of whole cinnamon sticks, cloves and dried orange peel curls
mulling-spices.what: A warming blend of spices for hot wine and cider.

facts: Mung bean sprouts are grown in the dark, which keeps them pale and crisp.
They are widely used in Chinese and Southeast Asian cooking, including stir-fries and pho.
mung-bean-sprouts.visual: a small heap of crisp white mung bean sprouts with pale yellow tips, lying on a plain background
mung-bean-sprouts.what: Crisp, pale shoots grown from green mung beans.

facts: Mung bean vermicelli is made from starch extracted from mung beans, and is often called glass noodles.
It is popular across East and Southeast Asia, in soups, salads and stir-fries.
mung-bean-vermicelli.visual: a small loose heap of dried mung bean vermicelli, fine translucent pale noodle strands, lying on a plain background
mung-bean-vermicelli.what: Fine, see-through noodles made from mung bean starch.

facts: Mung beans have been cultivated in India for thousands of years.
They are used whole for dal, sprouted for salads and stir-fries, and ground into flour or noodles.
In China, mung beans are cooked into sweet soups and desserts.
mung-beans.visual: a small heap of dried whole mung beans, matt green and loosely piled on the background
mung-beans.what: Small green beans, often cooked into dal or sprouted.

facts: Munster is named after the Munster valley in Alsace, north-eastern France.
Its orange rind comes from being washed in brine during ripening.
munster.visual: a small round wheel of soft pale-yellow cheese, orange washed rind, one wedge cut away
munster.what: A strong, soft washed-rind cheese from the Alsace region.

facts: Muntjac are small deer native to Asia, and the Reeves's species has spread to parts of Britain.
The muntjac is also called the barking deer, after the sharp call it gives when alarmed.
In Britain, muntjac are regarded as an invasive species, so some are culled and their meat is eaten.
muntjac.visual: a trimmed raw muntjac loin, deep red meat with a thin layer of fat, lying flat
muntjac.what: A small deer with lean, tender meat that cooks quickly.

facts: Muscadet is made from the Melon de Bourgogne grape, grown near the Atlantic coast of western France.
It is traditionally served with shellfish such as mussels, and is often drunk young.
The wine is often aged on its lees, which gives it a slightly yeasty character.
muscadet.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale straw-coloured white wine, standing alone
muscadet.what: A dry, crisp white wine from the Loire Valley in France.

facts: The name Muscat is linked to the Persian word for musk, a nod to the grapes' heady scent.
Some Muscat grapes are made into sweet dessert wines, such as those from southern France.
muscat-grapes.visual: a small bunch of plump pale green Muscat grapes on a short stem, with a dusty bloom on the skins
muscat-grapes.what: Sweet, musky grapes with a strong, flowery perfume.

facts: They are grown in countries such as Spain, Greece and Turkey.
The Muscat grape variety is named for its musky, perfumed aroma.
muscatel-raisin.visual: a small heap of large, dark-brown muscatel raisins, plump and glossy
muscatel-raisin.what: Large, sweet raisins made from sun-dried Muscat grapes.

facts: Unlike most domestic ducks, the Muscovy is not descended from the mallard.
In France, its breast is often sold as magret, usually cooked rare and sliced thinly.
muscovy-duck.visual: one whole raw Muscovy duck, plump with pale pinkish skin, lying breast side up
muscovy-duck.what: A large, lean duck with rich, dark meat and big breasts.

facts: Mushroom ketchup is an old British seasoning, and recipes for it appear in 18th-century cookbooks.
It was traditionally made by layering mushrooms with salt and leaving them to ferment before straining.
mushroom-ketchup.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of dark brown liquid
mushroom-ketchup.what: A dark, savoury sauce made from fermented mushrooms.

facts: Ravioli are small pasta parcels, traditionally made in Italy by sealing two sheets of dough around a filling.
Ravioli come in many regional styles in Italy, each with its own fillings and shapes.
Mushroom is a popular filling for vegetarian versions, often mixed with herbs and soft cheese.
mushroom-ravioli.visual: several pillow-shaped pasta parcels with pale golden dough, arranged on a small plain white plate
mushroom-ravioli.what: Fresh pasta parcels filled with savoury mushrooms.

facts: Mushroom sauce is traditionally made by cooking mushrooms in butter, then adding stock or cream.
It has long been served with grilled steak and roast chicken in European cooking.
Dried mushrooms can be soaked and used to add deep, earthy flavour.
mushroom-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, creamy pale brown mushroom sauce
mushroom-sauce.what: A smooth, creamy sauce made from mushrooms and cream.

facts: Dried mushrooms are ground into powder to give a concentrated savoury flavour.
Dried shiitake is a traditional Japanese ingredient for stocks, and its powder is used in similar ways.
mushroom-seasoning-powder.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, filled with fine pale brown mushroom powder
mushroom-seasoning-powder.what: A fine savoury powder of dried mushrooms for umami.

facts: Soy sauce originated in China and is now used across East Asia and far beyond.
Mushroom soy sauce is typically flavoured with straw mushrooms, which are grown in parts of Asia.
Dark soy sauce is aged longer than light soy, making it thicker and richer in colour.
mushroom-soy-sauce.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of dark brown liquid
mushroom-soy-sauce.what: A dark soy sauce, with a rich savoury taste from mushrooms.

facts: Stock is a flavoured liquid used as a base for soups, sauces and risottos.
Mushroom stock is traditionally made from the trimmings and stems left over from fresh mushrooms.
Dried porcini are often soaked and added to stock for a deeper flavour.
mushroom-stock.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of clear, golden-brown mushroom stock
mushroom-stock.what: A savoury broth made by simmering mushroom trimmings.

facts: Mushy peas are a traditional accompaniment to fish and chips, especially in northern England.
Dried peas have long been an important food in England, and they were mashed into a thick dish.
mushy-peas.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, bright green mashed peas, smooth and glossy
mushy-peas.what: Soft, mashed marrowfat peas served as a side.

facts: Mussels attach themselves to rocks and pier pilings with strong threads called byssus.
Many mussels sold today are farmed on ropes hung in coastal waters.
They are often steamed in a covered pan until their shells open, which shows they are cooked.
mussels.visual: a heap of fresh raw mussels with closed blue-black shells, on a plain background
mussels.what: Small blue-black shellfish, steamed open to eat.

facts: Mustard cress is sold as young seedlings, harvested within a week or two of sowing.
Egg and cress sandwiches are a classic British picnic and tea-time filling.
Garden cress has been eaten since ancient times and sprouts quickly on damp cloth.
mustard-cress.visual: a small bunch of bright green cress seedlings, tiny rounded leaves on thin pale stems
mustard-cress.what: Fast-growing peppery seedlings, often used in sandwiches.

facts: Mostarda is a traditional Italian preserve from the Cremona area in Lombardy.
Its heat comes from mustard essential oil, which is added to a sweet syrup.
mustard-fruits.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with glossy candied fruit pieces in pale amber syrup
mustard-fruits.what: Candied fruit in a hot, mustard-flavoured syrup.

facts: They are a traditional part of Southern American cooking, often slow-cooked with smoked pork.
In China, mustard greens are a common vegetable and are often stir-fried or pickled.
mustard-greens.visual: a bunch of fresh mustard greens with frilled, deep green leaves and pale stalks, tied at the base
mustard-greens.what: Peppery leaves from the mustard plant, good for braising.

facts: Mustard oil is widely used in Bengali, Bihari and north Indian cooking, especially for frying fish.
Its pungent flavour makes it a common base for pickles across parts of South Asia.
mustard-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of golden-yellow mustard oil
mustard-oil.what: A sharp, pungent oil pressed from mustard seeds.

facts: Mustard powder is made by grinding mustard seeds, and it becomes hot when mixed with liquid.
English mustard is traditionally hotter than French mustard, which is milder and often sweeter.
The name mustard is often traced to the Latin mustum, meaning new wine, as seeds were mixed with grape must.
mustard-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine pale yellow mustard powder
mustard-powder.what: Ground mustard seed that turns hot when mixed with water.

facts: Mustard seeds come from mustard plants, which belong to the cabbage family.
In Indian cooking they are fried in hot oil to bring out a nutty flavour.
Ground mustard has been used as a condiment in Europe since Roman times.
mustard-seeds.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of tiny round brown mustard seeds
mustard-seeds.what: Tiny round seeds that give a nutty heat when fried.

facts: Slow braising or stewing softens the tougher muscles of a mutton leg until they are tender.
mutton-leg.visual: a whole raw mutton leg joint with deep red meat and a thin white fat cap, lying on a plain white plate
mutton-leg.what: Meat from an adult sheep, with richer flavour than lamb.

facts: Mutton comes from older sheep, with a stronger flavour than lamb.
The shoulder has plenty of connective tissue, so it becomes tender when cooked slowly.
Mutton is used in many cuisines, including Indian and Middle Eastern cooking and British dishes such as Lancashire hotpot.
mutton-shoulder.visual: one whole raw mutton shoulder, deep red meat with a layer of fat, lying on a plain white background
mutton-shoulder.what: Strong, rich meat from an adult sheep, good for braising.

facts: Naan is a Persian word meaning bread, and it spread through South Asia.
Traditionally baked on the inner walls of a clay tandoor oven.
Naan is often brushed with butter or garlic after baking.
naan-bread.visual: a single soft golden naan flatbread with charred blisters, on a plain white plate
naan-bread.what: A soft, leavened flatbread cooked in a tandoor oven.

facts: Mastic and mahleb, both traditional flavourings of the Levant, are often used in it.
nabulsi.visual: a pale white block of brined cheese, one slice cut from its corner
nabulsi.what: A white, brined cheese from the Palestinian city of Nablus.

facts: Naengmyeon is a Korean noodle dish that began in the north of the Korean peninsula.
The noodles are traditionally made from buckwheat or potato starch and served in a chilled broth.
naengmyeon.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale, thin, chewy noodles in a clear cold broth
naengmyeon.what: Chewy Korean noodles, served cold in a tangy broth.

facts: Naga chillies are grown in north-east India, particularly in the state of Nagaland.
Chilli heat is measured on the Scoville scale, and naga chillies sit near the top of it.
naga-chilli.visual: a whole, wrinkled, orange-red chilli pepper with its green stalk
naga-chilli.what: An extremely hot chilli with a fruity, smoky edge.

facts: Nam prik pao is a Thai paste of roasted chillies, shallots and garlic, often with palm sugar.
The name means roasted chilli paste, which describes the way it is made.
It is used to flavour stir-fries, noodles and dips across Thailand.
nam-prik-pao.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with a thick dark red-brown chilli paste
nam-prik-pao.what: A thick, sweet-savoury Thai chilli paste used in cooking.

facts: Nameko is widely grown in Japan, where it is used in miso soup and hot pots.
The mushrooms are cultivated in Japan, often grown on blocks of sawdust.
When cooked, its coating thickens the liquid it is simmered in, giving soups a silky texture.
nameko-mushroom.visual: a small bunch of nameko mushrooms, golden-brown caps with a glossy, slippery coat, joined at the base
nameko-mushroom.what: A small, golden mushroom with a glossy, slippery cap.

facts: Togarashi is the general Japanese word for chilli pepper.
Nanami and shichimi both mean seven flavours, and the two blends are closely related.
Dried citrus peel gives the blend its bright citrus note.
nanami-togarashi.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with coarse, orange-red spice flakes
nanami-togarashi.what: A Japanese mix of chilli and dried orange peel.

facts: Napa cabbage is a type of Chinese cabbage, grown across East Asia for centuries.
It is the main ingredient in most Korean kimchi, where it is salted and seasoned.
Its loose, crinkled leaves make it quick to stir-fry or braise.
napa-cabbage.visual: a whole napa cabbage, pale green leaves with crinkled white ribs
napa-cabbage.what: A pale, crinkly, mild Chinese cabbage used in kimchi.

facts: Salsa napoletana is a basic sauce of tomatoes, garlic, olive oil and basil from southern Italy.
The name means Neapolitan, referring to the city of Naples in southern Italy.
Tomatoes came to Italy from the Americas in the sixteenth century and were soon used in local cooking.
napoletana-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, deep red tomato sauce, glossy on the surface
napoletana-sauce.what: A simple tomato sauce with fresh basil, from southern Italy.

facts: Both the flowers and the round leaves can be eaten and have a peppery taste.
The green seed pods can be pickled and used as a substitute for capers.
nasturtium-flowers.visual: a small heap of bright orange and yellow nasturtium flowers, petals open
nasturtium-flowers.what: Edible peppery flowers, bright orange, yellow and red.

facts: Nasturtiums come from the Andes of South America.
The whole plant is edible, including the flowers, which are often used as a colourful garnish.
The name comes from Latin, meaning nose-twister, for its sharp, peppery taste.
nasturtium-leaves.visual: a small bunch of bright green nasturtium leaves on their stems
nasturtium-leaves.what: Peppery round leaves with a bite like watercress.

facts: The native oyster of Britain is the European flat oyster, Ostrea edulis.
Native oysters were once very common around the British coast and were eaten widely.
Oyster flavour varies with the seawater where they grow, so each bed tastes different.
native-oysters.visual: one whole raw native oyster, rounded and flattened, rough grey-brown shell, shut tight
native-oysters.what: A small, flat shellfish with a mineral, nutty flavour.

facts: Natto is a traditional Japanese food made by fermenting soybeans with the bacterium Bacillus subtilis.
Its stickiness comes from strands of polymer that form as the soybeans ferment.
It is often mixed with soy sauce and mustard, and served over rice.
natto.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl holding a mound of sticky, pale brown fermented soybeans, glossy and stringy
natto.what: Fermented soybeans with a sticky texture and strong aroma.

facts: The word yoghurt comes from Turkish, where it has been eaten for centuries.
Bacteria turn milk's lactose into lactic acid, which thickens the milk and gives it a sharp taste.
In South Asia it is used in dishes such as raita and lassi, and in marinades.
natural-yoghurt.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, creamy white natural yoghurt with a smooth top
natural-yoghurt.what: Milk fermented with cultures, thick and tangy.

facts: Navel oranges are thought to have arisen as a mutation in Brazil in the nineteenth century.
The navel is a small, undeveloped second fruit growing inside the orange.
They peel easily and are popular for eating fresh and for segmenting into salads.
navel-orange.visual: one whole navel orange, bright orange peel with a small navel-like mark at the top, lying on its side
navel-orange.what: A seedless sweet orange with a navel-like mark on top.

facts: Nduja comes from Calabria in southern Italy, where it has been made for generations.
It is made from pork, chilli and spices, and is spread on bread or stirred into sauces.
The name is believed to come from the French word andouille, a type of sausage.
nduja.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with soft, brick-red spreadable paste, glossy and smooth
nduja.what: A spreadable Calabrian salami with a fiery kick.

facts: Its name refers to the Italian city of Naples in the south of the country.
The three flavours sit side by side in one block, so each slice shows a band of each.
neapolitan-ice-cream.visual: a rectangular block of ice cream in three bands, dark chocolate, cream vanilla and pink strawberry, with one slice cut away
neapolitan-ice-cream.what: A layered ice cream of chocolate, vanilla and strawberry.

facts: A nectarine is a variety of peach with a smooth skin rather than a fuzzy one.
Nectarines are grown in many warm regions, including Spain, Italy and parts of the United States.
The name is linked to nectar, the sweet drink said in Greek myth to belong to the gods.
nectarine.visual: one whole ripe nectarine lying on its side, smooth glossy skin blushed red over yellow
nectarine.what: A smooth-skinned fruit related to the peach.

facts: Stinging nettles have fine hairs that release irritating chemicals when touched.
The sting is lost when nettles are cooked or dried, so they are used in soups and teas.
People in Britain and Scandinavia have long eaten nettles as a cooked green.
nettles.visual: a small bunch of fresh stinging nettle tops, serrated green leaves, lying flat
nettles.what: Young green nettle tops, cooked to remove their sting.

facts: Neufchâtel is made in the Normandy region of northern France, as a soft bloomy-rind cheese.
Its heart shape comes from traditional moulds used to shape the soft curd.
Like Camembert, it ripens under a white mould that forms a soft outer rind.
neufchatel.visual: one whole heart-shaped soft cheese with a white bloomy rind, sitting on the background
neufchatel.what: A soft, heart-shaped French cheese with a white rind.

facts: New potatoes are harvested while young, before the skins have thickened.
Most new potatoes are sold in spring and early summer.
They are often boiled whole with butter and mint, a classic British side.
new-potato.visual: a small heap of thin-skinned new potatoes, pale brown and smooth, lying loosely together
new-potato.what: A young potato with thin skin and a waxy, sweet flavour.

facts: Wet garlic is harvested before the bulb has formed its papery skin, which is why it is soft and mild.
In parts of southern Europe and Asia, young garlic is sold in spring as a seasonal vegetable.
Young garlic leaves and stems can be chopped and used like spring onions.
new-season-garlic.visual: a bunch of fresh young garlic, pale white bulbs with green stems and leaves attached
new-season-garlic.what: Young garlic harvested early, before the bulb has dried.

facts: Niçoise olives are named after the city of Nice, and they are usually cured in brine or oil.
They are a classic ingredient in salade niçoise, a salad of tuna, eggs and tomatoes.
nicoise-olives.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of small, dark purple-black olives, slightly wrinkled
nicoise-olives.what: Tiny, nutty olives from Provence in southern France.

facts: Waxy potatoes have less starch than floury types, so they hold their shape in boiling and gratins.
Potatoes originated in the Andes of South America and reached Europe in the 16th century.
Gratins are often made with waxy potatoes, as they slice cleanly and hold together in the oven.
nicola-potato.visual: a whole raw yellow-skinned potato, smooth and oval, lying on its side
nicola-potato.what: A waxy yellow potato that holds its shape when cooked.

facts: The seeds are a traditional flavouring on naan and in Indian and Middle Eastern cooking.
Their name black onion seeds is misleading, because the plant is not related to the onion.
nigella-seeds.visual: a small heap of tiny black teardrop-shaped seeds, matt and slightly angular
nigella-seeds.what: Tiny black seeds with an oniony, peppery flavour.

facts: Nile perch is native to Africa, found in rivers and lakes including the Nile.
It was introduced to Lake Victoria in the twentieth century and became a major catch.
Its firm fillets hold together well for grilling, baking and curries.
nile-perch.visual: a raw Nile perch fillet, pale pinkish-white flesh and silvery skin, lying flat
nile-perch.what: A large freshwater fish with firm, mild, white flesh.

facts: Low-alcohol beers are made by stopping fermentation early or by removing alcohol after brewing.
Some cooks use non-alcoholic beer in batters and stews to add a malty flavour without alcohol.
Alcohol can be taken out of beer by vacuum distillation or membrane filtration.
non-alcoholic-beer.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale golden liquid with a small white head of foam
non-alcoholic-beer.what: A beer-style drink made with little or no alcohol.

facts: It is made from acetic acid and colouring, not from brewed malt like malt vinegar.
It became popular in British chip shops as a cheaper alternative to malt vinegar.
non-brewed-condiment.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of thin, pale amber liquid
non-brewed-condiment.what: A sharp, cheaper vinegar-style condiment for chips.

facts: Nopales are the pads of the prickly pear cactus, which is native to the Americas.
Nopales are a traditional part of Mexican cooking, eaten grilled, boiled or in salads.
The word nopal comes from the Nahuatl word nopalli.
nopales.visual: one whole green cactus pad, flat and oval, its surface smooth with small pale spine marks, lying on a plain background
nopales.what: Tender green cactus pads, eaten grilled or stewed.

facts: Nori is made from red algae that are harvested, washed, shredded and pressed into thin sheets.
Japan has a long history of cultivating nori, which is used for sushi and rice balls.
Nori is the Japanese name for this seaweed, and the English word is taken from it.
nori.visual: one whole dark green-black sheet of toasted seaweed, thin and slightly crinkled, flat on the background
nori.what: Thin sheets of dried seaweed, used to wrap sushi.

facts: Nori is cultivated seaweed, grown on nets in coastal Japan and pressed into thin sheets.
Kizami nori means finely shredded nori in Japanese.
Nori is traditionally used to wrap sushi rolls and sprinkled over rice dishes.
nori-strips.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, dark nori seaweed strips
nori-strips.what: Finely cut toasted seaweed for rice bowls and noodles.

facts: Prawns are crustaceans, part of the same group as crabs and lobsters.
Cooked, peeled prawns are commonly sold in Britain for sandwiches.
north-atlantic-prawns.visual: a small heap of peeled pink cooked prawns, curled, lying on a plain background
north-atlantic-prawns.what: Small, sweet cold-water prawns, often sold ready-cooked.

facts: Nougat is a honey-sweetened confection, and sweets like it have a long history around the Mediterranean.
Torrone is the Italian name for nougat, and the sweet is especially associated with Cremona in northern Italy.
Traditional nougat is made by beating hot honey into whipped egg white, then folding in toasted nuts.
nougat.visual: a single cut slab of pale cream-white nougat, with a neat, soft-looking cut face
nougat.what: A chewy, pale sweet of honey, egg white and nuts.

facts: Nuoc cham is made from fish sauce, lime juice, sugar, garlic and chilli, mixed with water.
It is served with many Vietnamese dishes, such as spring rolls, rice dishes and grilled meats.
Its name combines the words for liquid or sauce and for dipping, so it means dipping sauce.
nuoc-cham.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thin amber dipping sauce, smooth and runny
nuoc-cham.what: A thin, sweet, sour and salty Vietnamese dipping sauce.

facts: Brittle is a sweet made by cooking sugar until it caramelises and then stirring in nuts.
Peanut brittle is popular in the United States and is often made in thin sheets for snacking.
nut-brittle.visual: a loose heap of irregular golden-brown brittle shards studded with pale nuts
nut-brittle.what: Thin, crisp sheets of caramel set with nuts.

facts: Ground almonds have been used in European baking and confectionery for centuries.
Hazelnut and almond are common nut flours, each with a distinct flavour.
nut-flour.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, pale golden-brown nut flour
nut-flour.what: Finely ground nuts, often used in place of wheat flour.

facts: Almonds, walnuts, hazelnuts and pecans are among the nuts commonly blended for baking.
Chopped nuts are often folded into cake batter, sprinkled over ice cream and used in brittles.
nut-mix.visual: a small heap of mixed shelled nuts in varied pale and brown pieces
nut-mix.what: A blend of assorted nuts for baking and sprinkling.

facts: In France, praline originally meant almonds cooked in caramelised sugar.
The French word praline now covers many confections made from nuts and sugar.
Crushed praline adds crunch to desserts such as mousses, ice creams and cakes.
nut-praline-crunch.visual: a small heap of golden-brown nut praline shards, irregular glossy pieces of caramelised nut
nut-praline-crunch.what: Nuts cooked in sugar, then broken into crunchy pieces.

facts: It is grown on molasses, then heat-treated so the yeast can no longer grow.
It is popular in vegan cooking as a cheese-like seasoning sprinkled over pasta or popcorn.
The yeast is the same species used in baking and brewing, Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
nutritional-yeast.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale golden yellow yeast flakes
nutritional-yeast.what: Deactivated yeast dried into cheesy-tasting flakes.

facts: Oakleaf is a loose-leaf lettuce, so its outer leaves can be picked one at a time.
Its name refers to the lobed leaf shape, which resembles the leaf of an oak tree.
Red-tinged forms are also grown, and the soft leaves are popular in mixed salads.
oakleaf-lettuce.visual: a whole oakleaf lettuce with frilled, lobed leaves in green and red-tinged tones
oakleaf-lettuce.what: A tender, mild lettuce with lobed leaves like an oak.

facts: In Britain a flapjack is a baked bar of oats, butter and golden syrup, not a pancake.
The usual method is to melt butter with syrup, stir in the oats, press the mix into a tin and bake.
oat-bars.visual: a single oat bar cut into a neat rectangle, golden-brown, with a crumbly texture and flat cut edges
oat-bars.what: A chewy baked bar of oats, butter and golden syrup.

facts: Oatcakes and oat biscuits are a traditional part of Scottish and northern British baking.
Oats have long been grown across Scotland and the north of Britain, where the cool, wet climate suits them.
oat-biscuits.visual: a few round golden oat biscuits with a rough, speckled top, arranged on a plain white plate
oat-biscuits.what: Crisp, oaty biscuits baked with rolled oats and butter.

facts: Oat bran is the outer layer of the oat kernel, separated during milling.
It is traditionally stirred into porridge or baked into breads and muffins.
Oats have been eaten in Scotland for centuries, mainly as porridge and oatcakes.
oat-bran.visual: a small heap of pale golden oat bran, fine and light, in a small plain white ceramic bowl
oat-bran.what: The fine outer layer of the oat grain, sold as flakes.

facts: Oat milk was developed in Sweden in the 1990s as a dairy alternative.
It is made by blending oats with water, then straining out the solids.
oat-milk.visual: a clear drinking glass of creamy off-white oat milk, on a plain background
oat-milk.what: A creamy, mild plant milk made from oats and water.

facts: Oatcakes are a traditional part of Scottish cooking, made from oatmeal, water and fat.
Oatcakes are often eaten with cheese, and they keep well because they are dry and crisp.
oatcake.visual: a small plain white plate holding three round oatcakes, pale beige and rough-edged
oatcake.what: A thin, crisp biscuit made from oats.

facts: Oatcakes are a traditional food in Scotland, and in parts of northern England.
They were once made on a girdle, a flat iron griddle, over an open fire.
oatcakes.visual: a single plain pale oatcake, round and matt with a rough edge, lying flat
oatcakes.what: A thin, crumbly Scottish biscuit made from oats.

facts: Oaxaca cheese comes from the Oaxaca region of southern Mexico and takes its name from there.
It is a pasta filata cheese, meaning it is stretched while hot and then wound into balls.
It is traditionally used in quesadillas, and it melts into long, stringy strands.
oaxaca-cheese.visual: a whole round ball of pale ivory Oaxaca cheese with a smooth, slightly glossy surface
oaxaca-cheese.what: A mild, stringy Mexican cheese, ideal for melting.

facts: Oca is grown in the high Andes of South America, where it has been cultivated for centuries.
Despite its name, oca is not a true yam; it belongs to the wood sorrel family.
Its tubers come in pink, yellow, red and white varieties.
oca.visual: a small heap of knobbly raw oca tubers in pink, yellow and cream
oca.what: A tangy Andean tuber that turns tender when roasted.

facts: Ocean perch is the name for several deep-water rockfish in the genus Sebastes.
Despite its name, it is a rockfish and not a true perch.
ocean-perch.visual: a single raw fillet of ocean perch, skin on, pale pinkish-white flesh with a fresh sheen
ocean-perch.what: A mild, white-fleshed sea fish with delicate flakes.

facts: Octopus is eaten across the Mediterranean, in Spain and Greece, often grilled or simmered.
In Japan, octopus is known as tako and is a common sushi topping.
octopus.visual: one whole raw octopus, pinkish-grey skin, body and eight tentacles curled loosely on the background
octopus.what: A soft-bodied sea creature with eight arms.

facts: Ogi is a fermented porridge made from maize, sorghum or millet, widely eaten in West Africa.
The grain is soaked and left to ferment, which gives it a sour, tangy taste.
It is often eaten for breakfast, served warm with sugar or milk.
ogi-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, pale cream-coloured grain paste with a fine, soft texture
ogi-paste.what: A sour, fermented grain paste, cooked into a porridge.

facts: Okonomiyaki is a Japanese savoury pancake, and its name roughly means 'grilled as you like it'.
The sauce has a sweet, tangy flavour, similar to a Worcestershire-style sauce.
Bonito flakes are often sprinkled on top, and they seem to move as the heat rises.
okonomiyaki-sauce.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of thick, dark brown sauce
okonomiyaki-sauce.what: A sweet, tangy sauce for Japanese savoury pancakes.

facts: Okra is generally thought to have originated in north-east Africa and spread widely through trade.
In India the pods are most often called bhindi.
okra.visual: a small heap of fresh green okra pods, ridged and tapered, one pod cut in half to show the seeds, lying on the background
okra.what: Ridged green pods that thicken soups and stews.

facts: It was first blended in Baltimore, Maryland, in the late 1930s.
It is traditionally sprinkled over steamed crabs and shrimp on the Chesapeake Bay.
old-bay-seasoning.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with fine orange-brown seasoning powder
old-bay-seasoning.what: A celery salt and paprika blend for seafood and crabs.

facts: Olive bread is made in many countries around the Mediterranean, including Italy, Greece and Spain.
Olive oil is often added to the dough, which softens the crumb and adds richness.
olive-bread.visual: one whole round olive bread loaf on a plain white plate, golden crust, dark olive pieces visible in the crumb
olive-bread.what: A Mediterranean loaf studded with salty olives.

facts: Extra virgin olive oil comes from the first pressing of the fruit, without chemical refining.
Olive trees have been grown around the Mediterranean for thousands of years.
Spain, Italy and Greece are major olive oil producers.
olive-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with golden-green olive oil
olive-oil.what: A fruity oil pressed from olives, for cooking and dressing.

facts: Olive oil spreads are a fat blend made to stay soft straight from the fridge, unlike butter.
Many spreads blend olive oil with other vegetable oils such as sunflower or rapeseed oil.
olive-oil-spread.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale yellow soft spread, smooth glossy surface
olive-oil-spread.what: A soft spread blended from olive oil and vegetable oils.

facts: Oloroso is a style of sherry from Jerez in southern Spain, the town that gives sherry its name.
Its name comes from the Spanish word oloroso, meaning fragrant or aromatic.
It is aged in oak casks where it is exposed to air, which gives it a darker, nutty character.
oloroso-sherry.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of deep amber-brown liquid
oloroso-sherry.what: A dark, rich Spanish sherry with a raisin taste.

facts: The name comes from French, and the dish is now cooked in kitchens around the world.
A French-style omelette is cooked gently and folded into a neat oval, with the eggs still soft inside.
omelette.visual: a folded plain yellow omelette on a small plain white plate, one slice cut to show a soft pale interior
omelette.what: Whisked eggs cooked fast in a pan, folded around a filling.

facts: It hangs from the diaphragm, which is why it is also called hanger steak.
onglet.visual: a raw beef onglet steak, long thin dark-red cut with a visible central membrane line, lying on the background
onglet.what: A flavourful, tender cut of beef from the diaphragm.

facts: Bhajis are fritters from Indian cooking, and are widely sold in British takeaways and restaurants.
The batter is made from gram flour, which is ground from dried split chickpeas.
onion-bhajis.visual: a plain white plate of golden-brown onion bhajis, crisp and fried, arranged in a small heap
onion-bhajis.what: Crispy onion fritters in a spiced gram flour batter.

facts: Onion gravy is a classic British accompaniment to sausages and mashed potatoes.
Gravies thicken when flour or starch is stirred into the cooking juices.
Onions are cooked slowly until soft and sweet before the stock is added.
onion-gravy.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, glossy brown onion gravy
onion-gravy.what: A rich brown sauce of cooked onions, stock and flour.

facts: Gravy granules are a dried mixture that dissolves in hot water to thicken and flavour a sauce.
Caramelising onions slowly brings out their natural sugars, which gives sweet onion gravy its depth.
onion-gravy-granules.visual: a small heap of pale brown onion gravy granules in a small plain white ceramic bowl
onion-gravy-granules.what: Dried granules that make a quick, sweet onion gravy.

facts: Onion powder is made by drying onions and grinding them into a fine powder.
Onions belong to the Allium genus, which also includes garlic, leeks and chives.
onion-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, pale beige onion powder, smooth and level on top
onion-powder.what: Dried, ground onion, sweet and savoury, used as a seasoning.

onion-relish.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of soft, glossy brown onion relish
onion-relish.what: Sweet-sour cooked onions, a relish served with sausages.

facts: Onion salt is a blend of salt and dried onion powder, popular in American cooking.
It is often sprinkled on burgers, chips and popcorn.
It is one of several seasoned salts sold in the United States, alongside garlic salt.
onion-salt.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass jar filled with fine, pale cream seasoning powder
onion-salt.what: A seasoning of salt blended with dried onion powder.

facts: Oolong is made by partly oxidising tea leaves, so it sits between green and black tea.
Much oolong comes from Fujian and Guangdong, in southern China, and from Taiwan.
The name is often translated as black dragon, though its origin is debated.
oolong-tea.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dried, twisted oolong tea leaves in dark greenish-brown shades
oolong-tea.what: Partly oxidised Chinese tea with a floral, toasty flavour.

facts: Opah is found in tropical and temperate oceans around the world.
Unusually among fish, opah can keep parts of its body warmer than the surrounding sea.
Its firm, pink flesh holds together well on a grill and in a hot pan.
opah.visual: a thick raw steak of opah, deep salmon-pink flesh with fine pale fat lines, lying flat
opah.what: A large, rich deep-sea fish with firm, steak-like flesh.

facts: Sweet oranges are thought to have originated in Asia, where citrus fruits were first grown long ago.
The word orange passed through Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic and French before reaching English.
Seville oranges, bitter and sour, are the traditional choice for marmalade in Britain.
orange.visual: one whole ripe orange with a bright dimpled peel, lying on its side
orange.what: A sweet, juicy citrus fruit with a bright, thick peel.

facts: Bitters are concentrated flavourings, traditionally used a few drops at a time.
Bitters are used in classic cocktails such as the Old Fashioned.
Their citrus flavour comes from orange peel and other botanicals steeped in a neutral spirit.
orange-bitters.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of dark amber orange bitters
orange-bitters.what: A concentrated, bitter-citrus tincture used in cocktails.

facts: Orange blossom honey is made by bees that forage on the flowers of orange trees.
It is produced in citrus-growing regions such as Spain, Mexico and Florida.
Like other honeys, it is made from nectar that bees collect and ripen in the hive.
orange-blossom-honey.visual: a clear glass jar without a label, filled with pale golden, glossy honey
orange-blossom-honey.what: Light honey with a citrus perfume from orange blossom.

facts: Orange blossom water, distilled from the flowers, is common in Middle Eastern and North African sweets.
Orange blossom is the fragrant white flower of the citrus tree.
Citrus marmalades and jams are a traditional way of preserving fruit with sugar.
orange-blossom-jam.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label holding glossy amber jam
orange-blossom-jam.what: A delicate, floral preserve made with orange blossom.

facts: It is made by distilling the blossoms of bitter orange trees with water.
It is widely used in Middle Eastern, North African and Persian pastries and syrups.
orange-blossom-water.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale, transparent liquid
orange-blossom-water.what: A fragrant water distilled from orange blossoms.

facts: Orange cauliflower is grown in the same way as white cauliflower and belongs to the same species.
It is often roasted whole or cut into florets for a colourful side dish.
Its golden colour comes from a natural pigment in the florets.
orange-cauliflower.visual: a whole orange cauliflower, bright golden florets and pale green leaves
orange-cauliflower.what: A golden cauliflower with a sweeter taste than white.

facts: Lemon curd is a British classic, and orange curd is made in much the same way.
Orange curd has a milder, sweeter flavour than lemon curd.
orange-curd.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, filled with smooth, bright orange curd
orange-curd.what: A smooth, sweet spread of orange juice, eggs and butter.

facts: Jelly is a dessert set with gelatine and sold in packets and in cubes in Britain.
