Gelatine, the setting agent, is made from animal collagen, usually from pig or cow skin and bones.
orange-jelly.visual: a plain clear glass bowl of bright orange jelly, glossy and set, with a wobbly top
orange-jelly.what: A wobbly orange dessert set with gelatine.

facts: Oranges originated in South-East Asia and spread to Europe through trade routes.
Sweet oranges are the main variety used for juice, while bitter oranges are used for marmalade.
Orange juice is widely used in glazes and marinades, especially in Caribbean and Mexican cooking.
orange-juice.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with bright orange juice
orange-juice.what: Juice squeezed from oranges, sweet and tangy for cooking.

facts: Triple sec and curaçao are both orange liqueurs, usually flavoured with dried orange peel.
Curaçao takes its name from the Caribbean island of Curaçao, where a bitter orange was historically grown.
Orange liqueurs are classic in French cooking, including crêpes Suzette and soufflés.
orange-liqueur.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with clear amber-orange liquid
orange-liqueur.what: A sweet spirit flavoured with orange, used in desserts.

facts: Orange oil is pressed from the peel, where the fruit's aromatic oils are stored.
Its strong citrus scent is also used in perfumes.
orange-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of bright golden-orange oil
orange-oil.what: A concentrated citrus oil pressed from orange peel.

facts: Its slow growth and long lifespan mean some stocks have been heavily fished and need careful management.
Its flesh is white and firm, and it is usually sold as skinless fillets.
orange-roughy.visual: one raw orange roughy fillet, firm white flesh with a faint pink tinge, skin removed, lying flat
orange-roughy.what: A deep-sea fish with firm, mild, white flesh.

facts: Orange chicken is a dish popular in American Chinese restaurants.
The sauce usually combines orange zest or juice with sugar, vinegar and soy sauce.
Crisp fried chicken is typically tossed in the sauce just before it is served.
orange-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of glossy orange-brown sauce, smooth and thick
orange-sauce.what: A sweet, tangy citrus sauce for crispy fried chicken.

facts: Orecchiette originated in Puglia in southern Italy.
They are traditionally shaped by hand, pressing and dragging dough over a knife.
The name means 'little ears' in Italian, from orecchio, meaning ear.
orecchiette.visual: a small heap of dried ear-shaped pasta, cupped and pale cream in colour
orecchiette.what: Small, cupped pasta shaped like little ears from Puglia.

facts: Organic eggs come from hens kept under organic farming rules, which govern feed and outdoor access.
Yolk colour depends largely on the hen's diet, which is why yolks vary in shade.
organic-egg.visual: one whole brown-shelled egg, lying on its side with a slightly speckled shell
organic-egg.what: An egg from a hen fed organic feed, with a golden yolk.

facts: Orgeat takes its name from the French word for barley, the grain of the earliest versions.
It is a traditional ingredient in the Mai Tai cocktail.
Classic recipes sweeten it with sugar and flavour it with orange-flower water.
orgeat.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale, milky orgeat syrup
orgeat.what: A sweet syrup made from almonds and orange-flower water.

facts: Oro blanco was developed in the United States from a cross between pomelo and grapefruit.
The name is Spanish for white gold.
oro-blanco.visual: one whole large pale green-yellow citrus fruit with a smooth thick skin, lying on its side
oro-blanco.what: A sweet citrus fruit, a cross of pomelo and grapefruit.

facts: Orzo is Italian for barley, a name given to the pasta because of its grain-like shape.
It is common in Greek and Mediterranean cooking, in soups, salads and baked dishes.
In Italy it is also sold under the name risoni, which means large rice.
orzo.visual: a small heap of dry orzo pasta, pale ivory grains shaped like rice
orzo.what: Small rice-shaped pasta, good in soups and salads.

facts: Oscietra is one of the traditional caviars, made from the roe of sturgeon in the Caspian and Black Seas.
Caviar is salted sturgeon roe, and it has long been a luxury food in Russia and Persia.
Wild sturgeon are endangered, so much caviar today comes from fish raised on farms.
oscietra-caviar.visual: a small plain glass bowl of golden-brown glossy sturgeon eggs, loosely piled
oscietra-caviar.what: Golden-brown sturgeon roe with a firm pop and nutty taste.

facts: Oscypek is made from salted sheep's milk curd, shaped in carved wooden moulds and smoked.
It is traditionally made by herders in the Tatra and Podhale region of Poland.
Grilled slices are often served with cranberry jam in Polish restaurants.
oscypek.visual: one whole spindle-shaped smoked sheep's cheese, pale golden-brown with fine grooved ridges, lying on its side
oscypek.what: A smoked sheep's cheese from the Polish Tatra mountains.

facts: Ossau-Iraty is made from sheep's milk in the French Pyrenees, in the Basque and Béarn areas.
It is an AOC cheese, and its name combines the Ossau valley with the Iraty forest.
Basque cooks often serve it with cherry jam, a classic pairing in the region.
ossau-iraty.visual: a firm block of pale ivory cheese, one neat wedge cut out and lying beside it
ossau-iraty.what: A firm, nutty sheep's cheese from the Basque Pyrenees.

facts: Ostriches are native to Africa and have been farmed for their meat, eggs and feathers.
Ostrich eggshell has been carved into beads and containers in Africa for thousands of years.
ostrich-egg.visual: one whole raw ostrich egg, cream-white shell with a fine texture, resting on its side
ostrich-egg.what: A very large egg from the ostrich, with a thick shell.

facts: Ostriches are native to Africa and are the largest living birds.
ostrich-fillet.visual: one raw ostrich fillet, dark red meat, smooth and lean, lying flat on the surface
ostrich-fillet.what: Lean, dark red meat from a large flightless bird.

facts: Ouzo is made by distilling grape spirit with aniseed and other herbs, and is served with water.
It turns cloudy when water is added, a reaction caused by the oils in the aniseed.
Ouzo is closely related to the French pastis and Turkish raki, which are also anise drinks.
ouzo.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle, clear pale liquid inside
ouzo.what: A Greek spirit flavoured strongly with aniseed.

facts: Rum is distilled from sugarcane products such as molasses or fresh cane juice.
High-strength rum can be set alight, which is why it is used to flame Christmas puddings.
overproof-rum.visual: a clear drinking glass of golden-amber rum, filled to just below the rim
overproof-rum.what: A rum with much higher alcohol content than standard rum.

facts: Ox heart has traditionally been classed as offal, the term for edible organ meats.
ox-heart.visual: a whole raw ox heart, dark red muscle with pale fat around the top, lying flat on a plain background
ox-heart.what: Lean, dense beef heart, good sliced thin or braised.

facts: Kidney has long been used in British dishes such as steak and kidney pudding.
It needs careful preparation, as the fatty core is removed and the membranes trimmed before cooking.
Kidneys are eaten in many cuisines, including French and Spanish cooking.
ox-kidney.visual: one whole raw ox kidney, dark reddish-brown, smooth outer skin, lying on its side
ox-kidney.what: The kidney of a cow, with a rich, mineral flavour.

facts: Ox liver is a larger, firmer cut than calf's liver and is often sold sliced for frying.
ox-liver.visual: a fresh raw ox liver slice, thick, dark reddish-brown, smooth and glossy, lying flat on the background
ox-liver.what: Dark, firm liver from a cow, with a strong, rich flavour.

facts: Cooks have long used beef tongue in Central European and Jewish cooking, often sliced cold.
In Mexican cooking, lengua is beef tongue simmered until tender, then used in tacos.
Tongue is a tough muscle, so it needs long, slow cooking before its skin can be peeled off.
ox-tongue.visual: a whole raw ox tongue, pinkish-grey and smooth, lying in a gentle curve
ox-tongue.what: A cow's tongue, slow-cooked until soft and sliced thin.

facts: Oxtail is the tail of cattle, and its connective tissue turns silky when braised slowly.
Oxtail stew is a traditional dish in Jamaica and across the Caribbean.
oxtail.visual: several raw jointed oxtail pieces, dark red meat around pale bone, lying flat
oxtail.what: The meaty tail of a cow, rich and bony, for slow braises.

facts: Oyster mushrooms grow naturally on decaying wood and are cultivated on straw and other farm waste.
Their name comes from their shape, which resembles an oyster shell, though they are not related to oysters.
They are grown widely across Asia and Europe.
oyster-mushroom.visual: a small cluster of pale grey oyster mushrooms with fan-shaped caps, fanned out
oyster-mushroom.what: Fan-shaped mushrooms with a soft, velvety texture.

facts: It is made by simmering oyster extract with soy sauce, sugar and starch until thick.
It is widely used in Cantonese cooking, especially in stir-fried greens.
It is named for the oysters in its recipe, though the sauce tastes savoury rather than fishy.
oyster-sauce.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle holding thick, glossy dark brown sauce
oyster-sauce.what: A thick, savoury brown sauce for Chinese stir-fries.

facts: Paccheri are wide tubes that come from southern Italy, particularly the Naples area.
Their wide hollow centre holds chunks of seafood and thick sauces well.
paccheri.visual: a loose heap of large smooth pasta tubes, pale cream colour, lying on a plain background
paccheri.what: Large, wide tubes of pasta that hold chunky sauces well.

facts: Pacific halibut is found across the North Pacific, from Japan to the coasts of North America.
Like other flatfish, the young halibut has eyes on both sides of its head, and one moves across.
Halibut is often grilled or baked, as its firm flesh holds together well.
pacific-halibut.visual: a fresh halibut fillet with firm, pale pink-white flesh and the skin removed, lying flat on the background
pacific-halibut.what: A large, mild white flatfish from the North Pacific.

facts: Pacific oysters are native to the north-west Pacific, around Japan and Korea.
They were introduced to many coastlines around the world, including Europe, for shellfish farming.
Their shells grow in long, ridged layers, and they are often farmed on racks or ropes.
pacific-oysters.visual: one whole raw Pacific oyster in its rough, ridged grey shell, closed
pacific-oysters.what: Mild, plump shellfish, eaten raw or grilled.

facts: Instant mash was developed in the twentieth century and is made by cooking and drying potatoes.
Potatoes were domesticated in the Andes of South America, thousands of years ago.
packet-mash.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dry, pale cream instant mashed potato powder
packet-mash.what: Dried potato powder that turns into mash with water.

facts: Pad thai was promoted as a national dish in Thailand during the 1930s.
It is stir-fried with tamarind, fish sauce and palm sugar, which give it a sweet and sour taste.
Pad thai is usually made with eggs, tofu or prawns, then topped with crushed peanuts and lime.
pad-thai-noodles.visual: a small loose heap of dried rice noodles, pale off-white ribbons about a centimetre wide, lying on the background
pad-thai-noodles.what: Medium-width rice noodles that suit a quick stir-fry.

facts: Padron peppers come from the Galicia region of north-west Spain, around the town of Padron.
A Galician saying goes that some Padron peppers are hot and others are not.
They are usually blistered in hot oil and sprinkled with sea salt as a tapas dish.
padron-pepper.visual: a small heap of whole green Padron peppers, small and wrinkled-skinned, with short stalks attached, lying on the background
padron-pepper.what: Small green peppers that are fried whole and salted.

facts: Paella takes its name from the wide, shallow pan in which the dish is cooked.
Short-grained rice soaks up liquid while keeping a firm bite, which suits paella well.
paella-rice.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dry, pale short-grain rice, plump white grains
paella-rice.what: A short, plump rice that absorbs stock without going soft.

facts: Pain au chocolat is a French pastry made with the same laminated dough used for croissants.
The name means chocolate bread in French, though it is a pastry rather than a loaf.
It is a popular breakfast pastry in France and is sold in bakeries across the country.
pain-au-chocolat.visual: a golden baked pain au chocolat with flaky layers and visible dark chocolate batons, on a plain white plate
pain-au-chocolat.what: A flaky, buttery pastry rolled around dark chocolate.

facts: Pain aux raisins means raisin bread in French, though it is a spiral pastry rather than a loaf.
Bakers often soak the raisins and spread a thick custard inside the coiled dough.
Viennoiserie, the family of pastries it belongs to, takes its name from Vienna.
pain-aux-raisins.visual: a single golden spiral pastry, glossy and flaky, dotted with dark raisins, on a plain white plate
pain-aux-raisins.what: A spiral pastry filled with custard and raisins.

facts: Pain de campagne means country bread, a rustic loaf from rural France.
It is usually made with wheat flour, a natural starter and a long, slow rise.
pain-de-campagne.visual: a whole round country loaf with a floury, cracked, golden crust
pain-de-campagne.what: A rustic French loaf with a crisp crust and a mild tang.

facts: Its name comes from Cantonese, where bok choy means white vegetable.
The stems cook quickly and can be stir-fried or steamed whole.
pak-choi.visual: one whole pak choi with pale green stems and dark green leaves, base trimmed
pak-choi.what: A mild Asian cabbage with crisp white stems.

facts: Pale ale is a style that developed in England, and its name refers to the pale colour of its malt.
Beer is often used in batters, where its carbonation adds lightness to the coating.
pale-ale.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale amber beer with a thin off-white head
pale-ale.what: A hoppy, golden beer, lighter in colour than a dark ale.

facts: Palm hearts are the tender growing bud of certain palm trees, and cutting one usually kills the tree.
Palm hearts are a traditional ingredient in Brazilian and wider South American cooking, often served in salads.
palm-hearts.visual: several pale cream-coloured palm hearts cut into short rounds, lying flat on the background, showing their tender white centres
palm-hearts.what: The soft pale core of a palm tree, eaten as a vegetable.

facts: Palm oil is pressed from the fleshy fruit of the oil palm, which grows in tropical regions.
Unrefined red palm oil keeps a deep orange colour from natural pigments.
It is widely used for frying across West Africa and Southeast Asia.
palm-oil.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, filled with deep orange-red palm oil
palm-oil.what: A reddish oil pressed from palm fruit.

facts: Palm sugar is made by boiling the sap of coconut or sugar palm trees.
It is widely used in Thai and Indonesian cooking, in curries and desserts.
Palm sugar sold in blocks is often shaved or grated before use.
palm-sugar.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of golden brown palm sugar granules
palm-sugar.what: Caramel-flavoured sugar made from the sap of palm trees.

facts: Palm sap is collected by tapping the trunk or flower stalks, then boiled down.
In South and Southeast Asia, palm sugar is widely used in desserts and curries.
Palm syrup has a deep, caramel-like flavour with hints of toffee.
palm-syrup.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of thick dark amber syrup
palm-syrup.what: A dark, sweet syrup made from the sap of palm trees.

facts: Palourdes are prized in France and Spain, where they are often steamed with wine and herbs.
Clams like palourdes feature in many Portuguese and Spanish seafood dishes.
palourde-clams.visual: a small heap of raw palourde clams in their shells, ridged brown and cream, closed tightly
palourde-clams.what: A sweet-tasting clam with a ridged, brownish shell.

facts: Panang is a Thai curry, generally thicker and sweeter than many other red curries.
It is often simmered with coconut cream and used with meat, seafood or tofu.
panang-curry-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, deep red-brown curry paste
panang-curry-paste.what: A thick, nutty red curry paste with a sweet spice.

facts: Pancakes have been cooked in Britain for centuries, and Shrove Tuesday is traditionally Pancake Day.
pancake-mix.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with fine off-white pancake mix powder, level at the top
pancake-mix.what: A ready-mixed flour blend for quick, fluffy pancakes.

facts: Thin flatbreads and pancakes are eaten in many cuisines, including Chinese, Mexican and Indian.
Mandarin pancakes, served with Peking duck, are thin soft wheat pancakes.
Thin wheat pancakes are made from flour, water and sometimes oil, cooked on a hot flat pan.
pancake-wrap.visual: a single thin flexible pancake, pale golden and flat, lying open on a plain background
pancake-wrap.what: A thin, flexible pancake for rolling around fillings.

facts: Pancetta is Italian pork belly that is salted, seasoned with spices and left to dry.
pancetta.visual: a whole rolled block of pancetta, pale pink meat and creamy fat in stripes, lying on a plain background
pancetta.what: Italian salted pork belly, used like bacon in pasta.

facts: Pancetta is Italian pork belly, and arrotolata means rolled.
Unlike bacon, pancetta is seasoned with salt and spices but not usually smoked.
It is often used to flavour sauces, soups and pasta dishes in Italian cooking.
pancetta-arrotolata.visual: one whole rolled pancetta, a cylinder of pork with a visible spiral of pink-red meat and white fat, lying on its side on a plain background
pancetta-arrotolata.what: Pork belly rolled up and seasoned with salt and spices.

facts: Whole seeds are fried briefly in hot oil to release their aroma before other ingredients are added.
It is used in dals, vegetable dishes and pickles across Bengal and neighbouring regions.
panch-phoron.visual: a small heap of mixed whole spice seeds, tiny and dark, brown and black, lying loose
panch-phoron.what: A Bengali mix of five whole seeds, toasted in hot oil.

facts: Pandan is a tropical plant whose long, fragrant leaves are used across South-East Asia.
Its leaves are often knotted and simmered with rice or coconut milk to scent them.
It is often called the vanilla of South-East Asia, although it is not related to vanilla.
pandan-extract.visual: a small plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of bright green liquid
pandan-extract.what: A green, grassy flavouring made from pandan leaves.

facts: Pandan is a screwpine plant widely grown across South-East Asia.
The leaves are used to flavour rice dishes and sweets across Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
Cooks often bruise or knot the leaves before simmering to release their fragrance.
pandan-leaf.visual: a loose bunch of long, narrow, glossy green pandan leaves, one leaf curled at the tip
pandan-leaf.what: Long, grassy leaves used to scent rice and desserts.

facts: Pandan leaves are long, grass-like leaves from a plant common across Southeast Asia.
The leaves give a sweet, vanilla-like aroma to cakes, rice and drinks.
Pandan is often called the vanilla of Southeast Asia, though it is a different plant.
pandan-paste.visual: a plain glass jar without a label holding bright green pandan paste, smooth and glossy
pandan-paste.what: A green paste made from fragrant pandan leaves for sweets.

facts: Pane carasau is a traditional flatbread from Sardinia, baked twice to dry it out.
It is nicknamed carta da musica, or music paper, because the sheets are so thin.
pane-carasau.visual: a single large thin golden flatbread sheet, lightly blistered, lying flat
pane-carasau.what: A paper-thin, crisp flatbread from Sardinia.

facts: Unlike many cheeses, paneer does not melt when fried, so it keeps its shape.
Dishes such as palak paneer and paneer tikka use it widely across India.
paneer.visual: a block of white paneer with one wedge cut, edges clean and square
paneer.what: Firm, mild curd cheese from the Indian subcontinent.

facts: Pangasius is a catfish farmed mainly in the Mekong Delta, in Vietnam.
In some markets it is sold under the name basa, as a mild, flaky white fish.
Its fillets are boneless and mild, so they suit quick curries and breadcrumb coatings.
pangasius.visual: a single raw white fish fillet, pale and soft-textured, lying flat on the background
pangasius.what: A mild, white freshwater fish from South-East Asia.

facts: Panko is widely used to coat tonkatsu, a breaded Japanese pork cutlet.
Because the flakes are large and dry, the coating stays crisp after frying.
panko-breadcrumbs.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale golden panko breadcrumbs, light and flaky
panko-breadcrumbs.what: Light, flaky Japanese breadcrumbs for a crisp coating.

facts: Pansies belong to the violet family and have been grown in gardens for centuries.
The name pansy comes from the French word pensée, meaning thought.
pansies.visual: a small heap of fresh pansy flowers, velvety petals in purple, yellow and white
pansies.what: Small, velvety edible flowers with a mild, fresh taste.

facts: Pansotti come from Liguria in north-west Italy, where they are traditionally filled with wild herbs.
The filling is often made with borage, a wild green, and mixed with ricotta.
Pansotti are traditionally served with a walnut sauce, a dish known as pansotti con salsa di noci.
pansotti.visual: a small heap of fresh, pale cream triangular pasta parcels, pinched along their edges
pansotti.what: Triangular Ligurian pasta parcels filled with wild greens.

facts: Papaya is native to the tropical Americas and has spread to tropical regions worldwide.
Unripe papaya is eaten as a vegetable in parts of Southeast Asia, often shredded in salads.
Papaya seeds are black and peppery, and are sometimes ground and used as a seasoning.
papaya.visual: a halved ripe papaya, orange flesh and a cluster of round black seeds visible, cut face up on the background
papaya.what: A tropical fruit with soft, musky orange flesh.

facts: The name comes from the Italian verb pappare, meaning to gobble up.
It is traditionally associated with Tuscany, where it is served with hare sauce.
Its wide surface holds thick, meaty sauces well.
pappardelle.visual: a small heap of uncooked wide pappardelle ribbons, pale golden yellow and flat
pappardelle.what: Wide, flat egg pasta ribbons, good with rich meat sauce.

facts: It takes its name from its umbrella-like cap, which opens wide as the mushroom matures.
The cap is often dipped in egg and breadcrumbs and fried, much like a schnitzel.
Parasol mushrooms grow in grassland and at woodland edges, mostly in late summer and autumn.
parasol-mushroom.visual: a whole fresh parasol mushroom with a tall, brown scaly cap and a long slender stem, on a plain background
parasol-mushroom.what: A tall wild mushroom with a broad, scaly cap.

facts: Paratha is thought to have begun in the Indian subcontinent, where wheat flatbreads have long been made.
Its flaky layers come from rubbing fat into the dough, folding it and rolling it out before cooking.
It is eaten widely across northern India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, often alongside curries.
paratha.visual: one round paratha flatbread, golden-brown with visible flaky layers, lying flat on a plain white plate
paratha.what: A flaky, layered flatbread, often cooked with butter.

facts: Parmigiano Reggiano is made in northern Italy within a defined, protected area around Parma, Reggio Emilia and Modena.
The name Parmigiano means 'of Parma', the city where the cheese has long been made.
Its crumbly, crystalline texture comes from long ageing, which lets tiny crunchy crystals form in the cheese.
parmesan.visual: a block of pale golden hard cheese with one wedge cut away, showing a crumbly, granular face
parmesan.what: A hard, salty Italian cheese with a nutty flavour.

facts: Parsley root is also called Hamburg parsley, a name that points to German growing traditions.
It is grown mainly for its roots, though the leaves can also be eaten.
In central and northern Europe, it has long been used in soups and stews.
parsley-root.visual: one whole raw parsley root, pale creamy-white and tapered, with a few fine side rootlets
parsley-root.what: A pale, sweet root with a hint of parsley, like a parsnip.

facts: Parsley sauce is a traditional British sauce, often served with ham, fish or boiled vegetables.
It is built on a roux of butter and flour, thickened with milk and finished with chopped parsley.
Parsley grows wild around the Mediterranean and has been cultivated for many centuries.
parsley-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth pale green sauce, flecked throughout by finely chopped leaves
parsley-sauce.what: A creamy white sauce, turned green by fresh parsley.

facts: Parsnips are native to Eurasia, and were a staple root vegetable in Europe before potatoes arrived.
Their sweetness increases after the first frosts, as the starch in the root turns to sugar.
parsnip.visual: One whole pale cream parsnip, tapered, with fine rootlets, lying on its side.
parsnip.what: A pale, sweet root vegetable with an earthy flavour.

facts: Parsnips are a root vegetable related to the carrot, and were eaten in Europe before the potato arrived.
In Britain, parsnips are harvested through the autumn and winter.
parsnip-crisps.visual: a small heap of thin, golden-brown parsnip crisps, some slightly curled, on a plain background
parsnip-crisps.what: Thin, crisp slices of fried parsnip, sweet and earthy.

facts: Partridges belong to the pheasant family and are found across Europe, Asia and parts of Africa.
The grey partridge is native to Britain and has long been a traditional game bird.
partridge.visual: a whole raw partridge, plucked, pale skin and small tucked legs, breast uppermost
partridge.what: A small game bird with fine, delicate meat.

facts: Pasilla means little raisin in Spanish, a nod to its wrinkled, dried skin.
Pasilla chillies are the dried form of the chilaca chilli, which is grown in Mexico.
They are a key ingredient in Mexican mole sauces and are often toasted before soaking.
pasilla-chilli.visual: a small heap of dried pasilla chillies, long, wrinkled and dark brown-black
pasilla-chilli.what: A dark, dried Mexican chilli with a raisin-like flavour.

facts: Passata is made from crushed tomatoes that have been pushed through a sieve to remove skins and seeds.
It is widely used in Italian cooking, especially for simple tomato sauces.
The word passata comes from the Italian verb passare, meaning to pass or strain.
passata.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with smooth bright red tomato passata
passata.what: Smooth, sieved tomatoes, a simple base for sauces.

facts: Passion fruit is native to South America and was carried to other warm regions by early European traders.
Its tart pulp is often spooned over desserts such as pavlova.
Both the pulp and the small seeds are edible, and the fruit is eaten by scooping out the contents.
passion-fruit.visual: one whole ripe purple passion fruit with a wrinkled skin, on its own
passion-fruit.what: A wrinkled purple fruit with tart, seedy yellow pulp.

facts: The fruit is named after the passion flower, the blossom of the climbing vine it grows on.
Curd is often spooned into tarts or sandwiched between layers of sponge cake.
passion-fruit-curd.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, glossy yellow passion fruit curd
passion-fruit-curd.what: A tangy yellow curd made from passion fruit juice.

facts: Passion fruit liqueur is usually made by blending the fruit's juice with a neutral spirit and sugar.
Passion fruit is native to South America, and its name comes from the flower's resemblance to Christ's Passion.
passion-fruit-liqueur.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with deep golden-orange liqueur, its cap off
passion-fruit-liqueur.what: A sweet-tart tropical liqueur flavoured with passion fruit.

facts: Tomato sauces for pasta developed in Italy after tomatoes arrived in Europe in the sixteenth century.
Sugo is the Italian word for sauce, and tomato sugo is a common base for spaghetti dishes.
pasta-sauce-jar.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, full of smooth red tomato pasta sauce
pasta-sauce-jar.what: A smooth tomato sauce, ready to heat and toss with pasta.

facts: Fresh egg pasta is made by rolling a dough of flour and eggs until it is very thin.
Lasagne, tagliatelle and ravioli are typically made from sheets like this.
In Emilia-Romagna, hand-rolled egg pasta is a long-standing local tradition.
pasta-sfoglia.visual: one large flat sheet of pale yellow fresh egg pasta, lying flat with slightly translucent edges
pasta-sfoglia.what: A thin, hand-rolled sheet of fresh egg pasta.

facts: Pastina means little pasta in Italian, and it is made in many small shapes.
In Italy, pastina is often cooked in broth and served in family kitchens.
Stars, rings and tiny seeds are among the most common shapes of pastina.
pastina.visual: a small heap of tiny pale yellow pasta shapes, mostly stars and rings, scattered together
pastina.what: Tiny pasta shapes, traditionally cooked in soup or broth.

facts: Pastis is flavoured mainly with aniseed and liquorice root, along with other herbs.
It is traditionally diluted with water and ice, especially in the south of France.
pastis.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale yellow spirit, turned milky white and cloudy
pastis.what: A French aniseed spirit that turns cloudy with water.

facts: It is traditionally coated in black pepper and coriander seed before it is smoked.
The word pastrami is thought to come from the Turkish word pastırma, a dried meat.
Thin slices are often served on rye bread, sometimes with mustard.
pastrami.visual: a neat stack of sliced pastrami, dark peppery crust on the edges and pink smoked beef within, on a plain white plate
pastrami.what: Salted, smoked beef with a spiced crust, sliced thin.

facts: Tartlet cases are made from shortcrust or sweet pastry, pressed into small tins and baked empty.
In American English they are often called tart shells.
pastry-case-tartlets.visual: a small heap of empty golden baked pastry tartlet cases, fluted edges visible
pastry-case-tartlets.what: Small baked pastry cups for savoury or sweet fillings.

facts: It lives in cold, deep waters of the Southern Ocean, including around southern South America and sub-Antarctic islands.
Its marketing name, Chilean sea bass, is misleading, since the fish is not a true bass.
patagonian-toothfish.visual: a fillet of white fish with moist, flaky flesh and the skin removed, lying flat
patagonian-toothfish.what: A deep-sea fish with rich, buttery white flesh.

facts: Pâté de campagne means country-style pâté, made from coarsely chopped meat rather than a smooth paste.
It is a traditional part of French charcuterie, often served sliced with crusty bread.
pate-de-campagne.visual: a thick slice of coarse-textured pork pâté, visible flecks of herb, served on a plain white plate
pate-de-campagne.what: A rustic French pork pâté, herby and rich with brandy.

facts: Its name comes from the small, shallow baking tins that it resembles.
Patty pan squash is a variety of a species first domesticated in the Americas.
It is usually picked young, when the skin is tender and can be eaten without peeling.
patty-pan-squash.visual: a whole small pale green patty pan squash, flat and scalloped at the edge, lying on its side
patty-pan-squash.what: A flat, scalloped summer squash with a mild flavour.

facts: Pav bhaji is a dish from Mumbai of spiced vegetable mash served with buttered bread rolls.
The masala is a mix of ground spices that varies from cook to cook and from one stall to another.
Pav is the soft bread roll served alongside the mash, and it is an everyday part of the dish.
pav-bhaji-masala.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, brick-red spice powder with a smooth surface
pav-bhaji-masala.what: A tangy, spicy blend of spices for Mumbai street food.

facts: It grows wild in the eastern United States and southern Ontario, in forest understories.
Pawpaw is not the same as papaya, though the two are sometimes confused.
pawpaw-fruit.visual: a whole ripe pawpaw fruit, oblong and green-yellow with dark spots, lying on the background
pawpaw-fruit.what: A creamy North American fruit with custard-like flesh.

facts: Peas have been grown as a crop for thousands of years, with early evidence from the Near East.
Plant milks such as soya and oat are sold in many countries alongside pea versions.
pea-milk.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with pale, creamy off-white milk
pea-milk.what: A creamy plant-based milk made from ground yellow peas.

facts: Pea shoots are the young tips of pea plants, picked before the plant matures.
In Chinese cooking they are known as dou miao and are stir-fried briefly.
They are often eaten raw in salads, or lightly wilted in a hot pan.
pea-shoots.visual: a loose bunch of bright green shoots, with small leaves and curling tendrils
pea-shoots.what: Tender green tips of young pea plants, sweet and fresh.

facts: Peaches were first cultivated in China, where they have been grown for thousands of years.
The peach's scientific name, Prunus persica, reflects the old belief that it came from Persia.
Peaches belong to the same genus as plums, apricots and cherries.
peach.visual: a single whole ripe yellow peach with a soft pink blush and fuzzy skin, lying on its side
peach.what: A juicy stone fruit with fuzzy skin and sweet flesh.

facts: Jam is made by cooking fruit with sugar until the mixture thickens and sets.
Peach jam is often spread on toast or used in cakes and glazes.
peach-jam.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with soft golden-orange peach jam
peach-jam.what: A soft, sweet preserve made from cooked peaches.

facts: Peanuts are native to South America and spread worldwide through early Spanish and Portuguese trade.
Peanut butter became popular in the United States in the early 1900s as a spread for bread.
In West Africa, ground peanuts are used to thicken stews such as groundnut stew.
peanut-butter.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with smooth golden-brown peanut butter
peanut-butter.what: A spread of ground roasted peanuts, toasty and rich.

facts: Peanuts originated in South America and were grown there long before European contact.
Peanut-based stews and sauces are traditional in West African cooking.
peanut-flour.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine pale beige peanut flour
peanut-flour.what: Ground roasted peanuts, dried to a fine powder.

facts: Peanut sauce is a classic partner for Indonesian satay, grilled meat on bamboo skewers.
Peanuts are native to South America and spread to Asia through Portuguese and Spanish trade.
peanut-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth golden-brown peanut sauce, glossy and thick
peanut-sauce.what: A rich, nutty sauce for noodles and skewers.

facts: Peanut flowers open above ground, but their pods then bury themselves in the soil to ripen.
Peanuts are native to South America and were carried to Africa and Asia by European traders.
Peanut butter is made by grinding roasted peanuts into a smooth or chunky paste.
peanuts.visual: a small heap of shelled raw peanuts with thin brown skins still on
peanuts.what: Crunchy legumes that grow underground, often eaten as nuts.

facts: Pear drops are a traditional British boiled sweet, sold loose in old-fashioned sweet shops.
Their sharp pear taste usually comes from amyl acetate, a fruity-smelling ester also used as a solvent.
Boiled sweets are made by cooking sugar syrup to a high temperature, then letting it set hard.
pear-drops.visual: a plain white ceramic bowl heaped with translucent pale yellow boiled sweets
pear-drops.what: Hard, fruity boiled sweets that taste sharply of pear.

facts: Pearl barley is barley with its husk and bran removed, then polished.
It has been used in British and European soups and stews for centuries, such as Scotch broth.
As it simmers, its starch is released, which slightly thickens the liquid.
pearl-barley.visual: a small heap of pale cream, round, polished barley grains
pearl-barley.what: Polished barley grains, soft and chewy when cooked.

facts: Pearl couscous is made from semolina dough rolled into small balls and then dried.
It was first made in Israel in the mid twentieth century, and is also called Israeli couscous.
Unlike fine couscous, its larger grains take longer to cook and are often toasted first.
pearl-couscous.visual: a small heap of pale golden, pearl-sized couscous grains, smooth and round
pearl-couscous.what: Small, chewy pasta balls that hold their shape in salads.

facts: Pearl onions are a small variety of onion, and they are often pickled in vinegar.
They are a classic part of French beef bourguignon, where they are glazed and braised with the stew.
pearl-onion.visual: a small heap of tiny round onions with papery pale-brown skins
pearl-onion.what: A small, sweet onion often served in creamy sauces.

facts: Pearl semolina is made from wheat flour rolled into small pellets, which keep their shape when cooked.
Semolina is a coarsely ground wheat, most often durum, and is also used for pasta and couscous.
pearl-semolina.visual: a small heap of pale cream pearl semolina grains, tiny and round, on a plain background
pearl-semolina.what: Tiny round wheat pellets that cook into a creamy pudding.

facts: Pearl sugar is made of large, dense sugar grains that hold their shape when heated.
It is traditionally scattered over Swedish sweet buns and baked pastries.
Belgian liège waffles are made with a dough that includes pearl sugar, which caramelises as they bake.
pearl-sugar.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of opaque white pearl sugar nuggets
pearl-sugar.what: Coarse white sugar nuggets that stay crunchy when baked.

facts: Pease pudding is a traditional dish in northern England, often served with ham.
The name keeps an old English word for peas, which is pease.
Split peas are dried peas that have been split along their natural seam.
pease-pudding.visual: a smooth, thick yellow-green pease pudding served in a small plain white ceramic bowl

facts: Trotters are the feet of pigs, and are used in dishes across Europe and Asia.
Trotter skin and cartilage turn soft and gelatinous when simmered slowly for a long time.
Trotters are braised, pickled or boiled in many traditions, including Chinese, Spanish and Portuguese cooking.
pig-s-trotter.visual: a whole raw pig's trotter, pale pink skin and a cloven hoof, lying on a plain background
pig-s-trotter.what: A pig's foot that releases gelatin and thickens stocks.

facts: Pigeon has been eaten since ancient times, and in medieval Europe dovecotes kept birds for food.
Squab is the name for a young pigeon, usually raised for the table.
In French cooking pigeon is often roasted or seared so that the meat stays pink.
pigeon-breast.visual: one raw pigeon breast fillet, deep dark red, skin side up, lying flat on a plain background
pigeon-breast.what: The rich, dark breast meat of a plump small bird.

facts: Pigeon peas are grown across the tropics and are a staple in many regions of India.
In Caribbean cooking, pigeon peas are often simmered with rice.
The plant is a shrubby legume whose pods are picked fresh or left to dry.
pigeon-peas.visual: a small heap of dried pigeon peas, round and tan-brown with a pale seam, scattered loosely
pigeon-peas.what: A round, nutty bean grown in warm climates.

facts: Pigs in blankets are a popular party food in Britain, especially at Christmas.
pigs-in-blankets.visual: a small plain white plate of four golden, cooked pigs in blankets arranged in a neat row
pigs-in-blankets.what: Mini sausages wrapped in bacon, roasted until golden.

facts: Pike is a predatory fish that lives in rivers and lakes across the Northern Hemisphere.
Its many fine bones make it a challenge to fillet, so it is often minced and shaped into quenelles.
Pike has been caught and eaten for centuries in northern Europe, where it is an important freshwater fish.
pike.visual: a whole raw pike fish, slim and long with a mottled green-grey back and pale belly, lying on the background
pike.what: A lean freshwater fish with firm white flesh.

facts: Pikelets are a traditional griddled cake in Britain, made from a thin batter.
They are close relatives of the crumpet, and both are cooked on a griddle.
Pikelets are often spread with butter, jam or honey while still warm.
pikelet.visual: a small stack of three plain round golden pikelets on a plain white plate
pikelet.what: A small, thin, round griddled cake, eaten buttered.

facts: Pili trees are native to the Philippines, where the nuts have long been eaten.
Pili nuts can be eaten raw, roasted or pressed for oil, and are used in sweets.
Pili nuts are often compared in flavour to cashews or almonds.
pili-nuts.visual: a small heap of shelled pili nuts, pale cream and pointed at one end, lying on a plain background
pili-nuts.what: Creamy, mild nuts from a tree native to the Philippines.

facts: Piloncillo is made by boiling cane juice until it thickens, then pouring it into cone-shaped moulds.
It is used to sweeten coffee, hot chocolate and syrups for Mexican desserts.
Its dark colour and molasses-like taste come from the cane juice being cooked down slowly.
piloncillo.visual: one whole cone-shaped block of dark brown raw cane sugar with a flat base and rough surface
piloncillo.what: Unrefined Mexican cane sugar pressed into a cone.

facts: Piment d'Espelette is named after the village of Espelette in the French Basque Country.
The peppers are hung in the sun to dry, a tradition seen on house fronts in Basque villages.
Chillies came to the Basque Country from the Americas, likely brought by European traders.
piment-d-espelette.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with bright red pepper powder
piment-d-espelette.what: A mild, fruity red chilli powder from the Basque Country.

facts: Pimento is a variety of sweet pepper with thick, soft flesh, which is why it is often stuffed into olives.
The name comes from the Spanish word pimiento, which simply means pepper.
Pimentos are commonly roasted, peeled and packed in jars or tins before sale.
pimento.visual: one whole glossy red pimento pepper, heart-shaped and smooth-skinned, lying on its side
pimento.what: A small, sweet red pepper, often sold in jars.

facts: Pine nuts are the seeds of several pine species and are harvested from the cones.
Pine nuts are a key ingredient in traditional pesto, a sauce from Liguria.
Pine nuts have been eaten around the Mediterranean and parts of Asia for thousands of years.
pine-nuts.visual: a small heap of pale ivory pine nut kernels, slightly elongated and loose
pine-nuts.what: Small, creamy seeds from pine cones, soft and resinous.

facts: Pineapples are native to South America and were later carried by explorers to other tropical regions.
A pineapple is not a single fruit but many berries fused together around a central core.
Enzymes in pineapple break down protein, so fresh pineapple can stop gelatine from setting.
pineapple.visual: a whole ripe pineapple, golden-brown skin with green crown, standing upright on a plain surface
pineapple.what: A tropical fruit with spiky skin and sweet, juicy flesh.

facts: Pineapples are native to South America and were carried across the world by European traders.
In Britain, pineapple was once a costly treat grown in heated glasshouses.
Its name means pine cone in English, because the fruit looks like one.
pineapple-jam.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, holding golden, chunky pineapple jam
pineapple-jam.what: Sweet, tangy spread made from cooked pineapple and sugar.

facts: Pineapples are native to South America and were carried to other tropical regions by traders.
Fresh pineapple is used in marinades because its juice softens meat.
pineapple-juice.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with pale golden pineapple juice
pineapple-juice.what: Sweet, tangy juice pressed from ripe pineapple fruit.

facts: Its leaves smell strongly of pineapple when crushed, which is why it is used in drinks and fruit salads.
Its red flowers are edible and are sometimes used to decorate desserts and cocktails.
pineapple-sage.visual: a small bunch of pineapple sage stems, bearing bright red tubular flowers and soft green leaves
pineapple-sage.what: A sage with fruity-scented leaves and bright red flowers.

facts: The name refers to the fir-cone shape of the tubers.
Its waxy flesh holds its shape after boiling, making it good for potato salads.
Cooks often boil it whole and dress it while warm so it absorbs the dressing.
pink-fir-apple-potato.visual: a small heap of knobbly, long potatoes with pale pink skin and uneven shapes
pink-fir-apple-potato.what: A knobbly, waxy salad potato with a nutty flavour.

facts: Grapefruit is a hybrid citrus, thought to have arisen from a cross between pomelo and sweet orange.
Pink and red varieties have flesh coloured by natural pigments, and are often sweeter than white ones.
Grapefruit is often eaten halved at breakfast, or used in salads and cocktails.
pink-grapefruit.visual: a whole pink grapefruit with a pale yellow skin blushed with pink, lying on a plain background
pink-grapefruit.what: A large citrus fruit with sweet, blush-pink flesh.

facts: The Pink Lady apple was bred in Western Australia in the 1970s, from a cross of two other apple varieties.
The apple is also known as Cripps Pink, after the grower who developed it.
Its firm, crisp flesh holds its shape well, so it is often sliced for salads and cheeseboards.
pink-lady-apple.visual: one whole pale yellow-green apple with a rosy pink blush on one side, shiny skin, lying on a plain background
pink-lady-apple.what: A crisp, sweet-tart apple with a pink blush on its skin.

facts: Oyster mushrooms are named for their resemblance to the shape of an oyster shell.
Pink oyster mushrooms are grown commercially on straw and sawdust in many warm countries.
Their colour fades when cooked for a long time, so they are best fried quickly over high heat.
pink-oyster-mushroom.visual: a small bunch of pink oyster mushrooms, fan-shaped pale pink caps on short white stems
pink-oyster-mushroom.what: A pink, fan-shaped mushroom with a smoky, meaty smell.

facts: Pink peppercorns are not true pepper; they are the dried berries of South American shrubs in the cashew family.
Unlike black pepper, they come from a different plant family and taste milder and fruitier.
pink-peppercorns.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dried pink peppercorns, papery and rose-coloured
pink-peppercorns.what: Dried pink berries with a fragrant, mildly peppery taste.

facts: Pink salmon is a Pacific species that spawns in rivers around the North Pacific.
Pink salmon is often called humpy in North America, after the hump that males develop before spawning.
Pink salmon is commonly canned, and it works well in fishcakes and rich spreads.
pink-salmon.visual: a fillet of raw pale pink salmon, skin removed, lying flat on the background
pink-salmon.what: A small Pacific salmon with pale, delicate, soft flesh.

facts: Pink shrimp are small cold-water shrimp, often fished in northern seas.
They are often sold cooked and peeled, ready to use in salads and sandwiches.
Fishing for them is important in several northern countries, including Norway.
pink-shrimp.visual: a small heap of peeled raw pink shrimp, glossy and loosely piled
pink-shrimp.what: Small, sweet, cold-water shrimp, good in salads.

facts: Pinot grigio is the Italian name for the pinot gris grape, whose skin is greyish.
Italian versions are usually crisp and light, while versions from other regions can be richer.
The wine is often drunk young and is also used in cooking, such as in risotto.
pinot-grigio.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale straw-coloured white wine, filled to just below the rim
pinot-grigio.what: A light, dry white wine from the pinot grigio grape.

facts: Pinot Noir is a thin-skinned grape, which makes it a demanding grape to grow.
Its name comes from the French words for pine and black, from the grape's cone-shaped clusters and dark colour.
Burgundy in eastern France is the traditional home of Pinot Noir.
pinot-noir.visual: a clear drinking glass half full of translucent ruby-red wine
pinot-noir.what: A light, silky red wine grape from Burgundy in France.

facts: Pinto means painted in Spanish, a reference to the beans' speckled colour.
Pinto beans are a staple of Mexican cooking and are often refried.
pinto-beans.visual: a small heap of dried, mottled beige pinto beans speckled with pink-brown
pinto-beans.what: Speckled, earthy beans that turn creamy when cooked.

facts: It is widely cultivated and is popular in Italian and East Asian cooking.
Its stems stay firm when cooked, so the whole mushroom can be sauteed.
pioppino-mushroom.visual: a small cluster of pioppino mushrooms with dark brown caps and pale stems, joined at the base
pioppino-mushroom.what: A brown-capped mushroom with firm, nutty flesh.

facts: Piquillo means 'little beak' in Spanish, a nod to the pointed tip of the pepper.
They are traditionally grown in Navarre in northern Spain.
Roasting them over fire gives piquillo peppers a smoky flavour and blistered skin.
piquillo-pepper.visual: a whole roasted red pepper, small and tapered, its skin blistered and charred
piquillo-pepper.what: A small, sweet-smoky red pepper, roasted and often jarred.

facts: Piri piri is taken from the Swahili word pili pili, meaning pepper.
Grilled chicken with piri piri is a popular dish in Portugal and in Portuguese restaurants abroad.
piri-piri-marinade.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of deep red chilli marinade, glossy and thick
piri-piri-marinade.what: A fiery Portuguese chilli marinade for grilled chicken.

facts: The chilli at its heart came from the Americas and reached Africa and Portugal through trade.
Grilled piri piri chicken is a popular dish in Portugal and in South Africa.
piri-piri-paste.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of thick red-orange paste with visible chilli seeds
piri-piri-paste.what: A hot paste of chilli, garlic and lemon from Portugal.

facts: Peru and Chile both claim pisco as a national spirit.
Its name is thought to come from the Peruvian port of Pisco, though its origin is debated.
It is the base for the Pisco Sour, a cocktail made with lime juice, egg white and sugar.
pisco.visual: a clear drinking glass holding a measure of clear spirit, plain and unadorned
pisco.what: A clear grape brandy from Peru and Chile.

facts: Pistachios are native to the Middle East and Central Asia and have been eaten for thousands of years.
pistachio-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of vivid green pistachio oil
pistachio-oil.what: A vivid green oil with a rich, nutty taste.

facts: Pistachios grow on trees in the cashew family and come from the Middle East and Central Asia.
Iran and Turkey use pistachios widely in sweets, ice cream and savoury dishes.
Pistachio paste is a common flavouring in Italian gelato and in pastries.
pistachio-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, bright green nut paste
pistachio-paste.what: A smooth, bright green paste made from ground pistachios.

facts: Sicilian pistachios from the town of Bronte are a protected regional product.
The name pesto comes from the Italian pestare, meaning to pound or crush.
Pistachio trees are native to western Asia and have been grown there for a very long time.
pistachio-pesto.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, bright green pesto
pistachio-pesto.what: A bright green sauce of ground pistachios and oil.

facts: They have been grown in the Middle East for many centuries, and Iran is a major producer.
Their shells split naturally as they ripen, which is why many are sold in the shell.
pistachios.visual: a small heap of shelled bright green pistachio nuts on the background
pistachios.what: Green nuts from a small tree, with a delicate taste.

facts: Pistou is the Provençal cousin of Italian pesto, and it is usually made without pine nuts.
The name comes from the Provençal word for pounding, which describes how the paste is made.
Pistou is famously stirred into vegetable soup in the south of France.
pistou.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of bright green basil paste with a glossy, slightly oily sheen
pistou.what: A fresh basil and garlic paste, made without nuts.

facts: Pitta is a flatbread that puffs up in a hot oven, creating a hollow pocket inside.
Pitta is widely used for falafel and kebab wraps across the Middle East and Greece.
pitta-bread.visual: one whole round pale pitta bread, lightly golden, lying flat on the background
pitta-bread.what: A soft round flatbread with a pocket for stuffing.

facts: Pitta is a round flatbread from the Middle East and eastern Mediterranean.
Pitta puffs up in a very hot oven, which forms the pocket used for filling.
pitta-crisps.visual: a small heap of golden, crisp, irregular flatbread shards, lightly seasoned
pitta-crisps.what: Crunchy seasoned shards of baked flatbread for dipping.

facts: Dates grow on palm trees and have been cultivated in the Middle East for thousands of years.
Medjool dates are a large, soft variety often eaten as a snack or used in baking.
Dates are used across North Africa and the Middle East in tagines, stews and sweet pastries.
pitted-dates.visual: a small heap of glossy, dark brown pitted dates, lightly wrinkled
pitted-dates.what: Soft, sweet dried fruit with the stones removed.

facts: A pizza base is the flat dough that forms the foundation of a pizza, usually made from flour, water, yeast and salt.
Pizza grew from flatbreads baked in Naples, in southern Italy, and the city is still famous for it.
Ready-made bases let cooks skip the dough step, and many are sold chilled or frozen.
pizza-base.visual: one whole raw round pizza base of pale dough, lightly dusted with flour, lying flat on the plain background
pizza-base.what: A ready-rolled round of dough to top at home.

facts: Pizza dough as we know it took shape in Naples, in southern Italy.
The dough is left to rise slowly, and its flavour develops during that time.
pizza-dough-ball.visual: one smooth, round ball of raw pizza dough, slightly sticky and pale cream, resting on a plain white surface
pizza-dough-ball.what: A soft ball of yeasted dough, stretched into a pizza base.

facts: Pizza sauce is usually made from crushed tomatoes, cooked down with herbs such as oregano and basil.
Tomatoes reached Europe from the Americas, and became central to Neapolitan pizza.
Many shop-bought versions add sugar, salt and garlic to a smooth tomato purée.
pizza-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, deep red tomato sauce, smooth and glossy
pizza-sauce.what: A thick, seasoned tomato sauce spread over pizza bases.

facts: Pizzoccheri come from the Valtellina valley in northern Lombardy, Italy.
They are traditionally made with buckwheat flour, which gives a darker colour and a nutty taste.
A classic dish bakes the pasta in layers with potatoes, cabbage, butter and cheese.
pizzoccheri.visual: a small heap of short, flat, dark buckwheat pasta ribbons, slightly crinkled
pizzoccheri.what: Short, flat buckwheat pasta from the Italian Alps.

facts: Plaice is a flatfish, and both of its eyes sit on one side of its head as it matures.
Plaice is common in the North Sea and along the coasts of north-west Europe.
Fried plaice, served in batter with chips, is a classic of British seaside towns.
plaice-fillet.visual: a single raw plaice fillet, skin-on, its brown upper skin marked by reddish spots, lying flat
plaice-fillet.what: A mild, flat white fish, often fried in batter.

facts: Plain flour's lower gluten content makes it less stretchy than bread flour.
Wheat has been ground into flour for thousands of years, using hand-turned stones long before modern mills.
plain-flour.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of soft white flour, lightly heaped
plain-flour.what: A soft white flour for sauces, batters and cakes.

facts: Plantains are native to South-East Asia and were spread through the tropics by traders.
Unlike sweet dessert bananas, plantains are usually cooked, often fried or boiled.
In West Africa and the Caribbean, ripe plantain is fried as a sweet side dish.
plantain.visual: a whole ripe plantain, yellow skin with black speckles, lying on its side
plantain.what: A large, starchy cooking banana, usually eaten cooked.

facts: Ploughman's lunch is a classic English pub meal of bread, cheese and pickle.
Sweet brown pickles of this kind are usually made from chopped vegetables cooked in vinegar and sugar.
ploughman-pickle.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with chunky sweet brown pickle
ploughman-pickle.what: A chunky, sweet brown pickle eaten with cheese and bread.

facts: Chutney has a long history in India, where cooks combined fruit and spices with vinegar or sugar.
Plum chutney is often made in late summer, when plums are at their most plentiful.
plum-chutney.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, filled with dark, glossy plum chutney
plum-chutney.what: A sweet, spiced chutney made from plums and vinegar.

facts: Plum jam is a traditional way of keeping a plum harvest through the winter.
Damsons, a small sharp plum, are a classic choice for jam in Britain.
In Czech cooking, povidla is a thick plum spread used to fill dumplings and pastries.
plum-jam.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, filled with deep purple plum jam
plum-jam.what: A sweet spread of cooked plums and sugar.

facts: Plum sauce is a sweet condiment made from plums, sugar, vinegar and spices.
It is often served with crispy roast duck in Chinese restaurants in Britain and North America.
plum-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of glossy, deep reddish-brown plum sauce
plum-sauce.what: A sweet, tangy fruit sauce often served with crispy duck.

facts: Plum tomatoes are oval, fleshy tomatoes with fewer seeds, suited to cooking.
In North America they are often sold as Roma tomatoes.
Italian cooks have long used plum tomatoes in sauces, and they are widely tinned.
plum-tomato.visual: a whole ripe elongated red plum tomato with glossy skin and a small green stalk end
plum-tomato.what: A firm, oval tomato with dense flesh, best for cooking.

facts: The tomato is native to the Americas and was brought to Europe in the 16th century.
Plum tomatoes are oval and meaty, which makes them popular for sauces.
Canned tomatoes are used in cooking around the world, from Italian sauces to curries.
plum-tomatoes-in-tin.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of whole peeled plum tomatoes in their own juice
plum-tomatoes-in-tin.what: Whole, peeled plum tomatoes preserved in their own juice.

facts: Umeshu is made by steeping unripe green plums in spirit with sugar.
It has a long history in Japan and is often made at home each summer.
The Japanese plum, ume, is often considered closer to the apricot than to the plum.
plum-wine.visual: a plain glass bottle without a label, holding a clear amber liquid
plum-wine.what: A sweet, tart Japanese liqueur made from green plums.

facts: The pluot is a hybrid of plum and apricot, also called a plumcot.
Its flesh is juicy and sweet, and it is often eaten fresh or grilled.
pluot.visual: a whole ripe pluot with a mottled red-purple skin
pluot.what: A sweet cross between a plum and an apricot.

facts: Poaching cooks an egg out of its shell by gently simmering it in water.
Eggs Benedict, a classic brunch dish, is served with poached eggs on muffins.
The white sets at a lower temperature than the yolk, so gentle heat leaves the yolk soft.
poached-egg.visual: a single poached egg on a plain white plate, the white neatly set around a golden runny yolk
poached-egg.what: An egg cooked in simmering water, so the yolk stays soft.

facts: The poblano is native to Mexico and is named after the city of Puebla.
Dried, it becomes the ancho chilli, a sweet, mild chilli used in mole sauces.
It is often roasted, peeled and stuffed to make chiles rellenos.
poblano.visual: one whole fresh dark green chilli pepper, glossy skin, broad tapered tip, lying on its side
poblano.what: A large, mildly hot dark green chilli from Mexico.

facts: Red cabbage has been eaten in Europe for centuries, often braised with apple and vinegar.
The red colour comes from natural pigments that change shade with acidity.
Cabbage belongs to the brassica family, which also includes broccoli and kale.
pointed-red-cabbage.visual: a whole pointed red cabbage, tapered conical head, smooth purple-red leaves
pointed-red-cabbage.what: A tapered red cabbage with a tender, crisp texture.

facts: Poitin is an unaged spirit, and its name comes from the Irish word for little pot.
Distilling it was illegal in Ireland for much of its history, which is why it was made in secret.
Licensed distillers now make poitin legally in Ireland, and it can be bought in shops.
poitin.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with clear, colourless spirit
poitin.what: A strong, clear Irish spirit, traditionally made at home.

facts: Before maize reached Europe, similar dishes were made from grains such as millet and spelt.
In Italy it is often served soft beside stews, or left to set and cut into slices.
polenta-slices.visual: several firm pale yellow polenta slices, cut into neat rectangles, lying flat on the background
polenta-slices.what: Set cornmeal, sliced, then grilled or fried until crisp.

facts: Pollock is a cold-water fish found in the North Atlantic and North Pacific.
It belongs to the cod family and is often used in fish fingers and frozen fish products.
Its flesh breaks into flakes when cooked, which suits pies and fish cakes.
pollock-fillet.visual: one raw pollock fillet, pale grey-white flesh, moist and flaky-looking, lying flat, skin removed
pollock-fillet.what: A mild white fish, good for pies and fish cakes.

facts: Pomace oil is what remains of the olive pulp after the first pressing, which is then processed to extract more oil.
Pomace oil is refined to make it pale and neutral, so it suits high-heat frying.
pomace-olive-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with pale golden oil
pomace-olive-oil.what: Budget olive oil pressed from pulp, good for frying.

facts: Pomegranates have been grown in the Middle East and around the Mediterranean since ancient times.
Their name comes from Latin for seeded apple, which describes the many seeds inside.
pomegranate.visual: a whole ripe pomegranate with deep red leathery skin and a small crown at the top
pomegranate.what: A round fruit packed with sweet-sour, jewel-like seeds.

facts: Pomegranates have been cultivated for thousands of years across the Middle East and Mediterranean.
Pomegranate juice is widely used in Persian cooking, for stews, sauces and drinks.
The name pomegranate comes from Latin, meaning 'seeded apple', reflecting the many seeds inside the fruit.
pomegranate-juice.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with deep ruby-red pomegranate juice
pomegranate-juice.what: Tart, deep red juice pressed from pomegranate arils.

facts: Pomegranate molasses is widely used in Persian, Turkish and Levantine cooking.
It is made by simmering pomegranate juice slowly until it thickens into a syrup.
Its tart, sweet-sour taste is used in dressings, marinades and stews.
pomegranate-molasses.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle, full of thick dark reddish-brown syrup
pomegranate-molasses.what: A thick, tart syrup made by reducing pomegranate juice.

facts: Pomelo is thought to be one of the ancestors of the grapefruit.
It is native to Southeast Asia, where it has been grown for centuries.
Its thick pith is often peeled away, and the segments are eaten or used in salads.
pomelo.visual: a whole large pomelo with thick yellow-green skin and a slightly dimpled surface
pomelo.what: A huge, mild citrus with thick pith and sweet segments.

facts: It is a favourite in South Asian coastal cooking, often fried whole in a spiced coating.
Fresh and frozen pomfret are sold in many Asian food shops in Britain.
pomfret.visual: a whole raw silver pomfret, flat oval body and forked tail, lying on a plain background
pomfret.what: A flat, silvery sea fish with sweet white flesh.

facts: Pont-l'Évêque is named after a town in Normandy, in north-western France, where it has long been made.
It is made from cows' milk, and its rind is washed during ripening.
pont-l-eveque.visual: a whole square cheese with a soft, golden-yellow rind and a pale ivory interior visible at one edge
pont-l-eveque.what: A soft, square cheese from Normandy with a golden rind.

facts: Ponzu is a Japanese sauce that combines soy sauce with citrus juice, often from yuzu.
Yuzu is a small, very aromatic citrus fruit that grows mainly in East Asia.
Ponzu is often served with gyoza and sashimi, and is also used to dress salads.
ponzu.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with clear amber-brown liquid, smooth and still
ponzu.what: A tangy citrus and soy sauce, served as a dip.

facts: Popcorn is made from a special variety of corn with a hard shell around moisture-filled starch.
Indigenous peoples of the Americas popped corn long before European contact.
Its name comes from the popping sound the kernels make when heated.
popcorn.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with plain popped popcorn, light and fluffy, no toppings
popcorn.what: Light, crisp kernels of corn that have puffed when heated.

facts: It is commonly eaten at cinemas and fairs, where it is popped fresh.
popcorn-kernels.visual: a small heap of dried yellow popcorn kernels, hard and glossy
popcorn-kernels.what: Hard dried corn kernels that puff up when heated.

facts: They are usually fried briefly in hot oil or cooked over a flame until they puff up.
Poppadoms are a common accompaniment in Indian restaurants in Britain.
poppadoms.visual: a single round poppadom, thin, golden and crisp with slight bubbles, served plainly on a small plain white plate
poppadoms.what: A thin, crisp, spiced lentil wafer served before a curry.

facts: Popping candy is made from sugar crystals pressurised with carbon dioxide gas.
The gas is trapped in the crystals, and it crackles and fizzes as they dissolve on the tongue.
It is used in sweets, ice creams and desserts for its crackling texture.
popping-candy.visual: a small heap of fine pale pink popping candy crystals, granular and sparkling
popping-candy.what: Sugar crystals that fizz and crackle on the tongue.

facts: The seeds come from the opium poppy plant, which has been cultivated for thousands of years.
They are widely used in Central and Eastern European cooking, in cakes, strudels and bread.
They are often sprinkled on bread rolls, bagels and cakes for a crunchy finish.
poppy-seeds.visual: a small loose heap of tiny blue-grey poppy seeds
poppy-seeds.what: Tiny blue-grey seeds that add a nutty crunch to baking.

facts: Porcini are wild mushrooms found in European forests, especially in Italy.
Drying concentrates the mushrooms' flavour, which is why dried porcini are used in cooking.
porcini-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of golden-brown oil, dark flecks of dried mushroom visible
porcini-oil.what: A golden oil infused with earthy dried porcini mushrooms.

facts: Porcini, also called penny buns, are a wild mushroom prized in Italian cooking.
Drying concentrates their flavour, so a small amount of the powder goes a long way.
Dried porcini are sold across Europe and keep well in a cool, dry cupboard.
porcini-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine brown porcini powder, lightly mounded
porcini-powder.what: Ground dried porcini mushrooms for deep savoury flavour.

facts: Veal is meat from young calves, and it is paler and milder than beef.
pork-and-veal-mince.visual: a small heap of finely minced raw pork and veal, pale pink and loosely packed
pork-and-veal-mince.what: Minced pork and veal, mixed for a soft, tender texture.

facts: Pork belly comes from the underside of the pig, the same cut that is cured to make streaky bacon.
Roasted slowly, the fat melts away and the skin turns crisp, which is known as crackling in Britain.
pork-belly.visual: one raw pork belly slab, pale pink meat layered with white fat under a thick skin
pork-belly.what: A fatty cut of pork with layers of meat and fat.

facts: Pork belly is the cut from the underside of the pig, with alternating layers of meat and fat.
Slow cooking softens the fat and connective tissue, which is why belly suits braising.
pork-belly-strips.visual: several thin raw pork belly strips, pink meat layered with white fat, lying flat on the background
pork-belly-strips.what: Thin, fatty strips of pork from the belly.

facts: Tonkotsu is a Japanese style of ramen broth, made by boiling pork bones for many hours.
The broth turns creamy because collagen from the bones breaks down and dissolves into the water.
It is a classic base for Hakata-style ramen, which is usually served with thin noodles.
pork-bone-broth.visual: a small plain white bowl of pale, creamy, cloudy broth, opaque and smooth
pork-bone-broth.what: A rich, milky stock simmered for hours from pork bones.

facts: Caul fat is used to wrap forcemeats, pâtés and faggots during cooking.
In traditional British and French cooking, it wraps minced pork and offal for slow cooking.
pork-caul-fat.visual: a whole flat sheet of pale, lacy pork caul fat with its delicate net-like pattern visible
pork-caul-fat.what: A thin, lacy sheet of fat from inside a pig's abdomen.

facts: Pig cheeks are a traditional cut in Spanish cooking, where they are often braised in wine.
Cured pig cheek is called guanciale in Italy, and it is used in dishes such as carbonara.
pork-cheek.visual: a single whole raw pork cheek, deep pink with a thin layer of white fat
pork-cheek.what: Tender pig's cheek meat that softens during slow cooking.

facts: Chump chops are cut from the back of the loin, close to the leg.
Pork chops like this one are often brined before cooking to keep them moist.
pork-chump.visual: a single raw pork chump chop, pale pink meat with a thin band of white fat, lying on the background
pork-chump.what: A meaty rump-end chop from the pig, good for roasting.

facts: The collar is cut from the top of the pig's shoulder, close to the neck.
Collar is sold as a joint, steak or chop, and is often slow-roasted or grilled.
pork-collar.visual: one raw pork collar joint, pink flesh with fine streaks of white fat running through it, lying flat
pork-collar.what: A well-marbled cut from the neck of the pig.

facts: Crackling is the crisp skin of a roast pork joint, and it is prized in British Sunday roasts.
Scoring the skin and salting it helps the crackling blister and crisp in the oven.
pork-crackling.visual: one raw piece of pork skin with a thick layer of white fat, scored in parallel lines, lying on the background
pork-crackling.what: Salted pork skin, roasted until it blisters and crunches.

facts: Schnitzel is a thin, breaded cutlet, and the Austrian Wiener schnitzel is traditionally made with veal.
The word cutlet comes from the French côtelette, meaning a small rib.
pork-cutlet.visual: one raw boneless pork loin cutlet, pale pink meat, flat and oval, lying on the background
pork-cutlet.what: A boneless pork loin slice, often flattened and fried.

facts: Escalope is a French word for a thin slice of meat, usually beaten flat before cooking.
Escalopes are often coated in breadcrumbs and fried, a dish found across Europe.
pork-escalope.visual: one thin pork escalope, pale pink and flattened, lying flat on a plain background
pork-escalope.what: A thin slice of pork, beaten flat so it cooks quickly.

facts: Fatback is the layer of fat that lies along the back of a pig, just under the skin.
In the American South it is traditionally used to season beans, greens and other slow-cooked dishes.
Italian lardo is cured pork back fat, and its name comes from the Latin word for lard.
pork-fat-back.visual: a single raw rectangular block of firm white pork back fat, one edge neatly trimmed, lying on the plain background
pork-fat-back.what: Firm, unsmoked fat cut from the back of a pig.

facts: Hocks come from the lower leg, close to the ankle joint, and are rich in connective tissue.
Cured hocks are often smoked, and in the United States they flavour beans and greens.
In Germany, Eisbein is boiled pork knuckle, often served with sauerkraut.
pork-hock.visual: a single raw pork hock with pale pink skin and a flat cut end at the top
pork-hock.what: The lower leg of a pig, cooked slowly until tender.

facts: The leg is a large cut from the hind leg of the pig, often sold for roasting.
pork-leg.visual: a whole raw pork leg joint, skin scored in a diamond pattern, pale pink meat
pork-leg.what: A big roasting joint with crisp, crackly skin.

facts: A rustic pâté keeps a coarse texture because the meat is minced rather than blended smooth.
Herbs such as thyme and parsley are common in pork liver pâté.
pork-liver-pate.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of coarse pale-brown pâté, flecked with herbs and smooth on top
pork-liver-pate.what: A coarse, herby spread made from pork liver and fat.

facts: The loin runs along the pig's back, from the ribs to the hip.
In Britain the joint is often roasted with the rind scored, so it crisps into crackling.
Roast pork with crackling is a traditional British Sunday lunch.
pork-loin.visual: a whole boneless pork loin joint, pale pink meat, a thick fat cap and scored rind on top, lying on its side
pork-loin.what: A lean, tender cut from the back of the pig.

facts: The loin is the long muscle along the back of the pig, and chops are cut from it.
Apple is a traditional partner for pork in many European kitchens, from Normandy to Germany.
pork-loin-chop.visual: one raw pork loin chop, pale pink meat with a band of white fat along one edge, lying flat
pork-loin-chop.what: A lean, tender chop from the back of the pig.

facts: Meatballs are found in many cuisines, from Swedish köttbullar to Italian polpette.
Meatballs are often simmered in tomato sauce or broth.
pork-meatballs.visual: a small heap of raw, evenly shaped pork meatballs, pale pink and smooth
pork-meatballs.what: Small rounds of herbed minced pork, ready to simmer or fry.

facts: Pork medallions are cut across the tenderloin, a long lean muscle along the back.
pork-medallions.visual: three raw pork medallions, neat pale pink rounds, lying flat on the background
pork-medallions.what: Small round cuts of lean pork tenderloin, quick to cook.

facts: Pork mince is widely used in meatballs, burgers and sausage fillings around the world.
Minced pork is a common filling for Chinese dumplings and steamed buns.
pork-mince.visual: a small heap of raw pork mince, pale pink and flecked with white fat
pork-mince.what: Finely minced pork, used for meatballs and dumplings.

facts: Pigs were domesticated in the Near East thousands of years ago.
pork-neck-fillet.visual: one raw boneless pork neck fillet, pale pink meat with a band of fat, lying directly on the background
pork-neck-fillet.what: A boneless, fatty pork cut from the neck, good for grilling.

facts: Pork pies are a classic British food, traditionally eaten cold.
Its hot-water crust is made from hot water and fat, which lets it be shaped while warm.
pork-pie.visual: one whole golden-brown pork pie with straight sides, served on a plain white plate
pork-pie.what: A small raised pie of pork in a hot-water pastry case.

facts: Crisp pork skin is known as chicharrón in Spain and Latin America.
In the American South, fried pork rinds are a traditional snack sold in many shops.
Pork skin is also used to make gelatine and to thicken stocks.
pork-rind.visual: a whole raw pork rind, pale pinkish-white skin, small bristle marks, lying flat
pork-rind.what: Pig skin salted and roasted until light and crisp.

facts: Toad in the hole is a classic British dish of sausages baked in Yorkshire pudding batter.
pork-sausage.visual: a single raw pork sausage link, pale pink and glossy, lying in a gentle curve
pork-sausage.what: Minced pork seasoned with herbs, formed into a link.

facts: Pork shoulder is a hardworking muscle that becomes tender with long, slow cooking.
It is a rich, fatty cut used in roasts, stews and sausages.
pork-shoulder.visual: one whole raw pork shoulder joint, pink meat marbled in white fat
pork-shoulder.what: A marbled joint from the upper front leg of a pig.

facts: Spare ribs are cut from the belly side of the pig, below the loin.
Slow cooking breaks down connective tissue, so the meat becomes tender and easy to pull apart.
pork-spare-ribs.visual: a rack of raw pork spare ribs, pink meat and pale bones, lying flat on a plain background
pork-spare-ribs.what: Ribs from the belly, sticky and rich when slow-cooked.

facts: It is often roasted whole or cut into medallions and seared quickly in a hot pan.
pork-tenderloin.visual: a whole raw pork tenderloin, long and narrow, pale pink, lying straight on the background
pork-tenderloin.what: A lean, tender cut from along the backbone of the pig.

facts: A tomahawk chop is cut from the rib section, keeping a long section of rib bone attached.
The cut is named for its resemblance to a tomahawk, the axe with a long handle.
It is usually grilled or roasted, and the bone is often left exposed for presentation.
pork-tomahawk.visual: a single raw pork tomahawk chop with a long, clean bone handle and pale pink meat
pork-tomahawk.what: A thick pork chop cut long on the bone, like a steak.

facts: Port Salut takes its name from the Port-du-Salut abbey in Entrammes, in north-western France.
The cheese was first made by Trappist monks, and is now produced commercially.
port-salut.visual: a wedge of pale yellow semi-soft cheese, cut face showing, thin orange-brown rind, lying flat
port-salut.what: A mild, buttery French cheese with a thin orange rind.

facts: Porter is a dark beer that originated in London, where it was popular with street and river workers.
Porter is used in some cooking, such as stews and chocolate puddings.
porter.visual: a clear drinking glass of very dark brown porter with a thin creamy tan head
porter.what: A dark, roasty beer with chocolate and coffee notes.

facts: A porterhouse is cut from the rear of the short loin, where the strip and fillet meet either side of the bone.
Steaks of this kind are usually grilled or seared hot, then rested before they are sliced.
porterhouse-steak.visual: one thick raw porterhouse steak with a T-shaped bone and a band of fat, deep red beef
porterhouse-steak.what: A thick beef steak with a T-shaped bone and a fillet side.

facts: Portobello is the mature form of the cremini mushroom, itself a brown variety of the button mushroom.
Portobello caps can be grilled, roasted or stuffed, and are often used whole.
portobello-mushroom.visual: one whole large brown portobello mushroom, flat open cap with dark gills facing up
portobello-mushroom.what: A large, meaty brown mushroom with a wide, flat cap.

facts: Pot barley is barley with only the outer husk removed, so some bran remains.
It is cooked slowly in soups and stews, and needs a long simmer to soften.
Barley has been grown for thousands of years in the Near East and Europe.
pot-barley.visual: a small heap of pale tan pot barley grains, whole and unpolished
