facts: Rocamadour is named after a village in south-west France and is made from goat's milk.
If left to age, it becomes firmer and more pungent as it matures.
rocamadour.visual: one small whole round goat's cheese, pale ivory with a soft white bloomy rind, lying on the background
rocamadour.what: A small, creamy goat's cheese from south-west France.

facts: The Rocha pear is a Portuguese variety, grown mainly in the Oeste region of western Portugal.
Its green skin often turns yellow as the pear ripens, a sign that it is ready to eat.
It is traditionally eaten fresh and is enjoyed as a simple dessert fruit in Portugal.
rocha-pear.visual: a whole ripe Rocha pear, green-skinned and tinged yellow, lying on its side
rocha-pear.what: A soft, sweet Portuguese pear eaten at its ripe peak.

facts: Rock salt is mined from underground salt deposits left behind by ancient evaporated seas.
A salt crust, a cooking method, seals in moisture when meat or fish is baked inside a shell of salt.
rock-salt.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with large, irregular off-white salt crystals
rock-salt.what: Chunky salt crystals, used in grinders and for salt crusts.

facts: Rock samphire grows on sea cliffs and rocky coasts around Britain and western Europe.
Its name is thought to come from the French herbe de Saint-Pierre, meaning herb of Saint Peter.
Shakespeare's King Lear describes a man gathering samphire on a cliff edge, showing how it was once picked there.
rock-samphire.visual: a small bunch of fresh rock samphire, slender fleshy green stems and narrow pointed leaves, lying on a plain background
rock-samphire.what: A salty, aromatic plant that grows on sea cliffs.

facts: Rock sugar is made by slowly crystallising sugar syrup, which forms large, clear lumps.
It is mildly sweet and is used in Chinese cooking to add gloss and sweetness to braised meats.
In China it is also used in sweet soups and desserts.
rock-sugar.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of large clear golden sugar crystals
rock-sugar.what: Large clear sugar crystals used in Chinese braises.

facts: Rocket is an annual plant from the cabbage family, grown across the Mediterranean.
Its peppery taste comes from natural mustard-like compounds in the leaves.
Roman writers mention rocket as a salad leaf.
rocket.visual: a small bunch of fresh, deep green rocket leaves, stems tied together
rocket.what: A peppery salad leaf, also called arugula in America.

facts: Pesto takes its name from the Italian pestare, meaning to pound or crush, as it is traditionally made in a mortar.
Rocket, also called arugula, is a peppery salad leaf native to the Mediterranean.
rocket-pesto.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, dark green rocket pesto with a glossy surface
rocket-pesto.what: A thick, peppery green sauce made with rocket leaves.

facts: Rockfish is a name used for many species of fish that live around rocky reefs.
Many rockfish species grow slowly and live for many decades.
rockfish.visual: a whole raw rockfish with speckled reddish skin and spiny fins, lying on its side
rockfish.what: A mild white fish, good in tacos and soups.

facts: Rocoto is a chilli species domesticated in the Andes and grown there for centuries.
Rocoto relleno, a stuffed pepper dish from Arequipa in Peru, is made with this chilli.
rocoto.visual: one whole round red rocoto chilli, thick glossy skin, dark seeds visible at the stalk end, lying on its side
rocoto.what: A thick-walled, fiery chilli pepper from the Andes.

facts: Roe deer are small native deer of Europe and parts of Asia.
roe-deer-fillet.visual: one raw roe deer fillet, dark red meat that is fine-grained, lying on the background
roe-deer-fillet.what: Fine-grained, tender venison from the small roe deer.

facts: Rogan josh is a lamb curry associated with Kashmir and the Mughal kitchens.
Kashmiri chillies are prized for their deep red colour more than their heat.
rogan-josh-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of deep red-orange spice paste
rogan-josh-paste.what: A paste of chilli and spices used in lamb curries.

facts: Rolling and tying a joint helps it cook evenly and keeps it in a neat shape for carving.
A beef joint is the centrepiece of the traditional British Sunday roast.
Topside, silverside and top rump are common cuts used for rolled roasts.
rolled-beef-joint.visual: one whole raw rolled beef joint tied with string, dark red meat and white fat visible, on the background
rolled-beef-joint.what: A boneless beef roast, rolled and tied for even cooking.

facts: Oat grains are steamed, then pressed flat between rollers, which makes them cook faster.
Porridge made from oats is traditional in Scotland and across northern Europe.
Oats are a cereal grass suited to cool climates, and Canada and Russia are among the biggest growers.
rolled-oats.visual: a small heap of pale golden rolled oat flakes, flat and oval, loose and dry
rolled-oats.what: Oats flattened into flakes, used for porridge and baking.

facts: Rollmops are a traditional dish across Northern Europe, especially in Germany and Scandinavia.
The herring is cured in a vinegar brine, which keeps it firm and tangy.
In Germany, rollmops are often served on dark rye bread or with potatoes.
rollmop-herring.visual: one whole rolled pickled herring fillet, silvery skin with a pale centre, lying in a gentle curve
rollmop-herring.what: A pickled herring fillet rolled around onion and gherkin.

facts: Washed-rind cheeses are brushed or bathed in liquid during ripening, which gives them a strong aroma.
Many British cheeses take their names from the places they come from, such as Cheddar in Somerset.
rollright.visual: a whole round of soft cheese with a pale orange washed rind, one wedge cut out to show the creamy paste
rollright.what: A savoury washed-rind cheese from Oxfordshire.

facts: Romanesco is a type of Brassica from Italy, and is related to broccoli and cauliflower.
Its florets form a self-similar spiral pattern, where each small bud repeats the shape of the whole head.
romanesco.visual: one whole romanesco head, lime-green with pointed spiralling florets, on a plain background
romanesco.what: A lime-green cousin of cauliflower with a spiral pattern.

facts: Peppers are native to the Americas, and were spread around the world by traders.
Romano peppers belong to Capsicum annuum, the same species as most sweet peppers.
Long peppers like this are often roasted whole or sliced into strips for salads and stews.
romano-pepper.visual: one whole long, tapering bright green pepper with glossy skin, on a plain background
romano-pepper.what: A long, sweet, mild pepper, often roasted or grilled.

facts: Romesco comes from Catalonia in north-east Spain, where it is served over grilled vegetables.
It is often served alongside grilled calçots, a long, young onion from Catalonia.
romesco-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, brick-red sauce, smooth and flecked brown
romesco-sauce.what: A thick Catalan sauce of roasted peppers and almonds.

facts: Rooibos means red bush in Afrikaans and is grown in the Cederberg mountains of South Africa.
The needle-like leaves are bruised and oxidised, which turns them a deep red-brown.
It is often drunk without milk and is popular across South Africa and beyond.
rooibos-tea.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with deep reddish-brown tea
rooibos-tea.what: A red herbal tea brewed from a South African shrub.

facts: Potatoes were first domesticated in the Andes of South America.
Potatoes reached Europe in the sixteenth century, brought from the Americas by Spanish explorers.
Red-skinned varieties get their colour from pigments in the skin.
rooster-potato.visual: a small heap of raw red-skinned potatoes with smooth, pale-yellow flesh
rooster-potato.what: A red-skinned potato that suits chips and roasting.

facts: Root beer was traditionally made in North America, flavoured with sassafras root.
Modern root beer is usually flavoured with vanilla, wintergreen or other plant extracts instead.
It is often served as a root beer float, with a scoop of ice cream added to the drink.
root-beer.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with dark brown fizzy root beer
root-beer.what: A sweet, fizzy soft drink flavoured with roots and bark.

facts: Roquefort is named after a village in southern France, where it has been made for centuries.
It is aged in natural limestone caves near the village, where the blue mould develops.
roquefort.visual: a block of pale cream blue cheese with green-blue veins, one wedge cut away to show the marbling, lying on the background
roquefort.what: A sharp, salty blue cheese made from sheep's milk.

facts: Harissa is a chilli paste from Tunisia, now widely used across North African cooking.
Rose petals have long been used in Middle Eastern and North African cooking for their perfume.
Traditional harissa is often blended with garlic, cumin, coriander and olive oil.
rose-harissa.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of deep red, thick harissa paste
rose-harissa.what: Chilli paste from North Africa, with a floral rose note.

facts: Rose petal jam has been made in the Middle East and South Asia for centuries.
Gulkand is the Persian and Indian name for a preserve of rose petals and sugar.
It is often made from fragrant Damask roses, which are prized for their scent.
rose-petal-jam.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with deep pink rose petal jam
rose-petal-jam.what: A sweet, fragrant preserve made from crushed rose petals.

facts: Rose syrup has a long history in Persian and Middle Eastern cooking, where it flavours sweets and drinks.
It is made by simmering rose petals with sugar and water, often with a little lemon juice.
In India, rose syrup is mixed with milk or water as a refreshing summer drink.
rose-syrup.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of bright pink syrup, cap on
rose-syrup.what: A perfumed pink syrup flavoured with rose petals.

facts: Rose water has long been made in Persia and the wider Middle East, where it flavours sweets and drinks.
It is used in Turkish delight and many Middle Eastern and South Asian sweets.
rose-water.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale, faintly pink liquid with a plain stopper
rose-water.what: A fragrant liquid distilled from rose petals and water.

facts: Rosé is the French word for pink, and the wine takes its name from its colour.
Provence in southern France is especially known for pale, dry rosé wines.
rose-wine.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale pink wine, filled about two-thirds full
rose-wine.what: A pale pink wine, usually made from red grapes.

facts: Rosehips are the fleshy fruit that forms after a rose flower has been pollinated.
Rosehip syrup was widely made in Britain during the Second World War as a source of fruit.
The seeds inside the fruit have fine hairs, so they are removed before the pulp is cooked.
rosehip.visual: a small heap of glossy red rosehips, oval and shiny, with dry brown stalks
rosehip.what: Tangy red fruit from wild roses, used for syrups and jam.

facts: Rosemary is a woody evergreen herb native to the Mediterranean region.
Infusing oil with herbs is a long-standing kitchen method for carrying flavour into a dish.
rosemary-infused-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with pale golden oil
rosemary-infused-oil.what: Oil steeped with rosemary for a piney, herbal flavour.

facts: Rosemary is a Mediterranean herb with needle-like leaves and a piney flavour.
Flaky salt forms in thin crystals and is often used as a finishing salt.
rosemary-salt.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of flaky pale salt, flecks of dark green rosemary visible
rosemary-salt.what: Flaky salt crushed with rosemary, for lamb and potatoes.

facts: Roti canai is widely linked to Indian paratha and is popular in Malaysian mamak restaurants.
The dough is stretched and tossed in the air, then folded into layers.
roti-canai.visual: a golden, flaky roti canai folded in layers on a small plain white plate
roti-canai.what: A flaky Malaysian flatbread, often served with curry.

facts: Its twisted shape traps sauce and small pieces of vegetables in its grooves.
Rotini is typically made from durum wheat semolina and water, then dried.
rotini.visual: a small heap of dried, tightly twisted pasta spirals in a pale golden colour
rotini.what: Short, tightly twisted pasta spirals that hold sauce well.

facts: The word rotisserie comes from the French rôtir, meaning to roast.
rotisserie-chicken.visual: a whole roasted chicken, golden-brown crisp skin, lying breast-side up
rotisserie-chicken.what: A whole chicken, roasted slowly on a rotating spit.

facts: Rouille is a Provençal sauce, traditionally spread on toasted bread and floated in bouillabaisse.
Its name is French for rust, a reference to its deep orange-red colour.
It is made by whisking saffron, chilli and garlic into a mayonnaise-style base.
rouille.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick orange-red sauce, smooth and glossy
rouille.what: A saffron and chilli garlic sauce for fish soup.

facts: Round courgettes are a variety of summer squash, picked young and eaten skin and all.
Courgette is the British name for the young squash, and it is called zucchini in the United States.
round-courgette.visual: a whole round pale green courgette, lying on its side on a plain background
round-courgette.what: A small round courgette, good for stuffing and baking.

facts: Rowan berries grow on the rowan tree, also called mountain ash, across Europe and Asia.
Rowan jelly is traditionally served with game such as venison in Britain.
The berries contain natural pectin, which helps the jelly set.
rowan-jelly.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, filled with glossy orange-red jelly
rowan-jelly.what: A tart, bitter-sweet jelly made from rowan berries.

facts: It is made from icing sugar mixed with egg white or dried egg white powder, and it dries hard.
Royal icing is traditionally used to decorate Christmas cakes and to pipe fine details on biscuits.
royal-icing.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, bright white royal icing
royal-icing.what: Hard-setting white icing for piping and decorating cakes.

facts: Its natural pink colour and tart flavour come from the cocoa beans, rather than from added berries.
Chocolate is made from the beans of the cocoa tree, which grows in tropical regions.
Ruby chocolate is often used in desserts, drinks and sweets for its pink colour.
ruby-chocolate.visual: a glossy rose-pink block of chocolate with one square snapped off, lying flat
ruby-chocolate.what: A pink chocolate with a tart, berry-like flavour.

facts: Brandy is added during fermentation, which stops the process and leaves some sugar.
Ruby is the youngest style of port, blended for bright fruit and deep colour.
ruby-port.visual: a clear drinking glass of deep ruby-red port wine, about half full
ruby-port.what: A sweet, fruity red fortified wine from Portugal's Douro.

facts: Rue is a Mediterranean plant that was once widely grown in European herb gardens.
Its flavour is strongly bitter, so cooks use only a few leaves at a time.
rue.visual: a small bunch of rue stems with blue-green, finely divided leaves, lying on a plain background
rue.what: A bitter, pungent herb with small blue-green leaves.

facts: Rum is distilled from sugarcane products such as molasses or sugarcane juice.
Rum has long been produced in the Caribbean, and it is central to many Caribbean drinks.
Rum flavourings are popular in British fruitcake and icing recipes.
rum-flavouring.visual: a small plain clear glass bottle without a label, filled with pale amber liquid
rum-flavouring.what: Concentrated essence that adds rum flavour to baking.

facts: Rump steak is cut from the cow's hindquarter, close to the hip.
rump-steak.visual: one raw rump steak, deep red beef, a thin strip of fat along one edge, lying flat on the background
rump-steak.what: A lean, full-flavoured beef steak from the cow's rear.

facts: The pods are picked young while still tender, because older pods grow tough and stringy.
In Britain they are often sliced thinly on the diagonal before being boiled or steamed.
runner-beans.visual: a small bundle of fresh green runner beans, long flat pods with a slight curve, lying loose on the background
runner-beans.what: A long green pod bean that is sliced and boiled.

facts: Honey is made by bees that collect flower nectar and store it in the hive to thicken.
Ancient Egyptians used honey as a sweetener and in offerings to the gods.
runny-honey.visual: a plain glass jar filled with clear golden runny honey, without a label
runny-honey.what: Clear, pourable honey, made by bees from flower nectar.

facts: The russet Burbank variety was developed in the United States in the 1870s.
Russets are grown mainly in the United States and are known for their netted, brown skin.
Their dry, fluffy flesh suits baking, mashing and frying, rather than waxy salads.
russet-potato.visual: one whole raw russet potato, oval and brown with a rough, netted skin, lying on its side
russet-potato.what: A fluffy, starchy potato made for baking and frying.

facts: French tarragon is prized in cooking, while Russian tarragon is a hardier relative.
Its flavour is generally considered weaker than French tarragon's.
russian-tarragon.visual: a small bunch of narrow, bright green Russian tarragon leaves on slender stems
russian-tarragon.what: A hardy, milder kind of tarragon with grassy leaves.

facts: Rye bread is made with rye flour, which gives a dense, dark loaf with a slightly sour flavour.
It is especially common in Northern and Eastern Europe, from Germany and Scandinavia to Russia.
Rye bread is often served with pickled herring, smoked fish and cured meats.
rye-bread.visual: a slice of dark, dense rye bread lying flat on a plain white background, crumb visible
rye-bread.what: A dense, earthy bread made with rye flour.

facts: Rye crispbread is a traditional bread in Scandinavia, where it has been baked for centuries.
Its long shelf life made it a useful food in northern winters.
Rye tolerates cold and poor soils better than wheat does.
rye-crispbread.visual: two round dark rye crispbreads, speckled brown with a dotted surface, lying flat on a plain white plate
rye-crispbread.what: A thin, crisp rye bread with a faintly sour taste.

facts: Rye is a cereal grass that grows well in cold, poor soils where wheat struggles.
Rye bread is traditional across northern and eastern Europe, especially in Germany, Scandinavia and Russia.
rye-flour.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dark grey-brown rye flour, finely milled
rye-flour.what: A dark, earthy flour milled from rye grain.

facts: Rye bread has been baked in northern and eastern Europe for centuries, where rye grows better than wheat in cold soils.
Rye sourdough is often served with smoked fish, such as smoked salmon.
rye-sourdough.visual: a thick slice of dark, dense rye bread lying flat, crumb visible
rye-sourdough.what: A dark, dense, sour loaf made with rye flour and a starter.

facts: Rye whiskey was once the traditional spirit of Pennsylvania and Maryland, and was widely made across the eastern United States.
In the United States, rye whiskey must be made from a mash that is at least half rye grain.
The rye grain gives a spicier, drier taste than the sweeter corn-based bourbon.
rye-whiskey.visual: a clear drinking glass holding a small measure of deep amber rye whiskey
rye-whiskey.what: A spicy American whiskey made mostly from rye grain.

facts: The saddle is the back section of the lamb, covering both loins either side of the spine.
saddle-of-lamb.visual: one raw saddle of lamb, two long pale pink loins joined along a bone, thin fat cap on top
saddle-of-lamb.what: A whole double loin of lamb, joined along the backbone.

facts: Safflower is a thistle-like plant, grown for its oily seeds and for its petals.
Safflower petals have long been used to make red and yellow dyes for cloth and food.
safflower-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden oil, with the cap on
safflower-oil.what: A mild oil pressed from the seeds of a thistle-like plant.

facts: Saffron milk caps grow in partnership with the roots of pine trees.
In Catalonia and parts of Spain they are prized, and are often grilled simply with garlic and olive oil.
saffron-milk-cap.visual: a whole orange mushroom with a funnel-shaped cap, rings of darker colour and a pale stem
saffron-milk-cap.what: A bright orange wild mushroom from Mediterranean woods.

facts: Saffron comes from the dried stigmas of the crocus flower, Crocus sativus.
It takes a great many crocus flowers to produce a small quantity of saffron.
Saffron has coloured and flavoured food across Europe, Asia and North Africa for centuries.
saffron-pasta.visual: a small loose heap of fresh golden pasta ribbons, smooth and pale yellow
saffron-pasta.what: Fresh golden pasta, coloured and scented with saffron.

facts: Saffron is harvested from the stigmas of the purple crocus flower, Crocus sativus.
Saffron is picked by hand, which is why it is expensive, and it has been used in cooking since ancient times.
Saffron is used in dishes such as paella, Persian rice and Italian risotto alla milanese.
saffron-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, deep orange saffron powder
saffron-powder.what: Ground saffron that colours and flavours rice and milk.

facts: Saffron comes from Crocus sativus, and each flower yields only three threads, which are picked by hand.
Saffron has been used for thousands of years in Persia, Greece and India, to flavour food and colour cloth.
Saffron is harvested by hand, which makes it expensive by weight compared with most spices.
saffron-threads.visual: a small heap of fine crimson saffron threads, each a slender orange-red strand
saffron-threads.what: Dried crimson threads from a crocus flower.

facts: Saganaki is named after the small, two-handled frying pan the cheese is cooked in.
saganaki-cheese.visual: a thick slab of firm pale yellow cheese with one cut edge, lying flat on a plain background
saganaki-cheese.what: A firm Greek cheese, fried until golden and crisp.

facts: Sage and onion stuffing is a traditional British accompaniment to roast chicken, turkey and goose.
Stuffing was once cooked inside the bird, and it is now often baked separately in a dish.
sage-and-onion-stuffing.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of golden-brown breadcrumb stuffing, speckled green with herbs
sage-and-onion-stuffing.what: A herby breadcrumb stuffing eaten with roast poultry.

facts: Sage and onion stuffing is a traditional British accompaniment to roast chicken and turkey.
Sage has been used as a herb in European cooking since ancient times.
sage-and-onion-stuffing-balls.visual: several round, golden-brown baked stuffing balls with a crisp surface, arranged on a plain white plate
sage-and-onion-stuffing-balls.what: Baked sage and onion stuffing, rolled into little rounds.

facts: Sage was added to the curd, giving the cheese its green marbling and herby flavour.
sage-derby.visual: a block of pale golden cheese with bright green veining, one wedge cut away
sage-derby.what: A mellow English cheese marbled through with sage.

facts: Sai ua is a speciality of northern Thailand, especially around Chiang Mai.
Lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaf and chilli are typical ingredients.
It is often grilled and eaten with sticky rice and fresh vegetables.
sai-ua.visual: a whole raw sausage link, pale pink pork flecked with green herbs, lying in a gentle curve
sai-ua.what: A spiced northern Thai pork sausage, often grilled.

facts: Saint-Nectaire is named after a village in the Auvergne region of central France.
saint-nectaire.visual: one cut wedge of pale golden cheese with a thin brownish rind, lying flat
saint-nectaire.what: A semi-hard French cheese, nutty and earthy in flavour.

facts: Sainte-Maure de Touraine is named after a town in the Loire Valley, in central France.
Traditionally the cheese is moulded in a log shape and left to develop a bloomy white rind.
sainte-maure-de-touraine.visual: a whole log-shaped goat's cheese with a thin straw through its centre, white rind
sainte-maure-de-touraine.what: A log-shaped goat's cheese with a straw through its centre.

facts: Sake is brewed from rice, which is fermented with a mould called koji.
Sake has been made in Japan for many centuries and is used in Shinto ceremonies.
Cooking sake often contains added salt, so it is seasoned for cooking rather than drinking.
sake.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden liquid
sake.what: A Japanese rice wine used for cooking and drinking.

facts: Salad burnet is a perennial herb native to Europe and western Asia.
salad-burnet.visual: a small bunch of fresh green salad burnet, serrated oval leaves on slender stems
salad-burnet.what: A small herb whose leaves taste faintly of cucumber.

facts: Its recipe is based on an egg yolk emulsion, with added sugar, mustard and vinegar.
salad-cream.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, pale yellow, creamy dressing
salad-cream.what: A tangy, pourable British dressing similar to mayonnaise.

facts: Waxy potatoes contain less starch than floury types, so they keep their shape after boiling.
Salad potatoes are often boiled whole and dressed while still warm, a common way to serve them in Britain.
Early in the season, potatoes are harvested young, when their skins are thin and easily rubbed off.
salad-potato.visual: a whole raw small smooth pale yellow potato, lying on its side
salad-potato.what: A small, waxy potato that holds its shape when boiled.

facts: Salak is a palm native to Indonesia, grown in forests and home gardens.
Its common name, snake fruit, refers to the scaly skin, which looks like snake skin.
Inside, the pale flesh splits into lobes around one or more seeds.
salak.visual: a whole brown salak fruit with overlapping triangular scales on its skin, on a plain background
salak.what: A scaly brown fruit with crisp, tangy, apple-like flesh.

facts: Salame Milano is named after Milan, the city in northern Italy where it has long been made.
It is made from finely ground pork, which gives it a smooth, mild texture.
salami-milano.visual: several thin round slices of salami, deep pink with small flecks of white fat, fanned out on a plain background
salami-milano.what: A fine, mild pork sausage from northern Italy.

facts: Salchichón is a cured sausage from Spain, often made from pork and sold ready to slice.
It belongs to the wider Spanish tradition of cured meats, known as embutidos.
Many Spanish sausages are dry-cured, which lets them keep for a long time without cooking.
salchichon.visual: one thin round slice of cured sausage, pale pinkish-brown, black peppercorns visible in the meat, lying flat
salchichon.what: Mild Spanish dry sausage with black peppercorns.

facts: Salmon belly is a fatty cut, often served grilled, roasted or cured.
Salmon is a key ingredient in many Scandinavian dishes, including gravlax.
salmon-belly.visual: a raw boneless salmon belly portion, pale pink flesh showing white streaks of fat, lying flat on the background
salmon-belly.what: The rich, fatty underside cut from a salmon.

facts: The collar is the area behind a salmon's head, where the meat is fatty and rich.
Salmon collar is often grilled or roasted with salt to crisp the skin.
Salmon is a fish that migrates between freshwater rivers and the sea.
salmon-collar.visual: one raw salmon collar cut, thick pink flesh with pale fat lines and skin on, lying flat
salmon-collar.what: A thick, fatty cut from behind a salmon's head.

facts: Ikura is the Japanese name for salmon roe, and it is often served on sushi.
Salmon roe is cured in salt or soy-based brine, which firms the eggs and gives them their pop.
Salmon roe comes from several salmon species, and Pacific salmon are the usual source.
salmon-roe.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with glossy bright orange salmon roe
salmon-roe.what: Bright orange salted salmon eggs with a briny pop.

facts: Salmon skin is often grilled or fried until crisp, and is used in some Japanese sushi rolls.
Salmon are anadromous fish, hatching in freshwater rivers and migrating to the sea.
The word salmon comes from Latin salmo, linked to a root meaning to leap.
salmon-skin.visual: a small pile of crisp golden salmon skin pieces, curled and glossy, served on a plain white plate
salmon-skin.what: Crisp, salty fried skin from salmon, used in sushi rolls.

facts: Salmon are born in freshwater rivers, migrate to the sea, and return to spawn.
The pink colour comes from pigments in the crustaceans and krill that salmon eat.
Salmon steaks are cut across the fish, so each piece includes a section of the backbone.
salmon-steak.visual: a single raw salmon steak, a thick round slice with pink flesh and a central bone visible
salmon-steak.what: A thick, bone-in slice cut across a whole salmon.

facts: Salmon trimmings are the spare pieces left after fillets are cut from a whole fish.
Rillettes are a French preserve of shredded meat or fish cooked slowly in fat.
Salmon is native to the North Atlantic and North Pacific, where it hatches in rivers.
salmon-trim.visual: a small heap of raw, irregular pink salmon trimmings, pale orange-pink at the edges
salmon-trim.what: Spare pink pieces of fresh salmon, good for minced dishes.

facts: Salmoriglio is a traditional sauce from Sicily, often served on grilled meat or fish.
Its name is thought to come from salamoia, an old Italian word for brine.
It is made by whisking lemon juice and olive oil with herbs, and is served at room temperature.
salmoriglio.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of glossy, pale yellow-green sauce, thin and speckled green
salmoriglio.what: A Sicilian sauce of lemon, oregano and olive oil.

facts: Onions were brought to the Americas by European colonists, where they became part of local dishes.
Peruvian cooks often soak the onion in lime juice, which softens its sharp bite.
Peruvian cooking blends Andean, Spanish, African and Asian influences over centuries.
salsa-criolla.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of finely chopped pale onion, glossy and moist
salsa-criolla.what: A zesty Peruvian relish of thinly sliced onion and lime.

facts: Salsa roja means red sauce in Spanish, and it is widely served across Mexico.
It is often made with dried chillies such as guajillo, or with fresh chillies.
salsa-roja.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, deep red cooked salsa
salsa-roja.what: A cooked red sauce of tomatoes and chillies from Mexico.

facts: Salsa verde means green sauce in Italian, and many regions of Italy have their own version.
Salsa verde was traditionally served with boiled meats, and it still accompanies them in many Italian kitchens.
Capers are the pickled flower buds of a Mediterranean shrub, a common ingredient in these sauces.
salsa-verde.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with finely chopped bright green herb sauce
salsa-verde.what: A tangy green sauce of parsley, capers and anchovy.

facts: Tomatillos are a small green fruit in a papery husk, native to Mexico and Central America.
Salsa verde means green sauce in Spanish, and Mexican cooks have made versions of it for centuries.
salsa-verde-mexicana.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth bright green sauce, flecks of herb and chilli visible
salsa-verde-mexicana.what: A tangy green sauce of tomatillos, chilli and coriander.

facts: Salsify is also called oyster plant, a name that refers to its flavour when cooked.
It is native to the Mediterranean and was grown as a vegetable in Europe for centuries.
Black salsify is a related species with dark skin, and it is sometimes called scorzonera.
salsify.visual: one long, thin, pale brown salsify root tapering to a point, lying straight on a plain background
salsify.what: A long, pale root vegetable with a mild oyster-like taste.

facts: Salt has been mined and traded for thousands of years, and it was once a valuable commodity.
Sea salt is made by evaporating seawater, while rock salt is mined from underground deposits.
Salt is one of the oldest seasonings and is used in almost every cuisine in the world.
salt.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine white salt crystals, level at the top
salt.what: A white mineral seasoning that brings out flavour in food.

facts: The flavour is made by dusting crisps with a powder of salt and dried malt vinegar.
The sharp taste comes from acetic acid in the vinegar powder, which gives a stinging tang.
salt-and-vinegar-crisps.visual: a small heap of thin golden crisps, pale salt crystals sprinkled over them
salt-and-vinegar-crisps.what: Potato crisps dusted with salt and a sharp vinegar powder.

facts: Salt beef is a traditional deli meat in Jewish cooking in Britain and North America.
Salting meat in brine was an old way of preserving it before refrigeration.
It is sliced thinly for sandwiches in Britain and in North America.
salt-beef.visual: a thick cut slice of pink-grey salt beef, fine-grained and lean, lying flat on a plain background
salt-beef.what: Brisket soaked in brine, then simmered until tender.

facts: Salting and drying cod preserved it for long voyages and winters, and made it a staple across Europe.
Salt cod is central to Portuguese cooking, and brandade is a famous salt cod dish from southern France.
salt-cod.visual: one dried, salted cod fillet, pale greyish-white and stiff, lying flat
salt-cod.what: Cod, salted and dried to keep, then soaked before cooking.

facts: Salting and drying preserved cod long before refrigeration, and it was traded widely across the Atlantic.
In Jamaica it is soaked to remove salt, then flaked and cooked with ackee as a national dish.
Soaking the fish overnight, changing the water, reduces its saltiness before cooking.
salt-fish.visual: a stiff block of dried, salted white fish with a pale, slightly crystalline surface
salt-fish.what: Dried, salted white fish, soaked before cooking.

facts: Anchovies have long been preserved in salt, a method used around the Mediterranean.
Before use, they are rinsed to remove much of the salt and often boned.
Their strong savoury taste adds depth to dressings like Caesar and sauces like Worcestershire.
salted-anchovies.visual: a small heap of whole salted anchovies, silvery and grainy with coarse salt clinging to them
salted-anchovies.what: Small silver fish cured in salt, with a strong flavour.

facts: Butter is made by churning cream until the fat separates from the buttermilk.
Salt was mixed into butter long ago to help it keep before refrigeration.
salted-butter.visual: a block of pale yellow salted butter with one thick slice cut away, lying directly on the surface
salted-butter.what: Sharp juice from green limes, used in drinks and cooking.

facts: Capers are the unopened flower buds of a shrub that grows around the Mediterranean.
Caper bushes thrive on dry, rocky ground and can grow out of old stone walls.
Salting is an old way to preserve capers, and they are rinsed before use.
salted-capers.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, holding small grey-green salted capers
salted-capers.what: Tiny salted flower buds, sharp and briny.

facts: Caramel is made by heating sugar until it melts and turns golden brown.
Salted caramel is a flavour pairing that is popular in many desserts and confectionery.
salted-caramel-sauce.visual: a plain clear glass jar of smooth golden-amber caramel sauce, glossy and thick
salted-caramel-sauce.what: A pourable caramel sauce finished with a pinch of sea salt.

facts: Salted duck eggs are a traditional food in China and parts of South-East Asia.
The egg is soaked in a salt brine or packed in salty clay for several weeks.
Cooked salted yolks are sometimes used in mooncakes and rice dishes.
salted-duck-egg.visual: one whole salted duck egg, rough chalky grey-white shell, lying on the background
salted-duck-egg.what: A duck egg cured in brine, with a rich, salty yolk.

facts: Herring was salted for long storage in medieval Europe, when it was an important food for fasting periods.
Pickled herring is traditional in Scandinavia, the Netherlands and Germany.
salted-herring.visual: a whole salted herring lying flat, silver-grey skin with a fine pale salt crust
salted-herring.what: A firm, salty fish, soaked to remove salt before cooking.

facts: Peanuts are not true nuts but legumes, related to beans and peas.
Peanuts were domesticated in South America many centuries ago.
Peanut oil and peanut butter both come from the same crop, grown in many warm regions.
salted-peanuts.visual: a small heap of roasted peanuts, pale golden skins, slightly glistening with salt
salted-peanuts.what: Roasted peanuts, coated in salt for a savoury snack.

facts: Popcorn is made by heating corn kernels until their moisture turns to steam and bursts them open.
Popcorn has been eaten in the Americas for thousands of years, long before European arrival.
Popcorn became a popular cinema snack in the twentieth century.
salted-popcorn.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of light, golden popped corn, glossy and lightly seasoned
salted-popcorn.what: Light, crisp popped corn, lightly buttered and salted.

facts: Belacan is a fermented, dried shrimp paste used widely in Malaysian cooking.
Sambal is the general name for chilli-based condiments in Malay and Indonesian cuisine.
The shrimp paste is toasted before use, which deepens its aroma and flavour.
sambal-belacan.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of glossy red chilli sauce with a coarse texture
sambal-belacan.what: A fiery chilli sauce flavoured with toasted shrimp paste.

facts: Sambal matah is a fresh, uncooked relish from the island of Bali in Indonesia.
The relish is traditionally made by hand, finely chopping or pounding its ingredients.
sambal-matah.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of finely chopped, glossy pale-green and white relish, loosely mixed
sambal-matah.what: A raw Balinese relish of shallot, lemongrass and chilli.

facts: Sambal is a family of chilli pastes from Indonesia and Malaysia, served as a condiment.
The name oelek comes from the Indonesian word for grinding or pounding in a mortar.
It is often used in stir-fries and sauces, or served alongside a meal.
sambal-oelek.visual: a plain glass jar without a label filled with bright red chilli paste, coarse and glossy
sambal-oelek.what: A hot, coarse chilli paste made with vinegar and salt.

facts: Sambar is a South Indian dish of lentils and vegetables cooked with tamarind and spices.
Sambar is typically served with rice, idli or dosa.
sambar-paste.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, holding thick orange-brown spice paste with a flat surface
sambar-paste.what: A spice paste for sambar, a South Indian lentil stew.

facts: Sambar is a South Indian stew of lentils and vegetables, flavoured with a blend of spices.
Spices such as coriander seeds and dried red chillies are often toasted before grinding.
sambar-powder.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with fine reddish-brown spice powder
sambar-powder.what: A South Indian spice blend used to flavour lentil stews.

facts: Sambuca is an Italian liqueur, traditionally flavoured with star anise.
In Italy it is often served with a few coffee beans floating in the glass.
It turns cloudy and milky when water is added, a reaction typical of anise liqueurs.
sambuca.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with a clear, colourless liquid
sambuca.what: A clear Italian liqueur with a strong aniseed flavour.

facts: Samphire is a succulent plant that grows in salt marshes and on rocky coasts.
Its name may come from the French herbe de Saint-Pierre, meaning herb of St Peter.
Samphire was traditionally gathered from the coast and pickled in vinegar.
samphire.visual: a small loose bunch of bright green, fleshy, jointed samphire stems on a plain white background
samphire.what: Crunchy, salty green shoots that grow on coastal marshes.

facts: San Marzano tomatoes are grown in the volcanic soil around Mount Vesuvius near Naples.
They have a protected designation of origin, which means only tomatoes grown in the defined area can use the name.
The variety has been grown in southern Italy for a long time and is prized for its sweet, pulpy flesh and few seeds.
san-marzano-tomato.visual: a whole elongated red plum tomato with smooth glossy skin and a small green stem end
san-marzano-tomato.what: A sweet, thin-skinned Italian plum tomato, good for sauces.

facts: Sand dabs are flatfish found along the Pacific coast of North America.
Sand dabs live on sandy and muddy seabeds, where they lie partly buried.
sand-dab.visual: a whole raw sand dab, a small flat fish with a greyish-brown top, lying flat on the background
sand-dab.what: A small flatfish with a delicate, mild white flesh.

facts: Its large crystals reflect light, which gives baked goods a sparkle.
It is also called coarse sugar, a name that describes the larger crystal size.
Sugar cookies are the classic use, often decorated with a sprinkling before baking.
sanding-sugar.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of large, sparkling white sugar crystals, coarse and clear
sanding-sugar.what: Large, coarse sugar crystals used to decorate baked goods.

facts: Sandwich spread is a mayonnaise-style condiment sold in jars, popular in Britain.
Similar relishes are made in many countries, often from cucumbers preserved in vinegar.
sandwich-spread.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale, creamy spread flecked with small green pieces of chopped pickle
sandwich-spread.what: A creamy, tangy spread of chopped pickles and mayonnaise.

facts: It is a traditional Japanese seasoning, sold ground or as whole dried berries.
Sichuan pepper comes from a closely related group of trees, so the two spices are often compared.
sansho-pepper.visual: a small heap of dried reddish-brown sansho pepper husks, scattered loosely, some tiny black seeds among them
sansho-pepper.what: A citrusy, tingling Japanese pepper, used on grilled eel.

facts: Sapodilla is native to Mexico and Central America and is grown across the tropics.
Its milky sap is the source of chicle, the traditional base of chewing gum.
Its flesh is grainy and sweet, often compared to brown sugar and pear.
sapodilla.visual: a whole ripe brown sapodilla fruit with rough matte skin and a slightly oval shape
sapodilla.what: A sweet tropical fruit with brown flesh and rough skin.

facts: The name comes from the Spanish zarzaparrilla, a word for prickly bramble vines.
Root beer is a close relative, and the two drinks are often confused.
sarsaparilla.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with dark reddish-brown fizzy soft drink, small bubbles rising, nothing else in the glass
sarsaparilla.what: A sweet, fizzy soft drink flavoured with plant roots.

facts: Sashimi is a Japanese dish of thinly sliced raw fish, traditionally served without rice.
Poke is a Hawaiian dish of cubed raw fish, seasoned and served in a bowl.
sashimi-grade-salmon.visual: a thick, pale orange salmon fillet cut into a neat block, skinless, lying flat on a plain background
sashimi-grade-salmon.what: Very fresh salmon, cut and kept chilled for raw eating.

facts: Sashimi is a Japanese dish of thinly sliced raw fish, served without rice.
Tuna is a large, fast-swimming ocean fish found in warm and temperate seas.
Bluefin tuna is highly prized for sushi and sashimi in Japan.
sashimi-grade-tuna.visual: a fresh tuna loin, with thin slices cut across the grain, deep ruby-red flesh, lying flat
sashimi-grade-tuna.what: Premium tuna loin, sliced thin for raw dishes like sashimi.

facts: Satay, the grilled meat skewers, is a popular street food across Southeast Asia.
Peanuts originated in South America and reached Asia through later trade routes.
Satay sauce is often made by grinding roasted peanuts with spices and coconut milk.
satay-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, smooth brown-yellow peanut sauce
satay-sauce.what: A creamy peanut sauce, often served with grilled skewers.

facts: The satsuma mandarin takes its name from Satsuma Province in southern Japan.
Satsumas are usually seedless, which makes them easy to share.
Satsumas are grown in many warm countries and are a common winter fruit in Britain.
satsuma.visual: a whole satsuma with loose, slightly puffy orange skin, one peeled segment beside it
satsuma.what: A small, loose-skinned citrus that peels easily by hand.

facts: Saucisson sec is cured by drying rather than by cooking, and the drying can take several weeks.
Its name is French for dry sausage, and it is made in many regions of France.
saucisson-sec.visual: one whole firm dry sausage with a rough brownish casing, lying in a gentle curve
saucisson-sec.what: A French dry-cured sausage, often sliced thinly.

facts: The name comes from German, meaning sour cabbage.
Fermentation is carried out by lactic acid bacteria that occur naturally on cabbage.
Cabbage has been fermented in parts of Europe and Asia for centuries.
sauerkraut.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with pale yellow-green shredded fermented cabbage
sauerkraut.what: Finely shredded cabbage fermented in salt until tangy.

facts: The sausage roll is a classic British snack, made by wrapping sausage meat in pastry.
The pastry is often puff or flaky, which rises into many layers in the oven.
Sausage rolls are eaten hot from a bakery or cold at picnics across Britain.
sausage-roll.visual: a whole golden sausage roll with flaky pastry, lying on a plain white plate
sausage-roll.what: Seasoned pork in flaky pastry, served hot or cold.

facts: Sausagemeat is raw pork mixed with seasoning, and it is used in stuffings, pies and rolls.
In Britain, sausagemeat stuffing is traditionally served with roast turkey, especially at Christmas.
Sage and onion are classic flavourings for British stuffing, and both often appear in sausagemeat versions.
sausagemeat-stuffing.visual: a small plain white bowl of cooked sausagemeat stuffing, crumbly golden-brown mixture with a loose texture
sausagemeat-stuffing.what: A savoury, herby stuffing made from seasoned sausagemeat.

facts: Sauternes is made in the Sauternes district of Bordeaux, France, from grapes affected by noble rot.
Noble rot is a fungus that shrivels the grapes and concentrates their sugar.
Sauternes is often served alongside foie gras, blue cheese or fruit desserts.
sauternes.visual: a clear drinking glass of golden dessert wine, filled about halfway
sauternes.what: A golden, honeyed sweet wine from Bordeaux in France.

facts: New Zealand's Marlborough region became world-famous for its bold, fruity Sauvignon Blanc.
It is often served with shellfish and goat's cheese, thanks to its sharp acidity.
sauvignon-blanc.visual: a clear drinking glass half full of pale straw-coloured white wine on a plain background
sauvignon-blanc.what: A crisp, zesty white wine from France and New Zealand.

facts: Its name is thought to come from the Savoy region of the Alps, in France and Italy.
Its crinkled, loosely packed leaves are easy to separate, which suits stuffing and rolling.
It is often shredded and stir-fried, or braised with butter.
savoy-cabbage.visual: one whole Savoy cabbage, dark green outer leaves with deeply crinkled veins, sitting on a plain background
savoy-cabbage.what: A crinkled, dark green cabbage with loose, tender leaves.

facts: Sazón is a seasoning blend popular in Puerto Rico and across Latin America.
Annatto seeds, from the achiote tree, often give sazón its bright orange colour.
It is commonly used to season rice, beans and meat dishes.
sazon-seasoning.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of bright orange-red seasoning powder with fine granules
sazon-seasoning.what: An orange spice blend for rice and beans in Latin cooking.

facts: Sbrinz is a Swiss hard cheese made in central Switzerland from cow's milk.
It is aged for many months, which gives it a dense, crystalline texture and a sharp flavour.
sbrinz.visual: a block of hard, pale golden cheese, one flat cut face showing fine grain
sbrinz.what: A hard, aged Swiss cheese, grated over pasta or shaved.

facts: Scallops are bivalve molluscs that can swim by clapping their two shells together.
Scallop coral is the reproductive part of the animal and is eaten in several cuisines.
Scallop roe becomes firm and loses its soft texture if it is cooked for too long.
scallop-roe.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of bright orange scallop coral, soft and rounded
scallop-roe.what: The bright orange egg sac of a scallop, rich and soft.

facts: Scamorza is made by stretching curd and then shaping it into a pear with a narrow neck.
It belongs to the pasta filata family of stretched-curd cheeses, which includes mozzarella and provolone.
scamorza.visual: one whole pear-shaped scamorza cheese, smooth pale ivory skin with a faint golden tint, lying on its side
scamorza.what: A pear-shaped Italian cheese with a firm, stretched curd.

facts: Early Scottish scones were often made from oats or barley and cooked on a griddle.
A cream tea is a British treat of scones served with clotted cream and jam.
Scones are made by rubbing cold butter into flour, then mixing quickly to keep them light.
scone.visual: a plump round golden-brown scone with a floury top, whole and uncut
scone.what: A small, crumbly tea bread, split and spread with jam.

facts: Scorzonera is native to southern Europe and was once grown widely as a root crop.
It belongs to the daisy family, Asteraceae, which surprises many cooks.
Its white flesh discolours quickly, so peeled roots are kept in acidulated water.
scorzonera.visual: a small bunch of long, thin, dark black-brown scorzonera roots, earthy and unpeeled
scorzonera.what: A long black-skinned root with a delicate, nutty taste.

facts: Scotch bonnets belong to the same species as habanero, Capsicum chinense.
The name is said to refer to the pepper's shape, which resembles a Scottish bonnet.
They are a key flavour in Jamaican jerk seasoning and across Caribbean cooking.
scotch-bonnet.visual: one whole fresh scotch bonnet chilli, lantern-shaped with a bright orange-yellow skin and a short green stalk
scotch-bonnet.what: A small, fruity and very hot chilli pepper.

facts: Scotch bonnet chillies are named for their shape, which resembles a traditional Scottish bonnet.
The scotch bonnet is a close relative of the habanero.
Caribbean cooks use scotch bonnet in jerk seasoning and pepper sauces.
scotch-bonnet-sauce.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of bright orange-red scotch bonnet hot sauce
scotch-bonnet-sauce.what: A fiery, fruity hot sauce made with scotch bonnet chillies.

facts: The origin of the name is debated, and it is not clear that the dish comes from Scotland.
scotch-egg.visual: one whole golden-brown Scotch egg on a plain white plate
scotch-egg.what: A boiled egg in sausagemeat and breadcrumbs, then fried.

facts: Sausagemeat is minced pork mixed with seasonings such as herbs, pepper and sometimes breadcrumbs.
The Scotch egg is a British snack, a boiled egg wrapped in sausagemeat and breadcrumbs and fried or baked.
Sausagemeat is sold skinless, and in Britain it is also used as a stuffing for roast poultry.
scotch-egg-sausagemeat.visual: a small heap of raw, pale pink sausagemeat, soft and crumbly, lying loose
scotch-egg-sausagemeat.what: Seasoned minced pork, often wrapped around an egg.

facts: Scotch whisky must be made in Scotland and aged in oak casks for at least three years.
Malt whisky is made from malted barley, and peated varieties take their smoky flavour from peat smoke.
scotch-whisky.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale amber whisky, filled to about two-thirds
scotch-whisky.what: A malt spirit from Scotland, aged in oak casks for years.

facts: Scrag end is cut from the neck of the lamb, and it has long been used in slow-cooked dishes because it is inexpensive.
Irish stew traditionally uses scrag end, with potatoes and onions, cooked slowly until tender.
Long, slow cooking breaks down the connective tissue in the bones and meat, making the stew rich and tender.
scrag-end-of-lamb.visual: one raw scrag end of lamb, a bony neck cut with a rim of pink meat around thick bones, lying on the background
scrag-end-of-lamb.what: A bony, inexpensive lamb neck cut, ideal for slow stews.

facts: Scrambled eggs are made by beating eggs and stirring them gently over low heat.
In France the dish is called oeufs brouillés, meaning mixed-up eggs.
scrambled-egg.visual: a small soft heap of creamy pale yellow scrambled eggs on a plain white plate
scrambled-egg.what: Eggs beaten and gently stirred until soft and creamy.

facts: European sea bass are found in the Mediterranean and along the Atlantic coasts of Europe.
In Mediterranean cooking, whole sea bass is often baked or grilled with herbs and olive oil.
sea-bass-fillet.visual: a single raw sea bass fillet, pale pinkish-white flesh, silvery skin on one side, lying flat on a plain surface
sea-bass-fillet.what: A mild, firm white fish whose skin crisps well in a pan.

facts: Sea beet grows wild on coasts in Europe, North Africa and parts of Asia.
Chard, beetroot and sugar beet all descend from this wild species.
sea-beet.visual: a bunch of fresh sea beet leaves, glossy dark green with thin reddish stems
sea-beet.what: A wild coastal plant, the ancestor of chard.

facts: Sea bream is a family of fish found in warm and temperate seas, including the Mediterranean.
Its skin turns crisp when fried, which is why it is often cooked skin-side down.
The fish has been prized around the Mediterranean since ancient times.
sea-bream-fillet.visual: a single raw sea bream fillet, pale pink-white flesh with silvery skin on one side
sea-bream-fillet.what: A mild, firm white fish, sold as fillets with skin on.

facts: Sea buckthorn is native to Europe and Asia and grows in cold, sandy or rocky ground.
Its berries are pressed into juice, syrup and sauces, especially in Russia, Mongolia and China.
The shrub's thorny branches make it useful as a hedge, and its roots host bacteria that fix nitrogen in the soil.
sea-buckthorn.visual: a small bunch of bright orange, glossy berries on thin woody stems, on a plain background
sea-buckthorn.what: A small, sharp orange berry from a thorny wild shrub.

facts: Sea cucumbers are marine animals related to starfish and sea urchins.
Dried sea cucumber must be soaked and rehydrated for days before it is cooked.
sea-cucumber.visual: one whole raw sea cucumber, dark brown and bumpy, lying on a plain background
sea-cucumber.what: A soft-bodied sea animal, valued for its chewy texture.

facts: Sea kale grows wild on shingle and sand beaches in parts of Europe, including Britain.
It is a member of the cabbage family and was once grown in gardens for its shoots.
Gardeners blanched the shoots by covering the plants with soil or pots to keep them pale.
sea-kale.visual: a small bunch of pale, thick sea kale stems with blue-green, crinkled leaves
sea-kale.what: A coastal plant whose shoots are eaten like asparagus.

facts: Ulva is the scientific name for sea lettuce, a genus of green seaweeds found in coastal waters worldwide.
Several coastal cultures have gathered sea lettuce as food, often adding it to soups and salads.
Its thin fronds grow in shallow, sunlit water and are often seen in rock pools.
sea-lettuce.visual: a small loose heap of thin, crinkled bright green sea lettuce fronds, wet and glossy
sea-lettuce.what: A thin, bright green seaweed from rocky shores.

facts: Plants that tolerate salt water, like sea purslane, are called halophytes.
Sea purslane leaves can be eaten raw or lightly cooked, and they taste naturally salty, so little seasoning is needed.
sea-purslane.visual: a small loose bunch of fleshy, grey-green sea purslane leaves on thin stems
sea-purslane.what: A salty, fleshy coastal plant that grows on salt marshes.

facts: Sea robins are gurnards, a family known for using their fins to walk along the sea bed.
They live in warm and temperate coastal waters, especially along the Atlantic coast of the Americas.
Their firm white flesh suits stews, soups and bouillabaisse-style fish dishes.
sea-robin.visual: one whole raw sea robin, reddish-brown body and large fanned fins, lying on its side
sea-robin.what: A bony sea fish with firm, sweet flesh for stews.

facts: Sea salt is made by evaporating seawater, often in shallow pans and under the sun.
Salt has been traded for thousands of years and was once a valuable commodity.
Sea salts vary in colour and texture, from coarse grey crystals to delicate pyramid flakes.
sea-salt.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of coarse, pale grey sea salt crystals, filled to the rim
sea-salt.what: Coarse salt made by evaporating seawater.

facts: Crisps are thin slices of potato fried until crisp, a snack that became popular in the twentieth century.
Black pepper has been traded and used as a seasoning for many centuries.
Seasoning is usually added straight after frying, so the salt and pepper cling to the oily surface.
sea-salt-and-black-pepper-crisps.visual: a small heap of golden crisps speckled with black pepper and salt, lying loose on the background
sea-salt-and-black-pepper-crisps.what: Crisps with a peppery bite, seasoned with salt and pepper.

facts: Coastal communities in many countries have gathered sea snails from rocks for centuries.
In French kitchens, small sea snails are often simmered with garlic and herbs in their shells.
sea-snails.visual: a small heap of raw sea snails in their pale shells
sea-snails.what: Small marine snails, often stewed whole in their shells.

facts: Sea trout are a migratory form of brown trout that feed at sea and return to rivers.
Their pink flesh comes from the crustaceans they eat at sea, as in salmon.
In Britain, sea trout are prized by anglers for their summer runs up rivers.
sea-trout.visual: a fillet of raw sea trout, pink flesh with fine white lines, lying directly on the background
sea-trout.what: A silvery fish with pink flesh, between salmon and trout.

facts: The edible part is the sea urchin's gonads, the organs that produce its eggs and sperm.
Uni is the Japanese name, and it is served raw on sushi or in simple seafood dishes.
Japan, Korea and parts of the Mediterranean have long traditions of eating sea urchin.
sea-urchin-roe.visual: a small neat portion of bright orange-gold sea urchin roe, soft lobes, glossy and moist, lying directly on a plain background
sea-urchin-roe.what: Golden roe from spiny sea urchins, creamy and briny.

facts: Paella is a rice dish from Valencia in eastern Spain, traditionally cooked in a wide, shallow pan.
Prawns, mussels and squid are all widely eaten in coastal cooking around the Mediterranean.
Squid is a soft-bodied sea creature with arms and tentacles, eaten widely in southern Europe and East Asia.
seafood-mix.visual: a loose heap of seafood pieces: pink prawns, dark mussels and pale squid rings, seen from above
seafood-mix.what: A mix of prawns, mussels and squid for cooking.

facts: Seasoned salts combine common salt with dried herbs, spices and flavourings.
Garlic salt and onion salt are the simplest forms, made by mixing salt with the dried powder.
seasoned-salt.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, pale orange-brown seasoning salt
seasoned-salt.what: Salt mixed with paprika, garlic and onion powder.

facts: Sedanini is an Italian pasta shape, and its name means little celery.
Ridged pasta shapes are made to hold sauce in their grooves.
sedanini.visual: a small heap of short, slim, ridged pasta tubes, dry and pale yellow
sedanini.what: Short, slim, ridged pasta tubes, good for baking.

facts: The batch loaf is a traditional British bread, sold in bakeries and supermarkets.
Seeded loaves are popular across Europe, where the seeds add crunch and a nutty flavour.
Pumpkin seeds, known as pepitas, come from the Americas and feature in Mexican cooking.
seeded-batch-loaf.visual: one whole unsliced batch loaf, golden-brown crust speckled with seeds, lying on its side
seeded-batch-loaf.what: A crusty loaf studded with sunflower and pumpkin seeds.

facts: Sourdough rises on a starter of wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria, not commercial yeast.
Seeded loaves add toasted seeds such as sunflower, pumpkin or sesame to the dough.
seeded-sourdough.visual: one whole round sourdough loaf, golden crust dotted all over in pale and dark seeds
seeded-sourdough.what: A tangy, chewy loaf made with a wild yeast starter.

facts: It has a long history in Buddhist vegetarian cooking in East Asia.
In Japan it is known as fu, and it is sold in many forms.
seitan.visual: a pale golden-brown block of seitan with one thick slice cut from its end, showing a fine fibrous texture
seitan.what: Chewy wheat gluten, seasoned and sliced to look like meat.

facts: In French, sel gris simply means grey salt, a name for coarse, unrefined sea salt.
The salt is raked by hand from shallow pans on the Atlantic coast of Brittany.
The grey colour comes from the clay lining of the salt pans, which the salt picks up as it dries.
sel-gris-de-guerande.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with coarse grey sea salt crystals, slightly damp and clumpy
sel-gris-de-guerande.what: Coarse grey sea salt from the coast of Brittany, France.

facts: Self-raising flour contains a raising agent, usually baking powder, so it rises without extra leaven.
It is common in British baking, where recipes for sponges and scones often call for it.
Plain flour has no raising agent, so a recipe that uses it must add one separately.
self-raising-flour.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine white flour, soft and smooth
self-raising-flour.what: Flour with raising agent added, for light sponge cakes.

facts: Selles-sur-Cher is a village in the Loire Valley of central France, and the cheese is named after it.
selles-sur-cher.visual: a small round goat's cheese coated in grey-black edible ash, one wedge cut away to show the firm pale interior
selles-sur-cher.what: A firm, ash-coated goat's cheese from the Loire Valley.

facts: Semi-skimmed milk has had some of its cream removed, so it is lighter than whole milk.
Milk is partly skimmed by separating out some of its cream in a centrifuge.
In Britain, semi-skimmed milk is a widely sold type of cow's milk for everyday use.
semi-skimmed-milk.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of white milk, filled to the neck
semi-skimmed-milk.what: Milk with less fat than whole milk, for everyday use.

facts: Gnocchi alla romana, from Rome, are made from semolina rather than potato.
The semolina is cooked into a thick porridge, spread to set, cut into discs and baked.
Semolina is milled from durum wheat and is also used for pasta and some puddings.
semolina-gnocchi.visual: several round, golden-browned semolina discs with crisp edges, lying on a plain white plate
semolina-gnocchi.what: Baked discs of semolina dough, cheesy and golden on top.

facts: Serrano means mountain in Spanish, and the chilli is grown widely in central and eastern Mexico.
They are often eaten fresh in salsas and pico de gallo, or pickled.
It is a common chilli in Mexican cooking, used both fresh and dried.
serrano-chilli.visual: a small heap of slim, bright green chillies, smooth and shiny
serrano-chilli.what: A small, hot green chilli, hotter than a jalapeño.

facts: Bagels are thought to have developed in Jewish communities in Poland, where they were boiled before baking.
Sesame seeds have been cultivated for thousands of years and add a nutty flavour and crunch to baked goods.
sesame-bagel.visual: one whole sesame bagel with a golden-brown crust covered in toasted sesame seeds, lying on its side
sesame-bagel.what: A chewy, ring-shaped bread roll topped with sesame seeds.

facts: Grissini, the Italian breadstick, are traditionally associated with the city of Turin.
Sesame is one of the oldest oilseed crops and has been grown for thousands of years.
Breadsticks are often served with dips or soup, or eaten as a crisp snack.
sesame-breadsticks.visual: a small heap of slender golden breadsticks, crisp, with pale sesame seeds clinging to the crust
sesame-breadsticks.what: Crisp bread sticks coated in toasted sesame seeds.

facts: Sesame seeds have been pressed for oil and eaten for thousands of years.
Ginger is a rhizome, an underground stem, that has long been used in East Asian cooking.
sesame-ginger-dressing.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden, creamy dressing
sesame-ginger-dressing.what: A nutty, zesty dressing for slaws and noodle salads.

facts: Sesame oil is pressed from sesame seeds, which have been grown for thousands of years.
Toasted sesame oil is darker and nuttier, and is often used as a finishing oil.
It is a staple in Chinese, Korean and Japanese cooking.
sesame-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden sesame oil, cap on
sesame-oil.what: Nutty oil pressed from sesame seeds, used in stir-fries.

facts: Chinese sesame sauce is made from toasted sesame paste, often thinned with oil, vinegar or stock.
Sesame sauce is a common dip for cold noodles and for hot pot.
Sesame has been cultivated for thousands of years and is grown in many warm regions.
sesame-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth pale beige sesame sauce, thick and glossy
sesame-sauce.what: A smooth, nutty dipping sauce made from ground sesame.

facts: Burger buns are typically soft, enriched breads designed to hold a patty and its toppings.
The seeds are usually sprinkled on the bun before baking, so they toast in the oven.
sesame-seed-burger-bun.visual: one whole round burger bun on a plain white plate, golden domed top, pale sesame seeds scattered across it
sesame-seed-burger-bun.what: A soft round bun topped with toasted sesame seeds.

facts: Sesame is one of the oldest crops grown for its seeds and oil.
Tahini is a sesame paste that is a staple of Middle Eastern cooking.
Hummus is often made with tahini, along with chickpeas, lemon and garlic.
sesame-seed-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, pale beige sesame paste, thick and glossy
sesame-seed-paste.what: A smooth, thick paste made by grinding sesame seeds.

facts: Sesame is one of the oldest cultivated oilseeds, and has been grown for thousands of years.
Toasted sesame oil is made from roasted seeds, and gives many East Asian dishes their characteristic aroma.
Sesame seeds are sprinkled over bread, bagels and buns, and are used to make Middle Eastern tahini.
sesame-seeds.visual: a small heap of pale cream sesame seeds, tiny oval grains
sesame-seeds.what: Tiny nutty seeds for bread, stir-fries and dressings.

facts: Honey crystallises naturally over time, as glucose separates out of the liquid.
Set or creamed honey is made by controlling crystallisation, so it stays smooth and spreadable.
Bees gather nectar from flowers and store it in wax comb, where it slowly ripens.
set-honey.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with thick creamy pale golden honey, lid off
set-honey.what: Thick honey that has crystallised into a smooth spread.

facts: Set yoghurt is made by warming milk, adding live cultures and leaving it undisturbed until it thickens.
Yoghurt is made across the Middle East, the Balkans and South Asia, where it is a long-standing part of everyday cooking.
In India, set yoghurt is known as dahi and is used in curries and raitas.
set-yoghurt.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with smooth, thick, creamy white yoghurt
set-yoghurt.what: Thick, spoonable yoghurt set in the pot with a gentle tang.

facts: Seville oranges are grown in Spain, especially around the city of Seville, and are too sour to eat fresh.
Their bitterness and high pectin content make them the traditional choice for marmalade.
seville-orange.visual: a whole Seville orange, rough dimpled deep-orange skin and a small green stem end, lying on the plain background
seville-orange.what: A bitter, aromatic orange grown mainly for marmalade.

facts: Seville oranges are a bitter variety, and they are used to make marmalade in Britain.
Marmalade is a preserve made by cooking citrus peel, pulp and sugar together until it sets.
Seville oranges are harvested in winter, which is why marmalade is traditionally made in the colder months.
seville-orange-marmalade.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, full of chunky dark orange marmalade
seville-orange-marmalade.what: A chunky preserve made from bitter Seville oranges.

facts: Sevruga is a caviar from the sevruga sturgeon, a fish of the Caspian and Black Seas.
Caviar is the salted eggs of sturgeon, and sevruga eggs are smaller than beluga eggs.
Caviar has long been prized in Russia and Persia as a luxury food.
sevruga-caviar.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of small, glossy grey caviar eggs
sevruga-caviar.what: Small grey sturgeon eggs with an intense, salty flavour.

facts: Shabu-shabu is a Japanese hotpot in which thin slices of meat are swished through a pot of simmering broth.
Diners dip each cooked slice into a sesame or ponzu sauce before eating.
shabu-shabu-beef.visual: a neat overlapping fan of very thin raw beef slices, each nearly see-through, lying flat
shabu-shabu-beef.what: Very thin slices of beef, cooked by swishing in hot broth.

facts: Shad are anadromous, living in the sea and swimming up rivers to spawn.
Shad roe is a traditional spring delicacy, often grilled or pan-fried.
Shad is famously bony, with many fine bones that need careful filleting.
shad.visual: a whole raw shad, silver-blue skin with a sheen, lying on its side
shad.what: A rich, bony herring-family fish prized for its roe.

facts: Shad is a herring-like fish that swims up rivers in spring to spawn.
Shad roe is prized in North America, where it is often pan-fried with bacon.
shad-roe.visual: a pair of raw shad roe sacs, pale pink-grey and smooth, lying side by side on the background
shad-roe.what: Fish eggs from the shad, a seasonal spring delicacy.

facts: Shakshuka is a dish of eggs poached in a sauce of tomatoes, peppers and onions.
It is particularly associated with North Africa and is widely eaten across the Middle East.
shakshuka-eggs.visual: a plain white bowl holding a deep red sauce and two eggs, the whites set and yolks still soft
shakshuka-eggs.what: Eggs gently poached in a spiced tomato and pepper sauce.

facts: Shallots grow in clusters, with several bulbs joined from one root.
The name is thought to come from Ascalon, an ancient city in the Levant.
Shallots are widely used in French cooking, where they flavour sauces and dressings.
shallot.visual: a small heap of whole shallots, copper-brown papery skins
shallot.what: A milder, sweeter member of the onion family.

facts: Shaoxing wine takes its name from Shaoxing, a city in Zhejiang province.
It is a fermented rice wine, often aged and used in marinades and braises.
Rice wine has been made in the Shaoxing area for many centuries.
shaoxing-wine.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with amber-coloured rice wine, on a plain background
shaoxing-wine.what: An amber rice wine from Zhejiang, used in Chinese cooking.

facts: Most astringent persimmons must ripen until very soft before eating, while Sharon fruit can be eaten firm.
Persimmons are native to East Asia, where they have been grown for centuries.
sharon-fruit.visual: a whole glossy orange-red Sharon fruit with a small green leaf-like cap on top
sharon-fruit.what: A sweet, firm persimmon eaten crisp, like an apple.

facts: The name shawarma comes from a Turkish word meaning 'turning', after the rotating spit.
Spice blends vary from cook to cook, but cumin, turmeric, paprika and cinnamon are common.
Versions of the dish are found across the Levant, Turkey and the Arab world, and in many cities abroad.
shawarma-spice.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with a warm orange-brown ground spice blend
shawarma-spice.what: A warm, earthy spice blend for rotisserie-style meats.

facts: Cheddar takes its name from the village of Cheddar in Somerset, England, where cheese has been made for a long time.
Cheddar-style cheeses are made by cutting, stacking and milling the curd to press out whey.
sheep-s-cheddar.visual: a block of pale ivory sheep's milk cheese with one wedge cut away to show a firm, creamy-white interior
sheep-s-cheddar.what: A firm, sweet sheep's milk cheese, made cheddar-style.

facts: Feta is a brined white cheese that has been made in Greece for centuries.
Traditional Greek feta is made mainly from sheep's milk, sometimes mixed with goat's milk.
The word feta comes from an Italian word meaning slice.
sheep-s-feta.visual: a rectangular block of white crumbly sheep's feta cheese with one clean slice cut from the end
sheep-s-feta.what: Crumbly, tangy white cheese made from sheep's milk.

facts: Roquefort, the blue cheese from France, is made from sheep's milk.
Sheep's milk is traditionally made into yoghurt in the Middle East and the Balkans.
Sheep's milk has a higher solids content than cow's milk, which gives cheese a rich texture.
sheep-s-milk.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with creamy white sheep's milk
sheep-s-milk.what: Rich, creamy milk from sheep, used for yoghurt and cheese.

facts: Edamame are soybeans picked young, while the pods are still green and tender.
In Japan they are often boiled in salted water and eaten as a snack.
shelled-edamame.visual: a small heap of shelled edamame beans, bright green, plump and smooth
shelled-edamame.what: Young green soya beans, shelled and ready to eat.

facts: Pistachio trees come from Central Asia and the Middle East, and grow in dry climates.
Pistachio nuts grow inside a split shell, which opens naturally as the nut ripens.
shelled-pistachios.visual: a small heap of shelled unsalted pistachio kernels, pale green, some with papery skins
shelled-pistachios.what: Sweet green nut kernels, used in baking and desserts.

facts: The word comes from the Persian or Arabic sharbat, meaning a sweet drink.
In Britain, sherbet is a childhood sweet, often sold in a paper tube with a liquorice straw.
Its fizz comes from bicarbonate of soda reacting with an acid, usually citric acid, when it meets moisture.
sherbet.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine pale yellow sherbet powder
sherbet.what: A tangy, fizzing sugar powder for sweets and dipping.

facts: Sherry vinegar is made in Spain's Jerez region in Andalusia, from sherry wine.
It is aged for a long time in oak barrels, which gives it a mellow flavour.
Producers often age it by the solera system, in which barrels are gradually blended over time.
sherry-vinegar.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of deep amber-brown sherry vinegar
sherry-vinegar.what: A nutty, mellow vinegar made from sherry wine in Spain.

facts: Shetland black is a heritage potato variety associated with the Shetland Islands in northern Scotland.
Potatoes first grew in the Andes of South America and reached Europe in the 16th century.
shetland-black-potato.visual: one whole raw Shetland black potato, dark purple-black skin, a knobbly oval shape, lying on its side
shetland-black-potato.what: A knobbly, dark-skinned potato with violet flesh.

facts: Its name combines shichi, meaning seven, with mi, meaning flavour, and togarashi, the Japanese word for chilli.
It is a common sprinkle on noodle dishes such as udon and soba.
Blends vary between makers, but chilli is always included, and the rest often includes orange peel, sesame and seaweed.
shichimi-togarashi.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of mixed, flecked red-orange and dark spice powder
shichimi-togarashi.what: A Japanese seven-spice blend of chilli, citrus and sesame.

facts: Shiitake is native to East Asia, where it has been grown on logs for a long time.
Its name combines 'shii', a native tree, and 'take', the Japanese word for mushroom.
Dried shiitake are widely used in East Asian stocks and are rehydrated before cooking.
shiitake-mushroom.visual: one whole raw shiitake mushroom, brown domed cap with pale gills on the underside, on the background
shiitake-mushroom.what: A brown, umami-rich mushroom with a smoky, meaty flavour.

facts: Shiitake is native to East Asia, where it has been grown on logs for centuries.
Drying concentrates its savoury, umami flavour, which is why the powder suits stocks and rubs.
shiitake-powder.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with fine, grey-brown mushroom powder
shiitake-powder.what: Dried shiitake mushrooms ground to a rich, savoury powder.

facts: Shimeji is the Japanese name for several mushroom species that grow in dense clusters.
Brown shimeji are cultivated in Japan and often used in soups, noodles and hotpots.
shimeji-mushroom.visual: a small cluster of brown shimeji mushrooms with slender stems joined at the base and small smooth caps
shimeji-mushroom.what: These small clustered mushrooms taste nutty when cooked.

facts: Koji is a mould, Aspergillus oryzae, grown on rice or soybeans and used in Japanese cooking for centuries.
Shio koji is made by mixing koji with salt and water, then leaving it to ferment into a paste.
Japanese cooks use shio koji to marinate meat and fish before grilling or frying.
shio-koji.visual: A small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, creamy pale beige paste with a slightly grainy texture.
shio-koji.what: A salty koji paste that softens meat and adds depth.

facts: The noodles are made from konjac flour mixed with water and a little lime to set.
Konjac is a plant grown in East and South-East Asia, and its corm is used as food.
In Japan, konjac has long been used in dishes such as oden, a simmered hot pot.
shirataki-noodles.visual: a small plain white bowl of translucent, pale noodles resting in their water
shirataki-noodles.what: Clear, springy Japanese noodles made from konjac.

facts: Shiro shoyu is a Japanese soy sauce with more wheat than soybeans, giving a paler colour.
Its light colour lets cooks season soups, sauces and dressings without darkening them.
Japanese soy sauce is traditionally brewed from wheat, soybeans, salt and a fermenting mould.
shiro-shoyu.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with pale golden liquid, cap removed, standing upright
shiro-shoyu.what: A pale Japanese soy sauce that keeps dishes light.

facts: Shishito peppers come from Japan, where they have been grown for a long time.
Most are mild, but a few can be surprisingly hot, which is part of their appeal.
They are often blistered in a hot pan with a little oil and salt.
shishito-pepper.visual: a small heap of slim, wrinkled, bright green shishito peppers with a few dark blistered spots
shishito-pepper.what: A thin, wrinkled green pepper that is usually mild.

facts: Shortbread is strongly associated with Scotland and is a traditional treat at Christmas and Hogmanay.
Its name comes from its high butter content, which makes it 'short', meaning crumbly.
shortbread-fingers.visual: a small plain white plate of pale golden shortbread fingers, one broken in half
shortbread-fingers.what: Thick, buttery biscuits, made from flour, butter and sugar.

facts: Shortcrust pastry is made by rubbing cold butter into flour until it resembles breadcrumbs.
Its short, crumbly texture comes from a high proportion of fat to flour.
shortcrust-pastry.visual: a single round ball of raw pale shortcrust pastry dough, smooth and slightly floury, sitting on its own
shortcrust-pastry.what: A crumbly, buttery pastry used for pies and tarts.

facts: Shredded wheat was first made in the United States as a breakfast cereal in the 1890s.
The biscuits are made by cooking whole wheat, shredding it into strands and pressing them into shape.
