shredded-wheat.visual: one whole shredded wheat biscuit, a pale golden oval of layered crisp strands, standing alone
shredded-wheat.what: A pale biscuit of cooked, shredded whole wheat.

facts: In Cajun and Creole cooking, shrimp heads are simmered to make a rich stock.
Classic shrimp bisque is made by simmering shrimp shells and heads with stock, wine and cream.
Shrimp heads hold much of the shellfish flavour, which is why they are saved for stock.
shrimp-heads.visual: a small heap of raw pink shrimp heads, shells and feelers intact, with no tails
shrimp-heads.what: The head of a shrimp, rich in flavour and used in stocks.

facts: Shrimp paste is made by salting and fermenting tiny shrimp, then pounding them into a block.
It is widely used in Malay, Indonesian and Thai cooking, especially in chilli sambals and curry pastes.
shrimp-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dense, dark pinkish-grey shrimp paste, smooth and firm
shrimp-paste.what: Pungent fermented shrimp pressed into a block for curries.

facts: Its orange colour comes from annatto, a natural colouring from the achiote tree.
shropshire-blue.visual: a block of orange-yellow blue cheese with one wedge cut out, showing blue-green veins
shropshire-blue.what: A creamy English blue cheese with a mild, mellow bite.

facts: Oysters are bivalve molluscs that have been eaten since ancient times.
Oyster shells left in ancient rubbish heaps show that people ate them for thousands of years.
shucked-oysters.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of plump pale shucked oysters in their clear liquor
shucked-oysters.what: Oysters removed from their shells, ready to fry or cook.

facts: Sichuan pepper is not a true pepper; it comes from a prickly ash tree and gives a tingling sensation.
The sediment is the crisp chilli and spice pieces that settle, often spooned over noodles or dumplings.
sichuan-chilli-oil-with-sediment.visual: a plain glass jar without a label holding deep red oil flecked with dark chilli flakes, with spice sediment settled at the base
sichuan-chilli-oil-with-sediment.what: Red chilli oil with a numbing, spicy kick from Sichuan.

facts: Sichuan chillies are named for the Sichuan region of south-west China, famous for its spicy cooking.
Facing heaven chillies get their name because the pods grow upright, facing the sky.
They are often fried in oil to release their aroma, a key step in Sichuan cooking.
sichuan-dried-chillies.visual: a small heap of dried, wrinkled red chilli pods, reddish-brown and curled
sichuan-dried-chillies.what: Small dried red chillies with a fragrant, medium heat.

facts: Paocai is a brine-fermented vegetable dish from Sichuan province in south-west China.
Vegetables such as mustard greens are sealed in brine, where lactic acid bacteria ferment them.
Sichuan households traditionally kept a jar of paocai fermenting for use in stir-fries and soups.
sichuan-pickled-vegetables.visual: a plain glass jar without a label holding thin pale green pickled vegetable strips in clear brine
sichuan-pickled-vegetables.what: Crisp, sour, spicy vegetables pickled in brine.

facts: Sicily has grown olives for thousands of years, with groves across the island.
Sicilian oils are often made from Biancolilla, Nocellara and Tonda Iblea olives.
The island's dry, sunny climate suits olive trees well.
sicilian-olive-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with golden-green olive oil, with a plain stopper, on a plain background
sicilian-olive-oil.what: Fruity olive oil from Sicily, with green, peppery notes.

facts: Tofu is made by curdling soy milk, a method developed in China and later spread across East Asia.
In Japan, it is often served chilled in hiyayakko, with soy sauce and grated ginger.
silken-tofu.visual: a block of pale ivory silken tofu with one smooth-edged slice cut away, lying flat
silken-tofu.what: A very soft, smooth tofu with a custard-like texture.

facts: Silver balls are used on celebration cakes, especially wedding and birthday cakes.
Decorating balls are made by building up layers of sugar around a small centre.
They are sprinkled on iced cakes, cupcakes and biscuits, usually for celebrations.
silver-balls.visual: a small heap of tiny, shiny silver sugar balls, round and smooth
silver-balls.what: Tiny shiny sugar balls used to decorate celebration cakes.

facts: Silverskin onions are small pale onions, often sold as pickling onions.
They are commonly pickled in vinegar and served in cocktails, such as the Gibson.
silverskin-onions.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with tiny pale pickled onions in clear liquid
silverskin-onions.what: Tiny pale onions pickled whole in a sharp brine.

facts: Bartenders use it in cocktails because granulated sugar dissolves poorly in cold drinks.
Bakers brush it onto sponge cakes to keep them moist after baking.
simple-syrup.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with clear, colourless syrup
simple-syrup.what: Sugar dissolved in water, for sweetening drinks and cakes.

facts: Single cream has less fat than double cream, so it is thinner and pours easily.
Because it is lighter, it does not whip as stiffly as double cream does.
single-cream.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, pale ivory pouring cream
single-cream.what: Light pouring cream used in soups, coffee and sauces.

facts: Gloucester cheese has been made in Gloucestershire, England, for centuries.
Single Gloucester is the lighter cousin of the richer Double Gloucester.
single-gloucester.visual: a wedge of pale golden cheese with a thin, pale rind, lying flat on the surface
single-gloucester.what: A mild, delicate cheese from Gloucestershire, England.

facts: Sirene is Bulgaria's everyday white cheese, stored in brine, and it is closely related to feta.
Brined white cheeses like sirene have been made in the Balkans and Eastern Mediterranean for centuries.
sirene.visual: a block of crumbly white brined cheese with one wedge cut away, showing a pale moist texture
sirene.what: A brined, crumbly white cheese from Bulgaria.

facts: Skate is a type of ray, so it is related to sharks and has a cartilage skeleton.
Once cooked, the flesh separates from the cartilage in soft, fine strips.
Skate with beurre noir, a brown butter sauce, is a classic French dish.
skate-wing.visual: one whole raw skate wing, flat diamond shape, pale greyish-brown skin, lying flat
skate-wing.what: A flat sea fish whose wings have soft, sweet flesh.

facts: Skimmed milk has had its cream removed, so it contains much less fat than whole milk.
In the UK, skimmed milk is sold alongside whole and semi-skimmed milk.
skimmed-milk.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with thin, bluish-white skimmed milk
skimmed-milk.what: Milk with nearly all the cream removed, thin and light.

facts: The origin of fried potato strips is disputed, with both Belgium and France claiming them.
Thinner cuts cook faster because they have more surface area for their weight.
Frozen fries are usually blanched and partly fried at the factory before freezing.
skinny-fries.visual: a neat small pile of thin golden crisp fries on a plain white plate
skinny-fries.what: Thin, crisp potato fries that cook quickly from frozen.

facts: Skirret is a member of the carrot family and was grown in Europe and Asia.
It was grown in English kitchen gardens for several centuries before falling out of use.
Its roots grow in a cluster from one crown, so several are harvested together.
skirret.visual: a cluster of pale creamy skirret roots, knobbly and thin, joined at the crown
skirret.what: An old sweet root vegetable, boiled in clusters.

facts: Skordalia is a traditional Greek sauce, pounded from garlic, bread or potato and olive oil.
It is often served with fried vegetables, salt cod or boiled beetroot in Greece.
The name comes from the Greek word skordo, meaning garlic.
skordalia.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, creamy pale beige dip, its surface lightly peaked
skordalia.what: A thick Greek dip of garlic, potato and olive oil.

facts: Skyr has been eaten in Iceland for centuries, made by culturing milk and straining off the whey.
The name is Icelandic, and skyr is strained more than yoghurt, giving it a denser texture.
skyr.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick white skyr with a smooth, spoonable surface
skyr.what: A thick, tangy Icelandic dairy, like strained yoghurt.

facts: Bread-slicing machines were developed in the 1920s, and pre-sliced loaves soon became common.
In Britain, sliced white bread is the everyday base for toasties, sandwiches and bread and butter.
It is made from refined wheat flour, which gives it a soft, fine crumb.
sliced-white-bread.visual: a soft white sliced loaf with one slice pulled out to show the pale crumb
sliced-white-bread.what: Soft, pale bread, sliced ready for toast and sandwiches.

facts: Wholemeal flour keeps the bran and germ, which gives bread its darker colour and nutty flavour.
Bread is one of the oldest prepared foods, baked from ground grain for thousands of years.
Wholemeal is mainly the British term; in America a similar flour is called whole wheat.
sliced-wholemeal-bread.visual: a brown wholemeal loaf with three thick slices cut from one end, the crumb visible, lying directly on the plain background
sliced-wholemeal-bread.what: A brown loaf made from flour that keeps the whole grain.

facts: It grows under pine trees, forming a partnership with their roots.
Its cap is slimy when wet, which gives the mushroom its common name.
Cooks usually peel the sticky skin from the cap before frying or drying the slices.
slippery-jack.visual: one whole slippery jack mushroom, glossy brown cap, pale yellow pores underneath
slippery-jack.what: A brown edible mushroom with a sticky, slippery cap.

facts: Sloes are the fruit of the blackthorn, a spiny shrub found in hedgerows across Britain and Europe.
Sloes are traditionally steeped in gin with sugar to make sloe gin, usually after the first frost.
sloe.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dark blue-black sloe berries, lightly dusted
sloe.what: A small, dark wild plum with a very sharp, sour taste.

facts: Sloes are the small, wild fruit of the blackthorn tree, and are picked in autumn.
Sloe gin is a traditional British drink, and it is often made at home in autumn.
sloe-gin.visual: a clear drinking glass of deep ruby-red sloe gin
sloe-gin.what: A ruby-red gin infused with tart, dark sloe berries.

facts: Fresh smelt have a faint scent often compared to cucumber.
Smelt are usually cooked whole, and their bones are fine enough to eat.
smelt.visual: several whole raw smelt, slender silver bodies lying side by side
smelt.what: A tiny silver fish, eaten whole and often fried.

facts: Smen is butter that is salted and left to age for months, often stored in earthenware jars.
It is a traditional ingredient in Moroccan cooking, used to flavour tagines, couscous and bread.
smen.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with golden-amber aged butter, a little cloudy and soft
smen.what: Moroccan preserved butter, salted and aged until funky.

facts: Almonds are the seeds of the almond tree, which is a member of the rose family.
Almonds are widely grown in California and the Mediterranean region.
smoked-almonds.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with whole, golden-brown smoked almonds, their skins slightly darker
smoked-almonds.what: Crunchy nuts roasted over smoke for a savoury, smoky snack.

facts: Bacon is cured pork, usually salted and sometimes smoked to add flavour.
Back bacon comes from the loin, while streaky bacon is cut from the belly.
Smoked bacon is flavoured by hanging it over smouldering wood, a method used for centuries.
smoked-bacon.visual: three raw smoked back bacon rashers, lying flat, pink meat with a golden-brown smoked rind
smoked-bacon.what: Cured pork cut into rashers, then smoked over wood.

facts: Cold smoking exposes cheese to smoke at low temperatures, so it does not melt.
Cheddar takes its name from the village of Cheddar in Somerset, England.
Cheddaring is the process of stacking and turning cut curd blocks to drain off whey.
smoked-cheddar.visual: a block of smoked cheddar with one wedge cut, golden-brown smoked rind and pale yellow cut face
smoked-cheddar.what: Cheddar that has been smoked slowly over oak wood.

facts: Smoking cheese is an old method, used to help preserve it before refrigeration.
smoked-cheese.visual: a block of pale golden smoked cheese with one wedge cut away to show a firm, smooth interior, lying on the background
smoked-cheese.what: Firm cheese cured over wood smoke for a savoury flavour.

facts: Smoking fish was a traditional way to preserve it before refrigeration.
Smoked cod is often used in chowders and fish pies.
smoked-cod.visual: a skinless fillet of smoked cod, pale golden-yellow flesh with a light smoky colour, lying flat
smoked-cod.what: A white cod fillet cured over smoke for a savoury flavour.

facts: The Greek name comes from taramas, the word for salted roe, and salata, the word for salad.
Cod roe is the eggs of the cod fish, and it is sold smoked, salted or fresh.
smoked-cod-roe.visual: one smoked cod roe, a plump pale pinkish-orange sac with a glossy, lightly smoked surface
smoked-cod-roe.what: Salty, smoky cod roe, the base of taramasalata.

facts: Eels are long, snake-like fish that live in fresh water and return to the sea to breed.
Smoked eel is a traditional food in parts of Britain and northern Europe, often served cold in thin slices.
smoked-eel.visual: one whole smoked eel with glossy bronze-brown skin, lying in a gentle curve
smoked-eel.what: A rich, oily fish, cured and smoked for a savoury taste.

facts: Garlic is native to Central Asia and has been cultivated for thousands of years.
Smoked garlic is made by exposing whole bulbs to wood smoke at low temperatures.
smoked-garlic.visual: one whole bulb of smoked garlic, pale golden-brown papery skin, cloves visible at the top, lying on the background
smoked-garlic.what: A garlic bulb cold-smoked over wood for a campfire flavour.

facts: Gouda takes its name from the town of Gouda in the Netherlands.
Cheese-making has a long history in the Netherlands, and Gouda is among its best-known exports.
smoked-gouda.visual: a block of smoked Gouda with one wedge cut away, pale golden paste and a smoky amber rind
smoked-gouda.what: A Dutch cheese with a mellow, gently smoky aroma.

facts: Finnan haddie takes its name from Findon, a fishing village near Aberdeen where it was traditionally smoked.
Kedgeree, a dish of rice, eggs and flaked fish, was adapted in Britain from the Indian dish khichdi.
smoked-haddock.visual: one smoked haddock fillet, golden yellow flesh with a flaky texture, skin side down, lying flat
smoked-haddock.what: A mildly smoked white fish, golden and flaky.

facts: Halibut is a large flatfish found in cold northern seas.
Smoking preserves fish and gives it a gentle, woodsmoke flavour.
smoked-halibut.visual: a fillet of smoked halibut cut into thin pale pink slices, lying flat
smoked-halibut.what: A firm white fish, smoked for a mild, silky flavour.

facts: A ham hock is the lower part of a pig's leg, often cured or smoked before sale.
Pea and ham soup is a classic British dish that often uses a smoked hock.
smoked-ham-hock.visual: one whole smoked pork hock with golden-brown skin and pink meat showing at the cut end
smoked-ham-hock.what: A pig's lower leg, cured or smoked for deep flavour.

facts: Mackerel are oily fish that shoal in the Atlantic and other temperate seas.
Smoked mackerel is often flaked into pâté, salads or sandwiches.
Smoking fish was traditionally a way to preserve it before refrigeration became common.
smoked-mackerel-fillet.visual: a smoked mackerel fillet, its glossy golden-brown skin and pale flesh showing, lying flat on the background
smoked-mackerel-fillet.what: Oily, smoky fish fillet, ready to eat without cooking.

facts: Smoking is one of the oldest ways of flavouring food, and mushrooms are smoked in many cuisines.
Hot smoking cooks the mushrooms as it flavours them, while cold smoking adds flavour without cooking.
smoked-mushrooms.visual: a small heap of smoked mushroom caps, golden brown with darker smoky edges, lying loose
smoked-mushrooms.what: Caps smoked over wood for a savoury, woody flavour.

facts: Smoked paprika, called pimenton, is made in the Vera valley of Spain.
The peppers are dried over smoked oak fires, which gives the powder its woody flavour.
It is a key flavour in Spanish dishes such as chorizo and paella.
smoked-paprika.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of brick-red smoked paprika powder
smoked-paprika.what: A brick-red powder of dried peppers smoked over oak.

facts: Salmon has been smoked in northern Europe for centuries as a way to preserve it.
Cold-smoked salmon is not cooked, which gives it a silky texture when sliced thinly.
It is served on bagels in New York and on blinis in Russian cooking.
smoked-salmon.visual: a few thin, translucent slices of smoked salmon, pinkish-orange, laid flat and overlapping
smoked-salmon.what: Thin, silky slices of salmon cured and smoked over wood.

facts: Salmon has been smoked and cured in Scandinavia for centuries, as a way to preserve it.
Smoked salmon is widely eaten in Britain, often served on brown bread with lemon.
smoked-salmon-trimmings.visual: a small heap of pink smoked salmon offcuts, irregular pieces with a silky texture
smoked-salmon-trimmings.what: Pieces left over when smoked salmon is sliced for sale.

facts: Smoking was once a common way to preserve meat and fish, long before refrigeration.
Smoked salts are made by exposing sea salt to wood smoke, often oak, hickory or apple.
Sea salt is made by evaporating seawater, leaving crystals behind.
smoked-sea-salt.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of coarse grey-brown smoked sea salt flakes
smoked-sea-salt.what: Sea salt flakes smoked over wood for a smoky flavour.

facts: Sprats are small members of the herring family, found in the North Atlantic and Baltic seas.
Smoking was a traditional way to preserve oily fish before refrigeration.
Smoked sprats are often eaten as a snack with bread or crackers.
smoked-sprats.visual: a small heap of smoked sprats, golden-brown whole fish, tails visible
smoked-sprats.what: Small smoked fish, often sold whole and eaten on bread.

facts: Sturgeon are large fish found in northern rivers and seas, and their roe is used to make caviar.
Smoking is a traditional way of preserving sturgeon in parts of Russia and Eastern Europe.
smoked-sturgeon.visual: a smoked sturgeon fillet with bronze-brown skin, one end sliced to show pale pink flesh, on a plain background
smoked-sturgeon.what: A large fish whose rich flesh is smoked and sliced.

facts: Tofu was developed in China, where soya milk was curdled and pressed into blocks many centuries ago.
Smoked tofu is popular in vegetarian cooking, where its smokiness stands in for meat flavours.
Soya milk is set with a coagulant such as nigari or calcium sulphate to form tofu.
smoked-tofu.visual: a firm block of smoked tofu, golden-brown outside, with one slice cut and lying flat in front of it
smoked-tofu.what: Firm tofu that has been smoked for a deep, savoury taste.

facts: Trout has been smoked in Europe and North America as a way to preserve the fish.
Smoked trout is either hot-smoked, which cooks it, or cold-smoked, which only flavours it.
smoked-trout.visual: one smoked trout fillet, pinkish-orange flesh, glossy skin on one side, lying flat
smoked-trout.what: Delicate, moist fish, cured and smoked for a rich flavour.

facts: Turkeys were first domesticated in Mexico and Central America, and later spread across Europe.
Smoking meat was a way to preserve it long before refrigeration, and it gives turkey a deep, woody flavour.
smoked-turkey-breast.visual: a smoked turkey breast with a golden-brown smoked surface and one slice cut away
smoked-turkey-breast.what: Turkey breast smoked for flavour and sold as deli slices.

facts: Potato crisps are thin slices of potato fried or baked until crisp, which gives them their crunch.
smoky-bacon-crisps.visual: a small heap of golden thin potato crisps with a dusting of smoky seasoning
smoky-bacon-crisps.what: Crisps with a salty, smoky flavour that tastes like bacon.

facts: Barbecue sauce is usually based on tomato, vinegar and sugar, with added spices.
Its smoky taste can come from smoked ingredients such as paprika or chipotle chillies.
Barbecue sauces vary widely, from thin vinegar styles to thick, sweet tomato ones.
smoky-bbq-sauce.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of dark reddish-brown smoky barbecue sauce
smoky-bbq-sauce.what: A dark, thick barbecue sauce with a strong smoky flavour.

facts: Chipotles are smoked, dried jalapeno chillies from Mexico.
Chipotle salsa is made by cooking tomatoes, onion and chipotles together.
The smoky flavour comes from the chillies being dried over wood smoke.
smoky-chipotle-salsa.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of chunky, smoky reddish-brown salsa
smoky-chipotle-salsa.what: A smoky, chunky tomato sauce with a little chilli heat.

facts: Snake gourd is a tropical vine crop whose fruit can grow surprisingly long and thin, hence its name.
It is widely used in South Indian cooking, often in curries, stir-fries and dals.
Young fruit is picked while tender, because older fruit becomes fibrous and bitter.
snake-gourd.visual: one whole long, thin snake gourd, pale green with faint white stripes, lying straight on the background
snake-gourd.what: A long, thin, mild-tasting gourd eaten in South Asia.

facts: Snipe are wading birds of marshes and wet meadows, known for their zigzag flight when flushed.
Their long bills probe soft mud for worms and insects.
Once roasted whole and served on toast, the bird was prized in British and Irish cooking.
snipe.visual: one whole raw bird, long slender bill, speckled brown feathers, lying on its breast
snipe.what: A small wading game bird with rich, dark meat.

facts: Snow crab lives in cold, deep waters of the North Pacific and North Atlantic.
Snow crab is usually sold cooked and frozen, and the legs are cracked open to reach the meat.
snow-crab-legs.visual: a cluster of three pale orange-red cooked crab legs with the shell intact, lying flat
snow-crab-legs.what: Long, slender crab legs with sweet, delicate white meat.

facts: Snow fungus is also called silver ear or white fungus, and grows on decaying hardwood trees.
It is widely cultivated in China, where it has been used in soups and desserts for centuries.
Dried snow fungus softens and swells when soaked, becoming translucent and jelly-like.
snow-fungus.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dried, curled, creamy white snow fungus pieces
snow-fungus.what: A pale, jelly-like fungus for soups and sweet desserts.

facts: Soba is the Japanese word for buckwheat, and the noodles are often made with some wheat flour.
Buckwheat is not a true wheat, and soba is traditionally eaten at New Year in Japan.
It is served hot in broth or chilled with a dipping sauce.
soba-noodles.visual: a small loose heap of thin, greyish-brown dried buckwheat noodles on a plain background
soba-noodles.what: Thin Japanese noodles made from buckwheat flour.

facts: Sobrasada is a cured sausage from the Spanish island of Mallorca.
It is made from minced pork and paprika, and is often spread on bread.
sobrasada.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of soft, deep red spreadable sausage
sobrasada.what: A soft, spreadable pork sausage flavoured with paprika.

facts: Sockeye salmon hatch in freshwater, migrate to the sea, and return to their home streams to spawn.
Their deep red flesh comes from the tiny crustaceans and plankton they eat at sea.
Sockeye has long been fished on the Pacific coast of North America and is sold fresh, smoked or canned.
sockeye-salmon.visual: a skinless fillet of bright deep-red sockeye salmon with firm flesh and fine white lines, lying flat
sockeye-salmon.what: A deep red Pacific salmon with rich, firm flesh.

facts: Soda bread became a staple in Ireland after bicarbonate of soda became widely available in the 1800s.
Bicarbonate of soda reacts with the acid in buttermilk to make the loaf rise, so no yeast is needed.
Many Irish bakers mark a cross on the top before baking.
soda-bread.visual: one whole round loaf of soda bread, floury golden crust, a cross cut on top
soda-bread.what: A crumbly Irish loaf raised with bicarbonate of soda.

facts: Soda water was developed in the 18th century by adding carbon dioxide to water.
The fizz comes from dissolved carbon dioxide, which forms bubbles when the pressure is released.
soda-water.visual: a clear drinking glass of plain, fizzing water with small bubbles rising
soda-water.what: Plain sparkling water, used for light, crisp batters.

facts: Soft-boiled eggs are cooked in boiling water for a few minutes, leaving the yolk runny.
In Britain it is often served in an egg cup with buttered bread strips.
Cooking time is key, since the white sets while the yolk stays soft.
soft-boiled-egg.visual: one whole peeled soft-boiled egg, smooth pale white surface, lying on its side on a plain background
soft-boiled-egg.what: An egg boiled just long enough to keep a runny yolk.

facts: Flour tortillas are associated with northern Mexico, where wheat grows more readily than maize.
Corn tortillas are the older tradition in central Mexico; flour versions became popular in the north.
The word tortilla comes from Spanish, a diminutive of torta, meaning a small round cake.
soft-flour-tortilla.visual: a single round, soft flour tortilla, flat and pale with a few light golden spots, lying open
soft-flour-tortilla.what: A soft, thin wheat flour wrap for rolling and folding.

facts: Goat's cheese is an ancient food, and in France the word chèvre is used for it.
Goat's cheese is produced across Britain, France, Spain and the Middle East in both soft and aged forms.
soft-goat-s-cheese.visual: a small soft white log of goat's cheese with one slice cut from its end, lying on the background
soft-goat-s-cheese.what: A fresh, tangy goat's cheese that crumbles easily.

facts: Herring roes are the egg sacs of female herring, prized in Scottish and Scandinavian cooking.
Herring roes on toast is a traditional dish in Scotland, often served for breakfast or tea.
soft-herring-roes.visual: two soft pale orange-cream herring roes, glossy and whole, lying side by side
soft-herring-roes.what: Soft, creamy fish roes, usually fried on buttered toast.

facts: Traditional pretzels are dipped in an alkaline solution before baking, which browns their crust.
They are often eaten warm with mustard, a traditional pairing in Germany.
soft-pretzel.visual: one whole soft pretzel twist on a plain white plate, glossy dark brown crust, coarse salt grains on top
soft-pretzel.what: A chewy, salted bread twist with a dark crust.

facts: Soft-shell crabs are usually blue crabs, caught just after they moult while the new shell is still soft.
They are popular in the United States, especially along the Atlantic coast, where they are often fried.
Once cooked, the whole crab is eaten, shell included, because the new shell has not yet hardened.
soft-shell-crab.visual: one whole raw soft-shell crab, pale greenish-brown shell, legs tucked neatly underneath, lying on its side
soft-shell-crab.what: A crab that moults its shell and is eaten whole.

facts: Soju is traditionally distilled from rice, though modern versions often use other starches or sugar.
It is usually drunk neat from small glasses, often during shared meals in Korea.
In Korean drinking culture, soju is often mixed with beer, a combination known as somaek.
soju.visual: a clear drinking glass filled to the brim with clear, colourless liquid
soju.what: A clear, mild distilled spirit from Korea.

facts: Somen are made from wheat flour and salt, stretched into very thin strands and dried.
Somen are traditionally eaten chilled in summer, and a version called nagashi somen is served flowing down a bamboo channel.
Somen are often dipped in a broth called tsuyu, and served with grated ginger and spring onion.
somen-noodles.visual: a small neat bundle of very fine, pale dried noodles lying straight, on a plain background
somen-noodles.what: Very thin Japanese wheat noodles, often served chilled.

facts: Traditional soppressata is made from coarsely chopped pork, salt and pepper, and cured for weeks.
soppressata.visual: a whole flattened round soppressata salami with a dark red-brown casing, marbled with flecks of white fat
soppressata.what: A coarse Italian salami, sometimes spiced with chilli.

facts: Sorghum is a cereal grass that has been cultivated in Africa for thousands of years.
Today it is grown widely in Africa, India, China and the Americas.
Sorghum is also grown for syrup and for animal feed, not only for people to eat.
sorghum.visual: a small heap of pale cream sorghum grains, round and smooth, spread on a plain background
sorghum.what: A chewy cereal grain, rather like a tiny wheat berry.

facts: Sorghum is a cereal grass grown in Africa, Asia and the southern United States.
Sorghum syrup was a common sweetener in the rural American South.
The syrup is made by crushing the stalks and boiling down the juice.
sorghum-syrup.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of dark amber syrup, standing upright
sorghum-syrup.what: A thick, dark syrup made from sweet sorghum stalks.

facts: Sorrel has been eaten in Europe since medieval times and grows wild in many temperate regions.
Sorrel's sharp taste comes from natural acids in the leaves, so it is used in small amounts.
In French cooking, sorrel is used in soups and sauces, and is often served with fish.
sorrel.visual: a small bunch of fresh garden sorrel, broad bright green arrow-shaped leaves, stems tied
sorrel.what: A tangy green herb with leaves that taste sharply lemony.

facts: Sour cherries, also called morello cherries, are grown across central and eastern Europe and Turkey.
Their sharpness suits pies, jams and sauces, which is why cooks often preserve them for winter.
sour-cherry-preserve.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with dark red cherries in thick, glossy syrup
sour-cherry-preserve.what: Tart cherries cooked slowly in a thick, sweet syrup.

facts: Sour cream is a cultured dairy product made by fermenting cream with lactic acid bacteria.
Crisps are thin slices of potato, fried or baked until crisp, and the flavour is added afterwards.
Snipped chives are a common topping for baked potatoes, in Britain and beyond.
sour-cream-and-chive-crisps.visual: a small heap of pale golden crisps, speckled with small green herb flecks, served on a plain white plate
sour-cream-and-chive-crisps.what: Crunchy crisps with a tangy cream and herb flavour.

facts: Sour cream is cream soured by lactic acid bacteria, which gives it a tangy taste.
Chives belong to the onion family and have a mild, grassy onion flavour.
sour-cream-and-chive-dip.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick pale cream dip flecked with bright green chopped chives
sour-cream-and-chive-dip.what: Cool, tangy dip of soured cream and snipped chives.

facts: Tortilla chips are made from corn tortillas cut into triangles and then fried or baked until crisp.
Tortillas are a staple of Mexican cooking and have been made from maize for centuries.
sour-cream-and-chive-tortilla-chips.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with pale triangular tortilla chips, lightly flecked in green
sour-cream-and-chive-tortilla-chips.what: Crisp corn chips with a creamy, herby coating.

facts: Boule is the French word for ball, and the name describes the classic round shape of the loaf.
Sourdough is among the oldest methods of making bread, long predating commercial yeast.
sourdough-boule.visual: one whole round artisan loaf with a deep golden-brown crust and a scored pattern across the top
sourdough-boule.what: A round loaf raised with a natural wild-yeast starter.

facts: Crumpets are a traditional British griddle cake, cooked in metal rings on a hot griddle.
Crumpets are cooked on one side only, and the holes form as the batter bubbles.
A sourdough starter is a fermented mix of flour and water, used to raise bread for centuries.
sourdough-crumpets.visual: a single round golden sourdough crumpet with a holey top, on a plain white plate
sourdough-crumpets.what: A chewy, tangy British griddle cake with a holey top.

facts: Sourdough is leavened by a starter of wild yeasts and bacteria, not by commercial yeast.
Bread made this way has been baked for thousands of years, long before commercial yeast.
The sour flavour comes from lactic acid produced by bacteria during long fermentation.
sourdough-loaf.visual: one whole uncut round sourdough loaf with a blistered, floury golden crust
sourdough-loaf.what: A tangy, chewy bread leavened with wild yeast culture.

facts: Sourdough uses a wild culture of yeast and bacteria, instead of commercial yeast.
Neapolitan-style pizza is cooked quickly in a very hot oven, giving a blistered crust.
sourdough-pizza-base.visual: a round sourdough pizza base, baked, with a blistered golden crust and charred spots, served plainly on a plain white plate
sourdough-pizza-base.what: A chewy, tangy round base made from fermented sourdough.

facts: Sourdough starters can be kept alive for many years and passed between bakers.
Wild yeasts and bacteria in the starter give sourdough bread its tang and open crumb.
Bakers have leavened bread with fermented starters for thousands of years.
sourdough-starter.visual: a plain glass jar without a label holding pale, bubbly sourdough starter, a creamy paste with bubbles on top
sourdough-starter.what: A living mix of flour and water that raises tangy bread.

facts: Sour cream has been eaten in Eastern Europe for centuries, where it is served with soups and dumplings.
In Britain it is often called soured cream, and in the United States sour cream.
soured-cream.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick white soured cream with a smooth glossy surface
soured-cream.what: A thick, tangy cream that has been soured with cultures.

facts: Soursop is native to the tropical Americas and is widely grown across the Caribbean.
Graviola is its Portuguese name, widely used in Brazil.
The soft white flesh is often blended into juices, smoothies and ice cream.
soursop.visual: one whole soursop fruit, large oval green fruit with soft spiky skin and a few dark spines
soursop.what: A large spiky tropical fruit with creamy white flesh.

facts: Soused herring is a traditional northern European preparation, popular in Britain, Germany and Scandinavia.
Soused herring is cured in vinegar with spices such as allspice, bay leaves and peppercorns.
Rollmops are a related dish, where each fillet is rolled around a pickled gherkin or onion.
soused-herring.visual: a portion of soused herring fillets, pale and firm, curled neatly on a plain white plate
soused-herring.what: A cold dish of fish fillets preserved in spiced vinegar.

facts: Ajitsuke tamago is the Japanese name for this egg, which is seasoned by soaking in soy and sweet mirin.
The yolk stays soft because the egg is cooked only briefly before it is marinated.
It is a common topping for ramen noodle soup, served halved so the soft yolk shows.
soy-marinated-egg.visual: one whole peeled soft-boiled egg, glossy amber-tinted white, lying on a plain white plate
soy-marinated-egg.what: A soft-boiled egg with a jammy yolk, steeped in soy sauce.

facts: Soya beans have been grown in East Asia for thousands of years.
In Korea they are called kongnamul and are often served as a side dish.
soya-bean-sprouts.visual: a small heap of raw soya bean sprouts, pale white stems with yellow-green tips
soya-bean-sprouts.what: Crisp pale shoots sprouted from soya beans.

facts: Soya was domesticated in East Asia, where it has been grown for thousands of years.
Soya beans are used to make tofu, soy sauce, tempeh and miso, among many other foods.
Today large quantities are grown in the Americas, including the United States and Brazil.
soya-beans.visual: a small heap of dried pale yellow soya beans, smooth and round, loosely piled
soya-beans.what: Pale round beans that become tofu, tempeh and miso.

facts: Soya was first domesticated in East Asia, where it has been eaten for centuries.
They are soaked in hot water before being added to curries and stir-fries.
soya-chunks.visual: a small heap of dried soya chunks, pale tan and irregular, with rough, porous surfaces
soya-chunks.what: Dried soya pieces that soak up water and become chewy.

facts: Soya milk has been made in China for many centuries, from soaked and ground soya beans.
Soya milk is a common dairy alternative and is used in tea, coffee and baking.
soya-milk.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of creamy off-white soya milk
soya-milk.what: A creamy milk made from ground soya beans and water.

facts: Textured soya was developed in the 20th century as a meat alternative.
Soya is a legume native to East Asia and is grown widely around the world.
soya-mince.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dry, pale brown textured soya granules
soya-mince.what: Dried soya granules that swell into a mince-like texture.

facts: Soya oil is a common frying and salad oil, valued for its very mild flavour.
Soybeans were first domesticated in East Asia, where they have been eaten for centuries.
soya-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden oil, the oil filling the lower half
soya-oil.what: A pale, neutral oil pressed from soya beans.

facts: The name is a South German word that is a diminutive of the word for sparrow.
The dough is pushed or scraped through a sieve or grater into boiling water.
It is often tossed with cheese and butter, or served with gravy.
spaetzle.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of small, soft, pale yellow egg dumplings, irregular and slightly golden at the edges
spaetzle.what: Tiny, soft egg dumplings from southern German cooking.

facts: Spaghetti means little strings in Italian, and it is one of the best-known pasta shapes.
Dried spaghetti is traditionally made from durum wheat semolina, which holds its shape when cooked.
Spaghetti is cooked in boiling salted water in Italy and around the world.
spaghetti.visual: a loose heap of dry, uncooked spaghetti strands, pale golden yellow
spaghetti.what: Long, thin strands of pasta, usually made from durum wheat.

facts: Chitarra means guitar, after the wooden frame strung with wires that cuts the pasta.
The dough is pressed through the frame so the wires cut it into square strands.
Chitarra pasta is often served with rich sauces such as lamb ragù, which cling to its square edges.
spaghetti-alla-chitarra.visual: a small neat heap of uncooked pale yellow square-section spaghetti strands, matte and dry
spaghetti-alla-chitarra.what: Square-cut egg pasta from Abruzzo in central Italy.

facts: It is a variety of Cucurbita pepo, the same species as courgettes.
When baked, the flesh separates into long strands that resemble spaghetti.
It is usually halved, baked, and then the strands are scraped out of the shell.
spaghetti-squash.visual: one whole raw spaghetti squash, oval and pale yellow with fine lengthwise ridges
spaghetti-squash.what: A yellow winter squash whose cooked flesh forms strands.

facts: Spaghettini is a thinner version of spaghetti, made in the same long strand shape.
Its name is the Italian diminutive of spaghetti, meaning little spaghetti.
Dried pasta like this is usually made from durum wheat semolina and water.
spaghettini.visual: a neat heap of thin, straight dried spaghettini strands, pale golden-cream, lying loosely
spaghettini.what: Very thin spaghetti, often used with light sauces.

facts: Spanish mackerel is a fast-swimming fish found in warm coastal seas.
Mackerel as a group are fast, schooling fish that often migrate over long distances.
Its firm flesh suits grilling, and it is often cut into steaks for cooking.
spanish-mackerel.visual: a whole raw Spanish mackerel, silvery blue back with dark streaks, lying on its side
spanish-mackerel.what: A firm, meaty fish with dark streaks along its back.

facts: Onions are thought to have been cultivated in Central Asia for thousands of years.
Mild onions like the Spanish type are often eaten raw in salads and sandwiches.
Sliced into rings, onions are fried, battered or pickled in many cuisines around the world.
spanish-onion.visual: one whole raw onion, papery golden-brown skin, lying on its side on the background
spanish-onion.what: A large, mild brown onion, good sliced raw.

facts: Many sparkling wines get their bubbles from a second fermentation inside the bottle.
Champagne is a sparkling wine from the Champagne region of France, and other regions make their own.
Prosecco, from Italy, is a widely drunk sparkling wine and is also used in cooking.
sparkling-wine.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with pale golden sparkling white wine, bubbles rising
sparkling-wine.what: A fizzy white wine for toasts, sauces and cocktails.

facts: Spatchcocking means removing the backbone and flattening a bird so that it cooks evenly.
spatchcock-chicken.visual: one whole raw spatchcocked chicken, backbone removed and flattened, pale skin, lying flat
spatchcock-chicken.what: A chicken flattened for quick, even roasting or grilling.

facts: Spearmint is Mentha spicata, and it is widely used in mint sauce served with lamb.
spearmint.visual: a small bunch of fresh spearmint with bright green, pointed, toothed leaves on thin stalks
spearmint.what: A sweet, fresh mint with bright green, soft leaves.

facts: The ham is salted and seasoned with juniper and pepper, then lightly smoked and air-dried.
The name is the German word for bacon.
speck.visual: a neatly cut thin slice of dark smoky ham, rosy pink meat and white fat, edge of brown rind
speck.what: Smoked, cured ham from the Alps, flavoured with juniper.

facts: Spelt is an ancient wheat relative that has been grown in Europe for thousands of years.
Its flour has a nutty flavour and is often used in breads and baking.
Spelt loaves are popular in Germany and parts of central Europe.
spelt-bread.visual: a whole rustic loaf of spelt bread, its crust pale golden and lightly floured
spelt-bread.what: A nutty, easy-to-slice loaf made from an ancient wheat.

facts: Spelt is an ancient wheat that has been grown in Europe for thousands of years.
Its flour is used in breads, pasta and cakes as an alternative to ordinary wheat flour.
Spelt has a tough husk, so the grain is usually hulled before it is milled into flour.
spelt-flour.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale spelt flour, fine and loosely heaped
spelt-flour.what: An ancient wheat flour with a mild, nutty taste.

facts: Spelt is an ancient species of wheat that has been grown in Europe for thousands of years.
Spelt is a hulled wheat, so its grains must be separated from tough husks after harvest.
spelt-grains.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale golden spelt grains
spelt-grains.what: A nutty, ancient wheat grain with a chewy texture.

facts: It is made from pork seasoned with hot red pepper, which gives Calabrian salami its heat.
Its name comes from the Italian word for flattened, referring to its shape.
spianata-piccante.visual: a whole flat round salami, dark red-brown casing, rustic and slightly uneven, lying flat
spianata-piccante.what: A flat, spicy salami from Calabria in southern Italy.

facts: Rum is distilled from sugar cane juice or molasses, and is made in the Caribbean and beyond.
It is often used in Caribbean cocktails and in rich cakes and puddings for its warm flavour.
spiced-rum.visual: a clear drinking glass of amber-brown spiced rum, filled to just below the rim
spiced-rum.what: Dark rum infused with vanilla, cinnamon and warm spices.

facts: Spiced vinegar is flavoured with spices and sugar, and is often served on chips.
It is closely associated with the city of Sheffield in South Yorkshire.
spiced-vinegar-relish.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of dark amber spiced vinegar liquid
spiced-vinegar-relish.what: A sharp, sweet and spiced vinegar sauce from Sheffield.

facts: The mix is a classic Mexican way to season fruit, cucumber and corn.
Chilli and lime salt is often rolled on the rim of a glass for a michelada.
spicy-salt-tajin-style.visual: a plain glass jar without a label holding bright red-orange chilli and lime salt
spicy-salt-tajin-style.what: A bright mix of dried chilli, lime and salt.

facts: Their sweet meat is found mainly in the legs and claws, and it is prized by seafood cooks.
Spider crab is eaten in Britain and France, usually cooked and picked for its meat.
spider-crab.visual: one whole raw spider crab, orange-brown shell with long spiny legs folded in, on a plain white background
spider-crab.what: A crab with long legs and sweet, delicate meat.

facts: Spinach is thought to have originated in ancient Persia.
Spinach reached Europe through Moorish Spain during the Middle Ages.
In India, spinach is cooked into dishes such as saag and palak paneer.
spinach.visual: a loose bunch of fresh spinach, dark green crinkled leaves with the stems trimmed
spinach.what: Dark green leaves that wilt in seconds when heated.

facts: Feta is a brined white cheese traditionally made in Greece from sheep's milk or a sheep and goat blend.
Spinach is thought to have originated in ancient Persia, and it later spread across Europe.
Spinach and feta pies such as spanakopita are a well-known part of Greek cooking.
spinach-and-feta-tart.visual: a wedge of spinach and feta tart, golden short pastry edge, pale green filling and crumbled white cheese, on a plain white plate
spinach-and-feta-tart.what: A savoury pastry tart filled with spinach and salty feta.

facts: Tortellini are small filled pasta from northern Italy, traditionally made by hand.
Ricotta is a soft cheese made from whey, the liquid left after cheese curds form.
Spinach is a leafy green that was grown in Persia and later spread across Europe through trade.
spinach-and-ricotta-tortellini.visual: a small heap of fresh tortellini, small pale-yellow pasta rings with a green-flecked filling showing
spinach-and-ricotta-tortellini.what: Small pasta rings filled with spinach and soft ricotta.

facts: Green lasagne gets its colour from spinach puree mixed into the pasta dough.
Lasagne is a wide, flat pasta layered with sauce and cheese, then baked.
The word lasagne is thought to come from the Greek lasanon, meaning a cooking pot.
spinach-lasagne-sheets.visual: one whole uncooked green lasagne sheet, rectangular, bright green and flat
spinach-lasagne-sheets.what: Flat, wide pasta sheets tinted green with spinach.

facts: Tagliatelle is a long, flat egg pasta from Emilia-Romagna in northern Italy.
Spinach pasta is made by blending cooked spinach into the egg dough, which colours it green.
Spinach reached Europe from the Middle East and became popular in Italian cooking.
spinach-tagliatelle.visual: a small loose heap of fresh green tagliatelle ribbons, flat and smooth, bright emerald colour
spinach-tagliatelle.what: Flat pasta ribbons coloured green with spinach.

facts: Wraps are flatbreads made from flour, water and fat, rolled around a filling.
Flatbreads have been baked in many parts of the world for thousands of years.
spinach-wrap.visual: a single round, flat, pale green tortilla-style wrap, folded neatly in half
spinach-wrap.what: A soft flatbread wrap coloured green with spinach.

facts: Spiny lobsters lack the large front claws of the true lobster, and their shells are covered in spines.
Their tails are often grilled, or poached and served with melted butter.
spiny-lobster.visual: one whole raw spiny lobster, reddish-brown shell covered in spines, long antennae
spiny-lobster.what: A clawless warm-water lobster with sweet, firm tail meat.

facts: Black gram is a pulse native to the Indian subcontinent and has been grown there for a long time.
Once hulled and split it turns pale and cooks quickly, giving dal a creamy texture.
Urad dal is central to idli and dosa batter, which is fermented before it is cooked.
split-black-gram.visual: a small heap of split, hulled pulse halves, creamy pale and matt, loose on the background
split-black-gram.what: Hulled and split dried pulse, common in Indian dal.

facts: Split mung beans are a staple of Indian cooking, where they are simmered into dal.
Mung beans have been cultivated in South Asia for thousands of years.
split-mung-beans.visual: a small heap of split yellow mung beans, pale golden with the dark green skins removed
split-mung-beans.what: Small yellow beans that have been split and hulled.

facts: Split tin loaves are a traditional British bread, often baked as a plain white loaf.
The loaf rises above its tin, and the crust opens along the split as the dough expands.
Bakers cut the top of the dough so that the loaf rises in a controlled way.
split-tin-loaf.visual: one whole split tin loaf, pale golden crust with a deep split along the top, lying on the background
split-tin-loaf.what: A tin-baked loaf with a deep split along its top.

facts: The Italian name, savoiardi, is linked to the Savoy region in the Alps.
They are baked dry, so they absorb liquid and soften when dipped.
They are a key layer in tiramisu, the Italian dessert soaked in coffee.
sponge-fingers.visual: a small heap of pale golden, finger-shaped sponge biscuits, crisp and dry
sponge-fingers.what: Light, dry, finger-shaped biscuits for trifles.

facts: Spotted dick is a traditional British pudding, usually made with suet and steamed or boiled.
It is traditionally served hot, often with custard.
spotted-dick.visual: a thick slice of steamed suet pudding, pale sponge speckled with dark currants, served on a plain white plate
spotted-dick.what: A steamed sponge pudding studded with dried currants.

facts: They are often coated in flour and fried whole, so the small bones are eaten too.
Sprats are also salted, smoked or pickled as well as fried.
sprats.visual: a small heap of tiny silver whole sprats, slim bodies and dark-blue backs
sprats.what: A small, oily sea fish, often fried whole and eaten.

facts: Spring greens do not form a firm head, and they are harvested young in early spring.
Spring greens are a type of cabbage, closely related to kale and Brussels sprouts.
In Britain they are commonly shredded and steamed, or quickly stir-fried.
spring-greens.visual: a loose bunch of crinkled pale green spring greens, leaves unwrapped and fresh
spring-greens.what: A loose-leafed cabbage with crinkled, pale green leaves.

facts: Spring onions are young onions harvested before their bulbs have fully formed.
In Britain they are often called salad onions, while in the United States they are called scallions or green onions.
Spring onions are used raw in salads and cooked in stir-fries across East and Southeast Asia.
spring-onion.visual: a small bunch of fresh spring onions, white bulbs and long green stems, roots trimmed
spring-onion.what: Young onion with a mild flavour, eaten white and green.

facts: Wrappers are made from wheat flour, water and a little salt, rolled out very thin.
Rice paper rolls use a related wrapper, made from rice flour and water instead.
spring-roll-wrapper.visual: a few thin pale spring roll wrappers stacked on a plain white plate
spring-roll-wrapper.what: Thin, pale sheets of pastry that fry to a crisp.

facts: Squab is a young domestic pigeon, typically killed before it fledges, which gives it tender, dark meat.
Pigeon has been kept for food for thousands of years, and squab is still served in French and Chinese cooking.
squab.visual: one whole plump raw young pigeon, pale skin, lying on its breast
squab.what: A young farmed pigeon with tender, rich meat.

facts: In Britain, squash usually means a concentrated fruit cordial, often blackcurrant or orange.
Cordial is the general term for fruit syrups that are mixed with still or sparkling water.
Diluting it lets each drinker adjust the strength to their taste.
squash.visual: a clear drinking glass half full of bright orange fruit squash
squash.what: A sweet fruit concentrate, mixed with water to drink.

facts: Squid are found in seas around the world, and many species live in deep water.
Squid is eaten in many cuisines, from Italian fried seafood to Spanish and Japanese dishes.
squid.visual: a whole raw squid with a pale speckled body and curled tentacles, lying flat on the background
squid.what: A soft sea creature with eight arms and two tentacles.

facts: Squid ink has long been used in coastal Italian cooking, both to colour pasta and to make risotto.
The ink is taken from the sac of a squid or cuttlefish and is mixed into the pasta dough.
Nero di seppia means black of the cuttlefish, a reference to the ink's source.
squid-ink-pasta.visual: a neatly coiled nest of jet-black dried pasta strands, lying directly on a plain background
squid-ink-pasta.what: Thin black pasta made with squid ink.

facts: Squid have eight arms and two longer tentacles, which they use to catch prey.
Fried squid, known as calamari in Italy, is a classic dish across the Mediterranean.
squid-tentacles.visual: a small pile of raw, pale creamy-white squid tentacles, with suckers faintly visible, lying on the background
squid-tentacles.what: The long arms of squid, eaten crisp when quickly fried.

facts: Squid is found in oceans around the world and is eaten in many cuisines, from Mediterranean to East Asian.
Squid are cephalopods, relatives of octopus and cuttlefish, with a soft tubular body.
Squid turns rubbery if cooked for a moderate time, so cooks either sear it briefly or braise it slowly.
squid-tubes.visual: one whole cleaned raw squid tube, smooth, pale white and translucent, lying straight on a plain background
squid-tubes.what: They are cleaned squid bodies, ready to stuff or slice.

facts: Whipping cream works by trapping air bubbles in its fat, which is why cream thickens as it is beaten.
squirty-cream.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl holding a soft swirl of white whipped cream
squirty-cream.what: Sweetened cream whipped to a soft, airy foam.

facts: Sriracha takes its name from Si Racha, a coastal town in eastern Thailand.
The sauce is now widely used in both Asian and Western kitchens as a table and cooking condiment.
sriracha.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with glossy bright red chilli sauce
sriracha.what: A smooth, garlicky chilli sauce with sweet and hot flavours.

facts: Sriracha is a hot sauce named after the coastal town of Si Racha in Thailand.
Mayonnaise is an emulsion of oil and egg yolk, thickened by slowly whisking the oil in.
sriracha-mayonnaise.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of creamy pale orange-pink mayonnaise with a smooth surface
sriracha-mayonnaise.what: A creamy, pale orange mayonnaise with a warm chilli kick.

facts: Ssamjang is a Korean condiment made from soybean paste mixed with chilli and garlic.
Its name combines the Korean words for wrap (ssam) and sauce or paste (jang).
Koreans eat it wrapped in lettuce or perilla leaves alongside grilled meat.
ssamjang.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, dark red-brown paste, glossy and smooth
ssamjang.what: A thick, spicy Korean paste for dipping lettuce wraps.

facts: It is named after St George's Day, 23 April, when it often appears in spring.
It often grows in grassland and can form fairy rings, found across Europe.
st-george-s-mushroom.visual: a small bunch of pale cream mushrooms with broad caps and a dry, fine surface
st-george-s-mushroom.what: A spring mushroom with a fresh, floury smell.

facts: It is a key ingredient in Chinese five-spice and is used to flavour Vietnamese pho.
Star anise is not related to the anise plant, though both taste of liquorice.
star-anise.visual: a small cluster of whole, glossy reddish-brown star-shaped pods, each with eight points
star-anise.what: An eight-pointed brown pod with a warm liquorice flavour.

facts: Starfruit is native to Southeast Asia and Sri Lanka, and is now grown in many warm countries.
Its scientific name is Averrhoa carambola, and it belongs to the wood-sorrel family.
Cut across, each slice forms a five-pointed star, which is why it is used as a decoration.
starfruit.visual: one whole yellow starfruit with five ribbed edges, waxy skin, lying on its side
starfruit.what: A yellow tropical fruit that slices into stars.

facts: The pie was traditionally made with pilchards, a small oily fish once plentiful off the Cornish coast.
stargazy-pie.visual: a single portion of golden baked pie on a plain white plate, small fish heads poking through the crust
stargazy-pie.what: A Cornish pie with fish heads poking through the crust.

facts: Steak and ale pie is a traditional British pub dish, with beef slowly stewed in a dark ale.
The filling is slowly stewed before the pastry lid is added and baked until golden.
steak-and-ale-pie.visual: a plain white plate holding one portion of steak and ale pie, golden pastry crust on top and dark gravy showing at the cut edge
steak-and-ale-pie.what: Beef in dark ale gravy under a flaky pastry lid.

facts: It is made with flaky pastry wrapped around diced beef in gravy.
steak-bake.visual: a golden flaky pastry steak bake, cut open to show chunks of brown steak in gravy, on a plain white plate
steak-bake.what: A flaky pastry slice filled with steak and gravy.

facts: In Britain and Ireland, chips means fried potato strips, while in North America the word means crisps.
Potatoes were first cultivated in the Andes of South America long before they reached Europe.
Thick-cut chips are often fried twice, first to cook the middle and then at a hotter heat to crisp.
steak-cut-chips.visual: a small heap of thick potato chips with the skin still on, pale yellow and raw, on a plain background
steak-cut-chips.what: Thick, chunky chips cut from potatoes and sold frozen.

facts: Oats were grown as a crop in Scotland and northern Europe for centuries.
Steel-cut oats are whole grains sliced into pieces by steel blades, so they cook more slowly than rolled oats.
In Scotland, porridge made with oats is a long-standing breakfast tradition.
steel-cut-oats.visual: a small heap of pale, chopped oat grains, loose on the surface
steel-cut-oats.what: Chopped whole oat grains, slow-cooked into chewy porridge.

facts: Stelline means little stars in Italian, and it is a small pasta shape for broth.
It is traditionally added to clear broth in Italian home cooking.
Stelline belong to the family of small pastina shapes made for soups.
stelline.visual: a small heap of tiny star-shaped dried pasta, pale yellow and matt
stelline.what: Tiny star-shaped pasta, traditionally served in soup.

facts: Stem ginger is young ginger, harvested before its skin toughens, then cooked in sugar syrup.
The syrup is often used as a sweetener or spooned over cream and ice cream.
stem-ginger-in-syrup.visual: a plain glass jar without a label holding pale gold ginger pieces in clear amber syrup
stem-ginger-in-syrup.what: Tender young ginger root preserved in a sweet syrup.

facts: Sticky toffee pudding is a British dessert, widely associated with the Lake District.
The sponge is made with chopped dates, which soften and give it a moist, dense crumb.
The sauce is often made from butter, brown sugar and cream, and it soaks into the sponge.
sticky-toffee-pudding.visual: a small plain white bowl of sticky toffee pudding, dark brown moist sponge and glossy toffee sauce
sticky-toffee-pudding.what: A moist date sponge served warm with rich toffee sauce.

facts: Sticky toffee pudding is a British dessert, usually a sponge made with dates.
The sauce is made with butter, brown sugar and cream, and it is poured over the warm sponge.
The pudding is often associated with the Lake District, though its exact origin is disputed.
sticky-toffee-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, glossy dark brown toffee sauce
sticky-toffee-sauce.what: A dark, sweet sauce of dates and sugar for puddings.

facts: Stilton is a protected name, so it can only be made in specified counties of England.
It is named after the village of Stilton in Cambridgeshire, though it was never made there.
Blue veins form when the cheese is pierced so air reaches the mould inside.
stilton.visual: a wedge cut from a round creamy-white cheese, blue-veined, its natural rind intact
stilton.what: A rich, crumbly English blue cheese, veined and tangy.

facts: Stinking Bishop is made in Gloucestershire, England, and its rind is washed in perry, a pear cider.
The cheese is named after a pear variety, Stinking Bishop, used to make the perry it is washed in.
Washed-rind cheeses are bathed or rubbed with brine or alcohol while they ripen, which encourages a sticky rind.
stinking-bishop.visual: a round wheel of soft orange-rinded cheese with one wedge cut out, pale creamy paste visible
stinking-bishop.what: A pungent English cheese with a sticky orange rind.

facts: It is soaked in a fermented brine, which gives it its famous strong smell.
The crisp fried shell and soft centre contrast strongly, and it is often served with a spicy sauce.
stinky-tofu.visual: several cubes of golden-brown deep-fried tofu with crisp shells, served in a small plain white bowl
stinky-tofu.what: Fermented tofu, deep-fried until crisp and very pungent.

facts: Stir-frying is a Chinese cooking method that uses a wok and very high heat.
Soy sauce, a key ingredient, has been made in China for many centuries.
Ginger has been used in Asian cooking for a very long time and is grown across tropical regions.
stir-fry-sauce.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of dark brown glossy sauce
stir-fry-sauce.what: A ready-made soy and ginger sauce for quick stir-fries.

facts: Stockfish is cod dried in cold, windy air, a method used in Norway for centuries.
The name is thought to refer to fish dried on wooden racks or sticks.
stockfish.visual: a whole air-dried cod, stiff, pale tan and flat, lying flat
stockfish.what: Air-dried cod, rock hard, soaked for days before cooking.

facts: Stone crabs are caught off the coast of Florida, and only the large claws are harvested.
A stone crab can regrow a lost claw, which is one reason the fishery takes only the claws.
In Florida, the cooked claws are traditionally served cold with a mustard-based dipping sauce.
stone-crab-claws.visual: a pair of whole cooked stone crab claws, shells bright orange-red with black-tipped pincers
stone-crab-claws.what: Sweet, cooked claws from a Florida crab, served chilled.

facts: Stout grew out of porter, a dark beer style that was popular in eighteenth-century London.
Roasted barley gives stout its dark colour and its bitter, coffee-like taste.
In cooking, stout is used in stews, pies and cakes, where its roasted flavour adds depth.
stout.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with almost black stout, thick creamy off-white head on top
stout.what: A dark, roasted beer with a thick, creamy head.

facts: Stracchino is traditionally made from cow's milk in Lombardy and other northern regions of Italy.
It is typically eaten fresh, when it is soft, milky and easy to spread.
stracchino.visual: a soft white block of cheese with one thick wedge cut and lying flat beside it
stracchino.what: A soft, mild, spreadable Italian cheese from the north.

facts: Stracciatella means little rags in Italian, a name that describes its torn, shredded texture.
It is made from fresh mozzarella curd, torn into strands and mixed with cream.
It is the creamy filling of burrata, a fresh cheese from Apulia in southern Italy.
stracciatella.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of soft, pale, stringy white cheese shreds, moist and creamy
stracciatella.what: Soft shreds of cheese and cream, found inside burrata.

facts: Straw mushrooms are grown on beds of rice straw, which gives them their name.
They have been cultivated in China for centuries and are widely eaten across Southeast Asia.
They are often used in Thai curries and stir-fries and are also sold canned.
straw-mushroom.visual: a small heap of smooth, egg-shaped pale grey-brown mushrooms, whole and unbroken
straw-mushroom.what: Small egg-shaped mushrooms with a soft, silky texture.

facts: Garden strawberries are hybrids, first bred in Brittany in the eighteenth century from American and Chilean species.
Strawberries spread by sending out runners, long stems that root to form new plants.
Botanically the strawberry is not a true berry; the fleshy part is an enlarged stem tip with the seeds on the outside.
strawberry.visual: a whole ripe red strawberry with its green leafy top, lying on its side on a plain background
strawberry.what: A sweet, juicy red berry with seeds on its surface.

strawberry-ice-cream.visual: a round scoop of pale pink strawberry ice cream in a small plain white bowl
strawberry-ice-cream.what: A sweet, pink frozen cream flavoured with strawberries.

facts: Jam is made by boiling fruit with sugar, which helps it thicken into a spreadable preserve.
Many strawberry jams add lemon juice to help them set.
strawberry-jam.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with deep red preserve, plain lid
strawberry-jam.what: A sweet spread made from cooked strawberries and sugar.

facts: Jelly in Britain means a gelatine-set dessert, while in America jelly usually means a fruit spread.
Gelatine, the setting agent, is made from animal collagen, and it has been used in set desserts for centuries.
strawberry-jelly.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of bright red strawberry jelly cubes, glossy and set
strawberry-jelly.what: A wobbly, fruity dessert set with gelatine.

facts: Berry sauces are a simple way of sweetening puddings and have long been used with desserts.
The modern garden strawberry was bred in Europe from wild species native to the Americas.
Strawberry sauces are often made by cooking the fruit with sugar until it thickens.
strawberry-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, deep red strawberry sauce, glossy and thick
strawberry-sauce.what: A sweet red fruit sauce for ice cream and cheesecake.

facts: Streaky bacon is cut from the belly of the pig, where meat and fat form alternating layers.
In Britain, streaky bacon is commonly fried until crisp and served in sandwiches.
The name streaky refers to the streaks of fat running through the meat.
streaky-bacon.visual: two raw streaky bacon rashers lying flat, alternating bands of pink meat and white fat
streaky-bacon.what: Pork belly rashers with fine layers of fat and meat.

facts: Strong flour is milled from hard wheat that contains more gluten-forming protein.
Bakers use strong flour for bread because its gluten traps the gas that makes dough rise.
Wheat was among the first crops cultivated for flour in the Fertile Crescent.
strong-white-bread-flour.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with fine white bread flour, level surface, fine and powdery
strong-white-bread-flour.what: Wheat flour high in protein, for chewy loaves.

facts: Wholemeal flour is milled from the whole grain, with the bran and germ included.
In Britain, strong flour is made from hard wheat and sold for bread-making.
strong-wholemeal-flour.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, brown wholemeal flour, level and smooth
strong-wholemeal-flour.what: Wholegrain flour, ground for strong, chewy loaves.

facts: Strozzapreti means priest-strangler in Italian, a name whose origin is uncertain and told in many folk stories.
The pasta is traditionally made from flour and water and rolled into thin ropes that are twisted.
It comes from Romagna, a region of north-east Italy, where it is often served with rich tomato or meat sauces.
strozzapreti.visual: a small heap of dried strozzapreti pasta, short twisted shapes with a rough spiral
strozzapreti.what: Short, twisted pasta shaped by hand in Romagna.

facts: Stuffed crust pizza was first introduced by a major American chain in the mid-1990s.
The rim is typically filled with mozzarella or cheddar, which melts as the pizza bakes.
Frozen pizzas are sold ready-made and are cooked straight from the freezer in an oven.
stuffed-crust-frozen-pizza.visual: a whole uncooked round pizza with a thick, pillowy raised rim
stuffed-crust-frozen-pizza.what: A frozen pizza with a cheese-filled rim, ready to bake.

facts: Olives are pitted before filling, and the stuffing is pushed into the gap where the stone was.
Almonds and garlic are among the common fillings, and they are popular on cocktail and tapas plates.
stuffed-olives.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of whole green olives, each showing a small filling at one end
stuffed-olives.what: Green olives filled with a savoury stuffing, for snacking.

facts: Stuffing has been made in Britain for centuries, traditionally to flavour roasted poultry and meat.
Sage and onion is a traditional English stuffing flavour, often baked alongside a Sunday roast.
Dried stuffing mixes are rehydrated with water or stock and then baked or cooked.
stuffing-mix.visual: a small heap of dry, pale golden stuffing crumbs in a small plain white ceramic bowl
stuffing-mix.what: Dried sage and onion crumbs, moistened and baked.

facts: Large cup mushrooms are the mature form of the common button mushroom.
They are often filled with breadcrumbs, garlic and herbs, then baked until tender.
Their broad, open caps hold stuffing well and soak up juices as they cook.
stuffing-mushrooms.visual: two large whole cup mushrooms with deep brown open caps, lying side by side
stuffing-mushrooms.what: Large, deep cup mushrooms made to be filled and baked.

facts: Sturgeon are an ancient family of fish, with bony plates rather than scales along their bodies.
They live in rivers and seas across the Northern Hemisphere, and some species migrate between them.
Sturgeon flesh is firm and meaty, and it is often roasted, grilled or smoked.
sturgeon.visual: a fillet of pale cream-pink sturgeon flesh, skin removed, lying flat on a plain white background
sturgeon.what: A large, ancient fish whose roe is made into caviar.

facts: Suan cai means sour vegetables in Mandarin, and the name describes its tangy, fermented taste.
It is a staple of northern China and is cooked with pork or stir-fried in many home dishes.
suan-cai.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of shredded pale green pickled cabbage in its clear liquid
suan-cai.what: Sour, crunchy cabbage pickled in brine by fermentation.

facts: Suckling pig is a traditional dish in Spain, Portugal and parts of Asia, usually roasted whole.
It is named for young pigs still feeding on their mother's milk when they are killed for the table.
suckling-pig.visual: a whole raw young pig, pale pink, lying on its side on a plain surface
suckling-pig.what: A whole young pig roasted with crisp, crackling skin.

facts: Sudachi is grown mainly in Tokushima Prefecture on the island of Shikoku.
Cooks often squeeze it over grilled fish, noodles and soups in Japanese cooking.
The fruit is picked while still green, before it ripens to yellow.
sudachi.visual: a whole small green citrus fruit, round, with a thin slightly bumpy skin
sudachi.what: A small green Japanese citrus, used for its sharp juice.

facts: Suet is the hard fat that surrounds the kidneys and loins of cattle and sheep.
It has long been used in British steamed puddings, dumplings and mincemeat.
suet.visual: a small heap of pale white shredded beef suet
suet.what: Hard animal fat from beef or lamb, used in dumplings.

facts: Suet is hard fat found around the kidneys of cattle and sheep, and it has long been used in British cooking.
Vegetable suet is also sold, so vegetarian cooks can make dumplings without animal fat.
suet-dumpling-mix.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale off-white suet dumpling flour mix, level at the top
suet-dumpling-mix.what: A flour and suet blend for light, savoury stew dumplings.

facts: Suet is hard fat from around the kidneys of cattle or sheep, traditionally used in British puddings.
Suet dumplings are usually simmered on top of a stew, which lets them rise and puff up.
Suet pastry and dumplings have been part of English home cooking for centuries.
suet-dumplings.visual: three round, pale golden suet dumplings with a soft, slightly crumbly surface on a plain white plate
suet-dumplings.what: Light, savoury dumplings made with suet and flour.

facts: Sugar cane vinegar is made by fermenting cane juice first into alcohol, then into vinegar.
It is widely used in the Philippines, where it is a traditional dipping and cooking vinegar.
Cane vinegar is often milder than wine vinegars, so it suits dressings and marinades.
sugar-cane-vinegar.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale amber vinegar, cap on
sugar-cane-vinegar.what: A mellow vinegar made from fermented sugar cane juice.

facts: Cinnamon comes from the inner bark of several Cinnamomum trees, which is dried into quills.
Cinnamon sugar is a traditional topping for churros in Spain and Mexico.
In North America, cinnamon sugar is commonly sprinkled over toast and doughnuts.
sugar-cinnamon-mix.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of fine, pale brown powder, evenly blended
sugar-cinnamon-mix.what: A blend of cinnamon and sugar for dusting sweet bakes.

facts: Sugar snap peas were developed in the United States and first introduced in 1979.
Unlike snow peas, the whole pod of a sugar snap is thick and fleshy, so it is eaten along with the peas.
They are often eaten raw, or quickly steamed or stir-fried so that they stay crisp.
sugar-snap-peas.visual: a small heap of bright green sugar snap pea pods, plump and glossy, with the stalks trimmed
sugar-snap-peas.what: Sweet, plump pea pods that you eat whole, pod and all.

facts: Sugar strands are known by different names, including sprinkles, depending on the country.
They are made by pushing a stiff sugar dough through small holes and then drying the strands.
They have long been used to decorate cakes and biscuits in Britain and North America.
sugar-strands.visual: a small heap of fine, bright multicoloured sugar strands, thin and curled, loose on the background
sugar-strands.what: Thin coloured sugar threads for decorating cakes.

facts: Sugared almonds, called dragées in French, have been given at weddings and celebrations in Europe for centuries.
The sugar coating is built up in thin layers, which gives the hard, smooth outer shell.
In Italy they are known as confetti and are traditionally given at weddings.
sugared-almonds.visual: a small heap of pale pink and white sugar-coated almonds
sugared-almonds.what: Almonds with a hard sugar coat, often in pastel colours.

facts: Sultanas are dried from pale green grapes, often of the Thompson Seedless variety.
The word sultana means a queen or a sultan's wife in several languages.
Sultanas are used in British baking, for scones, teacakes and Christmas cake.
sultana.visual: a small heap of plump golden dried sultanas, slightly wrinkled
sultana.what: A small, golden dried grape, plump and sweet.

facts: Sumac has long been used across the Middle East as a souring agent instead of lemon.
It is a traditional topping for salads, kebabs and flatbreads in many Middle Eastern kitchens.
sumac.visual: a plain glass jar without a label, filled with deep crimson sumac powder
sumac.what: A tart, deep red powder ground from dried berries.

facts: Summer truffles grow underground in association with tree roots, often oak or hazel.
A truffle is the fruiting body of a fungus that grows below the ground.
summer-truffle.visual: one whole summer truffle, knobbly dark brown-black skin with a dusting of earth
summer-truffle.what: A milder, nuttier truffle with a knobbly, dark brown skin.

facts: Sun-drying tomatoes concentrates their sugars and flavour, a method long used in the Mediterranean.
Dried tomatoes are often packed in olive oil, a common style in Italian delis.
Tomatoes were brought to Europe from the Americas in the sixteenth century.
sun-dried-tomato.visual: a small heap of wrinkled, dark red dried tomato halves, slightly glossy
sun-dried-tomato.what: Tomatoes dried until chewy and concentrated in flavour.

facts: Tomatoes originated in South America, and were first domesticated in Mexico before reaching Europe.
Sun-dried tomatoes were traditionally preserved in Italy and other Mediterranean countries, where hot summers dry them naturally.
Tomato paste is made by cooking tomatoes down until most of the water has evaporated, leaving a concentrated flavour.
sun-dried-tomato-paste.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, deep red tomato paste, glossy and slightly oily
sun-dried-tomato-paste.what: A thick, sweet-sharp paste made from sun-dried tomatoes.

facts: Sun-dried tomatoes are a traditional way of preserving tomatoes in southern Italy and around the Mediterranean.
Tomatoes are native to South America and reached Europe only after contact with the Americas.
sun-dried-tomato-puree.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of deep red tomato paste
sun-dried-tomato-puree.what: A thick, sweet paste made from dried tomatoes.

facts: Sunflower oil is pressed from the seeds of the sunflower, a plant native to North America.
Ukraine and Russia are major producers of sunflower oil.
sunflower-oil.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden sunflower oil, filled to the shoulder
sunflower-oil.what: A light, neutral oil pressed from sunflower seeds.

facts: It is made in much the same way as peanut butter, but from seeds rather than nuts.
Sunflower seeds are pressed for oil in large quantities in Ukraine and Russia.
sunflower-seed-butter.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth pale golden-brown sunflower seed butter
sunflower-seed-butter.what: A smooth spread made by grinding roasted sunflower seeds.

facts: Sunflower oil is pressed from the seeds and is widely used for frying and baking.
The flower is named for its bright, sun-like head.
sunflower-seeds.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of shelled sunflower seed kernels
sunflower-seeds.what: Mild, nutty seeds that add crunch to breads and salads.

facts: Sunflowers are native to North America and were domesticated there thousands of years ago.
Shoots like these are grown in trays and cut young, and are popular in modern restaurant kitchens.
sunflower-shoots.visual: a small bunch of tender sunflower shoots, pale green stems each with two broad, bright green leaves
sunflower-shoots.what: Tender young sunflower sprouts with a nutty, crunchy bite.

facts: Sungold is a cherry tomato variety bred in Japan and now grown widely in gardens.
Tomatoes reached Europe from the Americas in the sixteenth century and were first grown as ornamental plants.
The word tomato comes from the Nahuatl word tomatl, spoken in Mexico.
sungold-tomato.visual: a small bunch of glossy bright orange cherry tomatoes still attached to a short green stalk, on the plain background
sungold-tomato.what: A small, very sweet orange cherry tomato variety.

facts: The Atlantic surf clam lives buried in sandy seabed offshore and is harvested by dredging.
Its meat is firm and chewy, so cooks often chop it for chowders or fry it in fritters.
surf-clams.visual: one raw strip of surf clam meat, creamy white with a darker edge, lying flat
surf-clams.what: A large, sweet Atlantic clam, usually sold as firm strips.

facts: Surströmming is traditionally fermented in tins, which bulge as gas builds up inside.
It is especially associated with northern Sweden, where it is traditionally eaten in late summer.
Herring has been preserved by salting and fermenting in Scandinavia for centuries.
surstromming.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale fermented herring pieces in a little liquid, silvery skin
