wasabi-root.what: A knobbly root with a clean, sharp heat when grated.

facts: The washing encourages bacteria and moulds that give the cheese its strong smell and sticky orange rind.
Many famous examples come from France, Italy and Switzerland, such as Epoisses and Taleggio.
washed-rind-cheese.visual: a round washed-rind cheese with one wedge cut away, sticky orange-pink rind and a pale creamy interior
washed-rind-cheese.what: A pungent cheese with a rind washed in brine or beer.

facts: Water covers most of the Earth's surface, though only a small share is fresh water.
Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.
water.visual: a clear drinking glass full of still water, a few small bubbles on the inside edge
water.what: A clear liquid used in drinks, stocks and many recipes.

facts: Water biscuits are a traditional British cracker, often served with cheese.
They are pricked with small holes before baking, so they stay flat and crisp.
water-biscuit.visual: a few thin, pale, flat water biscuits with small pricked holes, arranged on a plain white plate
water-biscuit.what: A plain, crisp cracker made from flour, water and oil.

facts: Water caltrop is the fruit of Trapa natans, a plant that floats on still fresh water.
The nuts have been gathered and eaten in parts of Asia and Europe since ancient times.
The nut is usually boiled or roasted, and it is eaten in a similar way to chestnuts.
water-caltrop.visual: one whole dark brown-black water caltrop nut, four sharp horn-like points, on its own
water-caltrop.what: A horned water nut with a floury, starchy centre.

facts: Water chestnuts grow in muddy ponds and paddy fields, rooted in the mud.
Their flesh stays crunchy even after cooking, which makes them popular in stir-fries.
They are widely eaten across China and other parts of East and South-East Asia.
water-chestnut.visual: a few whole brown water chestnuts, one halved to show crisp white flesh
water-chestnut.what: A crisp, sweet-tasting corm from an aquatic sedge plant.

facts: Water kefir grains are clusters of bacteria and yeasts, strained out of the drink before serving.
Water kefir is a non-dairy alternative to milk kefir, which is made from milk.
Dried fruit or lemon is often added during fermentation for extra flavour.
water-kefir.visual: a clear drinking glass of pale golden, slightly cloudy liquid with a few bubbles
water-kefir.what: Lightly fizzy, sweet drink made by fermenting sugar water.

facts: Water spinach grows in shallow water and wet soil, and it is widely eaten across South-East and East Asia.
In English it is also called morning glory, a name shared with flowering relatives in the bindweed family.
It is often stir-fried quickly with garlic and chilli, a simple method used across South-East Asia.
water-spinach.visual: a loose bunch of long, hollow green stems and arrow-shaped leaves, freshly picked and untrimmed
water-spinach.what: A hollow-stemmed leafy green from South-East Asia.

facts: Watercress belongs to the mustard family, which explains the peppery bite of its leaves.
Watercress grows in cool, fast-flowing streams, and many commercial beds are in chalk streams in England.
Watercress is a classic ingredient in British soups, sandwiches and salads.
watercress.visual: a small bunch of fresh watercress, bright green round leaves on thin pale stems
watercress.what: Peppery aquatic leaves grown in clear running water.

facts: Bloomy-rind cheeses are ripened from the outside in by a white mould on their surface.
Brie and Camembert are the best-known examples of bloomy-rind cheese.
The white rind is edible and adds to the flavour and soft texture of the cheese.
waterloo.visual: a block of soft pale cream cheese with a white bloomy rind, one wedge cut away
waterloo.what: A soft, creamy cheese with a white, bloomy rind.

facts: Watermelon is native to Africa, where it has been cultivated for thousands of years.
Watermelon was grown in ancient Egypt, and it is now cultivated in many warm regions.
In many countries watermelon is served in wedges, and the rind is sometimes pickled or stir-fried.
watermelon.visual: one whole watermelon with dark green striped rind, lying on its side
watermelon.what: A huge, juicy melon with a green rind and red flesh.

facts: Watermelon radishes belong to the East Asian group of large winter radishes.
Its pink colour is in the flesh, not only the skin, which is why it is called watermelon radish.
It is eaten raw in salads or sliced thinly, and keeps a mild peppery crunch.
watermelon-radish.visual: one halved watermelon radish, pale green-white skin, bright pink centre visible, lying flat on its cut side
watermelon-radish.what: A round radish with pale skin and a bright pink centre.

facts: Watermelon is native to Africa, where it has been grown for thousands of years.
Roasted and salted watermelon seeds are a popular snack across East and Southeast Asia.
Each seed is cracked open with the teeth or fingers to reach the pale kernel inside.
watermelon-seeds.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with roasted watermelon seeds, pale cream and speckled brown
watermelon-seeds.what: Crunchy roasted seeds of the watermelon, eaten as a snack.

facts: Weisswurst comes from Munich and is traditionally eaten before noon.
It is traditionally served with sweet mustard, soft pretzels and a wheat beer.
It is not smoked, which keeps its colour pale, and it is gently poached rather than fried.
weisswurst.visual: two pale, plump cooked white sausages on a plain white plate
weisswurst.what: A pale, mild Bavarian sausage, usually made with veal.

facts: Welsh cakes are cooked on a bakestone or griddle, not baked in an oven.
In Welsh they are called picau ar y maen, meaning cakes on the stone.
They are a traditional Welsh teatime treat, often dusted with sugar.
welsh-cake.visual: a single round Welsh cake, golden-brown, dotted with currants, resting on a small plain white plate
welsh-cake.what: A small, round, griddled cake studded with currants.

facts: Welsh onion is a hardy, many-stemmed onion grown widely in East Asia.
The name Welsh probably comes from an old English word meaning foreign.
It is also called bunching onion because it grows in clumps rather than forming a bulb.
welsh-onion.visual: a bunch of slender green hollow-leaved onions with their white roots trimmed, lying on the background
welsh-onion.what: A slim onion with hollow green leaves, used fresh.

facts: The cheese takes its name from Wensleydale, the valley in North Yorkshire where it is made.
Young Wensleydale is mild and creamy, while older cheese becomes crumblier and sharper.
wensleydale.visual: a block of pale creamy-white Wensleydale cheese with one wedge cut, lying on a plain background
wensleydale.what: A crumbly, mild cheese from Yorkshire, England.

facts: Westphalia is a region of north-western Germany, and this ham takes its name from it.
westphalian-ham.visual: a whole smoked ham joint with a dark brown crust, lying on its side
westphalian-ham.what: A German smoked ham, salted and dried, with a dark crust.

facts: Weissbier, meaning white beer, takes its name from its pale, cloudy appearance.
Wheat beer is a traditional style from southern Germany and Bavaria.
Its fruity flavour often comes from yeast compounds that give notes of banana and clove.
wheat-beer.visual: a tall plain clear drinking glass of cloudy pale golden beer with a foamy white head
wheat-beer.what: A cloudy, pale beer brewed with a large share of wheat.

facts: Wheat berries are whole wheat kernels, so the bran and germ are kept intact.
Wheat has been cultivated in the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East for many thousands of years.
wheat-berries.visual: a small heap of plump, dry, pale golden-brown wheat berries in a loose pile
wheat-berries.what: Whole, unmilled wheat kernels that stay chewy when cooked.

facts: Shredded wheat was developed in the late 19th century in the United States.
The biscuits are made by cooking wheat, shredding it into strands and pressing it into shape.
wheat-breakfast-biscuits.visual: a single rectangular pale golden shredded wheat biscuit with a ridged, woven texture, lying flat on a plain background
wheat-breakfast-biscuits.what: Pressed whole wheat biscuits, eaten with milk at breakfast.

facts: Whelks are sea snails found on rocky shores and seabeds around Britain.
In Britain they were a traditional seaside food, often sold from stalls.
They are firm and chewy, and become tough if cooked for too long.
whelks.visual: a whole whelk in its brown, ridged spiral shell, lying on a plain background
whelks.what: A sea snail with a spiral shell, usually sold cooked.

facts: Whey is what remains after milk is separated into curds and liquid during cheesemaking.
Historically, farms gave whey to pigs and calves, since it was a by-product of cheesemaking.
Ricotta, the Italian soft cheese, is traditionally made by heating whey.
whey.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with pale, slightly cloudy yellow-green whey liquid
whey.what: The thin, pale liquid left when cheese curds form.

facts: Cream is the fatty layer that rises to the top of milk when it is left to settle.
Whipping cream has less fat than double cream, so it whips to a softer texture.
Whipping adds air to the cream, forming a foam of tiny bubbles.
whipping-cream.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of soft whipped white cream, forming gentle peaks
whipping-cream.what: Dairy with enough fat to whip into a soft, airy foam.

facts: Egg whites can be whisked into foam because their proteins unfold and trap air.
Meringue, a dish of whisked whites and sugar, has been made in Europe for centuries.
Even a trace of fat or yolk can stop egg whites from whipping to full volume.
whisked-egg-whites.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of whisked egg whites, glossy white peaks standing up stiffly
whisked-egg-whites.what: Egg white beaten until it forms stiff, airy peaks.

facts: White anchovies, or boquerones, are a Spanish tapas dish, usually marinated in vinegar.
The fish are first salted, then soaked in vinegar, which turns their flesh opaque and pale.
Anchovies are small schooling fish found in Mediterranean and Atlantic waters.
white-anchovies.visual: several slim, silvery-white marinated anchovy fillets arranged in a neat row on a small plain white plate
white-anchovies.what: Small fish cured in vinegar and seasoned with garlic.

facts: White asparagus is grown under soil, so sunlight never turns the spears green.
It is a spring tradition in Germany and parts of France, where it is eaten each year in season.
Asparagus is a plant native to Europe and western Asia, and it has been eaten for a very long time.
white-asparagus.visual: a bunch of long, pale creamy-white asparagus spears with closed tips and evenly trimmed stems
white-asparagus.what: Pale spears grown under soil or cover, kept from the sun.

facts: White aubergines are a variety of the same plant as the purple aubergine.
Aubergine is central to dishes such as Turkish imam bayildi and Greek moussaka.
white-aubergine.visual: a whole white aubergine, smooth creamy-white skin, slightly rounded oval shape, lying on its side
white-aubergine.what: A creamy white-skinned aubergine with a mild, tender flesh.

facts: White balsamic is often made in Modena in Italy, using grape must and wine vinegar.
Unlike dark balsamic, its pale colour means it does not darken light dishes such as mayonnaise or fish.
white-balsamic-vinegar.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with pale golden vinegar
white-balsamic-vinegar.what: A pale, sweet vinegar that keeps sauces light in colour.

facts: Cabbage descends from wild plants that grew along the coasts of Europe.
Sauerkraut is made by fermenting finely shredded white cabbage in salt.
The word cabbage comes from the French caboche, meaning head.
white-cabbage.visual: a whole white cabbage, tight pale-green head with a few outer leaves
white-cabbage.what: A crunchy cabbage with a tight pale head, ideal for slaw.

facts: White chocolate contains cocoa butter but no cocoa solids, which gives it its pale colour.
Chocolate has been made from cacao since at least the Maya and Aztec peoples, and European makers later developed sweeter, milkier forms.
It is often used in blondies, cheesecakes and white chocolate mousse, where its sweetness balances tart flavours.
white-chocolate.visual: a whole rectangular bar of ivory white chocolate, with one square snapped off the corner
white-chocolate.what: A sweet, pale bar made from cocoa butter, sugar and milk.

facts: White chocolate is made from cocoa butter, sugar and milk solids, without cocoa solids.
Chips are designed to keep a recognisable shape when baked into cookies.
white-chocolate-chips.visual: a small heap of white chocolate chips, pale ivory drops scattered in a loose pile
white-chocolate-chips.what: Small sweet drops of white chocolate for baking.

facts: Crab meat is picked by hand from the shell, a slow job that has long been done in coastal communities.
Crabs are eaten across the world, and both Atlantic and Pacific crabs are used in cooking.
Crab cakes, popular in the United States, bind white crab meat with breadcrumbs and egg.
white-crab-meat.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of loose, pale cream crab meat flakes, fine and moist
white-crab-meat.what: Sweet, delicate flakes of pale meat from the crab's body.

facts: Eggs bind, lighten and enrich cakes, sauces and pastries.
The colour of an egg's shell depends on the breed of hen that laid it.
white-egg.visual: one whole raw white hen's egg, smooth white shell, resting on its side
white-egg.what: A plain white hen's egg with a mild, reliable flavour.

facts: These beans are a variety of common bean, first grown in the Americas before reaching Europe.
In Tuscany they feature in ribollita, a thick soup of bread, beans and vegetables.
Dried beans need soaking before cooking, which softens the skins and shortens cooking time.
white-kidney-beans.visual: a small heap of dried creamy-white oval beans, smooth and plump
white-kidney-beans.what: Creamy white Italian beans for soups, salads and stews.

facts: Kimjang, the autumn tradition of making kimchi in bulk, is recognised by UNESCO as cultural heritage.
White kimchi leaves out the red chilli powder that gives most kimchi its colour.
Napa cabbage and radish are common ingredients, salted and left to ferment in a brine.
white-kimchi.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of pale fermented cabbage kimchi, crisp leaves in a light brine
white-kimchi.what: A mild, non-spicy Korean dish of fermented cabbage.

facts: Miso is a traditional Japanese seasoning made from fermented soybeans, usually with grain such as rice or barley.
White miso is fermented for a shorter time than darker types, so it tastes milder.
It is often used in soups, glazes and salad dressings.
white-miso.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth, pale cream-coloured miso paste
white-miso.what: A mild, sweet soybean paste for soups and dressings.

facts: Onions have been cultivated for thousands of years and are grown across most of the world.
White onions are often used in Mexican cooking, especially in fresh salsas.
white-onion.visual: one whole white onion with pale papery skin and a small root end, lying on its side
white-onion.what: A crisp, clean-tasting onion with pale, papery skin.

facts: The peach began in China and spread westward along ancient trade routes.
White-fleshed peaches are often sweeter and lower in acid than yellow varieties.
The English word peach comes from the Latin persicum, meaning Persian, though the fruit began in China.
white-peach.visual: a whole ripe white peach with a pinkish blush and fine fuzzy skin
white-peach.what: A soft, fragrant peach with creamy white flesh.

facts: White pepper is made by soaking ripe peppercorns in water to loosen the outer skin.
It is traditional in Chinese and French cooking, especially in pale sauces.
Cooks use it where dark flecks would look out of place in a pale dish.
white-pepper.visual: a small heap of pale cream peppercorns, smooth and round
white-pepper.what: Peppercorns peeled of their dark skin, mild and earthy.

facts: Poppy seeds come from the opium poppy, a plant grown for its seeds in many countries.
In India, white poppy seeds, known as khus khus, are ground into a paste to thicken rich dishes.
Ground poppy seeds are also used in Central European cakes and pastries, such as poppy seed rolls.
white-poppy-seeds.visual: a small heap of pale cream poppy seeds, tiny and smooth
white-poppy-seeds.what: Small creamy seeds, ground to thicken curries and kormas.

facts: White port is made from white grape varieties grown in the Douro valley and fortified with grape spirit.
It is often served chilled as an aperitif, sometimes with tonic and a slice of lemon.
Port takes its name from the city of Porto, from which it was traditionally shipped.
white-port.visual: a plain clear drinking glass filled with pale golden white port wine
white-port.what: A pale, sweet fortified wine from Portugal's Douro valley.

facts: White pudding is a traditional sausage in Scotland, Ireland and parts of northern England.
Unlike black pudding, it contains no blood, which is why it has its pale colour.
white-pudding.visual: a single cut round slice of pale cream white pudding, lying flat, its surface lightly flecked
white-pudding.what: A pale, mild sausage of pork, oatmeal and suet.

facts: White rum is usually unaged or lightly aged, then filtered to remove colour.
Rum is made from sugar cane juice or molasses, a by-product of sugar refining.
It is a key spirit in many Caribbean cocktails, including the daiquiri and the mojito.
white-rum.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with colourless liquid, cap on
white-rum.what: A clear spirit distilled from sugar cane or molasses.

facts: Shimeji is a Japanese name for several mushroom species, and they are widely used in Japanese cooking.
White shimeji are cultivated, usually on sawdust-based growing material, rather than gathered in the wild.
They are often used in soups, hotpots and stir-fries across Japan.
white-shimeji-mushroom.visual: a small bunch of white shimeji mushrooms joined at the base, with slender stems and small pale caps
white-shimeji-mushroom.what: Small, pale mushrooms that grow in tight clusters.

facts: The name Stilton comes from a village in Cambridgeshire where the cheese was once sold.
White Stilton is made without the blue mould that gives blue Stilton its veins.
white-stilton.visual: a block of pale creamy white cheese with one wedge cut, the crumbly edge of the cut visible
white-stilton.what: A young, crumbly, mild cheese, often mixed with fruit.

facts: The name potato traces back to the Taino word batata, which referred to the sweet potato.
Sweet potatoes are native to Central and South America and spread worldwide after 1492.
White-fleshed varieties are drier and less sweet than the orange kinds common in British shops.
white-sweet-potato.visual: one whole raw white sweet potato, pale cream skin, tapered oblong shape, lying on its side
white-sweet-potato.what: A drier sweet potato with pale, chestnut-like flesh.

facts: Truffles grow in partnership with the roots of trees such as oak, poplar and hazel.
They are traditionally hunted with trained dogs or pigs that sniff out their scent.
white-truffle.visual: one whole white truffle, knobbly and pale ochre, small and irregular, on a plain background
white-truffle.what: A rare, strong-smelling fungus that grows underground.

facts: White turmeric is related to ginger and turmeric, both members of the ginger family.
It grows in tropical parts of South and South-East Asia, where it is a traditional ingredient.
white-turmeric.visual: a whole fresh white turmeric root, pale ivory skin with a few small knobbly fingers
white-turmeric.what: A pale, mango-scented root from the ginger family.

facts: White wine vinegar is made by fermenting white wine so its alcohol turns into acetic acid.
The French word for vinegar, vinaigre, comes from 'vin aigre', meaning sour wine.
It is widely used in French dressings and classic sauces such as béarnaise.
white-wine-vinegar.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle filled with pale golden white wine vinegar
white-wine-vinegar.what: A pale, crisp vinegar made from white wine.

facts: Whitebait is not one species but the young of several small fish, such as herring and sprat.
In Britain whitebait is often served with lemon and thin brown bread and butter.
Whitebait is a long-standing British seaside dish, often fried whole.
whitebait.visual: a small heap of tiny raw silver fish lying loosely together
whitebait.what: Tiny silvery fish, usually coated in flour and deep-fried.

facts: Whitecurrants are a pale colour variety of the redcurrant, not a separate species.
Currant bushes grow best in cool temperate climates such as northern Europe.
White currants are often used in tarts and desserts, or set in clear jellies.
whitecurrant.visual: a small bunch of fresh whitecurrants, translucent pale ivory berries hanging on thin stalks
whitecurrant.what: A pale, sweeter cousin of the redcurrant, used in tarts.

facts: They belong to the salmon family, Salmonidae, and are closely related to trout.
Smoked whitefish is a classic deli food in North America.
whitefish.visual: a whole raw whitefish showing silvery scales and a pale belly, lying flat on the background
whitefish.what: A mild, delicate freshwater fish from northern lakes.

facts: Whiting is a member of the cod family and is found in the cooler waters of the north-east Atlantic.
Its flesh is soft and fine, so it is best cooked gently and quickly.
whiting-fillet.visual: a single raw whiting fillet, pale white flesh and silver skin, lying flat
whiting-fillet.what: A small, mild white fish with delicate flaky flesh.

facts: Allspice is the dried unripe berry of a tropical evergreen tree, Pimenta dioica, native to the Caribbean and Central America.
Its name reflects a flavour that resembles a mixture of cinnamon, nutmeg and cloves.
Allspice is a key flavour in Jamaican jerk seasoning and is common in pickling spice blends.
whole-allspice-berries.visual: A small plain white ceramic bowl holding whole dark brown allspice berries, round and glossy.
whole-allspice-berries.what: Small dried berries that taste of cinnamon and clove.

facts: Roast chicken is a traditional British Sunday meal, often served with potatoes and gravy.
Chickens are kept on farms in almost every country in the world.
whole-chicken.visual: a whole raw chicken, pale yellowish skin, plump, lying on its back on the background
whole-chicken.what: A whole bird, ideal for a roast with butter and lemon.

facts: Cloves were once a valuable trade spice, prized in Europe and Asia.
The name clove comes from the Latin clavus, meaning nail, after the shape of the bud.
whole-cloves.visual: a small heap of whole dried cloves, dark brown nail-shaped buds with a short stalk
whole-cloves.what: Dried, unopened flower buds of a tropical evergreen tree.

facts: Ducks were domesticated in Asia thousands of years ago and later spread across the world.
Duck has a layer of fat under the skin, which melts away during slow roasting.
Peking duck, a famous Chinese dish, is roasted until the skin is crisp and glossy.
whole-duck.visual: one whole raw duck, plucked and pale-skinned, lying breast-side up
whole-duck.what: A rich, fatty bird prized for its crisp roasted skin.

facts: Cooking fish whole keeps the flesh moist, and the bones and skin add flavour.
Many cuisines, from Mediterranean to Chinese, cook fish whole, often steamed or grilled.
Whole fish is often sold gutted and scaled, ready for roasting or steaming.
whole-fish.visual: one whole raw fresh white fish, silver skin glistening, lying on its side on the background
whole-fish.what: A fresh fish, sold and cooked whole for roasting.

facts: Roast goose is a traditional dish at Michaelmas in Britain and at festivals across Europe.
Goose has been kept for food for thousands of years, and its fat was once prized for cooking.
Goose fat from roasting is often saved and used to cook potatoes and vegetables.
whole-goose.visual: one whole raw goose, pale skin, plump body, legs tucked in, lying breast side up on a plain background
whole-goose.what: A large festive bird with rich dark meat and lots of fat.

facts: Mackerel is a fast-swimming fish that shoals in large groups in the Atlantic and Mediterranean.
Mackerel was once a cheap, everyday fish in Britain, sold fresh from coastal fishing ports.
Its rich flesh is traditionally grilled, smoked or pickled in many European countries.
whole-mackerel.visual: one whole raw mackerel, silver-blue with dark wavy stripes along its back, lying on its side
whole-mackerel.what: An oily sea fish with bold dark stripes on its back.

facts: Whole milk is milk that has not had its fat removed, so it keeps more of the natural cream.
Milk is heated during pasteurisation, a process that makes it safe to drink.
whole-milk.visual: a clear drinking glass filled with creamy white milk, plain background
whole-milk.what: Milk with its natural cream, rich and creamy in texture.

facts: Nutmeg is the seed inside the fruit of an evergreen tree native to the Banda Islands of Indonesia.
Mace, the lacy red covering around the seed, is sold as a separate spice.
Nutmeg was once a highly prized spice traded across Europe and Asia.
whole-nutmeg.visual: one whole dark brown nutmeg seed, oval with a faintly wrinkled surface, lying on its side
whole-nutmeg.what: The hard, brown seed of a tropical evergreen tree.

facts: Quail are small game birds found across Europe, Asia and Africa, and some species migrate long distances.
Quail have been eaten since ancient times, and the Romans were known to prize them as a delicacy.
Domestic quail are now farmed for their eggs and meat, and their eggs are small and speckled.
whole-quail.visual: one whole raw quail, plucked and cleaned, breast up, lying directly on the background
whole-quail.what: A tiny game bird, often grilled or roasted whole.

facts: Atlantic salmon hatch in rivers, migrate to the sea, and return to their birthplace to spawn.
Salmon has been an important food in Scotland and Scandinavia for centuries, fresh and cured.
whole-salmon.visual: a whole raw salmon, silver skin with dark speckles, lying on its side on a plain background
whole-salmon.what: A large, silver fish with pink flesh, bought whole.

facts: Sea bass is a name used for several species of saltwater fish.
In Mediterranean cooking, whole sea bass is often baked with herbs, lemon and olive oil.
Whole fish baked in a salt crust is a traditional method in Mediterranean and Italian cooking.
whole-sea-bass.visual: one whole raw sea bass, silvery grey skin with a sheen, lying on its side
whole-sea-bass.what: A silvery, mild white fish, often roasted whole.

facts: Sea bream is found in the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic, and has long been eaten around these coasts.
Cooking it whole keeps the flesh moist, and the flesh comes away cleanly from the bones.
whole-sea-bream.visual: a whole raw sea bream with silver scales and red-tinged fins, lying on its side
whole-sea-bream.what: A silvery sea fish, often grilled whole with herbs.

facts: Turkeys were brought to Europe from the Americas during the early colonial period.
whole-turkey.visual: a whole raw turkey, breast-side up, plump pale skin with legs tied together
whole-turkey.what: A large domestic bird, often roasted whole for feasts.

facts: Wholegrain mustard is made from partly crushed seeds, not finely ground, which gives it a grainy texture.
Mustard comes from the seeds of plants in the brassica family, which also includes cabbage and broccoli.
wholegrain-mustard.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of coarse pale-brown mustard, whole seeds visible
wholegrain-mustard.what: A coarse mustard made from crushed or whole seeds.

facts: Pitta is a flatbread from the Middle East, baked at high heat so that it puffs up.
Wholemeal pitta is made with flour that includes the bran and germ of the wheat.
Pitta is widely eaten across the Eastern Mediterranean, around Greece, Turkey and Lebanon.
wholemeal-pitta.visual: one whole round wholemeal pitta bread, flat and lightly speckled with brown flecks
wholemeal-pitta.what: A flat bread with a pocket, made from wholemeal flour.

facts: Wholemeal flour keeps the bran and germ, which gives it a darker colour and a nuttier taste.
Because the oils in the germ can turn rancid, wholemeal flour keeps for a shorter time than white.
In Britain it is called wholemeal, while in America it is usually called whole wheat flour.
wholemeal-plain-flour.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl filled with fine, light brown wholemeal flour, surface level
wholemeal-plain-flour.what: Flour milled from the whole wheat grain, bran included.

facts: Sourdough is raised by a starter of wild yeasts and bacteria rather than commercial yeast.
Wholemeal flour keeps the bran and germ of the wheat, giving a nutty flavour and denser crumb.
wholemeal-sourdough.visual: a whole round wholemeal sourdough loaf with a dark brown crust and flour-dusted top
wholemeal-sourdough.what: A chewy, tangy loaf made with a natural starter.

facts: Wholemeal flour is milled from the whole grain, including the bran and the germ.
Flatbreads like wraps have been made across the Middle East, Asia and Latin America for centuries.
Wraps are often rolled around fillings, which makes them easy to pack for lunch.
wholemeal-wrap.visual: a single flat round wholemeal wrap, speckled light brown and soft, lying open
wholemeal-wrap.what: A soft, round flatbread made from wholemeal flour.

facts: Couscous is made by rubbing moistened semolina into tiny granules, a method long used in North Africa.
Couscous is a staple across the Maghreb, usually served with stews and vegetables.
Wholewheat couscous keeps the bran of the grain, giving it a darker colour and a nuttier taste.
wholewheat-couscous.visual: a small heap of dry wholewheat couscous grains, pale golden-brown and finely textured
wholewheat-couscous.what: Tiny granules of wholewheat semolina, steamed until light.

facts: Wholewheat noodles keep the bran and germ of the grain, which gives them a darker colour and nutty flavour.
Wheat noodles have a long history in China and are now eaten right across Asia.
wholewheat-noodles.visual: a small heap of raw wholewheat noodles, dried pale brown strands loosely tangled together on a plain background
wholewheat-noodles.what: Chewy, nutty noodles made from whole grain wheat flour.

facts: Spaghetti takes its name from the Italian word spago, meaning string.
Wholewheat pasta keeps the bran and germ of the grain, giving a darker colour and nuttier taste.
wholewheat-spaghetti.visual: a small portion of uncooked dried wholewheat spaghetti, strands lying loosely together
wholewheat-spaghetti.what: Long, thin strands of pasta made from wholewheat flour.

facts: The Romans grew asparagus, and it has been prized in Europe for a very long time.
Foragers pick the thin shoots in spring, before they grow into feathery ferns.
wild-asparagus.visual: a small bunch of thin, dark green wild asparagus spears with tightly closed tips
wild-asparagus.what: Slender, intensely flavoured spears gathered from the wild.

facts: Wild boar is native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, and is the ancestor of the domestic pig.
It has been hunted and eaten across Europe since prehistoric times.
wild-boar.visual: one raw boneless cut of dark red wild boar meat with a band of creamy fat
wild-boar.what: Dark, rich meat from the wild pig, with a gamey flavour.

facts: Wild boar are native to much of Europe, Asia and North Africa.
Wild boar meat has a stronger, gamier flavour than farmed pork.
Boar have been hunted in Europe for centuries, and their meat was a feature of medieval feasts.
wild-boar-haunch.visual: a large raw wild boar haunch, deep red meat with a thin fat cap
wild-boar-haunch.what: A lean meat joint from wild pig, ideal for slow roasting.

facts: Wild boar are wild relatives of the domestic pig, native to Europe, Asia and North Africa.
Sausages made from it are often flavoured with juniper berries, fennel or chestnuts.
Wild boar meat has long been valued in European game cooking, especially in autumn and winter.
wild-boar-sausage.visual: one whole raw wild boar sausage, deep reddish-brown coarse meat, lying in a loose curve
wild-boar-sausage.what: A rich, gamey sausage made from wild boar meat.

facts: Its flowers are white and star-shaped, and both leaves and flowers can be eaten.
Ramsons is an old English name for the same plant.
wild-garlic-leaves.visual: a small bunch of fresh wild garlic leaves, broad bright green and glossy on long stems
wild-garlic-leaves.what: Broad green spring leaves with a mild garlic flavour.

facts: Wild garlic, also called ramsons, grows in damp woodland and is foraged each spring.
Pesto comes from the Italian word for pounding, a nod to the old mortar and pestle method.
Its leaves and flowers are both edible.
wild-garlic-pesto.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of bright green pesto, coarsely blended and thick
wild-garlic-pesto.what: A bright green sauce made from wild garlic leaves.

facts: Geese were a traditional festive roast in Britain, especially at Michaelmas and Christmas.
wild-goose.visual: a whole raw wild goose, plucked and clean, lying breast-side down, its long neck tucked beside it
wild-goose.what: A lean, gamey wild waterbird with rich dark meat.

facts: Wild rice is not a true rice. It is the seed of Zizania, a grass that grows in shallow lakes and marshes.
It grew wild across the Great Lakes region of North America and was harvested by Indigenous peoples there for centuries.
Traditionally harvested by canoe, the grains are parched and hulled before they are cooked.
wild-rice.visual: a small heap of long, slender, dark brown grains with a matt finish
wild-rice.what: Long dark grains from an aquatic grass, with a chewy bite.

facts: Rocket belongs to the cabbage family, Brassicaceae, along with mustard and radishes.
Wild rocket is a separate species from the more common salad rocket, with smaller leaves and a sharper taste.
Rocket has long been grown around the Mediterranean, where it is eaten raw in salads.
wild-rocket.visual: a small loose bunch of fresh wild rocket leaves, narrow, deeply notched, bright green, pale stems
wild-rocket.what: Small, peppery salad leaves with deeply lobed edges.

facts: Salmon are born in freshwater rivers, spend time at sea, and return to the rivers where they hatched to spawn.
Wild salmon feed on small crustaceans and fish at sea, which gives their flesh a deeper colour.
Farmed salmon is now more common in shops, but wild salmon is still fished in Scotland and Norway.
wild-salmon.visual: a whole wild salmon with silver-blue skin and dark spots on its back, lying on a plain background
wild-salmon.what: Lean, deep-flavoured salmon from rivers and the open sea.

facts: Wild strawberries grow in woods and hedgerows across Europe and much of the northern hemisphere.
The French name fraise des bois means strawberry of the woods.
Their scent is far stronger than that of cultivated strawberries, so they are often eaten fresh.
wild-strawberry.visual: a small loose heap of tiny deep red wild strawberries, some with green caps still on
wild-strawberry.what: A tiny, fragrant strawberry that grows wild in woods.

facts: Its original name is Williams' Bon Chrétien, and it is widely grown across Europe.
It is used for canning, purées and eating fresh because its flesh is juicy and fragrant.
williams-pear.visual: one whole Williams pear, bright yellow-green skin with a rosy blush on one side and a short stalk
williams-pear.what: A juicy, aromatic pear with a buttery texture when ripe.

facts: Ham is pork from the hind leg, salted or brined to preserve it.
The name refers to Wiltshire, a county in south-west England.
Before refrigeration, curing was an essential way to keep pork through the year.
wiltshire-ham.visual: a thick slice of pale pink cured ham, lying flat on the background
wiltshire-ham.what: Mildly cured British ham, sliced from the bone.

facts: Wine cap mushrooms are also called king stropharia and are grown on wood chip beds.
Its name refers to the wine-red colour of its cap when it is young.
It is a woodland fungus that grows on decaying wood and mulch in temperate regions.
wine-cap-mushroom.visual: one whole wine cap mushroom, dark burgundy cap, pale stem and a few flecks of soil, lying on its side
wine-cap-mushroom.what: A meaty garden mushroom with a deep red-brown cap.

facts: Their pods, leaves, flowers and roots are all used in Southeast Asian cooking.
The name refers to the four flat wings running along each pod.
winged-beans.visual: a small bunch of fresh bright green winged bean pods, four-cornered with frilly edges, on a plain background
winged-beans.what: A tropical bean pod with four crunchy, frilled wings.

facts: Winkles are a common shellfish along the rocky coasts of Britain and Ireland.
They are traditionally eaten from the shell with a pin, often with vinegar.
winkles.visual: a small heap of cooked winkles in their dark, glossy shells
winkles.what: Tiny sea snails with spiral shells, eaten from the shell.

facts: Winter melon is a gourd native to Asia, grown in China and South-East Asia for centuries.
Its waxy white coating is why it is also called wax gourd.
Cooks often simmer its flesh in soups, where it takes on the flavour of the broth.
winter-melon.visual: a whole winter melon with a pale green, waxy-dusted skin, lying on its side
winter-melon.what: A pale green gourd with mild, subtly sweet flesh.

facts: Winter savory is a perennial herb native to southern Europe and the Mediterranean.
It has long been used in European cooking, especially to flavour beans and hearty stews.
Its flavour is often described as sharper than summer savory.
winter-savory.visual: a small bunch of winter savory, narrow grey-green leaves on thin woody stems
winter-savory.what: A robust, peppery herb often used in hearty stews.

facts: Witch sole is also called Torbay sole, after the bay near Torquay in Devon.
It lives on sandy and muddy seabeds around the coasts of Europe.
Its thin fillets cook quickly, so they are often grilled or pan-fried.
witch-sole.visual: a whole raw witch sole, a slim grey-brown flatfish with both eyes on one side
witch-sole.what: A slim flatfish with delicate, sweet white flesh.

facts: The name wonton comes from the Cantonese words wan tan.
Wrappers are made from flour, water and egg, rolled very thin and cut into squares.
Folded around a filling, they are boiled in soup or fried until crisp.
wonton-wrapper.visual: a neat stack of thin, square, pale yellow wonton wrappers lying flat
wonton-wrapper.what: Thin square dough sheets, folded around fillings.

facts: Wontons are a staple of Cantonese cooking, often served floating in broth.
Wonton wrappers are thin sheets of wheat dough, cut into squares.
The filling is usually minced pork, seasoned with ginger, soy and spring onion.
wontons.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl holding several cooked wontons, thin translucent wrappers with pleated edges
wontons.what: Small pork-filled dumplings with thin wheat wrappers.

facts: Wood ear is widely used in Chinese cooking, especially in hot and sour soup.
It grows on dead broadleaf wood, and in parts of Europe it is called Judas's ear.
It is usually sold dried and must be soaked in warm water before it is cooked.
wood-ear-mushroom.visual: a small heap of dried, dark brown wood ear fungus pieces, wrinkled and curled, lying loose
wood-ear-mushroom.what: A dark, ear-shaped fungus with a crunchy texture.

facts: The wood pigeon is a common wild pigeon in Britain and much of Europe.
Pigeon breast is usually cooked quickly and served pink, sometimes with blackberries or cherries.
wood-pigeon.visual: one raw wood pigeon breast, dark red meat with a thin pale skin, lying flat on a plain background
wood-pigeon.what: A wild woodland bird with dark, rich breast meat.

facts: Wood sorrel is a small woodland plant whose leaves fold up at night.
The name sorrel comes from an old word meaning sour, which suits its tangy leaves.
Wood sorrel grows in shady woods and hedgerows across much of Europe.
wood-sorrel.visual: a small bunch of delicate, bright green clover-shaped leaves, stems attached
wood-sorrel.what: Small clover-like wild leaves with a sharp, lemony taste.

facts: Traditional British cookery roasts woodcock with the innards left in, served on toast.
Its long bill is used to probe soft soil for food.
woodcock.visual: one whole raw woodcock, a plump brown-grey feathered bird with a long thin bill
woodcock.what: A woodland game bird with a long bill, prized by chefs.

facts: Pearmain is an old English name for a group of apples, and Worcester Pearmain is among the best known.
Its flesh is juicy and crisp, and its skin shows a bright red blush over a yellow base.
worcester-pearmain-apple.visual: a whole small round apple with a bright red blush over yellow-green skin, stalk attached
worcester-pearmain-apple.what: A crisp English eating apple with a bright red blush.

facts: Worcestershire sauce was first made in Worcester, England, by two chemists, John Lea and William Perrins, in the 1830s.
The recipe is built on anchovies, malt vinegar, molasses and tamarind, with spices added.
It is used in British cooking, in dishes such as Welsh rarebit and as a seasoning for meat.
worcestershire-sauce.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of dark reddish-brown sauce, cap closed
worcestershire-sauce.what: A dark, tangy sauce with a savoury, fermented depth.

facts: Worcestershire sauce takes its name from the English city of Worcester.
The sauce is traditionally made with vinegar, molasses and anchovies, among other ingredients.
worcestershire-sauce-crisps.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thin, dark golden potato crisps with a glossy brown seasoned finish
worcestershire-sauce-crisps.what: Thin, dark, tangy crisps with a savoury umami flavour.

facts: It is made by fermenting sugar with a bacterium, then drying and grinding the resulting gum.
Its name comes from Xanthomonas, the bacterium that produces it and is found on cabbage-family plants.
xanthan-gum.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl heaped with fine off-white powder
xanthan-gum.what: A fine powder that thickens sauces and stabilises doughs.

facts: XO sauce was created in Hong Kong in the 1980s and is said to be named after XO cognac as a mark of luxury.
Dried scallops form the base of the sauce and give it a concentrated, sweet and savoury flavour.
The sauce is used to flavour stir-fried vegetables, seafood and rice dishes in Cantonese cooking.
xo-sauce.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, filled with chunky dark reddish-brown sauce full of tiny flecks
xo-sauce.what: A rich, spicy seafood and chilli condiment from Hong Kong.

facts: Y Fenni is the Welsh name for Abergavenny, a market town in Monmouthshire.
y-fenni.visual: a block of pale golden cheese with one wedge cut away, flecked with dark seeds
y-fenni.what: A Welsh cheese flecked with mustard seed and ale.

facts: Yabbies live in rivers, lakes and farm dams across eastern and southern Australia.
Yabbies are often farmed in dams and ponds, and are a popular catch for anglers.
They are usually boiled or steamed whole until the shells turn bright red.
yabby.visual: one whole raw freshwater crayfish, small and olive-green with a dark shell, claws folded, lying on its side
yabby.what: A small Australian crayfish with sweet, tender meat.

facts: Yacon is native to the Andes of South America, where it has been grown for centuries.
It is a relative of the sunflower, and its crisp tubers are often compared to a pear.
In the Andes it is often eaten raw, sliced into salads or eaten as a fresh snack.
yacon.visual: a whole raw yacon root, knobbly light brown skin, lying on a plain background
yacon.what: A crisp, sweet root vegetable from the Andes mountains.

facts: Yakiniku means grilled meat in Japanese, and it is a style where diners cook thin meat on a table grill.
Yakiniku is closely related to Korean barbecue, and both use thin cuts of beef grilled quickly.
Marbled beef has fine streaks of fat through the lean meat, which melt as it cooks.
yakiniku-beef.visual: several thin raw slices of marbled beef, deep red with pale fat streaks, lying flat on the background
yakiniku-beef.what: Thin, marbled beef cut for quick grilling at the table.

facts: Yakitori is Japanese grilled chicken on skewers, and the sauce is usually made from soy sauce and mirin.
Mirin is a sweet Japanese rice wine used for cooking, and it gives the glaze its glossy shine.
In Japan this kind of sauce is called tare, and cooks often brush it on repeatedly during grilling.
yakitori-sauce.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, filled with dark brown glossy sauce
yakitori-sauce.what: A sweet soy glaze for grilled chicken skewers.

facts: True yams belong to the genus Dioscorea and are not the same as the orange sweet potato.
Yams are a staple crop across West Africa, where they are often pounded into a smooth dough.
The tubers grow large underground, and some varieties can be planted from pieces of the tuber.
yam.visual: a whole raw yam with rough brown bark-like skin, long and knobbly, lying on the background
yam.what: A starchy tuber, eaten boiled, pounded or fried.

facts: Yardlong beans are a variety of cowpea grown in south and east Asia.
They are often stir-fried in Chinese and Southeast Asian cooking.
Their pods can grow far longer than common green beans, which gives them their name.
yardlong-beans.visual: a small bunch of very long, slender green beans, their ends trimmed, lying flat on the background
yardlong-beans.what: A very long, thin green bean from Asia, cut into pieces.

facts: Yeast extract is made by breaking down yeast cells, often from brewing, then concentrating the liquid.
Savoury yeast spreads are popular in Britain, Australia and New Zealand, often spread thinly on toast.
Its strong, savoury taste comes largely from glutamates released as the yeast cell material breaks down.
yeast-extract.visual: a small plain glass jar without a label, holding a dark brown glossy spread
yeast-extract.what: A dark, salty spread made from yeast cells.

facts: Yellow bean sauce is a Chinese condiment made from fermented soya beans, flour and salt.
Fermenting soya beans into sauces and pastes has a long history across East Asia.
yellow-bean-sauce.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of thick, dark golden-brown bean sauce, smooth and glossy
yellow-bean-sauce.what: A salty, savoury sauce made from fermented soya beans.

facts: Courgette is the name used in Britain for the young fruit of a summer squash.
Yellow courgettes have golden skin instead of the usual dark green.
The courgette was developed in Italy in the nineteenth century and is now common across the Mediterranean.
yellow-courgette.visual: a single whole yellow courgette, golden skin, lying on its side on the background
yellow-courgette.what: A golden courgette with a mild, delicate flavour.

facts: Yellow mustard is made from white mustard seed, which is milder than brown or black varieties.
The American style of mustard is often coloured with turmeric, giving it its bright yellow tone.
It is a classic partner for hot dogs and is widely used in the United States.
yellow-mustard.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle holding bright yellow mustard, its surface smooth and glossy
yellow-mustard.what: A mild, bright mustard, made from pale mustard seeds.

facts: Yellow mustard seeds come from Sinapis alba, a plant grown in Europe and North America.
Mustard seeds have been used as a spice and condiment in India and Europe for thousands of years.
When crushed and mixed with liquid, mustard seeds release a sharp flavour that mellows with cooking.
yellow-mustard-seeds.visual: a small loose heap of tiny pale yellow mustard seeds, lying on the background
yellow-mustard-seeds.what: Mild seeds for pickling and making homemade mustard.

facts: Oyster mushrooms are named for their shell-like caps, which are said to resemble oyster shells.
Oyster mushrooms are grown commercially in many countries, and the yellow variety is common in Asian markets.
Oyster mushrooms grow on dead wood in the wild, and they are often cultivated on straw or sawdust.
yellow-oyster-mushroom.visual: a cluster of raw yellow oyster mushrooms, golden fan-shaped caps joined at pale stems, lying loose on the background
yellow-oyster-mushroom.what: A golden, fan-shaped mushroom with a mild, nutty flavour.

facts: Peppers and chillies originated in the Americas and reached Europe after Columbus.
Yellow peppers are sweet bell peppers that turned yellow as they ripened from green.
yellow-pepper.visual: one whole glossy yellow bell pepper, smooth skin, green stem cap on top, lying on its side
yellow-pepper.what: A sweet, mild capsicum with a fruity flavour.

facts: Yellow raspberries are varieties of the red raspberry that lack its red pigment.
They grow on the same kind of canes as red raspberries and are picked in summer.
yellow-raspberry.visual: a small heap of pale golden raspberries, soft and rounded, with no stems
yellow-raspberry.what: A pale golden berry with a honeyed, mild flavour.

facts: Pease pudding is a traditional English dish made from boiled split peas.
Peas are split so they cook faster than whole dried peas.
yellow-split-peas.visual: a small heap of dried yellow split peas, pale and smooth
yellow-split-peas.what: Dried peas split in half, cooking down soft and creamy.

facts: Yellow tomatoes belong to the same family as red tomatoes, the nightshade family.
Tomatoes were first grown in the Americas before spreading to Europe and beyond.
yellow-tomato.visual: a whole ripe yellow tomato with smooth golden skin and a small green stem
yellow-tomato.what: A mild, sweet tomato with golden skin and low acidity.

facts: Wax beans are a yellow-podded variety of the common bean.
The name refers to the waxy look of the pods' skin.
They are often lightly steamed or sautéed with butter, which suits their mild flavour.
yellow-wax-beans.visual: a small loose bunch of bright yellow wax beans, slender pods lying side by side
yellow-wax-beans.what: Long, buttery-tasting yellow pods that cook quickly.

facts: Yellowfin is a tuna of warm tropical and subtropical seas, and it has bright yellow fins.
Its name refers to its yellow fins, which contrast with its dark blue back.
In Japan raw tuna is served as sashimi, and in Hawaii cubed raw fish is served as poke.
yellowfin-tuna.visual: a single raw yellowfin tuna loin, deep ruby-pink flesh with clean cut edges, lying flat
yellowfin-tuna.what: A lean, deep-red tuna with a mild, meaty flavour.

facts: Hamachi is the Japanese name for the yellowtail, a fish of the jack family, and it is often served as sashimi.
The fish is farmed in Japan and parts of the Mediterranean as well as caught wild.
Its flesh has a soft, buttery texture because of its fat, which is why it is often eaten raw.
yellowtail.visual: a cut fillet of raw yellowtail, glossy pink-white flesh with a thin silver skin, lying directly on the background
yellowtail.what: A glossy, rich-fleshed fish, often eaten raw in Japan.

facts: The collar is the fleshy area behind the gills, which is prized in Japanese cooking for its fat.
Hamachi kama is often grilled over charcoal, where the skin crisps and the fat melts.
yellowtail-collar.visual: a raw yellowtail collar, a thick curved cut of pinkish-white flesh with silver skin, lying flat
yellowtail-collar.what: A fatty, rich cut from behind the head of a yellowtail.

facts: Yi mein is a Cantonese egg noodle, often served at birthdays as a symbol of long life.
Yi mein are used in dishes such as Cantonese fried noodles, sometimes called chow mein.
They have a springy texture because the dough is made with egg.
yi-mein.visual: a small heap of dry yellow yi mein noodle nests, wavy and pale golden
yi-mein.what: Springy egg noodles, often served at Chinese celebrations.

facts: York ham is a traditional English cured ham, associated with the city of York and Yorkshire.
Curing ham in salt, and sometimes sugar, was a long-established way to preserve pork.
york-ham.visual: A whole cooked pale pink ham joint, its outer fat cap lightly scored.
york-ham.what: A mild, sweet cooked ham, carved thick or thin.

facts: Originally, batter was cooked under roasting meat to catch its drippings, and the pudding was eaten first.
Yorkshire pudding is traditionally served with roast beef and gravy in Britain.
A very hot tin with hot fat helps the batter puff up sharply in the oven.
yorkshire-pudding.visual: one golden, crisp, puffed pudding with a hollow centre, served plainly on a plain white plate
yorkshire-pudding.what: A crisp, puffed batter made from eggs, flour and milk.

facts: Young coconuts are picked before the nut hardens, when the water inside is clear and sweet.
Coconut palms grow along tropical coasts, and the fruit has been eaten across the Pacific and Asia for centuries.
Coconut water from young nuts is drunk fresh in many tropical countries.
young-coconut.visual: one whole young green coconut with its husk on, lying on its side
young-coconut.what: An unripe coconut with soft, jelly-like flesh.

facts: Young ginger is harvested early, before its skin toughens and its fibres develop.
In Japan, young ginger is often pickled in sweetened vinegar, where it turns pale pink.
young-ginger.visual: one whole young ginger root, creamy pale skin with pink-tipped shoots, lying flat
young-ginger.what: Tender ginger, pink-tipped, with very little fibre.

facts: Gouda is a Dutch cheese named after the town of Gouda in the Netherlands.
Young gouda is aged only briefly, so it has a mild flavour and a soft, supple texture.
young-gouda.visual: a block of pale yellow young gouda cheese with one wedge cut away, showing a smooth creamy face
young-gouda.what: A mild, creamy Dutch cheese, easy to slice.

facts: It belongs to the brassica family, the same group as cabbage and broccoli.
It is widely eaten in southern China and Hong Kong, usually quickly stir-fried or blanched.
yu-choy.visual: a bunch of yu choy with pale green stems and bright dark-green leaves, stems cut neatly at the base
yu-choy.what: A tender Chinese green with sweet stems and leaves.

facts: Yukon Gold was bred in Canada, at the University of Guelph in Ontario.
Potatoes were first cultivated in the Andes of South America thousands of years ago.
Its yellow colour comes from natural pigments in the flesh, and it roasts and mashes well.
yukon-gold-potato.visual: a single whole raw Yukon Gold potato, smooth thin golden-yellow skin, lying on its side
yukon-gold-potato.what: A smooth yellow potato with a rich, buttery flavour.

facts: Yuzu is believed to have come from China and has long been grown in Japan.
Yuzu juice and zest are used in ponzu, a soy-based dipping sauce.
In Japan, yuzu is floated in baths on the winter solstice, a long-standing custom.
yuzu.visual: one whole bumpy, yellow-green yuzu fruit, round with a textured skin
yuzu.what: A tart, fragrant Japanese citrus with aromatic zest.

facts: Yuzu is a citrus fruit believed to have come from China, and it has long been grown in Japan.
Yuzu juice is often mixed with soy sauce to make ponzu, a tangy citrus dipping sauce.
yuzu-dressing.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale golden-yellow dressing, filled to just below the neck
yuzu-dressing.what: A tangy Japanese dressing made with yuzu citrus and soy.

facts: Yuzu is a citrus fruit thought to be a cross between mandarin and papeda.
Its juice and zest are used to flavour dishes, dressings and drinks.
yuzu-juice.visual: a plain unlabelled clear glass bottle of pale yellow juice
yuzu-juice.what: Sharp, fragrant Japanese citrus juice with a floral edge.

facts: It is made from yuzu peel, chilli and salt, and the paste is often aged for some weeks.
Yuzu is a small citrus fruit from East Asia, and its peel gives a sharp, floral aroma.
The name combines yuzu with kosho, a Japanese word for pepper.
yuzu-kosho.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of smooth bright green paste, speckled with small dark flecks
yuzu-kosho.what: A fiery paste of yuzu citrus peel and chilli, from Japan.

facts: In the Levant, za'atar is often mixed into olive oil and spread on flatbread.
Sumac, a tangy red spice, is made by grinding the dried berries of a shrub.
Recipes for za'atar vary widely between regions and households.
za-atar.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of dry, green-grey powdery herb mix, speckled evenly
za-atar.what: A dry blend of thyme, sumac and sesame seeds.

facts: Zabaglione is traditionally made in a bowl set over simmering water, whisking until thick and foamy.
It is a classic Italian dessert, often served warm on its own or with biscuits.
The Marsala used in classic recipes is a fortified wine from the Sicilian town of the same name.
zabaglione.visual: a small plain white bowl of pale golden, frothy whipped custard with soft peaks on top
zabaglione.what: A light Italian dessert of whipped yolks, sugar and wine.

facts: Zamorano takes its name from the province of Zamora in north-west Spain.
Like Manchego, it is a firm Spanish cheese made from sheep's milk.
zamorano.visual: a block of pale golden hard cheese with one wedge cut away, the rind visible at the edge
zamorano.what: A firm, nutty aged sheep's cheese from Spain.

facts: Zander is a predatory fish native to rivers and lakes across much of Europe and northern Asia.
Its name is German, and in English it is often called pike-perch.
Its firm white flesh holds together well when pan-fried, so it is popular as skinless fillets.
zander.visual: a whole raw zander fish with olive-grey skin and pale silvery sides, lying straight on a plain surface
zander.what: A freshwater fish related to perch, with firm white flesh.

facts: Zedoary is a rhizome native to South and South-East Asia, related to ginger and turmeric.
It is called white turmeric because its flesh is paler than the bright yellow of common turmeric.
Zedoary is used in pickles and curries in parts of India and South-East Asia.
zedoary.visual: a whole knobbly pale cream-yellow root with ring marks and a few dry rootlets, on a plain background
zedoary.what: A pale aromatic root that tastes of mango and ginger.

facts: Zhoug comes from Yemen, where it is served with bread and grilled meats.
It is traditionally made by pounding fresh chillies, coriander, garlic and spices into a paste.
Yemeni Jewish immigrants brought the sauce to Israel, where it is now very popular.
zhoug.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of bright green zhoug sauce, flecks of herbs and chilli visible
zhoug.what: A fiery Yemeni sauce of green chilli and coriander.

facts: Zhug is a spicy condiment from Yemen, and Yemeni immigrants made it popular in Israel.
Yemeni cooks serve it with bread, grilled meats and stews as a fiery table condiment.
Cardamom is the dried seed pod of plants in the ginger family.
zhug-spice.visual: a small plain white ceramic bowl of coarse, dried, reddish-green spice blend, loosely heaped
zhug-spice.what: A fiery Yemeni blend of chilli, coriander and cardamom.

facts: The name ziti is related to an Italian word for bridegroom.
Baked ziti is popular in Italian-American cooking, with tomato sauce and melted cheese.
It is usually sold in short lengths, so the tubes hold chunky sauces well.
ziti.visual: a small neat heap of dry, smooth ziti pasta tubes with straight-cut ends
ziti.what: Smooth, medium pasta tubes, often baked in the oven.
